text: [This book just has lore and no actual functions]
[The data slate contains information on a nearby mission]

The wreck came apart like rotten foil, but the black box did not. Its last seconds are clean, ordinary, then the course line bends a hair's breadth and everything tears loose. No interference spike, no pirate burn, just a neat little correction that should not exist. Listening to it on loop, I get the feeling the answer is right there in the numbers, as plain as basic nav, and somehow still refuses to resolve. All I really have is that lonely log from the edge of nowhere, a handful of "lucky" escapes, and a name nobody quite manages to say.

I keep thinking how none of this would have happened if some UC clerk had just signed the right deorbit order.  
They left the station up here to save a little fuel and a little face, then cut maintenance hours, then reassigned anyone who remembered its passwords.  
One cheap decision at a time, until this place turned into a quiet pocket where a person could reroute half a dozen lanes and no one would notice.  

Now I sit in the dark, watching old dishes groan as they track something they are not supposed to see, replaying every "temporary" cost-cut and overlooked warning I have lived through.

I docked here because the tanks were low and the crew was tired, not because I believe in ghost currents and cursed lanes like the locals do. Then I pulled yesterday's nav dump and watched our course bend three degrees starboard without a single correction logged, same as the old timers swear it always does over that valley. The station master just shrugged and said some paths are easier not to question, especially when the cargo keeps moving and the bodies stay far enough away to forget. I do not know if I am more afraid of phantom gravity or the way everyone prefers the story that hurts them least.

I heard it from a dockhand who swore her cousin saw the account screens stutter right before the lights flickered, like the city took a breath and forgot who it owed. Nobody can show you a clean record, of course, just half-scorched dataslates and freight manifests with the same routes crossed out in different hands. Some say it is a GalBank ghost, some say it is pirates, some swear it is a woman from the lower decks of New Atlantis who knows exactly where the old wiring runs. All I know is whenever the rumors start, the people in suits suddenly talk quieter and the ones who live under the pipes listen harder.

We were never meant to be out this far. Scarrunner was a hauler, not an explorer, but one little routing "optimization" slipped in during a maintenance cycle and nobody bothered to roll it back. Cheaper fuel, tighter jumps, the kind of thing captains brag about over drinks. Then the plotted paths started leaning, just a fraction, toward that junk-choked patch near the veil. Each run, same tiny adjustment, same quiet deviation that never tripped an alarm. Now I am floating in a dead ship, staring at logs that show how a minor tweak got copied, normalized, and finally steered us straight into the teeth of someone else's math.

They say every tower in Neon has a ghost in the basement, but this one walks in numbers and routing codes instead of chains. I used to think the stories about vanished freighters and bought shortcuts were just bar noise that got louder on the way up the Span; now the whispers have paperwork behind them. Out on the fringe I tripped over a lone dataslate that should have been slagged, then heard a Ryujin clerk stammer through the same missing names, and finally cracked a cutter's half-burned logs that described the exact same kind of jump, like the rumor had learned how to write itself into every system that tried to erase it.

I heard the story before I ever set down here, but it was already worn smooth by the time it reached my ears. First it was a convoy that never checked in. Then it was "pirates," or "drive failure," or "bad coordinates in a storm." Ask three haulers at the bar and you get four versions, all of them saying less than they know. Out in the yard the cutters work overtime on incoming husks with scrubbed transponders, and nobody writes down who paid to bring them in. The earliest telling of what really happened has already drifted into speculation; all that is left are scared glances, half-finished sentences, and a feeling that someone is using the dark between the lanes as both grave and bank.

Funny how something that started as bar talk in The Well is now riding the lifts up into the nice parts of New Atlantis. I keep hearing the story come back to me in different mouths, polished a little more each time. A clerk swears they knew a hauler whose whole family license vanished between one shift and the next. A tech on a maintenance crew claims they heard a voice on a dormant line reciting case numbers that do not exist anymore. I saw the original slate that kicked this off, glitched timestamps and dead transponders, and I still do not know what scares me more now: that the story has outgrown whatever really happened, or that the truth is worse than the version people feel safe repeating.

They say every story up here has three versions the official one, the one told over drinks, and the one nobody says out loud. I have heard all three today and they do not even agree on the color of the sky. One UC patrol officer swore the distortion was a calibration fault, nothing more. A freighter hand in a smoke choked backroom swore on his last credits that something slid past his ship without a transponder, humming in his teeth like bad grav. And in the alley outside, a Neon runner laughed and said it was just an old test profile, long buried, nothing anyone should be asking about. Funny how everyone uses different words for the same thin slice of orbit, and how their voices all dip when they get to that part.

I always trusted GalBank lanes. You fly the blue logo, you assume someone in a clean shirt and better pay has triple-checked the math. Maybe that is how they got away with it. We ran that corridor so often I could draw the buoy pattern from memory, right down to the little skip where the grav well makes your teeth hum. When the escort failed to report in, nobody flinched; consoles shrugged, called it a relay glitch, filed another green stamp. It took three missed convoys and one freighter limping back with its drive casing warped before anyone bothered to pull the raw logs. That is when we saw the extra projections tucked between routine updates, pointing toward a skinny band of rock and ice that was never on any of our official charts.

I keep replaying the approach in my head, but every time it runs a little different.  
The telemetry said clear lane, clean gravity, no debris worth naming, and still the hauler ahead of us drifted off-course like something was tugging at its teeth.  
We scooped three escape pods; the black took the rest.  
LIST stamped it down as pilot error, Argos called the basin a bad investment, and the official records all agree it was nobody's fault in particular.  
Only the stories in station bars refuse to line up, little fragments about the same burned pads, the same families, the same quiet pilot who swore the numbers were solid.  
Some days I think I imagined that extra ping on the scope; other days I am sure it was a hand on the wheel that never makes it into the logs.

I log beacon checks at the start and end of every shift. Always have. Flip through the same diagnostics, tap the same acknowledgements, watch the same green lights blink in the same order. Somewhere in the last year, that order changed and I did not see it. A handoff here took a heartbeat longer, a timestamp there drifted by a fraction. The system compensated, captains cursed their nav suites, and traffic flowed on. Only now, looking back over old traces, do I see how the routes bent, almost politely, around the same handful of worlds. The frozen outpost that did not get its evac, the survey run nobody could re-plot, the approvals a LIST clerk swears they sent. The pattern was there the whole time, threaded through my consoles like a quiet apology I never bothered to read.

I am recording this from a rented bunk bolted to bulkhead C, because if I say it out loud in the bar again it will turn into another story and I need it to stay a fact.\n\nThe TA broker here swears the manifests he showed me are just misfiled freight, nothing to see, just frontier bookkeeping. But his hands shook when he scrolled past the third ship with the same registry, three different captains, three different lien codes. Same audit signature on each. He told me, real soft, that if I wanted the rest of that pattern I should go where the metal and the money meet: the yards in Gagarin, where freighters are reborn with new names and old debts. Everyone else talks about a ghost auditor like a campfire tale, changing details each time, but her accent and those codes never change.

I have been sleeping next to the bunker wall, just to feel the hum through the metal. It is thin, a background tremor in the old UC wiring, but it matches the cadence I saw in the patrol logs I stole. Same gaps. Same timing. She is still riding the grid.\n\nNo one back at New Atlantis wanted to see it. They skimmed my report once, then started staring past my shoulder, like I was a static burst they could tune out. Out here, the bunker still listens to a sky the registry pretends is quiet, and tonight I caught something new: a tight-beam exchange, bouncing through an unlisted node, then vanishing toward that cluster of grav scars the Crimson crews call the blind corridor. Whatever she is doing next, she is staging it off a dead relay, just far enough outside the charts that no one has to admit it exists.

I keep telling myself I am just here to clean up a mess in the logs, but the deeper I dig, the less it looks like random corruption. The theft chain they handed me was supposed to be simple follow the unauthorized copies, close the holes, file the report. Instead I am staring at the same warped jump curves cropping up in places that should never share traffic, tagged with user IDs that do not exist in any personnel registry I can see. One of the senior analysts flagged this pattern weeks ago, left a half-finished trace on their console, then took urgent leave and never came back to finish what they started. Tonight I pushed their old trace one step further and found a match buried in offsite telemetry from a navy hull that should be nowhere near these experiments, let alone echoing the same impossible vectors.

Been picking through this dead node so long I can taste oxidized metal in my teeth. Most of the consoles here are ghosts, but one of the cores still had heat left in it, tucked behind a wall panel someone thought was welded shut. Jump data, tightened and cleaned in a way no company mechanic around here could dream of, all bent around the same kink in the lanes we have been chasing. Whoever pulled that Fleet package knew exactly what they were stealing; half these coordinates match the accidents everybody swears were just bad luck. The funny part is, the route strings keep referencing a salvage yard on Deimos, like the path always folds back through there before it disappears. I have heard that place mentioned in bar talk for months, always as a joke, always with eyes dropping to the floor the second anyone asks for details.

They started changing the duty roster about a year back, but it did not feel like anything at the time. Different pilots pairing with different convoys, a few routes shuffled off the public boards, the usual corporate "optimization" spin. I remember one morning at the TerraBrew stall near Dock 17, seeing a Vanguard jacket at a table that never hosted uniforms before, talking low with a Ryujin type who smelled like fresh plastic and old secrets. Nobody cared. Ships came and went, GalBank still paid out, LIST settlers still limped through bad systems with just enough fuel and just enough luck. Only later, when the same name started whispering through Neon bars and insurance disputes, did it hit me that all those small adjustments were drawing lines around one pilot, setting her apart from the rest of us without ever saying why.

I keep telling myself I am only here because the pay is good, that I do not care why some Aegis ghost bled out on this rock with their datapad hugged to their chest. But I walked the perimeter twice before I even cracked the casing. No sign of a fight, no distress beacon in the logs, just a gap in the record where a human being should have left noise. That bothers me more than any scorch mark would have.  \n\nThe file fragments mention a safety inspector who stopped filing reports, a freighter that never finished its jump, and a research contract whose number does not exist in the public registries. Nothing links on paper. Names change, timestamps drift, routes get reclassified. Every time I think I see the chain of events, it smears sideways, like the universe is refusing to hold still long enough for anyone to write it down.

They say some places in space hold on to things longer than they should. The microgravity platform I swung past today is one of them. It should be scrap and silence, just another drilling rig left to spin itself apart, but the patrol grid still flinches every time its old transponder breathes. I parked just outside the lane and listened; there is a thin, dirty signal riding the standard telemetry, nudging any tagged-for-disposal hull a few degrees off its proper course. Every dock rat back on the station "knows" to give this sector a wide berth, then suddenly forgets why when you press them. Between the dead spacer's slate and that corrupted buoy I burned, both pointing at misrouted wrecks and retired codes that refuse to die, it feels like this whole patch of sky is hanging onto someone else's mistakes until they can be quietly erased.

I am parked off this ore platform, watching it turn like it has for decades, still humming through a pattern nobody bothered to erase. Somewhere along the way, some clerk signed the wrong form or looked the other way, and that tiny shrug of bureaucracy carved out a blind lane in the sky. Now the platform's guidance is stitched into bar gossip and half-lost sensor logs, echoes of the same freighter silhouette skimming grids where no one should be. I keep thinking about that first dead homestead, the dirty telemetry from its orbit, the way local fauna started acting like they got new orders. None of it screamed conspiracy at the time. Just glitches. Just bad luck. But all those small, quiet mistakes and compromises nudged things toward this forgotten dot on the map, until everything strange seems to lean, just a little, in this direction.

Hard to tell where the real story starts, so I will pin it to that rusted relay I was paid to wake up last month. The work order called it routine: clear a backlog, reset a few buffers, bill some faceless office in New Atlantis. When I got there, half the panels were already scorched, and the logs did not read like simple neglect. Distress calls came in clean, went out smeared, registry tags folded over themselves. Some entries had been sliced and pasted so many times the timestamps looped. A tug crew swears they saw a hijacked signal bouncing through there weeks before; a dockhand insists those same ship IDs showed up later on a private auction list. None of their stories match perfectly, but every broken piece points at the same thing: someone very patient, nudging ghosts through forgotten circuits until the records forgot they were ever alive.

Been running cargo runs since before the Armistice, and I have never seen a ship fly itself like the Boneclaw did last week.

We were three days out, grav drive on cooldown, when the nav console lit up with a route I did not punch in.

Looked official, too, buried under old UC formatting nobody bothers with anymore.

Captain swore it was a relic subroutine, some legacy safety corridor from back when the war made everyone jumpy.

Crew laughed it off, let the autopilot ride it, because who argues with a path that clean.

Thing is, the more I dug into the logs after shift, the more I found those same corrections, repeating like a heartbeat, on runs years apart.

Different captains, different cargo, same quiet nudge.

Somewhere out there, something we forgot to shut down is still talking to our ships, and I do not think it is doing us any favors.

I was supposed to be on a six-month temp contract up here, the kind of nowhere posting you take when you want to disappear without quitting. The module hums and breathes like any other relic on the corporate leash, but the logs feel wrong under my hands. Years of clean mirrored transfers, then suddenly one chain fractures: inbound packets split, some land where they are supposed to, others slip sideways into dead space. The anomalies are tiny, like someone with surgeon hands nudged the code, trusting the redundancy to hide the cut. I flagged it in the maintenance queue, marked for a senior tech to review, and then nothing happened. No follow-up, no purge, just my ticket quietly closed without comment. The gaps stayed in the archive, hanging there like half-erased handwriting, as if whoever was meant to come back and tidy the mess simply never made it this far.

I was a kid when the first version of the story did the rounds, so I only have thirds and fourths by now. The ones who were there do not agree on much anymore. Some swear the sky over the fields tore open, others say it was just a freighter that came in too hot and shook itself apart. The only constant is that the official report never lined up with what people remember, and every retelling drops another hard detail and picks up another maybe. By the time I was old enough to fly, it was just a warning: do not trust the lanes just because they are lit.\n\nNow there is a new name attached to the old unease, a navigator who walked out on the big flags, a whisper about trials buried in some staryard server. Funny thing is, no one here can tell you exactly when he appeared in the tale; it is like he was always part of it, waiting in the gaps where the truth got rubbed smooth.

I keep thinking someone is coming back.

The garage is loud enough that no one hears the hum from the old core, not really. Fans rattling, music leaking from a busted speaker, arguments over parts prices. But every time I walk past that one bay, the air feels thinner. Bench wiped spotless in a sea of grime, wrappers folded into a neat little pile, like somebody packed up in a hurry and promised themselves they would finish the job later.

The kid they pulled off the floor swears he blacked out, woke up with his arm set better than UC ever did it. Others say he tripped, patched himself, end of story. Except the med stock sheet does not match, and the Static Hackers keep glancing at that core like it is rigged to bite. If there is a ghost in those logs, it is waiting on the same thing I am: the one who cut here, cleaned here, and walked away before the erase cycle finished.

Found the packet in the last place anyone checks the old relay's maintenance queue. No alarms, no lockouts, just a half finished transfer flagged "deferred" three years running, sitting in a forgotten subdirectory like somebody fully intended to come back and scrub it clean, then got reassigned or spaced. Atmospheric sweeps layered over patrol routes, with one ship path threaded right through the gaps every time. Same vector, same speed, same little pauses in burn where a careful pilot checks their own work. I pulled the trace forward one more hop and the endpoints start clustering around a junk field that is not on any public navchart, but shows up in system grav noise like a bad memory. First it was that stray record out on the rock, then the cut patterns in the Deimos yard, now this: all of it saying the same thing he has a favorite graveyard, and he keeps going back to it.

I am logging this from the old drop can, sitting under a flickering strip that should have burned out a decade ago. The place hums with half-dead fans and forgotten protocols; I swear I heard a decon cycle spin up on its own two hours after I powered the generator, like some buried routine still thinks infantry are due in from orbit. That is what got me looking deeper. Under the rust and bootleg wiring, the shelter's systems were still filing traffic, still mirroring route updates to a secondary endpoint nobody bothered to wipe from the registry. Buried in a nav cache I pulled off the liaison's terminal was a repeating destination tag hardwired into his latest corridor updates, same code cross-referenced three times in the old system handshakes. All point toward a relay node tucked in the undergrid of Neon, exactly where no honest captain wants their beacon to light up: Ebbside.

First time I docked here, I thought it was just another junkyard orbiting the edge of nowhere. Now I cannot shake the feeling that this depot is where the story started, even if nobody remembers the first telling. Every Deadspace loader I talk to starts their version with, "I heard from a guy who heard it from a crew that is gone now," and the details never match, just the punchline: ships that jump out fat and healthy, never ping another beacon, and leave behind drive logs that look like they were written by the same careful hand. The corrupted files I pulled at that remote rock and the whispers from the broken yard point back here, but whatever really happened the first time someone "tested to failure" in this place has already been chewed into rumor. All that is left is the pattern, and the quiet way these people lower their voices when they think the depot itself might be listening.

I am not saying I know where she is, just that the pattern is wrong. I have been stuck on this rusting module for three tours watching traffic for Ryujin, and data does not just decide to jump manifests on its own. The archive pulls show a neat little chain of thefts, then one transfer hits this node and comes out sliced, like someone reached in with a scalpel and rerouted only the parts they cared about. One of the techs swears he saw an old bionics prefix in the checksum, the kind tied to that shuttered lab they swore was scrubbed years ago. Another tech says that prefix is a ghost tag, leftover junk, that we are all seeing shadows because of the stories about a red-haired doc and melted implants. All I know is: every time code goes missing around her name, it leaves the same faint trace, and this time the trace points straight at that dead bionics facility everyone pretends not to remember.

I have been sitting in this cramped berth on The Den long enough to know why nobody volunteers for this posting. Everything is beige and half-asleep, the kind of place where reports get filed, stamped, and then quietly forgotten. Which is exactly why whoever hid those numbers chose it. If you want something buried, you do not drop it in a warzone; you tuck it under a bored clerk in a dead system and let routine smother it.\n\nThe stories I picked up on the way here all sound like they have been passed around too many tables. A hauler that was there, then was not. A rigger who saves people in one version and strands them in another. Every time someone tells it, the edges get rounded off, the guilt spread thinner. But underneath the smoke and barroom bravado, the same outline keeps showing through. Missing crews, altered manifests, and a line of drift that curves back toward the same invisible hand.

I was supposed to be gone before the storm rolled in. Just a simple refill, a few signatures, then back to hauling grain where the worst thing that happens is a clogged pump. Instead I am sitting in the office watching the wind shove dust against the viewport while the consoles spit out half-finished reports and error flags that no one ever cleared. Someone rushed through this place in a hurry, cut corners in the logs, pushed a few ships through on backdoor clearances, then ran before the numbers could catch up. The ledgers are messy in a very precise way, like a hand that knows exactly which fields matter and which can be left wrong for years without anyone noticing. I am no investigator, but even I can see the pattern of diverted routes and vanished transponders threaded through this depot, and it has me checking over my shoulder every time the comms crackle with another "routine" traffic update.

I am still shaking dust out of my hair from this bunker, and the consoles are older than half the patrol grid, but they still know how to keep a secret. The deserter was sloppy with his deletions; he scrubbed the export paths, not the cached scans. Buried under old meteor tracks and shuttle noise, I found a sequence of atmospheric spikes that do not belong to any registered thruster profile, cutting straight across restricted lanes like they owned the sky. Cross-checking the timestamps against patrol rosters gives me a heading and a hull class, and every line points toward a Navy combat ship that was never supposed to be on that circuit at all. Some of the techs back in the dive swear they saw it slip past on a dead transponder; others say it is all barroom exaggeration. Either way, the next piece of this mess is sitting in a silent UC hulk, waiting for someone brave or desperate enough to board it.

This module has a way of hanging onto things it is not supposed to. Old firmware, obsolete protocols, ghost accounts from contractors nobody remembers hiring it is all still here, just pushed one layer deeper every time someone does a "cleanup." I came in thinking I was tracing a straightforward breach, another bored tech moving proprietary routes offsite for a quiet sale. But the deeper I dug, the more I kept finding the same bent curves pressed into different logs, like a bootprint stamped over and over in fresh dust. Someone upstream noticed, tried to wipe it, then stopped halfway through, like they got called away or decided they did not want their name tied to this anymore. This place remembers them anyway. Even with lazy edits and truncated records, the system still clings to their mistakes and to the shape of those impossible paths, faint and overlapping where no sane corridor should ever cross.

I keep telling myself I only take the night shifts in the back corridors because the pay is better, but it is really because no one looks too hard back here. You sign off a crate as medical relief, watch it roll past the scanners, and by the time it hits storage someone has scraped the tags and called it scrap. Lately, though, the routes stamped on the cargo slates do not match the traffic boards upstairs, little course corrections that nudge whole loads away from the usual lanes. Some of the other handlers swear they saw a woman in a battered flight jacket, just standing at the junctions, fingertip tracing invisible paths on the bulkhead, but when I ask for details they laugh it off like bar talk. Maybe it is all exaggeration, but the manifests keep changing after she is supposed to have passed through, and the colony destinations on those shipments have a way of disappearing from the system altogether.

I spent half the cycle today under New Atlantis instead of in it, sitting in a humming archive room that smells like old ozone and cheaper coffee than they serve upstairs. One junior admin owed someone a favor and let me mirror a set of deprecated traffic models he swore nobody used anymore. The projections looked clean at first, then I started overlaying real freight logs. Tiny manual corrections, always in the same direction, always just enough to miss something the official charts do not admit is there. When I asked who signed off on those edits, every analyst I cornered said the same thing they had only seen the pattern after someone else ran it, and nobody was willing to say whose name was on the original run. There were other gaps too, places in their stories where words should have been and were not, like they had all agreed ahead of time which parts of the night sky did not belong in the conversation.

I am writing this down so I can stop replaying it in my head every time the grav drive spins up.

The buoy was supposed to be scrap, just another hazard marker drifting where nobody cares. I cracked it for parts and the data core spilled out a set of routes that should not exist, drift math nudged off by the same fraction every time. When I asked around on the dock, nobody claimed to know anything; they just said they had heard it from a friend, from a cousin, from some pilot who had already shipped out. Same name, different mouths, nobody willing to swear they were the first.

Dock records do not match the departure times. A freighter listed as lost took a path that never appeared on the official chart. Every time I try to trace the origin of those vectors, the line bends back into rumor and shrugs. It feels like catching a voice in the static and being told, over and over, that someone else heard it first.

I am logging this while the tug's reactor is still warm under my boots, before some supervisor edits the story into something cleaner. We were supposed to mark the derelict and move on, just another piece of junk drifting a few clicks off the lane. Then Nav said its drift did not match the model, Comms swore the beacon was just standard hazard code, and I said we did not have time to argue over scrap. Three different readings, three different priorities, and we split the difference like idiots. By the time we were close enough to see the extra plating and the way the drones orbited it like guard dogs, every channel on the board was full of that same faint, wrong signature. I keep thinking if I had pushed harder, or if Comms had not muted that one warning ping to clear space for a routine check-in, we would not have watched a whole cargo stack vanish off our scopes as if the lane itself opened a door and swallowed it.

I docked today at what should have been a dead node on the edge of nowhere. Old UC paint, dead beacon, the sort of relay you route around because nobody has maintained it since before you were born. Except the boards down in the well are still listening, running just enough juice to catch a little kick in the traffic a crooked bump in the timing that does not belong to age or dust. Silk Collective types are squatting here, running contraband through the blind spot, muttering about "lucky" jumps and refusing to look too closely at the diagnostics. Every time I ask about the missing convoy, voices drop, conversations thin out, like speaking the details aloud might ping the wrong set of ears. All I have right now is this whisper in the numbers, a relay that was supposed to be cold, and the memory of that analyst on Jemison who said her anomaly folders emptied themselves and then refused to say anything else above a murmur.

I keep telling myself it was just the Aurora talking, but it has been three nights and I still see that symbol when I close my eyes. Not the usual dock scribbles, not some drunk spacer's tally mark, but a clean little arrow cut into the edge of a table in the Astral Lounge, right where the noise is loudest and the cameras always seem to glitch. I watched a hauler trace it with his thumb while he argued over a fuel bonus, swearing a "Kyrgyz map-witch" had shaved whole days off his run. His buddy called it bar fiction, said the only thing getting shaved was his sense. Later, when the lights dimmed and the band took a break, I saw two of Neon's quieter brokers pass a napkin over that same spot. They looked around like they expected someone else to be there, someone who never showed. Next shift, that hauler's ship was still docked, cargo sealed, crew gone. Half the bar swears they saw it leave; the logs say it never undocked.

I am never going to admit this to SysDef, but the deserter was right about one thing the bunker's ears are better than its masters. Half the racks are dead, dust in the fans, but down in the cold storage I found a patrol grid slice nobody ever purged. Atmospheric sweeps, routine passes, then a smear of interference that keeps popping in the same place. Not over a colony, not over a lane. Out past the orbit tracks, right where the scouts say the rock field goes thin.  \n\nThe deserter swore some UC captain called it "the place your scopes forget," and that a certain pilot slipped through that gap more than once. I pulled old buoy chatter from a remote station that heard the same static, and way back on that farm rock I heard a drunk freighter hand mumble about a ship that crossed the sky without leaving a trail. Everyone pretends they are just telling stories, but all the stories point toward the same empty patch of stone.

I remember when the Scarrunner still smelled like new sealant and cheap coffee, back when our routing package was supposed to be a "trial build" for some contractor in New Atlantis. We were told the tweaks were temporary, just a test run on a mid-tier hauler. Nobody ever pushed an update to take them back out. Jump after jump, the little corrections stayed, got copied, got baked into our standard when nobody was looking. I only started logging the drift after our last three runs all brushed the same patch of nothing near that debris field, all flagged by the same unseen hand in the telemetry. Now I am sitting in a dead ship, in a cabin that still has two mugs strapped to the bulkhead, watching logs that prove our "temporary" settings nudged us here on purpose, and every line of code points back toward a quiet analyst who decided we were safer as numbers in his model than as people trying to make a living between the lanes.

Dock master logged this sector as routine hold space again today. Funny word, "hold." Out here it means everything from "waiting on parts" to "don't ask why that hull has not moved in six months." The local tug crews joke that ships come here to be forgotten; the old hands just shrug and say this pocket of orbit is where cargo and secrets both go to overstay their welcome.\n\nI walked past a viewport on break and caught sight of that dark courier, still drifting, still tagged as temporary layover. Nothing about its scorch pattern says temporary. I cannot stop thinking about the stories I have heard, the ones that get softer around the edges every time they are told in the back of the bar. A farm whose harvest turned to dust. A dome where the air went wrong but the paperwork stayed perfect. Now there is a dead ship parked in a zone that never lets go of what it is given, and everyone pretends their gaze just slid past it by accident.

I spent the afternoon on a busted crate outside Bay 6, pretending to fix a scanner that was not broken, just so I could watch the traffic. Same tugs, same bulk haulers, same bored crane ops running their loops. On paper, nothing wrong. In the air, though, you can feel the skips. Escorts that always seem to find a reason to break formation three klicks out, freighters that never actually touch the deck they are booked for. Nobody talks about it. Foreman changed the subject when I asked, like we had both agreed years ago that some routes just were not to be discussed.\n\nWhat bothers me is how neatly it all fits around that slate I pulled off the derelict last week. Wrong registry there, wrong tonnage here, and now these quiet detours that only show up in smudged grease-pencil on a wall no one admits to updating. Feels less like random error and more like somebody has been drawing a new map over the old one, and the rest of us decided not to see it.

I am writing this down because if I say it out loud again, someone will tell me to file it under "routing anomaly" and move on. I have been staring at traffic plots from this dustball for months, half asleep at the console, letting the patterns blur. Today I finally overlaid them with the old LIST settlement requests, the ones that never got a green light but also never got closed. That is when it snapped into place tiny course nudges on ore haulers and research ferries, always just a degree or two off declared vectors, always lining up with cargo that "went missing in transit." No one caught it because each tweak was nothing on its own, buried under years of lazy audits and cut budgets. Now I can trace the arc of those corrections out into an empty patch of sky where no beacon broadcasts and no chartered colony supposedly exists. Whatever she has been feeding lives out there, in the gap between what the records say should happen and what actually did.

I have been working this yard long enough to know when a story is supposed to die. Command cashed out the contracts, auditors stamped everything "decommissioned," and the patrols we picked up from the regulars walk like they were told to stop thinking about what happened around that wreck. Still, on long shifts, over cheap coffee and the clank of cutters, the same details leak out in different mouths civilian beacons that should not have been there, targeting orders that arrived a little too late, logs that got "reconciled" between one rotation and the next. Officially, it was all settled years ago. Unofficially, some of us kept scraps of residue, fragments of data, the way you keep a splinter after it works under your skin. They wanted the whole thing to rust away out here, but the whispers will not stay buried, and now someone is following the same trail from that forgotten rock to our piles of Deimos steel, listening harder than anyone has in a long time.

I was supposed to be working border disputes today, not chasing ghosts in the shipping lanes. One wrong routing code hit my console this morning, some clerk in Akila mixing up sectors, and suddenly I am looking at a convoy manifest that should not have passed anywhere near last year's incident. I pinged New Atlantis for clarification, got three different answers and a polite threat to drop it. The more they stumbled over themselves, the more that spiral pattern in the transit logs burned into my eyes. It is in the timing, the way the grav burns stagger just so. Cross-referencing old blackbox echoes with that misfiled manifest pointed to a dirty orbit above a dead-looking world, where the sensors keep flagging "background noise" and then clearing it. I logged it as a routine debris survey; dispatch signed off without reading. A few careless words, a few half-read requests, and now I am pretty sure I have the next breadcrumb to whoever has been rewriting our sky.

I docked at that rock expecting a routine inspection and a half-decent cup of TerraBrew, nothing more. From up close the facility is just another tired UC contract job, weld scars and patched plating, but the techs walk like they are carrying glass inside their skulls. One of them slipped, called the drive bay "the screaming room" before she caught herself and shut down, eyes on the nearest camera. I have heard three different versions of what happened here already, each one softer than the last, like someone has been sanding the edges off the story. Some say it was a test article that went sideways, some say sabotage, some say the logs were changed after the fact and nobody can remember the original numbers anymore. Whatever the truth was, it is buried under secondhand gossip and redacted files now, and all I have to go on are a falsified report, a slate full of panicked equations, and a whispered name that makes every engineer in this place change the subject.

I am writing this from a maintenance cubby three decks below the cargo office, where the walls still sweat dust from the last micrometeor strike. The relay feels wrong tonight. Dock queues are short, ships are holding in shadow, and every terminal I jack into shows the same thing: credits pushed through, then quietly walked back like they were never there. I finally traced the pattern past the forged manifests and dead shell firms the broker has been peddling. All those "corrections" bend toward one dead node off the main grid, a relay station that should have been decommissioned years ago but still drinks a trickle of power and bandwidth it is not supposed to have. Whoever is steering this tide thought the story would sink under paperwork and time, but the whispers from that farm foreclosure, from a frozen LIST rock, from bar gossip in Gagarin kept matching the same invisible signature, and now the route lines all point to that deserted hub waiting in the dark.

I asked dispatch about the Capitalwing again today and he did that thing with his eyes, looked past me like I was a bulkhead that needed repainting. Nobody forgets an escort that size, not out here, but they talk around it now, like a word you are not supposed to say in front of kids. I keep running into that same look: clerks shuffling printouts, techs suddenly very interested in cable routing, even the bartender wiping the same spot on the counter while I pretend not to notice his hands shaking. The stories do not line up, either. Official feed says grav-drive failure, quick loss, nothing to salvage. Haulers coming through three beers deep swear they heard about a test lane, faster, cleaner, if you did not ask too many questions. And somewhere between those versions there is this hollow in the logs, beacons that should have pings but do not, green ratings that appeared without scans attached. When a secret is that big, it makes people afraid to even meet your eyes.

Somebody wiped this place lazy, like they trusted time to finish the job. Half the terminals still think it is three years ago, half the cameras loop blank corridors, and the security daemon is chasing ghosts in its own logs. I was supposed to audit a simple breach trail, tick the boxes, bill whoever hired me. Instead I find a chain of connection requests that never should have routed through a backwater lab like this, all handshakes half completed, then neatly severed just before they reached the main archive. Ran them through my own rig, out of habit, and every one of those broken calls resolves toward the same patch of deep nothing a dead coordinate buried under layers of "temporary" redirects. It feels too clean to be an accident, too convenient to be just fear. Whoever she is, she knew exactly how much to cut so the system would keep limping along, and now I am holding the first clean vector to wherever she sends the people who do not want to wait in line anymore.

I should not be down here alone.

The pod still thinks it has a purpose. Consoles cycle through the same old sweeps on dead satellites, query beacons that have not answered in years, ping corridors UC stopped admitting existed. Nobody ever shut any of it off; they just stopped looking at the results. That is the only reason I found it. Buried in the rolling diagnostics, under three generations of "do not touch" tags, there is a route offset that repeats whenever one particular transponder pattern passes through the field. Cross-checking it against the fragments I pulled from that hillside cache, and the static-riddled jump data from the freighter that never arrived, it all lines up.  

Somewhere above this rock, between here and that stretch of wreck-strewn dark everyone pretends is just bad luck, the same tiny correction keeps being applied to ships that bought a certain kind of chart. The system is still nudging them, long after the people who set it up walked away.

I am writing this from the Riftblade, and the ship feels like it is trying to forget something. Drives are cold, power throttled down, but every bulkhead has that faint shiver you get after a hard abort, like the metal remembers being somewhere it should not have been. The manifest I am digging for should be routine cargo nonsense, but the routing stamps do not match the stories I heard back on the fringe. Same captain name, different paths. Same ports, different dates. Like someone took a perfectly straight haul and bent it just enough to slip between patrol sweeps. What gets me is how every step that led here was small, harmless on its own: a garbled ping from a monitoring shack, a miner talking about a missing cousin over cheap Erdebrau, a scratched-out line on an old service log. None of it screamed conspiracy, just little scuffs on the paint of reality, and somehow all of those quiet mistakes pushed me toward this dead ship and the name everybody swears they do not know.

They say if you stay too long in a dead GalBank hull, you start hearing old transactions whisper in the bulkheads. Sitting in the cold server bay of this vault ship, watching the power flicker over racks nobody is supposed to know about, I almost believe it. The logs do not match the public story; course changes are shaved by fractions, storm alerts delayed by minutes, payouts denied on worlds that should have been safe. I have heard this tale in bars and supply queues, passed around like a ghost story about a nav engineer who tilted the sky, but every retelling trims an edge, blurs a name, makes it sound like bad luck instead of design. Out at that first backwater homestead, all I saw were ruined fields and people who cursed the weather; at the old listening post, I found recordings cut off mid-warning. Now the patterns in these sealed ledgers say none of it was random, and that someone has been very careful about which parts of the truth survive the trip to the next backroom.

I picked up that dataslate because Rafi swore Juno swore her cousin had pulled it off a dead hauler out near Narion. That is how it always goes out here. No one ever finds anything themselves, they just pass along someone else's ghosts.

I ran the file on my bunk, lights low, just the hum of the recycler and that cold glow on my hands.

Course data, stamped like it came off a UC console twenty years ago, but nudging jumps by half a degree here, a full degree there.

Nothing dramatic, just a slow drift.

When I asked Rafi where Juno's cousin actually got it, he laughed and said he heard it from a Ranger who heard it from a smuggler who heard it from a Navy washout.

Every name was a step sideways, never forward.

Now I am sitting in a ship that hums the same way, staring at routes that look just a little too clean, and all I can think is that whatever started this never had to show its face.

It just needed people like us, trusting that somebody else checked the math.

I always thought banks were boring, even when they were floating in orbit. Turns out the quiet ones hide the worst rot.  

I have been on this derelict for three hours now, lungs full of recycled dust and old insulation, watching GalBank headers scroll past on dead consoles. The numbers say traffic, insurance, expected loss. Between the lines, I see ships nudged a little off the lanes, like someone was leaning on the galaxy with one finger. Nobody flagged it. Nobody wanted to.  

Out in that first backwater outpost, the locals just shrugged when routes shifted, said the sky changes. Later, that beacon in orbit with its jittery telemetry seemed like a one-off glitch. Now, buried in this courier's belly, I can feel the pattern tightening, realize how long this has been in the system, ignored because it was profitable to look away. Whatever I pull from here points toward Neon, toward high steel where someone has been rewriting how we travel while the rest of us pretend not to notice.

I signed on to Heat Ridge because it was supposed to be simple work. Guard duty, they said. Easy credits babysitting a dead UC husk no one remembered filing the decommission papers for. First few months it really was that dull; same patrol routes on half-lit catwalks, same hum of old scanners sweeping an empty sky out of habit. Felt like we were watching a locked door in a corridor no one walked anymore.\n\nThen the captain started checking the sensor room himself. Not just once, but every shift change. We got told not to touch certain consoles, not to ask why the old arrays were suddenly drawing more power. The logs started filling up with tiny course corrections for ships that, on paper, never passed within a system of us. No alarms, no flags, just little numbers pushed into folders marked routine. Somewhere along the way, standing post on a forgotten station turned into sitting on something someone else did not want found, and none of us could say when that change actually happened.

I keep replaying that day the crate lists, the loader jams, and suddenly we are staring at seals with medical hazard glyphs instead of processed grain. Trade Authority paperwork said "nutritional supplements." Smelled like antiseptic and metal, the way every battlefield clinic I have ever limped through smells. Jonas cracked a joke, Kira logged it under a different code, Elias just went very, very quiet. No one wanted to say the obvious out loud that somebody was shunting chems to places that do not show up on any of our route maps. Since then, every time some spacer in the dockside bar mutters about a ghost medic patching up people the system forgot, the crew shifts in their seats. They laugh it off, look at their drinks or the wall or anything that is not my face. Manifest says we jumped clean from Gagarin, but the nav buffer shows a burned-in echo of a different vector, a short, dirty hop toward nowhere. The closer I look, the more the gaps line up into a shape that feels like intent.

I keep replaying that intake shift in my head. One overworked Trade Authority clerk, three screens blinking orange, and a cargo ship with a routing anomaly that "looked like a sensor hiccup." Nobody wanted to hold the line over a few mismatched timestamps when there were paying haulers stacked behind it. We cleared Tidewalker TA-7207 with a shrug and a shared joke about phantom paperwork, and I told myself I would circle back to the discrepancy after shift. I did not.\n\nSince then I have watched settlement distress calls pile up from worlds stamped "marginal but viable," watched survey signatures come through with tiny calibration quirks that feel familiar now. The stories all sound the same: storms no model mentioned, groundwater souring overnight, coordinates bought from someone who swore the numbers were solid. One skipped follow-up turned into a corridor nobody questioned, the perfect place for a man who lives in the blind spots between what the data says and what people want to believe.

I keep telling myself I am not paranoid, just observant. Then I look around this box they call a command post and see how every wall is held up by things no one wants to say out loud. Manifests pinned under other manifests, patrol reports with whole hours missing, hauler complaints tagged "resolved" when I know damn well no one even sent a reply. Today I found three different versions of the same convoy's route, all stamped clean. Only the timing lines did not match. Little delays, a few seconds here, a minute there, always bending the same way. When I traced them on the board they curved into something like a spiral, neat as you please. I asked dispatch about it and got silence, then too much talking about unrelated sectors. Everyone pretended not to understand which files I meant, like we were all suddenly bad at our jobs at the same time. That is when I knew this was bigger than a bad routing algorithm and that whatever is sitting at the center of that spiral is not supposed to have a name.

I have been staring at these screens long enough that the afterimage of the graphs follows me when I close my eyes. No windows down here, just recycled air and the low whine of processors chewing on data no one officially collects anymore. Off the record, half the bureau will tell you they have heard of "those routes" in a bar somewhere between shifts. On duty, those same people swear the charts are clean, the lanes are safe, and any missing tonnage is bad bookkeeping or pirate work. Funny how the stories thin out when the recorder is running.\n\nI pulled a jump log from a small freighter that never arrived, overlaid it with half-erased telemetry from an old survey corridor, and there it was again: that same tiny course correction, like a hand on the rudder just off-center. Someone built that into the system, then everyone agreed not to see it. Whatever this cartographer is doing, it is stitched straight into the gap between what we know in private and what we are allowed to write in the report.

I met him at the edge of nowhere, where the dust eats boots and the only light is whatever you bring with you. He still had the posture, the haircut, the way of scanning horizons like someone who expects orders to drop into his ear at any second, but his badge never left his pocket. We talked like people who were not supposed to know each other, trading half phrases and old unit slang, and every time I pushed for something concrete his eyes slipped sideways, like there was a list of things he had decided not to remember. Ship names, dates, the exact wording of clearance codes no one uses anymore all brushed past, never quite spoken. I recognized the pattern; I have seen whole patrols swear they never saw the wrong kind of insignia on the wrong kind of corpse. Still, in between the gaps he gave me enough duplicated IDs, ghost cargoes, a flight plan that ends in empty coordinates to know there is a thread running through it all, and that everyone who has touched it is now pretending their hands are clean.

Docked at the relay again, grav low enough that every step feels like walking through someone else's dream. The broker finally talked, after enough credits and a reminder that rival haulers die messy when routes go bad. Under all the fake manifests and shuffled crate IDs, there it was a repeating drift in the routing tables, like someone had taught the system to breathe in a certain rhythm. Every third shipment, no matter the declared destination, nudged one or two degrees off into the same empty patch of sky. Cross it with the queue anomalies from New Atlantis and that half baked jump plan pulled from the dead survey cutter and it lines up with eerie precision. I flagged the coordinates, prepped a shuttle, told Jo I would ping back once I had eyes on whatever is floating out there. She joked I would probably find nothing but another derelict and a bad story. That was three cycles ago. Her berth is still empty, and the route is still there, pulsing quiet in the relay's old nav buffer, waiting for someone else to follow.

I have seen a lot of farms on the edge of nowhere, but this one hums wrong. The air smells of soil and synth-fertilizer, sure, but under the tractor chatter there is a steady, artificial rhythm in the power lines, like a heartbeat that forgot it was supposed to stop years ago. Someone bolted an extra antenna into this place and then never turned it off again. What was probably meant as a quick workaround, a temporary relay to skirt some inspection, just kept doing its job until it became part of the scenery.\n\nThe datapad I found on that rock should have been junk, yet its route times did not fit any legal lane. Then I kept hearing freighter crews complain about deliveries that arrived before they were even filed. Now I am watching a tired homestead push more power to its uplink at the exact moments those impossible shipments appear overhead. None of it screams conspiracy; it all just looks like systems that were supposed to be cleared, retired, forgotten  quietly left running until someone clever enough decided to use them.

I am writing this from a maintenance alcove that smells like coolant and old paper, which tells you everything about the kind of place this is. Out here, manifests change in the time it takes a bored clerk to look away, and no one notices if a freighter's mass reading is a little off or its route history does not match the stamp. I have been combing through half-burnt logs and ghost entries all shift and I keep seeing the same thing: jumps filed one way, radiation signatures insisting they went somewhere else first.  \n\nFunny thing is, none of this would be on my mind if I had not cut a corner two weeks back, letting a convoy through on a hunch because the queue was long and the supervisor was on my neck about throughput. Tiny decision, gone in a heartbeat. Now I see that same convoy's ID echoed in the dead survey site's data, and in a story a Neon dockhand swears he heard from "somebody who was actually there." It feels like I kicked a stone out of a wall without thinking, and only now do I hear the rocks shifting further in.

I am recording this from the quiet end of the module, where the fans drown out most of the guilt.

The Ryujin handler handed me a packet like it was nothing, just a side-channel scrape from an old routing experiment. I burned half a shift combing the telemetry, lining it up with the ghost vectors we pulled from that forgotten relay weeks ago. The same rounding quirks, the same microsecond drift on the time stamps, repeating like a nervous tic. Follow the offsets long enough and they stop looking random; they all curl back to one place, a dead ground station parked in orbit like a bad memory.

Everyone here swears they heard about her from someone else. A cousin on a freighter that jumped late and lived, a broker who paid extra to shave risk off a convoy, a UC analyst who saw their anomaly folder emptied overnight. No one has the whole story, just fragments traded in low voices when the room feels safe. But the traces in this packet all point to the same gap in the network, the same relay where the numbers stop making sense.

I do not usually give a damn what falls onto my table, so long as it weighs out and does not explode. Today felt different. Spacer came in shaking, said he pulled a datapack off a derelict that "went wrong" and wanted it gone, fast. Half the casing is slag, but the core still ticks if you sweet-talk it. I cracked it for parts, like always, and the screen flickered long enough to spit a string of drift coordinates before dying for good. The line it drew on my nav looked too clean for a random trader, too quiet.\n\nI traced the route as far as my old charts would take it. It threads right past that dead ice-world everyone pretends not to remember, skims a relay with missing logs, then sinks out toward a patch of empty system nobody ever files flight plans for. People around here say it is safer not to ask why certain lanes stay empty, that some places are unlucky, some cargo best left lost. I do not know if that is fear talking or just the comfort of not having to care, but the trail is there now, whether anyone wants to see it or not.

I am recording this from the old relay pit, the one UC swears was taken off the grid ten years ago. The walls still hum, just enough to rattle your teeth if you lean against them. Funny thing for a dead node, right

The deserter finally cracked after the third cup of bad coffee and a reminder that the Trackers do not file every name they hear. He handed over a slice of the patrol grid logs, the part he copied before his supervisor told him to "correct the anomaly and move on." Nobody here says that word out loud, anomaly. They talk around it, like it is a curse that might ride the comms back to whoever is listening.

I reran the scans on the bunker boards. Same ship signature, same wrong vector, threading through restricted air like it owned the place. The echoes converge on a relay that should not be handling anything but dust, way out past regular traffic. No coordinates in the open records, but the old maintenance tags still point the way. Every time I mention it to anyone, they drop their voice, like the signal itself can hear.

I used to think bad jumps were just part of the life, like rust on a bulkhead or dust in the air over Akila; you curse, you patch, you pour one out for whoever did not make it, then you fly the next lane they hand you. Lately the lanes feel like they are flying us. The last contract I ran was on one of those "optimized" routes everyone whispers about, the ones with just enough success stories to drown the wreck reports. Ship handled fine, drives within tolerance, but the timing in the chain itched at me, like a note played half a beat late. When we dropped, there was fresh debris spinning a few thousand klicks off vector and a buoy broadcasting the wrong correction by a hair. That is not random drift; that is a hand on the scale. Now I hear the same alias in spacer bars from Neon to the Stretch, always tied to quiet adjustments, cheap deals, and convoys that do not all come back. None of this started with me, but you can feel how every little cheat and covered-up "accident" bent the map, nudging us all toward this knot we are sitting in now.

Prime Deckhands is the informal name given to a loose fraternity of independent technicians, cargo hands, and systems wranglers who work the insurance and asset-protection routes around ships like GL-7623 Assetguard. They are not formally on GalBank payroll, but the bank's captains rely on them to coax aging vault-ships through decaying orbits, patch sensor arrays no one admits still exist, and negotiate with frontier crews for tug assistance without triggering legal scrutiny. \n\nLocal traders describe Prime Deckhands as quiet, methodical, and unnervingly well-briefed on which derelicts are truly dead and which are merely pretending to be. Recent unlogged course corrections and unexplained telemetry gaps in the region are often attributed to their unseen maintenance runs, or to private salvage operations carried out under the cover of "stabilization work." Rumor has it that on more than one occasion, they arrived at a drifting hull seconds after a catastrophe, as if someone had warned them which ship would start lying to its own instruments.

I am logging this from a maintenance crawlway because it feels safer talking to the bulkhead than to anyone else on this module. The air purifiers whine on a half-cycle, lights dimmed to conserve power, but the archive banks are still warm. That is all I needed. Took me most of the night to unwind the rerouted access trails, hidden under old agronomy reports and budget audits. Every time I found another redacted freight route tagged to the same hauler, my hands shook a little more. The last string was buried deep, crosslinked with soil-sample telemetry and crop failure alerts from a nowhere patch of land. Coordinates, property tags, even the irrigation layout point to an abandoned farm that should not matter to anyone anymore. Yet every story about the man in the dust circles back to places like that, and each retelling shifts a little, like the fear is editing the facts. First it was a convoy ghost, then a saboteur, then a protector no one asked for. Now the ledger in my hands says he keeps going back to ground everyone else walked away from.

I keep telling myself it is just space junk. Mech armor sloughed off some battle no one logged right, telemetry looping its own last moments until the batteries die. But the numbers in that wreck are too clean where they ought to be scarred, and bent exactly where they ought to be reliable, like someone meant to come back and finish rewriting the story and just never did. It feels like walking into a crime scene where the cleaner got interrupted mid-swipe.\n\nThe more I stare at it, the more it lines up with everything else I have tripped over by accident. A foreclosure on a farm that reversed itself while the owner was still packing. A dataslate half-buried in dust, full of draft entries that almost made it into the system. A jump node whose timing made my teeth itch even though the charts said it was fine. Little things, all of them, the kind you blame on tired clerks and lazy techs. But taken together, they look like someone started pulling on the threads of the Settled Systems a long time ago, and just got used to leaving the ends hanging.

HM-6310 is still out there, hanging between beacons like a bad thought no one wants to finish. I caught its ID in a rundown dockside bar, buried in a spacer s story he swore was just a joke. Dead Navy hull, clean cuts in the comms, no scorch marks from a boarding, no beacon loop. Just silence, and a notation buried three menus deep that says "operational loss" in the kind of language auditors use when they do not want to know more.  \n\nWhat sticks with me is not the ship itself, it is the pattern around it. Convoys rerouted for "efficiency," escorts arriving a little late, patrols shifted one sector over for reasons that sound reasonable until you realize they always leave one lane thin. Then something disappears and everybody shrugs and blames raiders, or equipment, or bad luck. Nobody ever mentions the matching blackout windows or the way records get neater the closer you get to New Atlantis. Every time I bring it up, people laugh it off too fast, like they are afraid if they stop joking the truth will land somewhere between cowardice and calculation.

Calen Rourke here, logging this before someone decides it is inconvenient and wipes the drive clean. The module is dead quiet, just fans and my own breathing, but the consoles tell a louder story than most captains ever will. I traced the data forks like any good thief would trace a payout, following the jumps where they should not bend, the packets that detoured through places no contract mentioned. Every time the trail went fuzzy, the same ship ID kept reappearing in scrubbed access notes and half-redacted audit flags from the Trade Authority. Someone thought routing that much traffic through a single cargo hauler was subtle, that if they buried it in routine freight no one would notice. Maybe they were right, for a while. But the broken beacon logs we pulled near the outer marker, the whispers in Neon's lower levels about ghost routes, and that LIST emergency broadcast everyone pretends not to remember, they all point back to the same thing: a cargo ship running too many "lucky" jumps and a pilot whose name keeps getting spoken in a lower voice every time.

I have been chasing this name in the margins for months now and I am still not sure if it belongs to a person, a program, or just the way crews talk when they do not want to say what they really mean. Every time a run threads between storms that were not on the forecast, somebody shrugs and jokes that "someone upstairs has a good broker," and the room gets just a shade quieter. I am sitting in the mess of this Alliance cutter now, listening to its empty hull tick and cool, trying to piece together how a ship built to haul bounty contracts ended up holding what looks more like a weather ledger than a job list. No one left a clean record; just half-finished notes, rerouted payments, corridors of fog that keep matching the same three or four departure points. All I know for sure is that it started on a dustball outpost with cargo that should have been delayed by a week of rain and was not, then a hunter's wreck drifting way off course with storm data in its black box, then manifests from a factory town whose harvests refused to line up with their own climate reports.

I came back to this rock because the noise would not shut up. You stand on the ridge and the wind is the only thing you hear, but jack into the local relay and it is like listening to a hoarder's attic: half-deleted pings, orphaned status codes, messages queued for recipients who have been dead a decade. This place should have been swept clean when the UC pulled their survey drones. It was not. Somebody skipped a step, or pretended to, and whatever he pushed through the buffer back then got caught in the same neglect.\n\nI keep replaying a fragment, a routing tag that does not match any registered ship, pulsing at intervals too regular to be ghost data. The dead agent's scribbled coordinates, that dataslate I bought off a frightened farmer, even the story about armed escorts circling a field that glowed after dark, they all bend toward the same name. Feels like everyone saw a piece and shrugged, too busy or too scared to add it up. Now I am standing in the middle of what they overlooked, wondering how long this signal has been waiting for someone to finally notice.

I am writing this before I lose my nerve and toss that slate back into the crate where I found it. Out here the manifests are still smeared in oil and bad handwriting, but the numbers are too neat around that one tug. Wrong hull ID, wrong routing stamp, and three different initials "fixing" the same mistake. I asked the clerk on duty who changed it; she swore she only copied what came from Gagarin. The yard boss said he signed off because a UC rep vouched for it. The rep, when I finally reached him on a laggy channel, insisted the request came from "higher up" and cut the call. Nobody owns the decision, but they all heard it from someone else first.\n\nI keep thinking about that cutter and the way its line just stops, replaced by a phantom courier that never shows on any legitimate docket. First it was a rumor from a hauler who swore a whole crew vanished off Titan. Then it was a half-burned name on a memorial wall. Now it is my own pen hovering over a ledger, deciding whether to pretend I did not see a ship quietly pushed into a graveyard route that should not exist.

I came up here to babysit a bank of half-dead sensors and drink bad coffee, not to stumble over someone else's ghost trail. The hut looks abandoned unless you know where to listen; under the wind and the creaking mast there is this steady tick of relays, software from three revisions ago still chewing on sky and ground like nobody ever told it the war was over. Half the crew cycles through, signs the maintenance sheet, never checks what the system is actually flagging. Today I dug into the ignored queue, the one that has been auto-filing anomalies as "atmospherics" for years, and there it was: a clean thermal line knifing across the ridge, too straight for weather, too smooth for wildlife, logged and time-stamped by a process nobody remembers writing. I asked around in town, and suddenly everybody's memory got real convenient; the sheriff recalls a storm, the pilot remembers "instrument noise," the bartender swears the night was quiet. The only thing not lying to me is this forgotten code, still doing its job long after the people who trusted it stopped paying attention.

I am not supposed to be working this, not officially. I am just the deputy they park in the field trailer to shuffle reports and pretend the border is quiet. But yesterday, while I was cleaning up an old convoy case, I pulled the raw traffic burst the UC shared with us for "coordination." Someone sliced our copy sloppily. A patch of static where their data shows a clean handoff, a time stamp that does not line up with engine burn logs, and a relay ID that should have been retired cycles ago.\n\nWhoever scrubbed it did it in a hurry and trusted nobody would look twice. They were almost right. I cross-checked that relay ID against older incidents and found it echoing behind three different "navigation failures," always the same forgotten listening post drifting just off the main corridor. The captains who survived keep blaming cheap charts or bad luck, and command is happy to let them. I have forwarded nothing yet. All I know is that the same interference that bent the buoy you are chasing once bounced through that dead UC ear, and every time it did, another convoy went dark.

I am recording this from the shack before I lose my nerve and sell the whole lot to the highest bidder. The walls here sweat condensation and stolen power, a tangle of rusted antennae and half-burnt routers humming on frequencies no sane port authority checks anymore. That is why her traffic washed up on my doorstep.  \n\nIt did not come as some grand revelation. Just a double-echo in the bands, two identical convoys that never existed on any manifest, both vanishing into a dead patch where no one flies unless they have to. I followed the ghosts back through weeks of chatter, past Crimson Fleet dead-drops and Ryujin side channels, until every route rebounded off the same cold coordinate string. Spacers in back rooms keep saying Deadchannel is a myth, or a hero, or a corporate hit piece, depending on who owes who, but every retelling shaves a little truth away. The raw recordings I pulled do not care about stories. They all point to the same place the next relay in her chain, a forgotten UC node floating in the dark, where the signals go silent and the lies stop being rumors.

I am writing this where no one can look over my shoulder. Out here the stars are too bright and the air is too thin for comfort, but at least the only ears are mine. I pulled the last three months of sensor sweeps from the patrol grid, buried behind routine smuggling alerts and meteor warnings. There is a pattern in the noise, a faint smear of grav interference that keeps showing up in the same narrow band of orbit. It is not on any flight plan, but it pulses with the same timing as those "isolated malfunctions" command keeps renaming.\n\nWhen I tried to bring it up in the ready room, the room went quiet in that careful way. Nobody told me I was wrong, nobody asked to see the data. They just found somewhere else to look. That is how I know I am close. The signature climbs out from the blind side of this rock and vanishes right where a derelict comms platform went missing six years ago. First the dead cache, then the jump-scarred freighter, now a grav shadow in empty orbit, all sharing the same geometry. Whatever she is doing, she is walking the same invisible line every time.

I am recording this before I lose the nerve to listen to my own voice.

The bunker is colder than outside. Systems half-dead, dust on every console, like nobody has breathed in here since the last war. I jacked into the relay expecting dead air and junk packets, but the patrol grid was still whispering to itself, looping old atmospheric scans like a nervous habit. Buried in all that static, the same transponder ghost kept reappearing over the border, slipping through restricted airspace and vanishing right over the old barracks line. No alarms, no flags, just quietly filed away and forgotten. Somebody trusted the summaries and never looked at the raw feed again.

I pulled the logs myself, traced the drift pattern, and there it was: a ship riding the same corridor, again and again, like it knew exactly where the blind spot lived. Every course correction points back to those ruined barracks outside Akila, like they are using the ghosts of old casualty reports as cover. Feels like this has been happening for years, hiding in full sight of everyone who stopped paying attention.

Should have burned the cache the first night. It was meant to be a quick skim while the relay was quiet check a few flagged packets, flip them for drink money, forget the rest. Then I saw the pattern tucked under all the spacer noise and Crimson chatter the same correction marks, same timing gaps, slipping through systems that do not share charts. I told myself I would just hold onto one clean slice, something I could trade if the wrong people ever decided I knew too much. That was the oversight. Word got around that I "had Vector on tape." Now I have captains leaning on my door and bounty types sniffing the air like they can smell the bits. I traced one of her cleaner jumps riding a Vanguard transponder they should not have been anywhere near the anomaly she used, but there they were, drive singing almost the same tune as her freelance runs. Whatever she is doing, she has their hardware in her hands, even if they pretend otherwise. From that little corporate lab to this shack, every scrap says the next solid piece of her trail is locked in a dead navy hull that never made it home.

I did not like coming back to this hole in the rock. The cavern sweats fuel and cold air, and the quartermaster counts crates like they are sins he will never confess. Still, credits loosened his tongue, a little. He never said her name, not once, but his eyes kept flicking to the ceiling, like something could be listening through stone.  

The manifests he finally showed me were scrubbed, but the nav offsets were wrong in a very particular way, a familiar kink in the numbers. Buried in the timing of those jumps is a rendezvous pattern that only resolves if you project it off-world, just above this system's gravity well.  

So the trail now runs: that forgotten outpost where someone left a data crumb, the mismatched docking records tied to a hauler in Neon, and a smuggler here who moved war junk on a schedule that matches neither trade lanes nor patrol sweeps. Three points on a curve that bends up into empty orbit, where someone has been hiding messages in the spaces between official routes, and everyone who has seen it only talks about it in lowered voices, if they talk at all.

I keep replaying the last clean jump in my head, trying to remember if anything felt wrong. On the scopes it was textbook smooth approach, green lights from the UC tower, a corridor plotted so tight you could shave with it. Nobody questioned it. Why would they We all trust those vectors like gravity.

Then the stories started trickling in, always secondhand. A cousin of a hauler swore a freighter vanished on the same track, but his captain heard it from a GalBank adjuster who blamed pirates. A bartender in New Atlantis told me of a courier that never docked, and she swore she heard it from a Vanguard pilot. Every time I leaned in, they leaned back, said someone else knew more, that they were just passing it along.

Now I am standing on CM-1304, UC crest still stamped over the airlock, and the logs do not match the bodies. The recorded course is pristine, the telemetry too clean, like someone scrubbed out the struggle and left only the math. Whoever laid these lanes knew exactly where they bent, and everyone who ever touched them swears they only heard the warning from someone else.

Docking log, personal copy, in case this all disappears like the rest.  

We were only supposed to babysit a drifting support ship for the Trade Authority, run basic checks, sign off on the tow. No one said why the TA tag looked like it had been peeled and re-stuck three times, or why every cargo cradle smelled of burnt lubricant and welding flux. In the cargo spine I found a slab of hull plate with seams too clean for any station yard out here, over-braced like someone expected to take fire. The manifest claimed it was scrap. The crew chief just stared at it, then at me, and changed the subject.  

Funny thing is, a few months back I rotated through an old UC relay where the consoles were full of ghost returns, unregistered work barges popping in and out of junk fields. The tech on duty swore it was sensor drift, then whispered later that the signatures had showed up before, always on routes that suddenly became very profitable for "the right people." Everybody talks like they have it all figured out in the mess, but the moment you suggest putting it in a report, the room goes quiet.

Dock's quiet now. Just the relay hum and the way the bulkheads creak when the rock flexes. Feels like the whole module is leaning in, listening to see if I talk.

They say this tug pilot never fires a shot. Ships just arrive light, containers written off, everyone shrugs and files the claim. I have seen the gaps behind those shrugs. Partial manifests that do not match hull capacity. Time stamps edited by a shaky hand. Credit transfers routed through dead accounts that somehow still pass Trade Authority checks.
