Today a spacer brought me another fragment, said it came off a crate that "never existed." Same route vector I saw on that corrupted record from the research outpost, same ghost ping that bounced off an old relay nobody admits is active. All of it points to the same kind of place: where cargo goes to be forgotten before someone like her makes it useful again.

I am not stupid enough to say the name in the open channel, but I know which depot she has been bleeding dry. Nobody here knows the whole story. We just pass pieces along to people we trust to live long enough to use them.

I am recording this from the relay bunker, in case someone needs to know why I walked back into a dead grid. The air still smells like old ozone and coolant, like the place is one power spike from remembering it mattered. I pulled the deserter's stolen scans off a buried buffer, the ones no one filed because they were easier to ignore than explain. Same patrol, same sweep pattern, but there is a shadow in the upper atmosphere that does not match any registered transponder, holding position right above that forgotten station on the ridge. It is all there in the timestamps and angles; you can almost feel the course corrections, like someone threading a needle through a gap the charts say does not exist. Maybe it is safer for everyone if that kind of flying stays a rumor, but pretending we never saw it is how we got here in the first place. The last listening post gave us ghost readings that did not line up with the public lanes, the deserter confirmed a ship cutting through restricted sky on a path nobody admits is real, and now the numbers point straight back to that same quiet station, waiting.

I keep replaying the last jump profile in my head, like if I stare at the numbers long enough they will admit what we all refuse to say out loud. The Trustsphere should not be here, cold and torn open on a lane that was sold to us as safer than dockside. I walked past a hundred holo-ads in New Atlantis promising that GalBank watches over its investments like family; funny how none of those clips show a vault deck vented to vacuum. The nav buffers are scarred with corrections that are too elegant to be accidents, little nudges lining us up with someone's private kill box. When I took this side contract out of that busted quarter on Akila, it was supposed to be a clean audit, a chance to prove to my old crew I still had a future. I tagged the corrupted chains, flagged the inconsistencies, left a note to myself that I would come back with proper tools and a clearer head. I never did. If anyone finds this, know that the pattern started with a cheap dataslate in the dirt and angry spacers muttering about discount routes; it led here, to a dead protection ship that proves the odds were never on our side.

I thought this would be another dead end like the rest of my assignments out here, one more "monitor and report" buried under nicer words. The outpost is barely more than a sealed room, a crackling comm dish, and a bunk that smells like whoever had it before me smoked in their sleep. Still, the relay hears everything the lanes whisper past. Today, buried inside routine telemetry and a half-corrupted freighter ping, I caught it again: that same fractional drift in the jump solutions, the same signature from a skiff we lost six months back when Command told me my timestamps were off. I only saw it because Ops sent the wrong filter profile, the deck tech typoed a ship ID, and I forgot to purge yesterday's buffer. A chain of small mistakes no one will ever admit. Crossed with that old LIST incident file I was told to "deprioritize," it all folds toward a scrapyard orbiting Deimos that somehow features in traffic patterns way above its importance. So far I have a trail of dismissed reports, an anonymous tip from a nervous hauler, and now a set of lane deviations all curving toward the same patch of rust.

I keep thinking if I say this out loud, it becomes real, so here it goes.

I ran manifests for a hauler out past New Atlantis, thought I knew how the numbers were supposed to look. Then we picked up that stray slate in the drift, all mismatched dates and dead transponders, pointing back to Trade Authority traffic it had no business knowing about. I laughed it off until I checked a personal account and half my life was suddenly "under review."

By the time I reached the city branch, the clerk downstairs swore my file had always been like that. Same tone at every window, the same little pauses when they read my name. Even the lawyer I found in the lower levels said there had been "another version" of my case once, but whatever it was got folded into rumor and bar talk a long time ago. Now I am sitting in the dark of this support ship, listening to its cooling metal, and the shape of it all is starting to show; quiet edits in station ledgers, cargo that moved without moving, and a whisper that the first person who tried to explain it disappeared from the records before anyone wrote down what they saw.

I am recording this from a borrowed bunk on a UC combat hull, and the hum here is wrong. Too clean. On my ship you could feel the drive's heartbeat through the soles of your boots, a little off-tempo, like it knew it was living on favors and hand-fit parts. They brought me aboard after the incident to "clarify my testimony," then parked me in a cold corridor while officers argued in a room I was not allowed to see. One of them slipped, mentioned a cryo facility well off-chart, then shut up when he saw I was listening. Later, a junior tech let me glance at a routing trace. Same coordinates we had been warned never to jump anywhere near, buried under layers of classification and "need to know." Whoever was supposed to chase that line left in a hurry; their duffel is still under the bunk opposite mine, folded uniforms never issued, slate blinking with an unfinished note. They told me to wait while they "verified a few things." That was three days and two course corrections ago, and the ship keeps drifting closer to those dead coordinates as if someone forgot to cancel an order nobody wants to admit was given.

I am recording this mostly so I can convince myself later that I did not imagine it.

The outpost is dead in all the obvious ways. Air smells like dust and coolant, screens dark, lab benches stripped. But the Lima Devils keep drifting through like they grew up here, stepping around certain doors without looking, using the same two jokes about "old science ghosts" and studiously not mentioning anything else. I asked one of them who used to run this place and he laughed, then froze, then said he "forgot" and changed the subject so fast it was almost clumsy. Thing is, the walls remember better than they do. Scratches where warning signs used to hang, faded tape outlines on the floor around equipment no one wants to describe, a schedule still pinned to a board with whole shifts blacked out instead of erased. 

Feels like everybody agreed, quietly, to stop recalling the details at the same time. Like names, dates, whole accidents just slid into a hole that someone dug on purpose. And now there is me, alone in the corridor, trying to decide whether following that gap in their memory is brave, or just stupid.

I am recording this because if I say it out loud again in the mess, they will just tell me I am reading ghosts into the traffic reports.

We were supposed to be running standard courier hops, comfortable little arcs between stations where the biggest worry is whose crate of snack packs leaks first. Then the route updates started coming in with gaps. Whole segments of flight plans redacted, replaced by neat, anonymous vectors threading right through places every pilot I know calls cursed weather. Ask who plotted them and people stop saying names. They tap the console, shrug toward orbit, talk about "the contractor" or "that navigator" like the sound might bite.

Trade Authority likes its deniability tidy. As long as the manifests balance and the couriers return, no one asks why the sensor feeds splice mid-storm. But I have seen the same signature in three different log sets now, a little pattern in the corrections like someone tightening screws in our sky. It feels like we are flying inside someone else's experiment, and the only time anyone mentions the architect, it is with a tilt of the chin, not a word.

Common Watch is the informal name given to the loose convoy of haulers, tugs, and survey cutters that habitually work the lanes around the derelict GC-5222 Stockwind. Originally a rotation of contract escorts keeping scavengers off GalBank traffic, the group has since grown into a semi-regular presence, trading drift warnings, selling updated debris charts, and quietly charging for "eyes-on" patrols when official coverage thins out.  \n\nTheir reputation is mixed: captains praise their vigilance, while more cynical traders claim Common Watch only sounds the alarm when there is no profit in staying quiet. One archived traffic control log notes a brief halt in their patrol while the crews burned minutes searching for a missing mug someone swore had been left on the main console, accompanied by open-band grumbling about how they lose the same junk every week out here. In that same exchange, a senior voice can be heard wondering aloud whether their old ritual of circling the drifting Stockwind at the start of each shift still means anything, or if they keep doing it only because no one wants to be the first to stop.

Filed on a dead shift, because nobody reads these unless something explodes.

I have been staring at the same stack of incident reports all week. Broken loaders, bad weather, bar fights out by the farms. Noise. Then I started cross-tagging the implant failures the way nobody pays me to do, and the noise turned into an echo. Same firmware fragment, same off-the-books installer, same shrug from every clinic that signed the contracts.

Today I pulled a robotics maintenance ticket for a site that is supposed to be mothballed. Power draw says otherwise. Parts orders rerouted there line up with the dates of those seizures planetside. When I mentioned it in the mess, the room went quiet in that special way, where people stop saying certain names and just tap their fingers on the table instead. So I logged the coordinates, flagged the lab in my own notes, and locked this entry where it will not be auto-archived into nothing. If anyone actually follows up, they will find their next step in that forgotten complex, where dead machines are learning new tricks from someone who knows exactly how to vanish between signatures.

I keep telling myself I only came to Neon for cheap parts and cheaper drinks, but I have been stuck in Ebbside three nights now, listening to pipes instead of music. The walls here sweat, little beads along the conduits, and every time the pressure drops the whole bar goes quiet for half a heartbeat. Folks pretend it is nothing, then start talking louder.

Dockhands swear the taps ran clean yesterday and sour today, that tankers dock at hours no one remembers logging. I saw a maintenance panel half-open in a service corridor, tools laid out just so, like somebody got called away mid-job and never came back to finish the tidy work. No lock, no seal, just that low hum through the metal and the taste of iron on the air.

I checked that corrupted slate I picked up out past nowhere, then listened to a drunk spacer mutter the same intake codes in his sleep. Different places, same feeling. Someone was supposed to smooth this over, file the reports, pretend the water still flows like it should. Instead, the mess is just sitting here, humming behind thin walls, waiting for someone stubborn or stupid enough to start pulling at it.

I am writing this down because if I say it out loud again, somebody will tell me to lay off the chems or get back to work. The lab should be dead. Power grid cut years ago, no traffic, no reason for anything out there to still hum. And yet that icebox glows on long-range like a bad tooth, and every time a hauler skirts its sky my console shows the same microscopic bend in their descent. Pilots blame weather, controllers blame worn sensors, command shrugs and files another "unexplained fluctuation."\n\nOff-duty, in the mess, you still hear the old stories. A Navy run that vanished after a routine ping. A convoy that never made the farmstead. Each tale told softer than the last, like everyone hopes if they whisper low enough the numbers will stop lining up. They have shuffled the reports, retired the officers, buried the families in condolences and statistics, but the pattern keeps bleeding through. I am not special; I just sat one watch too many with the scopes turned up and the volume down, and now I cannot unsee that all those missing ships seem to tip their wings over the same patch of frozen nowhere before they disappear.

I used to joke I could fly a SysDef hull blind just by the hum in the deckplates. PX-15 feels the same as every other combat frame I've patched on, same scuffed corridors, same stale TerraBrew in the galley, same officers treating techs like background noise. That is the problem. When you know every panel by heart, you stop questioning the ones that do not belong. I saw the first altered jump projections three shifts ago, tucked in among old interdiction charts. Thought some junior analyst had fat-fingered a waypoint, so I corrected it and moved on. Now I keep finding the same pattern, mirrored, inverted, threaded through legacy threat maps like someone stitching a new spine into dead data. Back on that dustball relay, there was a trader whispering about missing convoys and a name I had heard in The Well years before, buried in LIST chatter. I remember thinking it was all rumor. Then PX-15 turned up on my assignment list, tagged routine archival work, and I signed off without a second glance. Familiar callsigns, familiar procedures, and somewhere in that comfort, a whole new route was slipped past everyone who should have seen it.

I have worked manifests for the Trade Authority long enough to know when the numbers are lying.

On their own, they all looked clean. A crate here routed one system wider than it needed to be, a refuel stop added to a hauler that should have had the range, a timing window that cut it a little close to a patrol schedule. You shrug, you blame lazy clerks or overcautious captains, and you sign where you are told to sign.

Then one evening on the cargo deck I laid three runs side by side, all from different shippers, all stamped months apart. Same "optional" detour, same quiet refuel station, same gap in recorded telemetry. It felt like staring at a face I had seen a dozen times on passing crowds but never really looked at.

People whisper about someone who can sell you a route that slips between all the cracks. I used to laugh that off. Lately it feels like we have been freighting ghost footprints for him. The last batch of manifests I checked before we lost contact with the Starborne had that same detour buried in the route code. Coincidence stops feeling like chance when it starts repeating in the same cold, careful handwriting.

I am starting to think the worst damage on a SysDef ship never shows up on a hull scan. It is in the tiny gaps between what one person meant to say and what the next person actually heard. Naomi Khatri swore she logged the last change to our patrol lanes; Leah Ortiz insists she never saw it. Erin Cho thought Command's burst about "legacy triage assets" was just another dead file bouncing around the network. I thought the medic they flagged was a ghost story to keep us sharp on watch.\n\nToday, HM-7378 dropped out exactly where the amended orders said to, only to find a medical courier wreck that is not on any official chart and a string of reroutes buried under half a decade of "we will fix it later." Comms traffic does not quite line up with the nav logs, and nobody can explain why our previous shift burned three hours loitering off a rock that does not appear in the briefing. None of it is big enough on its own to raise an alarm, but all together it feels like we have been nudged, a few degrees at a time, into someone else's forgotten emergency response. If this is just a paperwork snarl, it is the most elaborate one I have ever seen.

Some nights I think half the Settled Systems lives off lies told in cargo bars. Gagarin is proof. Every time I ask about those lost convoys I get a different version, sanded smooth by whoever is talking. Dock clerks swear the lanes were straight and certified. Haulers over Erdebrau insist the routes kinked at the last second into the same patch of bad sky. No one ever agrees on details, just on one thing; it was not their fault. You can feel it in the way the story edges keep getting rounded off, like they have all told it too many times to themselves already.\n\nI started copying manifest numbers on the sly, lining them up against what little GalBank will still show, and the more I look the less the official record matches what people mutter in backrooms. Insurance spikes on runs that were supposedly uneventful. Traffic traces that look like someone took a handful of convoys and nudged them, just a little, onto the same strange three-forked pattern. Nobody wants to say the name tied to those adjustments out loud, but when it does slip through their teeth, it comes out soft, like they are afraid he might be listening on an open channel.

I was not supposed to take the job. Should have left that low-grade Alliance posting to some green kid with a patched suit and big dreams. But a derelict signaling from nowhere smells like clean salvage, and clean salvage pays.  

The shuttle was wrong the second I saw it. Hull creased in directions metal does not like to bend, cockpit torn open from the inside, like the jump itself had tried to eat its way out. I buried what was left of the pilot with my gloves still on, dust clinging to the suit, then found his slate half-melted under a rock he had not finished stacking.  

There was enough data left to scrape together a name, the same one I heard once in a bar on Gagarin when freighter captains got too drunk to watch their tongues. Short, sharp, the way spacers talk about storms. Nav noise on his last jump matched an old ghost blip I logged years back and forgot, filed under sensor glitch to keep dispatch off my back.  

Funny how the past leaves fingerprints on the present. One bad reading ignored, one rumor laughed off, and suddenly the lines all converge on a single path someone has been penciling into the dark for a long time.

I keep telling myself it is coincidence.

One farmer comes in, says his arm rig locked during harvest. Glitch, fine. Next week a hauler swears her vision implant fuzzed out right as she hit orbit. Different clinic, different brand, same shrug from the rep on the other end of the line. I log it, because that is what I do out here in the tin box while the real decisions get made in cities I will never see.

Then the numbers start to rhyme.

Same fragment in the diagnostics, same vague reference to an "independent tech," same way people drop their eyes when I ask who did the install. They stop saying names, start pointing with their chins, like the old days when you did not say a gang's tag out loud. The complaints get marked resolved upstairs, but they keep walking through my door, shaking, scared, angry.

Tonight I laid the reports out on the desk and followed dates and coordinates with my finger until the trail curled back on itself. Too many accidents lining up on the same curve for me to call it bad luck anymore. Coincidences stacked until they leaned, and once they leaned they pointed, and now I cannot pretend I do not see where.

I think this is still the Ananke Drift, but the nav keeps flickering like it does not want to admit we are really here. Suits me fine. No one likes logging this rock anyway.

Met the Aegis man today. He did not say Aegis, but you can hear it in the way he measures every word, like he is still on record even when his badge is gone. Face looked like he had not slept since the coolant incident everyone avoids naming directly. Ask three people what happened and you get three stories, all framed to make sure no one in uniform comes back with questions. Nobody pushes too hard; out here, curiosity is just a slower way to die.

He handed me a cracked slate, said he was "done chasing ghosts." The trace on it is not a ghost, though. It is a route signature, buried under maintenance pings and survey sweeps, repeating at intervals that match a very real ship. I crosschecked it with what little I have: that stray dataslate from the fringe homestead, the harvest that grew too well, and the way a certain name keeps surfacing in dockside rumors whenever someone mentions miracle grain and missing logs. Wherever that pattern leads next, it is not random.

I keep replaying that day on the outpost like a bad grav sim with a glitching reset. It was supposed to be routine: check the soil monitors, log the yields, complain about funding over cold TerraBrew. I saw the anomaly in the routing table, a little flag on a grain shipment that did not match the standard template. I remember thinking, "must be some clerk in Gagarin fat-fingering codes again," and I let it sit until after lunch.

By then the recall order had appeared and vanished in the queue, just a flicker. The samples still went out.

I told myself it was nothing, that people above my pay grade knew what they were doing. Then reports started drifting back months later, in rumor not in data: colonists coughing up dust, fields that would not stop producing even after the farmers begged for a fallow cycle. Someone down the chain kept calling it a miracle. Someone up the chain kept insuring it. I keep wondering if I had overridden that single shipment, forced a manual review, whether any of this would still be happening, or if they would have just found another technician too tired to double-check a harmless little deviation in the code.

I am done pretending this is random.

When I took this posting on the rock, it was supposed to be easy time. Push manifests, skim a little off the top, sign whatever the system fed me. Then the "variance" jobs started showing up. Same ship classes, same lanes, always shifted a hair off the standard corridor. Escorts dropped by just one hull. Refuel stops quietly deleted. First one, I thought the clerk before me was lazy. Fifth one, I told myself the computer was glitching. Twentieth, and my hands were shaking every time I hit confirm.

Tonight I dug deeper. Buried in the routing tables was an old UC code woven through the edits, a reference tag that should not exist on a backwater module like this. I followed it, line by line, until it pointed at a forgotten military node out-system, one of those posts they "decommissioned" on paper and left to rot in the dust. All my altered lanes bend toward it, like someone has been curving traffic around a blind spot for years and paying idiots like me to press the button.

I thought I was just helping cargo dodge fees and inspections. Turns out I have been nudging people onto a board I cannot even see.

I keep replaying that survey run in my head, the one that brought us down to this nobody rock. We were behind schedule, two drones already fried by static, so when the air samplers started flashing out-of-range, I just tagged the readings as localized contamination and pushed on. No budget for curiosity. We scraped a few cores, logged coordinates, lifted before the storm front ate the landing gear.  

Weeks later, back on the station, those same samples showed a pattern that did not match any refinery waste or colony runoff. A precise kind of wrong, like someone had been drawing lines through the atmosphere with a scalpel. I filed a note to Environmental, then watched it vanish under "non-critical." Ships kept jumping through the sector, captains grumbling about minor course corrections, nothing more.  

Now I have seen the half-burned log from that outpost, heard the nervy chatter about a freighter that never arrived, and skimmed the vault ship manifests that almost make sense if you ignore the gaps. It feels like whatever she did down there started as a rushed test, a small cheat in the math, and we all stepped over the stain without looking down.

I keep telling myself the array is just old hardware and lazy clerks, but sitting in this cramped console seat, listening to the static between pings, it feels more like I am eavesdropping on a lie everyone agreed not to talk about. The corridor it watches is not on any chart I can pull without favors, yet the sensors know it is there; tiny grav spikes, ships sliding through at angles that make my stomach tighten just looking at the vector math. Traffic control tagged them as calibration drift years ago and then, somehow, never circled back. Funny how nobody quite remembers who filed the original note, or why the budget never stretched far enough to decommission the array outright. I have seen that same silence before: at a frontier dock where a captain "lost" half his jump logs, in a station bar where people changed the subject as soon as Neon's power dips came up, in a maintenance bay where a tech swore she had never met a pilot named Vector but could trace his burns on the hulls she patched. Now this old watcher is staring straight down the throat of a path he is been rehearsing, and every omission around it feels less like ignorance and more like consent.

Funny how the story keeps changing, depending who is telling it and how close they are to a docking bay. First time I heard it, over watered whiskey in the mess, it was just a rumor about a liner that came apart mid jump, no names, no blame, just a bad roll of the grav dice. Next station over, the same tale had a villain, some engineer who signed off on cheap steel and vanished into the black. After that, I kept hearing about a shadow on the docks, a quiet tech who slipped aboard at night and fixed what the staryards pretended not to see.\n\nToday I ended up in that crooked little Freestar trailer at the edge of the pad, listening to a deputy whose hands shook just a little when they scrolled through failure reports. Same incidents, same ship classes, same manufacturer tags, but the way they talked about it was different: not curses, not campfire stories, just a pattern no one higher up wanted to acknowledge. They say the masked fixer is a saboteur in one port, a savior in another. The only thing that does not change is the silence whenever someone asks why the same hulls keep cracking in the same way and why the logs keep getting buried under other case numbers.

I am writing this down so I will not start believing the official version.

We were three ships running ore and machine parts toward HopeTown, nothing fancy, same corridor I have flown since before the Armistice. UC traffic pings in a correction, minor variance, cleaner path through the junk belt. I swear I checked the vector twice. Looked safe. Then we caught the echo of a wreck ahead that should not have been there, hull still warm on thermals, cargo already stripped clean. Somebody had got the tip before us rode the same correction, just a few hours earlier.

Afterward, in the bar at New Atlantis, the story turned into one more spacer tale bad luck, old charts, UC underfunding. The captains laughed it off, but when the drinks thinned out, they started whispering about a voice that sounds like ops, numbers that never show in the logs. Every time the rumor cooled, some tug limped in with a new near miss and the same quiet pattern, like the story is trying to die and keeps getting dragged back up by people who cannot unsee their own telemetry. I am no investigator. I just know my ship went exactly where I was told to go, and someone was already there, waiting.

I am writing this in the dark between shifts, because the ship feels wrong and I do not trust the official logs to remember that. We were not supposed to break route this close to Neon. Manifest said standard haul, no deviations, but the Trade Authority dispatcher slipped in a new vector at the last minute, barely a line of explanation. The bridge took it anyway. Credits make people move faster than they should. Now the Skyclipper hums unevenly, like the Grav core is holding its breath, and half the nav data from the last jump came through smeared, as if the stars themselves dragged. Ivy tried to scrub the errors, muttering that it was just interference from traffic around Volii, but I saw the look she gave that corrupted segment, like it was something alive. Someone pushed this course in a hurry, then turned their eyes away from what it might brush against. Out on a survey outpost we found the first stray blackbox, just a fragment. Then there were those odd beacon returns in high orbit, callsigns that matched ships marked as lost, and now this cargo run with its quiet addendum and a route line that bends closer to Neon's shadows than any normal hauler would risk.

I am recording this quietly, because people who talk too loud about lanes and disappearances stop getting invited back on good contracts. Learned that the hard way at a bar outside HopeTown two months ago. I mentioned a transport that never pinged its arrival beacon, and three captains suddenly remembered somewhere else they had to be. The fourth just stared into his drink and told me, very carefully, that the frontier eats ships and stories the same way.\n\nToday I put down on an old relay they swore was decommissioned. No traffic, no maintenance drones, just a dead lattice hanging where three routes used to meet. Inside, the boards are burned but not empty; you can still see faint traces of jumps that do not match any published corridor. Someone carved their own path through here, again and again, so clean the drives barely left a bruise. I mentioned that pattern once to a LIST clerk I know, and watched her face close up like an airlock. She changed the subject to fuel prices and never answered my messages after. Out here, everyone has noticed something wrong in the map, but the smart ones keep their opinions small, like they are afraid the vacuum might be listening.

Hard to say when it started feeling inevitable. Maybe back on that rock out past the lanes, when I cracked open a discarded slate and saw numbers that did not belong to any homestead that size. Maybe in Gagarin, watching freight hands swear a shipment existed while the manifest swore it did not. Either way, it brought me here.

The Fundrunner is dead metal outside, but inside you can still feel the hum of old credit flows, like a ghost current under your boots. GalBank stamped their logo everywhere, as if repetition makes trust. It does not. Every sealed rack I pass smells like another story that ended the same way: someone in the black, someone in the ground.

The trail says whoever taught her how to cut debts loose used ships like this as a pulpit. Phantom yields at an extraction site that should be dry, families whose ledgers just blinked clean, a pattern of erased risk that always arcs back toward Helium-3 and quiet corridors like these. I followed rumors from a forgotten outpost to noisy docks, from there to this drifting vault, and every step made it clearer this was never random; the numbers were always steering me toward the plants that feed the whole game.

Everybody swears they heard it from someone else first.

The deserter whose bunk I borrowed said a friend in SysDef mentioned it over cards. The tech running the power in this rusted hide said it came down from some analyst on Jemison. I am sitting in the dark with the last of the juice running through an old overwatch console, and no one will admit they were the one who actually saw it.

Thing is, I have seen it now.

Buried three layers down under scrubbed patrol logs, there is a jump trace that does not fit any sanctioned corridor. The ship on that feed slides between pings, just outside where the net is supposed to be solid, like it knows exactly where the blind spots live. Every time it reappears, its vector lines kiss the same set of coordinates orbiting Deepala. The Clinic.

People say that station sees everything the war broke and everything the lanes keep breaking still. If he is sampling the damage his numbers do, that is where he would go to listen. I have got the timestamp, the entry window, and the angle his drive flared when he dropped into local space. It is not much, but it is the first time this ghost leaves the same fingerprint in two different systems.

I keep telling myself this is just another relay job, just another Trade Authority courier drifting between people who pretend they are not on the same side. The hull hums like always, life support purrs, the recycler coughs every few hours. Familiar noises. Comforting, until you notice the other sounds.

Tonight I heard the ship talk to no one.

Old UC diagnostic routines, buried deep in the nav core, spun up during downtime. Their pings went out into the dark, calling to beacons that were supposed to be decommissioned years ago. No one on the manifest ordered that. The captain shrugged, said legacy code sometimes ghosts the system. But I watched the patterns scroll by and they were too clean, too deliberate, like somebody had been tuning them while we ran cargo and looked the other way.

We docked at a rock last week, quiet place, barely a name. A freelancer handed over a data packet, eyes flicking to the stars every other breath, muttering about ships that arrive late or not at all. Since then, the old routines have been waking more often, pointing toward the same patch of sky. The pay on this route is better than it should be. Everyone pretends not to notice that, either.

I am sitting in a dead relay, listening to ghosts that never got the memo war is over.

The main board is red-lit and half the panels are fused, but when I tied a microcell into the backbone, the grid woke up like it had just been on break. Old patrol routines, still cycling after all these years, quietly logging every shuttle and ore hauler that screamed past the no-fly line. Nobody checked, nobody cared, so the system kept watching.

Buried under a decade of dust and recycled timestamps, I found it  a set of atmospheric returns that did not match any filed transponder, cutting through restricted airspace like they owned it. The pattern is clean, too clean for a smuggler guessing blind. Whoever plotted that path knew every blind arc in the grid and trusted the forgotten software to still be doing its job. I piggybacked the trajectory into orbitals and there it was, a residual signature stitched into traffic corrections around a processing hub hanging over the planet.  

So now I know where the next piece is waiting, caught in the same old procedures that outlived their operators. The brass turned their eyes away, but the machines never stopped watching, and she gambled on that.

I am writing this from the corner of the trailer, back to the bulkhead so I can see the door. The deputy went out for "fresh air," which is funny given the dust, and left their board on idle. They think I do not notice where their eyes slide whenever the subject comes up, how the room goes quiet when someone mentions that engineer in anything louder than a mutter. Nobody wants to be the one on record knowing too much.\n\nStill, patterns are hard to unsee once you trace them. Every jump failure, every emergency dock closure, every "miracle" overnight repair the deputy flagged sits on the same crooked line. The last report they filed, buried under a different case number, mentions a disposal site Deimos supposedly cleared years ago. Same prefix code on the ship that limped in last month with stress fractures on a frame that was "well within spec." They circled those coordinates twice, then closed the file without sending it. That is how I know it matters. The people closest to whatever happened will not meet my eyes when I ask about old scrapyards, and one of them quietly told me to avoid that sector if I valued my hull. Which is exactly why I logged the location before the board timed out.

I keep replaying the last jump in my head, like staring at a cracked grav plate and waiting for it to give. On paper it was simple: log the new corridor data, tag the anomaly signatures, pass everything along to the next set of hands. Trade Authority gets leaner lanes, we get a bonus that does not show on any official docket. But the vectors we pulled do not line up with any sanctioned chart I have ever seen, and the noise in the telemetry felt wrong, like something out there breathing against the hull. I brought it up in passing back in Neon, over cheap coffee and louder music than the bar could handle, and the broker who gave us the coordinates just smiled, said some ex-Navy genius had triple-checked the math. Since then, every rumor I have heard about vanished haulers or convoys that never reached HopeTown seems to trace back to the same kind of shortcut. I have logged everything I can on this recorder and flagged a follow-up survey for whoever takes Windcrier after us, told them to trace the signal all the way to that old listening post sitting off the lanes like a forgotten ear. Someone will need to go there, see how deep this pattern really runs. If they are smart, they will not come alone.

I am logging this from a maintenance alcove on the relay because the walls here feel thicker, like they will actually keep a secret for once.

Spent the last six hours peeling back Trade Authority manifests with my own hands. The broker who used to sit this post thought he was clever, hiding patterns inside mislabels and "transmission errors." He was not clever enough. Buried in the duplicates and ghost shipments, there is a cluster of traffic tags that never resolve to any port, just loop back through the same defunct military uplink on the edge of nowhere. UC registry says that listening post went dark years ago, but the timestamps on these routings are fresh.

Everyone in the bar stories talks about a pilot who can find ships after they disappear, steer them where no one is looking. Funny thing about stories: the first version, the real one, always gets swallowed by the second and third. All that is left out here are the edited copies, and in those copies the same anonymous hand keeps bending routes through a dead station that should not hear anything at all. I found the node that all his ghosts pass through. Now I just have to decide whether I am brave enough, or stupid enough, to follow.

I should have left this place two jumps ago.

The ridge hums at night, like the rock is holding its breath with us. In the common room they pass around chipped mugs and the same stories, sanded down by a dozen retellings. No one ever starts with "I was there." It is always a cousin, a crew mate, a stranger at some port whose name they forgot. An engineer who comes when the air goes thin, touches a console, and the gauges swing back to green. People stop coughing. Filters stop screaming. Everyone is so grateful they do not ask what she changed.

The missioner let me see the notes, reluctant, like they were sacred. Dates, ship IDs, settlement codes. I recognized two routes from my own hauling days and felt stupid for not noticing the pattern sooner. Same failures, same "miracle," same consultant moving just ahead of the real breakdowns. This has been going on longer than anyone here wants to admit; you can see it in the way they flinch from their own records. I keep thinking about all the times I docked, saw flickering status boards, and assumed it was just frontier life. We all overlooked it, because the air kept flowing and nobody wants to stare too hard at the thing that keeps them breathing.

I am logging this off the main board, tucked under a maintenance stub no one bothers to audit. The relay I just walked through was gutted in a hurry, like somebody got spooked mid-job. Panels hanging, fuse trays half-ripped, error lights frozen mid-blink. That is not how you mothball hardware, that is how you run when orders change faster than your hands can keep up. Whatever this place was listening to, it soaked it up deep; you can feel it in the way comms go thin and tinny as soon as you slide into this sector, like the channel is already half-occupied by echoes from somewhere else.\n\nBack at the bar, no one talks about this straight. It is always a mutter over a drink, a sideways glance at the door. Pilots say traffic control has been "off" along the old war corridors, that ships slip a little too close to debris and no one files complaints because no one wants the attention. You start asking for specifics and voices drop, sentences trail off. I keep hearing the same thing in different words though: misjumps, unlogged wrecks, distress calls that never hit the right receivers. People act like if they describe it too clearly, whoever is listening out there will turn their head and notice them next.

Primeway Flight is a small, semi-legitimate hauler outfit that works the under-served lanes around the derelict GC-8466 Depositron, taking contracts that larger lines deem unprofitable or too close to the insurance red zones. Port records describe them as "reliable, if chronically late," a reputation often blamed on their habit of lingering near drifting hulls and old traffic beacons to listen for distress calls and salvage rumors. Traders in the region note that Primeway crews swap corridor gossip as eagerly as they trade cargo manifests, repeating half-remembered tales about a vault ship that went dark and about quiet deals between GalBank clerks and UC officers who do not want their names in the same log. One dockside statement archived at a nearby station mentions the crew bickering loudly over a pilot's slurped noodles and mismatched socks while arguing whether the story of vented testbeds and redacted annexes is corporate myth or something far uglier. Whatever their internal frictions, Primeway Flight continues to chart courses uncomfortably close to GC-8466, citing "good salvage odds" while pretending not to notice how many transponders in that corridor have started flickering or falling silent.

I thought I was done being scared of numbers. Routes in, routes out, stress curves, tolerances it is all just math until the hull groans. But sitting here in the dark of this Vanguard hulk, listening to the residual power whisper through ruined conduits, I finally heard what the others meant when they said the lanes themselves sound wrong. The drive logs I pulled are not patrol profiles, they are something else sharp, stacked, like someone kept threading the same needle through narrower fabric, waiting for it to tear. The analysts back at that quiet little module told me, off the record, that certain vectors keep reappearing on ships that never should have shared charts. Now, sifting through this ship's black box, I see the same patterns buried under rewritten timestamps. People out in the fringe talk about a pilot who can slip a freighter through a sensor net like smoke, or drag a warship off its leash with a single corrected jump. It started as one lost convoy and a half-whispered complaint in a bar, but now the story has grown legs hulls going missing near dead listening posts, nav cores scrubbed clean except for that same curled signature. Whatever is tying all this together, it is not rumor anymore.

I am writing this between shifts, wedged behind a stack of mislabeled crates where the cams do not quite reach. The ship hums around me, same as it has for years, but it feels different now that I know how long we have been looking the other way.  

We got another batch of "scrap" yesterday, routed from a yard that is supposed to be half-dead. Seals blacked out, destination tags that loop through the same offworld pit before they vanish from the system. Nobody blinked. The loaders cursed about the weight, the clerk stamped the forms, and it slid into our hold like a hundred others.  

I should have noticed sooner. The route codes repeat, always back through that old mine that Deimos supposedly walked away from. I remember hearing about it over TerraBrew once, something about "reclamation" and "special contracts," but I filed it under spacer gossip and let it drift.  

Now the manifests keep glitching around those shipments, and I swear the automated checks skip entire lines when that mine comes up. Maybe it is nothing. Maybe it is everything.  

All I know is, somewhere out there is a hole in the rock swallowing hardware and names both, and we have been feeding it without even asking what it is for.

I thought this would be routine, signing those papers at the GalBank kiosk, nodding along while they talked about risk coverage and "weather volatility." Just one more form so we could keep the farm. That was, what, early 2329? The clerk barely looked up from their slate. I barely read the fine print.

Now I am floating through this dead protection ship, and every time a body turns in the stale air, I see my own hands on that screen again, ticking boxes I did not understand. The files I pulled mention our parcel by grid, same as the Waggoner place, tucked into a list of "exposure flags" next to clinical notes about yield spikes and respiratory cases. Someone in an office somewhere tagged us as a line item and forgot to untick the box.

Back home the soil started misbehaving. First it was just more grain than we could store, then the dust that burned your throat if you worked past noon. We called inspectors, they shrugged it off, said weather again. Later in Gagarin, I heard dock rats mutter about shipments like ours and a woman who kept showing up wherever the numbers went strange. They joked that if your crops were too good to be true, you would see her shadow in the manifests before you saw her in your fields.

Started this file three months ago, when it was still just a nagging feeling in the back of my skull and a handful of "unrelated" accidents on my desk.  
I told myself I was chasing noise in the telemetry. Now the coincidences are stacked too neatly to ignore.

Every time a freighter tore itself open near that debris field, I saw the same microscopic bias in the plotted jump. Different captains, different hulls, same invisible hand on the numbers. Then came the backcountry wreck with a registry that should have been retired, orbiting right where the math said it would fail, and that nameless slate we pulled off a scavenger, full of "efficiency tweaks" that all bent in one direction.

Tonight, out here on this forgotten rock, the pattern closed in on a name. Buried in a bundle of reroute authorizations, maintenance notes, and one unsent request for an internal review, the same analyst's signature keeps surfacing, always just upstream of the disaster. I cross-checked routing timestamps with those misjumps and the quiet redirects through that comm hub they call a relay; every path backtracks to him. Whatever this Tariq really is, I have him narrowed to a handful of corridors and one last waypoint the others somehow missed.

They say this place was built for mundane things like spectral analysis and rock samples. Funny, because nobody I have met can tell the same story twice about what really went on in these labs. When the resupply shuttle dropped me here last week, the pilot called it a "paper graveyard." The maintenance tech who greeted me just said "keep your head down and never, ever ask about missing ships" then laughed like it was a joke he wished it was.  \n\nI started hearing the rest in pieces. One version says some freelance navigator sold private shortcuts to smugglers, then used this module to scrub the evidence when convoys started vanishing. Another has him on a corporate retainer, tuning routes so insurance never had to pay out. A third paints him as some righteous saboteur trying to expose a system built on acceptable losses. Same name, different motives, always a trail of dead lanes behind him. Every retelling shifts a detail, like people are trying to talk around something they still do not want to see straight. All I know for certain is that the more I dig through these half-archived logs, the more I find the same hands adjusting jump patterns without ever signing them, and the more the room feels crowded even when I am alone.

I was supposed to be cataloguing soil samples this week. That is what the assignment packet said when they shipped me out here to this forgotten station, just another junior tech shuffling data no one on Jemison will ever read twice. Funny thing, though, about being the one who actually clears the archives; you see what people thought they had erased.  \n\nThere is a whole chain of access logs with gaps where there should not be any. Requests that hop from our lab to freight registries, then vanish mid-route, like somebody yanked the cord on the connection and hoped no one would notice the scorch mark. And buried under a stack of mislabeled experiment files I found a reference to a private relay, tagged only by coordinates and a contractor ID that got my supervisor suddenly very quiet. She told me to delete it, then later asked if I had "seen anything unusual" in that directory, like she was afraid of the answer. Out in the common room, the older staff still swap stories about lost convoys and a man who could twist corridors with a stylus stroke, always looking over their shoulders when they do. Someone wanted this trail dead, but they missed a step, and now I know exactly which off-grid node their phantom connection pointed to.

I keep replaying the moment the relay flagged that first spike.

It was late, nothing moving but survey drones and commuter buses, when the grid squealed about a ship cutting through restricted sky like it owned the air. I pulled the scan, saw the vector, and knew it was wrong in the way that makes your teeth hurt. Sent it up the line. Got a one-line reply: "Instrument drift. Clear and proceed." Simple. Neat. Done.

But if it was drift, why did the same ghost signature slide past again three nights later, and again after that, always just outside where the charts say people are allowed to be

I dug through archived diagnostics and found the old relay listed as "retired," except it is not. You can hear it in the floorplates, feel it when the consoles buzz a little hotter during those passes. Everyone talks about it in half-sentences and lowered voices, like saying too much might make the pattern solid enough to blame on someone real.

The truth feels small, one obvious step no one wants to write down, and somehow that makes it harder to grab. So I copy the scans onto a spare slate, lock it in my locker, and tell myself I am imagining things while the same nameless ship keeps sliding through the same forbidden slice of sky.

I am writing this with my back against a GalBank bulkhead, listening to the ship groan like it wants to fall out of orbit and be done with secrets.

Three years ago, give or take, I was running cargo through that nowhere depot the haulers use when they do not want questions. We were half-asleep, nursing cheap coffee, when the air on the dock went strange. Not a siren, not a fault, just this low tremor in the deckplates that set everyone's teeth on edge.

Some swear they saw a woman in coveralls at the access panel, hands buried in a conduit that should have been dead. Others say it was just a shadow and an overworked tech with a guilty conscience. All I know is the drives on three different ships tripped themselves offline inside an hour, and every log blamed "operator error."

Since then I keep hearing the same symbol described in different ports, the same name muttered like a curse, and the same story about systems that fail exactly the way an old buried report once predicted. Maybe it is all exaggeration. But when a GalBank vault ship like this one goes quiet in the same corridor, after the depot and that anonymous outpost, it starts to feel less like random bad luck and more like somebody is walking the map with a purpose.

I remember when the first set of manifests crossed my desk. Same old stamps, same old shippers, nothing that would have raised so much as an eyebrow if I had been three cups of TerraBrew deep and half asleep. That is the problem. After a few years with the Trade Authority, the formats blur together, and "routine" becomes a kind of blindness. You stop asking why a freighter needs an extra hop, or why a fuel charge does not line up with the tonnage.

It is only now, sitting in a quiet office with the comms dimmed, that I see how much we let slide because it looked familiar. The routes that double back near the same empty regions. The insurance claims on ships that "misjumped" along those paths. The way certain names in the ledgers come and go like they are testing the waters, then vanish altogether. None of it screamed fraud or sabotage. It just hummed along under the noise of a thousand legitimate runs, invisible because it copied the shape of normal traffic so well.

I used to pride myself on knowing every quirk of Authority paperwork, every lazy habit captains had. Now I am wondering how long someone has been hiding inside that certainty, using our comfort with the usual patterns as cover to carve their own paths through the dark.

I have been posted on this rock for eight months now, long enough that the hum of the equipment feels louder than my own thoughts. When I first arrived, the job was simple: compare traffic reports to corporate manifests, watch for the usual data skimming along the edges. Then someone upstairs pushed a firmware update through our routing tools and did not bother to brief anyone. The interface barely changed, just a few new flags, a different way it rounded jump estimates. Easy to ignore.\n\nExcept the patterns shifted. Routes that should have been clean started clipping the same thin corridor near that debris field; minor adjustments kept nudging freighters toward the same sparse beacons and forgotten relays. Our internal logs, the ones that used to double-check the math, began overwriting themselves in neat little windows of missing time. At first I chalked it up to bad code and lazy contractors. Now I am sitting on packet captures and mirrored archives that say otherwise, and I have a set of coordinates circled where three "unrelated" misjumps all pivoted off the same change order signed by the same analyst. Routines changed quietly, and nobody cared until the wreck counts lined up on my screen like someone had drawn a curve through them.

I am recording this in case I do not make it back to delete the evidence.

The bunker still listens, even with half its panels gutted. Old UC protocols pinging empty sky, catching ghosts no one filed. I pulled the sweep from the night that cutter vanished. Buried in the noise were microbursts in restricted airspace, too clean to be random, stitched like beads on a line. Same signature shift every time, same altitude, same timing just outside the official corridor.

Cross-referenced it against patrol routes and derelict notices. Only one hull fits the gap: a light tactical frame listed as "maintenance extended" for the last eighteen months. Same ship that forwarded those weird redacted jump reports to this bunker and never logged a receipt.

Someone upstairs meant to come out here, match the scans to that hull, and shut whatever this is down. They queued the follow-up, then never showed. Maybe they got scared. Maybe they got paid.

I tracked the transponder echo. That tactical is drifting just off the grid, still answering to UC credentials like nothing is wrong. If there is a trail left to this pathfinder everyone keeps pretending not to know, it is sitting in that hull's logs, waiting for someone else to make the mistake of looking.

East Division is the informal designation for a mixed support and escort cadre that operates in the shipping corridors surrounding the CB-6735 Trustsphere route network. Originally assembled from career hauler crews and a handful of former security pilots, the group built a reputation for steady, regulation-compliant work, the sort of people traders once described as "the boring ones you survive with." Recent months have marked a quiet change in both posture and temperament; reports note longer weapons drills, more sealed briefings, and deployments that linger near derelict tonnage and unlogged grav-scars. Off-duty, crew behavior has shifted from casual camaraderie to brittle, watchful silence: personnel who once swapped stories about shore leave now stand in long, shuffling lines at mess or resupply wondering when, exactly, they stopped feeling like transport hands and started feeling like expendable pieces in someone else's calculation. Rumors of sudden promotions, inexplicable demotions, and a few key figures who can bypass standard rotation boards suggest that internal politics, rather than flight hours, now decide who gets the safer patrol arcs and who is sent to shadow the ghosts that keep appearing near the Trustsphere's last known vectors.

I remember when cutters like the Prairiefire still came through Gagarin shining. Fresh paint, clean manifests, Trackers stepping off the ramp like they were the sharp end of justice. We used to turn those ships around in under six hours; grab a TerraBrew, grease a few couplings, stamp the contracts and wave them back to the stars. Somewhere between then and now, the jobs got stranger. Line items turned vague. Storm delays that should have cost weeks just stopped happening, and nobody upstairs wanted to hear why. "Temporary measures," they said. "Just until the grids stabilize."  \n\nLast month I pulled an overnight in the annex and found a string of old climate files misfiled under security footage, all tagged with the same consulting alias. Freight that always left on the wrong side of a cyclone and arrived bone-dry. At first I thought it was just us screwing up, some lazy clerk hiding mistakes where no one would look. But the more I dug, the more it felt like something that had been small once, half a workaround, half a favor, and then never stopped growing. Now the Prairiefire is parked out there like a bad memory, and her logs are the only place left where you can see how a lot of people quietly decided not to fix what they never meant to start.

I am recording this from a maintenance crawlspace two decks above the cargo ring, knees jammed against conduit, watching the relay's traffic map bleed red where it should be clean. Took me three days of sipping recycled air and pretending to be another overworked tech before the broker stopped flinching every time I walked past their office. They talked plenty about shell firms and "risk partners," but whenever certain names came up, they did not say them; they just tapped a knuckle on the table, or glanced at the ceiling, or said, "You know who" and moved on. That is how you know you are close to the real monsters, when people start speaking in silhouettes instead of words.\n\nThe manifests themselves were the key. Buried behind the usual Trade Authority double-talk, I found a sequence of scrap lots and "noncompliant hulls" diverted to a single disposal ring out past any profitable orbit. I cross-checked the beacon fingerprints we pulled from that Dogstar mess with the relay's routing history, and there it was the same corrupted signature, over and over, terminating at one dead Deimos facility nobody has paid to decommission. The broker pretended not to see it when I laid the pattern out. They just went quiet, closed the ledger, and asked if we were done.

I am writing this down so I remember I was not imagining it.

Neon's docks always feel like waking up mid-fall: noise, light, fuel stink, everyone pretending the chaos is planned. Tonight felt different. A berth that had been "blocked for maintenance" all week suddenly went green the second a hauler without a visible queue code drifted in. No hails, no argument over fees, just a tired clerk thumbing an override like muscle memory while the loadmaster stared a little too hard at the floor.

When I asked about it later, I got three answers from three people. Emergency medical relief. VIP corporate shipment. System glitch. Same ship, same berth, three stories that did not quite fit together. It reminded me of the time back in 2328 when we rushed a clearance on a freighter because some supervisor did not want to stay late. Only later did anyone notice that half its cargo never existed in the registry.

I am starting with almost nothing a dead slate I pulled off a derelict and a name that keeps changing in people's mouths whenever they talk about vanished debts and ships that always seem to leave on time. Whatever happened in haste back then is still echoing through these berths, and whoever is pulling the strings is counting on the rest of us being too tired to notice.

I am recording this because nobody down here says anything straight, and I need at least one thing that is not twisted by three different mouths before breakfast.

I am sitting on a crate in the salvage pit, boots in coolant, holding a half-melted datapack I did not pay enough for. Rafe swears he pulled it off a hauler that "just spun apart" near an old war corridor. He says he heard the job from a spacer who heard it from a GalBank courier who heard it from some UC tech. Every time I ask for a name, the story jumps one link further away, like everyone is afraid to admit they were this close to it.

The casing is cooked, but the nav buffer inside is not dead yet. I scraped enough out to see a route stub, pointed right at a vault ship that has been dark longer than GalBank likes to admit. Same harmonics tag I caught on those redacted test logs years ago, same pattern in the drive entries that nobody wanted to hear about. I followed a ghost signature from a forgotten outpost to a dead freight yard and then into Neon's pipes; now the broken trail in this pack lines up with that vault's last declared jump. Whatever she is tracking, whatever she is trying to prove, the next piece of it is locked in that floating bank the galaxies pretend is still just "under maintenance."

I am recording this mostly so I can convince myself I did not imagine it.

Soil is not supposed to pull like that. You stand still and you can feel your weight slide a fraction sideways, like the ground is remembering a different center. The miners who were here before me turned it into a bar story, something to tell over cheap liquor about "crooked gravity" and tools that fell in the wrong direction. Funny how none of them ever wrote it down. The old survey logs skirt around it with phrases like "localized anomaly," then change the subject. Same with the rig failures, and the missing warning pings from that relay everyone pretends never existed.

The thing we dug up today hums with the same wrongness. Not loud, just enough that if you hold it long enough your fingers go numb. The foreman made a point of saying we were not to speculate about it over open comms, and the rest of the crew nodded like they had already made that agreement without me. Nobody mentioned the failed crops on that moon, or the storm beacons that drifted off target, or the quiet talk that some engineer somewhere is learning how to teach gravity new tricks. Those parts stay unspoken, but they are there, hanging in the air with the rust and the coolant, waiting for someone stubborn enough to pull on them.

They told me this posting was temporary. Six months underground, eyes on a dead corridor of space, then back to daylight work. That was three years and a dozen "routine extensions" ago. Somewhere along the way, the filters we flagged as provisional stayed, the back channels stayed, I stayed. Temporary turned into default, and nobody sent an update.

Today I finally saw why.

I was combing archived feeds, trying to prove to myself that all this quiet meant something, when I found the pattern. Same consultant ID buried in environmental telemetry from frontier farms, from a clinic that should not have had that kind of tuning, from an old weapons bay listed as decommissioned. Cross checked it against a blacked out operations file I was never supposed to open. There she was, walking through a restricted asset like she had clearance, under cover of one of our own codenames.

Followed the signal out, past the redactions. It terminates in a cargo registry marked as scrap, a hangar written off on every official chart I can access. Nothing is ever really gone; they just stop printing it. That hangar is where her trail surfaces again. I have tagged the coordinates and locked them in this log. If someone is finally hunting her, they will need a starting point that is not already a lie.

They told us the war was over before I was old enough to hold a rifle, but the dust out by the old trench line never got that message. I was hauling scrap plating for Salvage Crown Union when my cutter snagged something half-buried, a dataslate wedged under a rusted bunk frame. Should have logged it as waste, tossed it in with the rest, but the power light was still blinking and curiosity buys more trouble than credits out here.

The rosters inside do not match what they taught us in school. Names marked evacuated the day my father never came home. Medical sign-offs all bearing the same neat hand, attached to casualty clusters that locals swear were left screaming in the dirt. It looks like someone meant to come back, clean up the numbers, finish erasing whatever really happened in those barracks. The last entries are flagged for review, then nothing. No follow-up, no closure, just a frozen list of ghosts and a medic's signature that keeps turning up in backroom stories from Akila to New Atlantis.

I have been chewing on this all shift. Part of me wants to dump the slate in a GalBank drop and pretend I never saw it. The other part keeps thinking if those numbers can be bent once, they can be bent again. To hide the dead. Or to hide someone who is not as dead as they are supposed to be.

Among independent haulers operating in the same lanes as the derelict Tidewalker TA-7207, few names come up as often as Second Flight. The crew is known for taking contracts other captains quietly decline, running cargo and salvage through routes where patrol coverage thins out and navigation data stops lining up cleanly with official charts. They are not registered as a guild, nor do they maintain a fixed home port, but their transponder sig has been logged in proximity to more than one "administratively unresolved" incident near Trade Authority assets.\n\nThe name Second Flight is widely believed to reference a failed first venture, though records of any earlier ship under their banner are conspicuously absent from standard registries. What is documented is a pattern: whenever a cargo hull goes dark in that sector, Second Flight is never far from the next set of sensor echoes, either "assisting recovery" or arriving just late enough to claim salvage without contradiction. Station rumor paints them as necessary opportunists, tolerated because they know the blind spots between corporate liability and official response times. Whether they are simply quick to capitalize on abandoned tonnage or have a more intimate understanding of why certain ships go missing remains, for now, a matter of speculation.

I was on refuel watch when they brought in that little courier, the one they are calling Seamender. No tugs, no escort, just drift and a soft scrape as it kissed the berth. Running lights dead, hull scorched in the wrong places, like it had tried to leave somewhere faster than physics allowed. I watched the dock crew cycle the locks and nobody rushed, nobody called it out. Just another tired ship having a bad day.

Later, in the break room, one of the line techs let slip that the traffic data for its last leg had already been "cleaned up" by the time it arrived. Adjusted timestamps, smoothed routes, the kind of edits you only make when you want the story to move along. He laughed it off, said someone in New Atlantis pushed the wrong button, but his eyes did not match the joke.

What bothers me is how fast everyone moved on. No investigation team, no angry suits from MAST, just a quiet note that Trade Authority had the situation in hand. I heard about a Navy scout that went missing not long after, about a courier captain swearing their delay orders were forged. Maybe they are all unrelated. Still, when I think about how quickly those logs were wiped, how casually the berth was reassigned, it feels like someone slammed a door in a hurry and never stuck around to see what got caught on the other side.

Dock noise carries better than station announcements. You sit long enough at the edge of a cargo bay, nursing a warm drink and pretending to check fuel tallies, you hear more truth than any GalBank terminal will give you.

That is how this started.

One hauler swore his freighter got repossessed twice without ever docking at a bank port. Another said his lien vanished, then came back under a different name, same hull, different owner. They talk big when it is just spacers and smoke, but as soon as someone in a pressed jacket walks by, the story turns into "clerical error," "misunderstanding," "all sorted now." Funny how fear can edit a memory in real time.

Yesterday a broker pulled me aside behind a crate stack, eyes flicking at every camera. Showed me a string of manifests on a cracked slate, all with the same audit code buried deep where only another numbers rat would notice. Ships listed twice, three times, then not at all. He kept saying it was nothing, just frontier bookkeeping, but his thumb hovered over the delete icon like it was an airlock switch.

Everyone claims they have heard of the woman behind it, the one who can erase a ship with a signature. Ask for details and the room goes quiet. Out here, it is amazing how much people "know" that somehow never makes it into a complaint file.

I have been sitting in this shelter long enough to watch quick fixes turn into standard operating procedure. The first time I rerouted a hauler through an unsanctioned window, it was supposed to be a one-off favor for a captain who could not afford another inspection. I told myself it was temporary, a little patch over a broken system. Then the next captain wanted the same treatment, and the next, and pretty soon those off-the-books timings were written in more ledgers than the official lanes.\n\nThe consoles here hum with all of that history. You can still hear it in the way the traffic logs stutter around certain hours, little gaps where a ship should be but is not. Customs back at the mid-tier port keeps complaining their manifests do not line up with burn reports, but nobody is pulling the thread too hard; as long as the credits clear and the docks stay busy, no one wants to admit how much of their flow depends on shadows. The smugglers say there is a woman out there who can carve those shadows on demand, slide hulls between sweeps like she is drawing with light. All I know is that the temporary workarounds I built for her have been running long enough that the system would choke without them, and somewhere along the line I stopped being able to tell where the official routes end and her edits begin.

I was on break when the last one came in.

Just another half-heard story over a lukewarm TerraBrew, a junior controller griping that their corridor update got overwritten mid-shift, that a ship they were shepherding clipped junk it should never have been near. The supervisor brushed it off, blamed a bad timestamp, told them to re-sync and stop scaring the tourists. Later, in the Skyline feeds, I saw the same ship's path stutter, jitter one degree at a time, like three different hands had argued over where it belonged.

It is never one big lie with these things. It is a missed handoff in the relay, a misread notation on a shift change, someone assuming a senior already double-checked the math. A GalBank clerk ticking the wrong risk box. A captain trusting the green light instead of their gut. None of it malicious, not on paper. Add one quiet specialist with access to the back door of every route, and suddenly those tiny slips all lean the same way.

Most nights I tell myself it is just the noise of a crowded sky. Then I think about how many times Luca's name comes up in whispers, never in logs, and how often the miscommunications seem to benefit the same invisible pattern. I keep replaying small, forgettable moments, wondering which crossed wire actually killed people and which ones I only imagined.

I thought transferring onto a Navy hull would finally put that story to bed. New insignia, new bunk, same stars. But even out here, in the stale air of this derelict, I can still hear it in the way people lower their voices when they think the bulkheads are listening. The hauler that was written off. The crew that did not scream loud enough on the right channels.

They told us the case was closed. Wrong coordinates, corrupted logs, all very unfortunate. At a dusty bar near that old transfer station, a tug pilot slipped me a data scrap and said, "Check Gagarin if you want to know where the metal really went." I pretended I did not understand.

On the LX-2547, you can see the gaps if you know where to look. Manifests that balance too neatly. Mass readings that line up like they were arranged, not measured. The name that keeps turning up in half-erased work orders. Everyone important seems content to let it molder in forgotten archives, to let time sand the edges off. But in mess halls, at back tables in places like The Den, it still comes up. Not as a case. As a warning.

I am tired of being told to move on. If this log survives, if someone finds it and still cares, follow the freight trail down to Gagarin Landing. Someone there kept just enough of the story alive to make sure it never quite disappears.

I do not know why I am recording this. Habit, maybe. When you run cargo long enough, you start writing things down just to prove you were there.

Three years back, before the talk of "ghost windows" and missing ships got loud, my routes in UC space were boring in the best way. Same jump tables, same Harmonization signatures, same long stretches of nothing. Then, one week, the delays started. Five minutes slipped here, twelve there. "Weather in the lanes," the controller said. Same calm voice, same clipped phrases, just a different number on the screen.

I did not think much of it until a run out past Valo. A Navy scout swung through our corridor, close enough that my copilot swore he could see the pilot through the canopy. Our slot and theirs overlapped by sixty-three seconds. That does not happen. Not by accident. We raised it with the traffic desk later and got smiles, reassurances, new tables that made the near-miss disappear on paper.

Since then, I have heard about a courier that "vanished between pings," and a scout designated BL-6924 that broke contact mid-routine with no distress call. People blame pirates, drive faults, divine judgment, take your pick. What stays with me is the way the numbers shifted first, quietly, like someone testing how far they could bend a schedule before anyone noticed.

I logged this under "routine notes" so no one skimming the header bothers to read it.

I have been running freight and the occasional something-else through the same lanes for fifteen years. You get to know the way people talk about danger. They either brag, or they whisper. Lately, they do this other thing, where they talk around it. Some captain in the Den bar last week mentioned three ships gone quiet off the same corridor, then stopped mid-sentence and just traced a circle on the table instead of finishing the story.

Nobody says who plotted those jumps. They say, "I know a guy," or "someone did us a favor," and if you ask for a name, they shrug like they never had one. I heard about a route broker who used to drop a certain signature into his speech every time he drank too much; now he never does, like the word itself is bad luck.

Out at that broken survey shack, the one with the dead console and the angry log, there is a name half-scorched off the recording. The captain starts to say it, chokes on it, and switches to "the vector man." I keep thinking about that, about how often people reach for a pronoun instead of a proper noun. Maybe they forgot him. Maybe somebody made it easier to forget. But the jumps still curve the same way, and whoever he is, he has turned into an absence big enough to bend routes around.

They say every Trade Authority ship has at least three stories trailing behind it like exhaust. With Deepwater it is more like thirty, and none of them match. Dockhands swear she was boarded by pirates. A Ryujin broker told me, very quietly over coffee, that she was paid to drift. Someone on Gagarin insisted the crew turned on each other. Same ship, different ghosts.

What I know is this: every rumor ends with the same two names, spoken softer than the rest. A quartermaster who makes planets behave and a pilot who can slide a hull between sensor sweeps like a needle through skin. Freight manifests that never quite line up, patrol logs showing convoys bending off the usual lanes, then popping back in as if nothing happened. I have walked the perimeter of that derelict twice now, listening to her dead systems tick and cool, and I cannot shake the feeling that something living moved through her, used her, and then shed her like old skin.

The first clue came from a settlement that vanished but left its fences standing, animals calm inside and slaughtered outside. The next from a broken beacon in high orbit whispering a familiar transponder pattern. Now this courier in the dark, with its cargo hold wiped but its routes altered by a hand that knew exactly where the blind spots were. The stories keep changing. The pattern does not.

Stumbled across an unsecured maintenance terminal no one bothered to wipe before they scuttled us. I guess when the order came down to abandon ZT-7430, scrubbing logs was lower on the list than getting out alive. The whole event still feels like that: alarms, half-heard orders, a rerouted power surge through CIC, then we were burning hard for the nearest friendly hull, leaving a lot of questions behind in our wake.

Tonight I dug through what was left. Buried under system checks and training sims, I found transfer traces tied into places a combat ship has no business touching. Power usage spiking in quiet corners of New Atlantis, recalculated risk curves pointing straight down into the undercity, flagged in a way that looks like someone meant to come back and tidy up but never did. We ran scenarios based on those models without knowing whose lives they balanced.

I keep seeing the underbelly of Neon when I close my eyes, those cramped walkways where I first heard the name everyone whispers now. Back then it sounded like a story we told to make sense of seized accounts and frozen wages. Now, sitting in a dead SysDef shell with old code still humming in the dark, I am starting to think someone down below the pretty plazas is where this all converges next. Someone who learned early what happens when the numbers say you do not count.
