They tell me it is nothing, that weather is messy on the frontier and the satellites are old, and I should stop asking why three different colonies, in three different systems, use the same phrases when they talk about the sky going wrong. Out here at the outpost, folks come in dusted and tired, ask for water and a line home, and only when the room is half-empty do they mention how the clouds moved like they were being steered, how the forecast tickers lagged three days behind reality. Every time I press, they glance at the Ranger badge, then soften what they just said, shaving off the edges like they have been taught the hard way not to sound certain.\n\nI used to argue, loudly, in the mess about how command was ignoring the pattern. Lately I have noticed the people who did that before me transfer out or stop talking altogether. Now I keep my voice low too, mark up the incident board in pencil instead of ink. The liaison asked me today why I always request the storm reports, why I am chasing the same anonymous ship signature through half a dozen testimonies. I told him it was for a personal project. He nodded like he believed me and suggested, very gently, that I might want to be careful how I phrase things in my official notes. Apparently anyone who sounds too sure about the sky ends up reviewed by people who do not like surprises.

I keep replaying the numbers in my head, as if the math will suddenly confess. Route risk projection, claim probability, expected loss. All neat, all within tolerance, all signed off by people who smiled across a table in New Atlantis and told me GalBank takes care of its partners. Then I sat in that routing den on Gagarin and heard captains talk about the same "low-risk" lane we signed them onto, like it was a dare. Same bend, same blind patch, same rumor about a man who can squeeze the odds until ships crack.\n\nWeeks later I am alone on this transport, walking past pallets that were never meant to arrive, trying not to look too long at the pattern of damage on the hull feeds. Officially we lost guidance in a freak corridor fluctuation. Unofficially, the chatter in the underbelly of Neon says someone is selling lanes tuned to fail only for certain cargos, at just the right distance from just the wrong kind of outposts. When I pushed those rumors up the chain, I got polite shrugs and a suggestion to take some leave, maybe visit the Red Mile and "blow off steam." That is the part that sticks with me. The people who know the charts best are also the ones most eager not to know why our models keep pointing toward the same lonely crater, on the edge of nowhere, where a man who lives on probability can disappear into the roar of the crowd.

I keep replaying that run from three years back, the one no one writes down but everyone steers around. We were patrolling near a thin-atmo rock, nothing on the charts worth naming, when the grav shear started to sing through the hull. Not the usual shudder, either. This was a rhythm, like someone plucking a string the ship was resting on.

Nav said it was a localized anomaly and plotted a bypass. The junior tech next to me whispered that the pattern matched a corridor she had seen in an old sim at Jemison, then laughed it off like a bad memory. Command pushed us through the edge of it anyway. We came out clean, on schedule, and the log got stamped as routine. That night in the mess, nobody talked about how the stars had bent around us, or why the atmospheric telemetry from that nameless rock looked like it was expecting company.

Most of those people have shipped out to other billets by now. One took a payout and retired planetside, one signed on with Freestar haulage, a couple got themselves lost in Neon. They all moved on, thinking it was just another weird day in the black. I did too, until I saw the same pattern turn up in frontier distress calls, always near worlds with air too thin to argue with. Now there is an empty UC hull parked in that old anomaly, and someone else is following a line we traced without ever seeing where it led.

I am logging this before I change my mind and dump the whole lot into the recycler.

The module is quiet now, just the hum of old cooling loops and one stubborn status light that refuses to admit the system is dead. I finally traced the breach tonight. Not the first intrusion, not the loud one everyone documented to prove they had done their jobs, but the thin hairline cut underneath it. Buried in a backup schedule, there is a redirect that should not exist, pointing asset updates to a GalBank vault ship that was supposedly decommissioned three fiscal years ago.

When I called it out in the team channel, nobody argued. They just went silent in that practiced way, the one that says they have seen this shape before and have all agreed to forget it. Same way they "forgot" the missing storm logs on that frontier moon. Same way nobody talks about the partial audio from the abandoned relay, the one where a voice tried to warn someone and then cut off mid-word.

So now I have a route number, a hull designation nobody uses out loud anymore, and a headache that feels a lot like complicity. The next piece is sitting in that drifting vault, wrapped in layers of old insurance law and newer lies. And when this is over, I am not sure which will be harder: proving what was done, or getting anyone to admit they always knew where the evidence was hiding.

I was not supposed to be anywhere important that day. Just another junior tech checking latency on a half dead comms relay above some no name rock, arguing with a supervisor who kept mixing up time slots and routing codes. First miscommunication right there he swore my assignment was next week, I swore I heard "now," so I went anyway.

That is when I found the slate, half buried by the loading ramp, casing blackened like it had tried to die in a fire. I almost logged it as scrap, but the tag pinged our system in a way that did not match any of our manifests. I called it in, dispatcher said it was probably leftover survey junk, told me to wipe it and move on. She thought I was on a different shift, different sector. Second misstep.

I cracked it open on my own time. Most of it was static, but there was this fragment of traffic tied to a Trade Authority route and a firmware key that felt too sharp, too clean, to be random debris. I sent a copy to a contact in Neon, got an auto reply that did not sound like him at all flat, formal, as if someone had put the words in his mouth.

Since then small things keep slipping. People swear they answered a message they never saw, forget who told them a story about a woman who walks through vaults without touching anything. It feels like our whole lives are being edited one misheard instruction at a time.

Did not think I would ever come back to a place like this.

The relay bunker smells like stale coolant and dust, like the war hung up its coat here and forgot to leave. Most of the consoles are dark, but enough of the grid is still talking to itself that I could pry open the scan archive. The deserter who ran from this post knew what they were doing; the logs around the dates I needed were scrubbed so clean it hurt to look at them. No patrol chatter, no incident tags, just a neat band of silence where a whole flight's worth of traffic should have been.

Thing is, whoever did the cleaning missed the reflections.

Atmospheric scans bounce. You wipe the primary traces, you still get echoes in the background noise, ghost signatures where hulls pushed air aside. I layered the right bands, filtered for mass and vector, and there it was: the same drive profile I saw in that orphaned buoy's telemetry, sliding through restricted sky like it had every right to be there. It did not land on any registered pad. It just dipped low over a dead industrial zone and vanished off the board.

That zone feeds into a Deimos yard no one has funded in years, a scrapyard they pretend is shuttered but still keeps tug traffic in the middle of the night. Everybody in the bunker logs just called it "the graveyard" and left it at that. No one spelled out why. No one had to.

I keep replaying it in my head, all the tiny choices that felt harmless at the time.

The first time I let a route update slide even though the numbers did not quite match the weather feeds, it was because the shift was over and my eyes hurt. The second time, because the supervisor said the contractor knew more about storm lanes than we ever would. After that, it was habit. Click accept, file the correction, trust the invisible hand nudging freighters a few degrees off the safe corridors.

Nobody ever said his name in the control room. They just talked about "the vector guy," the one who could pull a ship through an ion front without losing a panel. The pilots were grateful, the accountants were thrilled, and we stopped looking too closely at the cuts in the safety margins because every successful run made the risk feel smaller.

Then one supply shuttle vanished between beacons and came back on a different heading with half its hull scorched and a manifest that did not match. We wrote it up as sensor interference and moved on. That was the moment, I think, when "just one more little adjustment" tipped into whatever this is now.

I am logging this because I can feel the pattern tightening around my station, and I cannot tell anymore if I helped build a safer route through chaos or just paved a road straight into it, one small approval at a time.

I am writing this in the back booth of a cheap bar in Neon, because the station noise is the only thing loud enough to drown out that story people keep telling.

It started as a freight joke a couple years back, just something haulers tossed around when a run was late. A Trade Authority courier takes a contract off some no-name rock, cuts a new lane, never shows on the main traffic boards again. First time I heard it, the ship was small, the jump short, the pilot greedy. Next time, it was a larger freighter, different system, heroic captain chasing a shortcut. Now, depending who is drinking, you get Crimson Fleet ambushes, UC coverups, cursed coordinates, or a ghost in the nav.

Every retelling adds a detail, sands off another. Sometimes they mention a woman who can thread a jump through the width of a needle, sometimes she is just a rumor tacked on at the end. Nobody agrees on where the route started or ended, but the shape of it stays the same, a line that goes somewhere it should not.

I used to laugh it off. Lately I notice people lower their voices when they reach the part about missing ships. I have seen the way certain captains flinch when an extra route segment shows up on their charts, unasked for. The facts are thin as vacuum, but the fear is thick, and fear has a way of rewriting the map long before anyone sees what really waits at the edge.

I started taking the "special" routes because they were easy credits.

First it was just a five-minute offset on a run out of Gagarin. The controller on the line sounded bored, professional, and the corridor he slid us into was clean as glass. No pirates, no traffic, no questions from anyone in Trade Authority when the manifest closed out. Then it became ten minutes here, twenty there, little nudges around Navy patrols and busy lanes, always accompanied by a quiet assurance that the windows were safe and well-compensated.

I did not notice when the voice on the other end stopped reading from standard tables and started anticipating our fuel load, our usual speed, the way our captain likes to cut burn. I did not mind when a few of our delivery times stopped matching the official charts, as long as the bonuses kept posting and no one from the Hub asked why our logs looked cleaner than everyone else's.

Now there is a Navy scout floating cold out where our last "adjustment" led, and a courier like mine has gone dark with its holds still full. People say it is coincidence, that routes shift every day and only the unlucky get caught in the gaps. But when I listen back to the old comms, to that calm voice telling me we are "just inside the safe window," all I can hear are the hundreds of little yeses I whispered to myself, lining up in a row I never meant to draw.

I snuck back to the bunker again after shift, even though they have taped half the doors and killed the main grid. The place hums anyway, like it remembers being useful. I jacked into the auxiliary and pulled the last week of atmospheric scans before shutdown. There it was, buried under routine traffic and supply flights and some smuggler who thought his heat profile looked like a mining shuttle. One thread that did not match any filed route, skimming the edge of restricted airspace, slipping in and out between pulses like it knew when the grid blinked.

The signature is subtle, but it repeats with the same timing as those anomaly reports everyone pretends they have never read. It angles away from the usual traffic lanes, then climbs hard toward that research spire they built out past the old farms, the one nobody talks about unless the doors are shut and the volume is low. In the mess, when the conversation drifts that way, people joke about "ghost inspectors" and change the subject quick, eyes on the corners like sound might carry farther than it should.  

Out on that lonely rock, where the first cache turned up, the gaps in the satellite recorder bothered me. The half-scrubbed safety audit from New Atlantis bothered me more. Now this flight path ties both to the same tower of glass and sealed labs, and I am starting to think none of this is random malfunction.

Personal log, unsent

I signed onto WK-9192 because I thought flying with SysDef meant clear lines: good ships, bad ships, and us in between. Turns out most of the time it is spreadsheets in vacuum. Patrol the same corridors, trust the same relays, let the traffic flow like it always has. Somewhere along the way, we stopped asking why the routes bent the way they do.

Lately the bends are sharper.

The last update from command pushed us closer to that dead relay chain, and nobody blinked. Nav just folded the new vectors in. I watched the model spin and, for a second, it looked like someone had reached in and dragged the whole pattern sideways with a fingertip. The numbers still balanced, so no one cared.

Back on that drop shelter a few weeks ago, a Fleet liaison swore their smuggling runs were arriving early without extra burn. I chalked it up to bravado and bad accounting. Now I see the same tiny discrepancies ghosting through our own logs, the same improbable timing, the same gaps where patrols should be. Different ships, different factions, one invisible hand nudging everyone toward the quiet spots between signals.

Feels like the lanes made their choice before any of us did, and we just kept following the glow on the console. If there is someone out there rewriting the map, we have been sailing along their ink the whole time, pretending the tide is natural.

I took this post because I thought it would be quiet.

End of the lane, moonside, nothing but rock dust in the vents and haulers too tired to argue about docking fees. You pour them a drink, bump their escort requirement down one ship, look the other way on a crate or two, and everyone goes home a little richer. That is how the clerk before me explained it, anyway, right before he shipped out on a transfer he did not deserve.

I have been going through his old logs, trying to make sense of the routing overrides he left half-finished. Same pattern keeps blinking back at me. Convoys pushed a little off the standard corridor, insurance coverages quietly adjusted, all flagged with an internal tag I cannot clear, like some ghost auditor riding shotgun on every change.

At first I figured it was some automated safety routine, overzealous system guarding cargo values. Then I noticed the dates lining up with raids you hear about in bar talk: that HopeTech freighter that never made its refuel, the Narion runs that "just disappeared" between beacons. Tiny edits, over and over, and everyone who touched them already rotated to better posts, patting themselves on the back for a few extra credits.

I cannot say what any of it means yet. All I know is somebody smart set this in motion a long time ago, and the rest of us have been pressing confirm without ever seeing the whole board.

It started as background noise. Little things the settlers tacked onto their complaints about broken pumps and missed supply drops. A hauler swore his escort peeled away just as the sky went white and somehow his ship rode the worst of it without a scratch. A mining foreman mentioned a quiet woman in a battered flight jacket who spent more time staring at the clouds than at her drink. At first I filed it under frontier exaggeration. Then the coordinates started to line up.

I keep a private overlay, separate from the reports I send up the chain. Storm incidents, convoy disappearances, odd sensor gaps. They were scattered across systems that have nothing in common except a habit of bad weather and neglect. But when I plotted the approach vectors people described, I started seeing the same thin corridor traced over and over, like someone was sewing through storms with the same needle.

The last batch of logs did it for me. Three separate captains, weeks apart, all mentioned ghost traffic in the same sector, right before their feeds went to static. One of them caught a partial transponder, old UC formatting, tagged to a long-range combat hull that is supposed to be mothballed. That is not the kind of coincidence you shrug off. Whatever she is doing out there, she is riding routes we built and buried, and the next step sits on a dead Navy ship that has no business being where it is.

I am recording this from the dorm pod on BX-1113, lights dimmed, drive offline, ship humming that empty kind of quiet where you hear every relay breathe. We are not where the manifest says we should be. We are too far off the lane, too close to a cluster that never appears on the standard route projections, and no one is logging a deviation.  

I watched the senior techs argue over the nav console yesterday. Voices low, faces tight. One of them slid a datapad into their jacket when they noticed me in the reflection. Later, over reconstituted soup, they joked about "creative routing" and changed the subject so fast it left a pressure drop in the room.  

There are gaps in the records. Whole jump segments summarized in one clean line, no residual data, like the ship decided not to remember where it had been. I heard someone mention an old UC array out this way, a listening post that "does not exist anymore." That was followed by a long silence and a lot of looking at the ceiling.  

I am not stupid. First there was that job on the fringe rock where we found a slate full of corrupted corridor data. Then the scientist on the research module who kept asking if our routes ever passed close to abandoned military infrastructure. Now this ship, off-course, carrying ledgers no one wants audited. There is a pattern here. The parts everyone refuses to say out loud are the ones that scare me most.

I am recording this from a bunk that smells like coolant and old socks, somewhere under the plating of the moonside relay. The broker is three doors down, pretending he is just a middleman, that the crates stacked in his bay are nobody's business but his. We both know that is a lie.

I ran diagnostics on his cargo feed under the excuse of checking for leaks. The route tags looked familiar in the wrong kind of way: same off-lane jumps, same quiet ports that somehow never appear in official traffic summaries. When I overlaid them with a copied harvest schedule from a frontier colony I worked last season, the pattern snapped into place. All those "anonymous" shipments pass through one dirtball farm that should have failed years ago.

The broker saw the plot come up on my slate. He glanced once, then looked away like we had both agreed not to say the name of the place out loud. No threats, no bargaining, just that shared understanding that some things stay between people who enjoy breathing. 

So now I know where the next piece lies, buried under glow-sick soil and old promises. Up to this point, all I had were rumors from a solitary homestead, a forgotten dataslate that should have been wiped, and the way certain cargo manifests kept looping back on themselves. Every new whisper has circled closer to the same man, the same routes, and that one farm sitting like a knot in the middle of it all.

The green wash from the consoles makes the frost on the bulkheads look like mold. I keep thinking if anyone else walked in here, they would call this place dead and shut the hatch again. But the logs keep turning over, same loops, same traffic, and then every so often, a gap where there should not be one. Salvage beacons that flare for a second and vanish, ship IDs that appear as a checksum error instead of a name. I flag them, send the notes up the line. The response is always the same: system artifact, ignore.

Thing is, I remember when this pod was installed. I remember the briefings, the strict rules about retention, who could touch what. Now, when I bring up those details in the break room, people look away or tell a different version, like we all dreamed the first part. They talk about some arbitrator who "used to" have clearance here, then change the subject mid-sentence. I am not stupid. You can feel when a story has missing teeth.

Then that dataslate came in from the survey team on the frozen rock, full of mismatched time stamps and the same broken IDs. The analyst called it a curiosity and buried it under a dozen other reports, but she passed me a copy off the record. Between that and what I see in the nightly loops, there is a thread running through these erased calls. Someone decided certain ships did not need to exist anymore, and everyone else decided they did not remember why.

I keep telling myself I am not spooked by an empty Navy hull, just cautious. That is what we are supposed to call it these days. Cautious. Not suspicious, not angry. Those words get you flagged in debriefs.  

Walking HM-6310 s corridors, with only the emergency strips lit and the air recyclers running on a tired wheeze, feels like boarding a story nobody finished writing. The log entries I have been able to scrape so far are a mess of half-sent status updates, patrol chatter, then gaps that feel too neat to be accidents. Someone here learned where the line was between reporting a concern and sounding like they were questioning the wrong people. After the last big blackout incident, everyone I talked to in the bars around New Atlantis dropped their voices when the topic drifted toward missing convoys or dead sectors. The ones who had actual data? They wrapped it in jokes, changed the subject, or blamed "equipment issues" with eyes that did not match their mouths.  

So when I see a ship like this, drifting with its comms carved up and its name quietly shuffled down the dispatch list, I hear all those careful silences louder than any alarm. People have been adjusting their tone, their words, their records for a long time to fit whatever story command is most comfortable with. Whatever is sitting in this ghost s memory core, it is something nobody wanted to say out loud in a room with a live recorder.

I am recording this off-shift, lights dimmed, just the hum of the LX-6790 and my own bad thoughts for company.

I used to think flight plans were clean things. Numbers, vectors, margins of safety. You plug in the data, trust the models, trust the people who swear they have tested every edge case. Then, back in 2328, a freighter went the wrong way through Sol and did not come out the other side. Official word was "unfortunate, unavoidable." The kind of phrase you use to close a file.

But the chatter never really stopped. A tech in the Titan relay mentioned a routing profile that did not match any signed update. A LIST homesteader forwarded a burst about a "helpful advisory node" that changed their approach seconds before a swarm of junk tore past. In Neon, over a stale drink, someone pointed at the boards and said, see that narrow corridor, the one no one admits exists? That is where the math goes when someone wants you to live, or not.

We were told to drop it, let command and insurers work it out. Most did. I tried. Every time the story started to fade, some dock rat or traffic controller would bring it up again, quieter, angrier. Different systems, same pattern: near misses, unlogged corrections, that same invisible hand on the wheel.

Now we are parked over Deimos, babysitting coordinates that should not belong to a Navy ship, waiting for the order to pretend none of this was ever in our log.

I am starting to hate the way people lower their voices when the conversation turns to bad air.

Every port we hit this quarter, it is the same half-story: a farm that lost half its crop overnight, a mining dome where the filters screamed for an hour and then shut up without anyone touching a thing. In the back corners of mess halls and cargo bars, the details change depending on who is buying the drinks, but it always ends tidy. Someone heroic stepped in. Someone important signed off. Somebody got paid. No one ever admits they were standing there, holding the wrong wrench, when the alarms went quiet.

The Silverwake is not supposed to be part of that kind of talk. We move what the Authority tells us to move, keep the ledgers balanced, pretend we do not notice when a crate of "agricultural supplements" weighs too much and hums like active hardware. Still, I watched a routing change come through today that bounced us past a nowhere maintenance dock out on the edge of Freestar traffic, and nobody could look me in the eye when I asked why. The last place that pinged that coordinate is some grease-stained garage where a mechanic swears the atmosphere went strange and the readings got scrubbed. All I have right now is a trail that starts at a lonely outpost, winds through stories polished in backrooms until they shine like lies, and points straight at people who treat the air itself like negotiable freight.

Core Division is an informal callsign used by a rotating cadre of UC SysDef specialists assigned to the troubled corridor around the derelict combat ship PX-15. Officially, they are tasked with cataloging and securing abandoned military assets in the region, updating old interdiction charts, and monitoring unexplained grav anomalies that have spiked along disused patrol arcs. Unofficially, traders and haulers say that when Core Division shows up in a sector, it means some forgotten piece of the last war has started humming again, and nobody in MAST wants to admit why. Recent incident summaries mention their cutters holding station near PX-15 for days at a stretch, lights dimmed, running quiet scans on jump telemetry that was supposed to have been purged decades ago. In one archived after-action note, a sensor tech briefly breaks tone, complaining that half the shift was wasted tearing apart lockers looking for a missing thermal mug, grumbling that "we lose more cups than drones out here," before adding that the only consolation was a hot TerraBrew Classic from the ship's recycler, which tasted burnt but at least cut through the recycled air. Small frustrations like that sit beside more sober lines about unlogged pings, corrupted route data, and the growing sense among Core Division crews that something in this stretch of space is being carefully, deliberately rewritten just beyond the edge of their instruments.

I used to joke that this hut was where Freestar forgot the rest of us existed. One ranger, one rack of half-broken gauges, and a sky full of dust no one bothers to map properly. Then, little by little, the numbers started lying.

At first it was small things. Flight paths from the same hauler shaving a few meters closer to the bad updrafts. Heat signatures riding the edge of the corridor instead of the middle. I figured it was pilots cutting corners, or my old sensors drifting. You tell yourself that so you can sleep.

But then the pattern kept repeating with different transponders, different registries. Every few weeks, a new ship traced the same crooked S through the air, right where the dust boils hardest. And every time, storms obligingly shifted just enough to leave a narrow, invisible lane. That is not bad luck. That is handwriting.

I backtracked the most recent run. Its last clean ping was not from any Freestar tower, but from a Navy bird sitting out past the shear, one they say went missing on a routine haul. Somehow its beacon and my sky-scars line up too neatly to ignore. I logged the anomaly, kicked it upslope through channels that will probably bury it, and kept the real coordinates in my personal slate.

Looking back, the routines did not break all at once. They bent, degree by degree, until the only straight line left in this mess points from this hut to that dead UC ship hanging in the dark.

They send us more forms than ammo out here, and most days I file them the same way: skim the headings, log the coordinates, move on. Weather anomalies, equipment failures, the usual litany of frontier complaints. I do not think anyone at central has actually read half of what we transmit. Maybe that is why it took me this long to notice the rhythm hiding in the noise.

Two nights ago I could not sleep, so I started flipping back through old incident reports. Grain colonies talking about rain arriving three days early, survey crews swearing the sky changed between sensor sweeps, miners in the belt claiming storms where there should not be a magnetosphere to speak of. Different systems, different months, but the same phrasing, the same uptick in power draw on local regulators, the same signature buried in the telemetry attachments if you know how to look.

It is like someone laid a transparent stencil over the Settled Systems and started tracing the same loop, again and again, trusting that no one would bother comparing notes. Now I have a list of dates, a scattering of worlds, and one shared pattern in the background code that does not belong to any sanctioned terraforming rig I have ever seen. The next station in that sequence is a Helium-3 operation that logged a "harmless calibration spike" and then quietly changed its maintenance schedule. No one thought twice about it at the time. I am thinking about it now.

Did not even mean to be on this rock past one cycle. In, hand off routes, out. That was the plan.

Instead I am sitting in a buzzing metal box with scorched paint, listening to recycled air wheeze and watching that UC hull spin lazy on the scopes. The big one, half-dead, like somebody took a bite out of its side and forgot to finish the meal. That is where I traced the pattern to in the end. Not to some pirate den or Neon backroom, but to a ship that used to write the patrols everyone else obeyed.

The smugglers keep arguing about how it went down. Some say she sold the corridor twice, once to the Fleet, once to SysDef, let them smash together for the payout. Others swear she warned the UC and hung the pirates out to dry. Same story, different villain, and nobody really wants to chase the details in case the truth ruins a good rumor or points back at their own crew.

What I know is simpler. Every ghost run I arranged for her, every too-perfect window that dropped us between sensor sweeps, left a fingerprint in our logs and theirs. I followed those smudges through GalBank insurance packets, through freighters that arrived too early with too much fuel left, through manifests that did not balance. All the stray timings line up on that crippled SysDef ship out there. Whatever she did to bend their routes, the record of it is still in that carcass, waiting for someone desperate or stubborn enough to go pull it loose.

I used to think there was no such thing as a haunted jump, just bad maintenance and worse captains.

Then I started hauling out of Gagarin more regularly, and the stories stopped being funny. Same kind of wrecks drifting back in, same scorch marks around the grav housing, and everyone swearing they had followed approved plots. Insurance blamed "operator error" every time, stamped, filed, forgotten. Funny how error keeps drawing the same curve across different ships.

The first time I saw it myself was last year, somewhere between Polvo and a nowhere mining rock. Nav threw a fit, all red bands and warning tones, then suddenly the display calmed down and smoothed into a new course like nothing had happened. ETA shaved by twenty minutes. My copilot whooped, said we had luck on our side. My stomach did not agree.

I pulled the raw telemetry later. Hidden in the noise were those neat little adjustments, burn durations that lined up on prime numbers, angles nudged just off what any auto-plotter would pick. It looked hand-drawn, like somebody had reached into the system and guided us past the worst of the debris while the machine thought it was still in charge.

For a while I told myself it was a software quirk nobody had patched. But the more logs I collected, the more clear it got: someone was carving secret lanes through the dark, and we had been following their handwriting for a long time before anyone bothered to notice.

There is still coffee dried into the grooves of the console, and I catch myself wondering whose mug it was before remembering how that ends. They tell us in training that Vanguard ships do not just disappear; every jump is logged, every variance audited. Someone forgot to tell this hull. We picked up the distress whisper by accident, a slurred echo buried under fuel reports from a quiet depot that should never have routed to my station. The ID read Vanguard, then blinked out as if embarrassed.

I have been cross-checking traffic for two days. The scout should have been on a patrol arc near a debris corridor. Instead, its last confirmed path threads neatly through a cluster of wrecks all marked with the same suspiciously efficient clearances. Dock logs at that dusty fuel stop did not match the tank levels on outgoing ships, and the clerk insisted their system just "rounded up." Somebody mis-typed a timestamp, someone else filed the wrong route, and in the gaps between those little errors, an entire crew dropped off the board.

Now I am sitting in their dead ship, listening to the hull creak, watching half-burned nav data redraw the same elegant curves over and over. Whatever is buried on this vessel will not just explain what happened here. It will tell me who has been quietly steering us all this time, and why every time a story about those perfect routes reaches my desk, the details never line up quite the same way twice.

I am recording this in the mess, lights dimmed, engines barely a hum through the hull. The banners on the bulkhead still carry the old slogans about duty and vigilance, but nobody repeats them out loud anymore. Out here, you learn that saying the wrong thing travels faster than any ship, and someone always has a reason to file it away.

Before we launched, I spent a night in Neon, up in one of the quieter lounges where the music does not quite drown out the deals. Heard a hauler talk about a phantom in the traffic nets, some ex-controller picking favorites in the lanes. People laughed, then checked their route clearances twice before boarding.

Now I am on this SysDef wreck, helmet lamp cutting across frozen consoles and bodies that died doing what the pamphlets called "essential work." The navigation logs are jagged, overwritten in places by something that does not look standard issue. Whoever rode this ship into silence got close to something they were not supposed to see, and every gap on these drives feels less like a malfunction and more like a warning to keep my own thoughts clipped and tidy.

The more I dig, the more the stories line up: captains in Neon muttering about lucky detours, a tech in The Well selling copies of hearings that never happened, a dead hauler from HopeTown whose "priority advisory" led straight into a killzone. Different systems, same invisible hand tracing the same sharp curve through the void.

I am recording this because I keep hearing the same story in different mouths, and out here with PX-9199 dead in the water, stories are all that move.

Dock 17 was the first time I heard her called by that callsign. Some Vanguard vet in a scuffed flight jacket, nursing a TerraBrew like it was the last decent thing left in the galaxy, said she threaded a convoy through a Crimson net without firing a shot. Two days later, in a corner booth on Neon, a Ryujin clerk swore she sold their analysts drift data that did not match any known jump physics. Same name, different angle. Hero. Traitor. Ghost.

Now I am standing in a darkened CIC, watching PX-9199's last jump log smear into static right where the squadron should have synced. That gap everyone pretends is a sensor error has the same taste as those bar stories, the same shape. Too clean to be chance, too ugly to be official. They say she walked away from this kind of ship when the record turned on her. They say command buried the truth to keep the lanes calm.

What gets me is how the tale keeps improving itself every time it is told, drifting from rumor to inevitability. A pilot who knows the places drives slip. A wing that vanished. A name that shows up wherever the math stops adding up. I used to file it with spacer superstition. Looking at this wreck, listening to its broken heart try to beat, I am starting to think the story has been circling the real coordinates all along.

I am filing this as a personal log because the official channel keeps timing out and, if I am honest, I do not really want anyone higher up reading it.

We have been shadowing these broken flight paths for three weeks now. First that empty rock where someone ditched a crate of nav slates like they were radioactive, then the busted relay with its guts rearranged so no one could tell where anything actually went. Now this little Navy scout, cut adrift in a place no one has business being, its course history knotted up in patterns that make my head hurt.

The weird part is how ordinary everyone treated it at first. Just another recovery op, just another derelict with a nice clean ID and a maintenance backlog we could bill for. The last team that touched these routes logged their work, signed off, and went home. They did not wait around to see why the same signature kept cropping up at abandoned farms and half-built outposts, or ask why every "optimized" vector seemed to pass close to the same dark patch of sky.

I keep replaying their notes, hearing how casual they sound. They tugged on a loose thread, filed their reports, and transferred to safer contracts. The mess they left behind has teeth. Standing on this dead ship, listening to the hull pop and settle, I cannot shake the feeling that all of us have been moving data and metal for someone else's idea of mercy, and we walked away long before we understood what we helped build.

I told myself I'd go back out there.

First time I saw the place was by accident, dropping cargo two valleys over. The foreman pointed it out like you'd point at an old scar, said the owners left in the night when the bank called in the note. What stuck with me wasn't the house, it was the glow on the metering panel. Dead farm, live power. Someone still feeding it credits.

I swung by once on the way home. Stayed in orbit, zoomed in with the scope. Saw the black-and-white armor at the doors, rifles cradled but not relaxed, a generator thumping steady in the yard. Mercenaries do not babysit empty soil for free. I logged the coordinates, marked it "follow-up" in my slate.

That was three months and too many runs ago. Every time I line up a free day, something gets in the way: late shipment, pirate scare, a "random" inspection that feels a little too targeted. Like the universe or the people who pay to shape it want that note on my slate to stay unfinished.

What bothers me is how the stories line up. A bar on Akila where they talk about a ranch that woke up debt-free. A LIST broadcast where a settler thanks an unnamed "friend in the system." Dockworkers humming that same tune about some fixer who can make numbers disappear. Someone out there pulled this farm back from the brink on paper, then let the land rot and paid Uniform Blackguard to keep everyone away.

Feels like I wasn't the only one who meant to loop back and never did.

I used to think shipping lanes were the closest thing we had to laws out here. Numbers, vectors, margins of error. Safe if you did the math right. Then, over the last year or so, jobs started coming in with strange caveats: "Use this corridor, not that one," "Ignore the published approach, follow the attached file." At first it was just more corporate paranoia, I figured. Fuel optimization. Pirate avoidance. The kind of thing smugglers brag about in bar corners. But run enough of those routes and you start to feel the ship lean toward places the charts do not name.\n\nI am looking at a cluster of jump traces right now, spread across three different contracts, three different clients who swear they never met. Same subtle deflection every time. Patrol logs around those dates got suspiciously tidy, no mentions of course corrections, just clean arrivals and clean departures for ships I know limped in scarred. Someone has been sanding down the rough edges in the records, one report at a time, until the pattern only shows if you stack months together. Feels like nobody meant for it to grow this big, like a little nudge here, a quiet override there, and suddenly half the traffic in this sector has drifted a few degrees off where it started. Now there are stories about convoys vanishing on "safe" approaches and an old survey file nobody wants to admit exists, and all of it lies along that same slow curve toward somewhere we were never supposed to go.

They keep calling it a derelict now, but I remember when this hull was alive.

I was on contract with UC SysDef two years back, riding shotgun on seizures out near Neon. LX-3802 was the big shadow hanging over us, the one that made smugglers fold without a shot. We were supposed to be cleaning up pirate ledgers, locking down accounts, making the traffic lanes safe. That was the story, anyway.

The first time I heard the rumors, we were linked to a remote station where some farmer from Freestar swore his foreclosure vanished the same night we impounded a ship. He even had the notice printouts to prove it. The SysDef officer I was with filed it under "clerical noise." But later, in the mess, people whispered about a ghost in the systems, someone editing lives from a public kiosk and using patrol ships as cover.

On LX-3802 there were days the cargo logs would change between shift checks. A crate that was here was suddenly never signed in. Some of the crew swore it was just delay in GalBank syncs, others muttered about invisible hands. I saw one tech pull a manifest backup onto a private slate, like they did not trust their own ship anymore.

I got out as soon as my term ended. Could not shake the feeling we were carrying more than contraband and seized credits. Now I hear talk around Neon that if you follow the bad numbers long enough, they lead under the city, where the lights never quite reach and debts are paid in faces, not credits.

I was going to wipe this, but my hands will not stop twitching, so I might as well leave myself a record in case someone else ends up staring at these screens.

Traffic here used to be simple. Small-timers moving medicine and machine parts through the shadows, a few smugglers who paid on time and did not shoot the place up. Then, about a year ago, the patterns changed. Same hull classes, same captains, but their routes started bending the wrong way. Jumps shaving too close to bad grav, arrival vectors just off enough to make my teeth itch when I plotted them.

Every time I tried to bring it up, the room got quieter. Dockhands changed the subject, the Trade Authority rep suddenly remembered paperwork, and the captains just smiled that thin smile you see right before someone decides you have asked one question too many. Nobody said the name, but everyone knew there was a new hand drawing the lines.

Tonight I finally traced one of those lines to its next anchor. Buried in a half-scrubbed manifest, embedded in the timing of a relay handoff and the way a stack of "lost" containers keeps reappearing, there it was: a dormant station on the edge of nowhere, its comms still linked to the same back-channel codes that keep showing up in these altered routes. I am flagging the location in a locked file; if this log is playing, I either got paid to forget or someone decided I knew too much about a navigation analyst who treats star lanes like a game board.

I do not know what day it is out here, exactly. Somewhere between port calls and dead drops, the calendar stopped mattering and we just counted jumps. Last clear date in my head is late 2329, watching the towers on Neon vanish in the aft cam while the courier slid into dark.

They told us it was a clean run. Old med hardware nobody cared about and a data spine routing update from a Trade Authority office too busy to bother with a proper briefing. First misstep right there nobody cared enough to explain why the spine needed us instead of an automated relay.

Second was letting that quiet engineer plug in "just for a diagnostic." She had the kind of eyes that measure rooms in signal paths, not meters. I signed off on a firmware patch I never really read because the manifest was already late and my comms officer misheard the clearance code. Three digits off, and nobody caught it.

After that, little things. Logs dropping a second here, a second there. Crew swearing they had already run checks they could not remember doing. A background ping in the nav console that always lined up with our vector back toward Neon, even when our paperwork said otherwise.

By the time I realized the courier was less ship and more moving conduit, we were already committed to the route overhead, to the rooftop grid where all those stray signals like to disappear into the storm. I keep replaying the small mistakes, wondering which one actually opened the door for her.

I am still not sure why they kept paying me to babysit this place.

Remote lab, skeleton crew, half the consoles running diagnostics on diagnostics. Most days it was just me, recycled coffee, and trying to convince the air scrubbers not to quit. The funny part is the only system nobody bothered to shut down properly was the one tagged "legacy routing monitor." Old code, older comments, nobody wants to touch it because if it breaks, they might have to explain why it was still running.

Tonight I dug deeper than I was supposed to. The monitor has been quietly flagging odd traffic for years, tucking copies of certain jump traces into a private buffer. Same origin points, same tug signature masking itself different ways, always shedding cargo mass somewhere off the published lanes. There is an argument in the logs: one tech calls it a glitch, another insists it matches three separate "acceptable loss" cases. Then the thread just stops. No closure, no incident report, just silence and a note to "let operations handle it."

I pulled the last set of coordinates before the buffer overwrote them. Sent them on a secure channel, no names, no commentary. Around here, people love to argue about what probably happened to those missing freighters, but nobody pushes too hard. Not when pay is on time and the lights are still on. Me, I have seen just enough of the pattern to want it off this station and in the hands of someone willing to keep asking after the room goes quiet.

I used to think the relay was where stories ended. Cargo comes in, cargo goes out, credits change hands, no questions. Turns out it is where this one started to make sense.

The broker did not want to talk. He never does. But debts stack, and I know which pressure seals on this module are overdue for maintenance. A little reminder of how fast air can disappear, and suddenly he remembered every crate that came through without an official sender, always on the same off-hour transits, always with the same soft-voiced courier who never stayed to drink.

He thought he was just shaving time off inspections, taking a little extra for himself when manifests did not line up. One missing scan here, one reprinted label there. Nothing that looked like treason when you squinted. But he kept copies. Of course he did. Greedy men archive everything that could bite them later.

Buried in his backups were route fragments, cross-referenced against private shuttle charters. Same unknown receiver tag keeps popping up on a backwater moon with a rest facility listed as spiritual retreat. I only noticed because I reran his filter, widened the tolerance by a single digit. Small decision, big shift.

Now the path runs clear enough to trace: a stray slate from an empty rock, ghosted logs at a clinic near Gagarin, panic stories out of Neon, and this relay's quiet profiteer, all pointing toward that isolated sanctuary where too many people went to mend their minds and never came back.

I keep thinking about how small the first mistake must have been.

Some junior tech in a tower somewhere, misreading a timestamp over their third TerraBrew, signing off on a course adjustment they meant to double-check later. A hauler captain too tired to question why the window shifted by a few minutes, just glad to be cleared in. A GalBank clerk noticing a pattern in payouts and deciding it was above their pay grade to ask.

By the time it reached me, it was just a rumor in a bar above Jemison. A retired supervisor with whiskey on his breath leaning close, telling me there was a controller who would not stop arguing with the system, someone who saw these little slips adding up to something uglier. He could not quite remember her name, only the callsign, and even that he spoke like it might be flagged on an open channel.

I wrote it off as drunk talk, until I started seeing the same corridor codes in different places, attached to different "accidents." Charts that should not match lining up a little too neatly, like someone kept tracing over old ink. Each time there was a reason a scheduling error, a sensor glitch, pirates in the wrong place at the wrong time.

It is almost funny, in a sick way, how many people shrugged and passed it along. Nobody lied outright; they just assumed someone else had already checked the math. Now I am floating here, staring at a dead relay and a Spacer gunship, wondering how many half-heard warnings it took to build a ghost lane.

I used to think the armor would make it easier to breathe. Funny how you can wear three layers of composite plating and still feel naked when someone drops a crate behind you. Today in the hangar, a loader slammed into its stops and I almost drew on it. Karina saw the flinch, pretended she did not. Later, she "casually" mentioned noise discipline drills, like that would sand down nerves that burned in years ago.

We got another briefing about the Vector contract. Command says it is just overwatch, pattern analysis, low-risk escort while some client chases ghosts in the lanes. Marcus does not buy it. He pointed out that every time a ship touches those routes, insurance rates spike and the paperwork comes through half-redacted. Nadia swears she saw UC tags buried in the metadata on our last packet. Nobody says it out loud, but it feels like we are walking between blades again, hired to stand in the space where bigger knives might cross.

I keep thinking about leaving. I have packed my duffel three times in as many years. Every time, someone from upstairs calls me in, lays out new pay scales, lighter rotations, "cleaner" jobs. Once they even mentioned a consultancy slot, no fieldwork. Within days, the inbox fills with the same old ops, just with different codenames and hazard bonuses tagged on. So I stay, jumpy at every bang and shadow, watching people like Karina and Marcus measure distances in escape vectors instead of meters, and pretending this is still just a job.

I used to write dates at the top of these, like that made anything official. Time is just burn and cooling metal out here, so what is the point.  

There was a stretch, right after the ring, where I could not sleep without hearing the collision in my head. Alarms, metal screaming, all of it layered over the memory of me, days earlier, pointing at the numbers and saying this will fail. At first I carried that like a broken rib I did not want anyone to see. After a while, the ache just became background noise. You learn to breathe around it.  

Funny thing: once the guilt went dull, the hesitation went with it. I stopped flinching at the idea that something I built might crack a hull, or that a drone I reprogrammed might miss a warning buoy. They already decided I was the problem, so why not become the variable they cannot control.  

This new yard, strung through forgotten metal where no one bothers to look, makes sense for a lot of reasons. Scrap is cheap, eyes are fewer, and every dead freighter is a lesson in where the big powers decided a life was not worth a repair ticket. I weld over their decisions, brace their failures, and sell the result to people who at least know what they are buying.  

What scares me is not being caught. It is being paraded. Some tribunal on Jemison, some carefully edited feed where I sit in a cage while they pretend this was one woman with a torch, not decades of cuts and lies. I will burn every bridge I have before I give them that.

I have been staring at dead screens in this rock for six months, so when one of them blinked tonight, I thought I was finally losing it.

We were supposed to be monitoring routine traffic, cataloging the usual noise; instead I found a sliver of an old ops file tucked behind a corrupted index. Half the headers are scrubbed, timestamps misaligned, but the pattern underneath is wrong in the same way as that stray dataslate we pulled off the abandoned outpost. Same cluster of derelict IDs. Same "administrative closures" on ships that never sent final manifests. And threaded through it, a repeated arbitration tag tied to someone who should not exist on UC channels at all.

The story in the mess is that years back there was a case that went bad, some arbitrator who signed the wrong ruling and vanished. Depending who you ask, she died in the blast, ran with a hold full of stolen cores, or got buried on a black payroll. Nobody remembers the original version, just a handful of contradictions that all start sounding like myth if you drink enough.

This fragment does not give me a name, but it does give me a path. The routing note points forward to an old listening post that was never formally decommissioned, just quietly taken off the books, the way you close your eyes and pretend the noise stopped. First clue from the outpost was dismissed as a glitch; now the decrypted file echoes it, and both point toward that silent station where someone thought no one would ever look again.

Recording this so if anyone digs OM-2098 out of her patrol loop and wonders how we missed it, they will know it was not one big conspiracy. Just a thousand little shrugs.

We got the revised manifest three days ago. Deimos hull IDs, nothing special, routine salvage oversight request. Ops flagged a checksum mismatch, but the watch officer said the system was "still syncing to central" and cleared it. I meant to follow up. Shift change hit, my relief was late, and by the time I handed the console over I had talked myself into believing him.

Next rotation, I noticed a courier entry buried under generic scrap classifications. UC science tag, old but not that old. I pinged for clarification. The reply came back from a junior clerk planet-side, canned language about decommission backlogs and a reminder about our queue. I asked Elena to take a second look at the routing codes. She nodded, said she would, then got pulled into a call with command. I never saw the result.

It feels different now, looking back. One missing annotation here, one misrouted query there, a night where I skipped logging a gut feeling because the air was too stale and my head hurt from grav-cycling glitches. None of it big enough to halt a Navy ship. All of it pointed the same direction, if anyone had taken the time to draw a line.

If this log survives and you are listening from some dead yard over Deimos, know this: we did not ignore the cracks. We just kept assuming someone else was already patching them.

I was never supposed to be on a Navy hull. Freight, sure. Charter runs, maybe. But steel with that emblem on the bulkhead? That belonged to people who knew what they were doing. Then one bad harvest on a dusty rock and a recruiter with a clean smile, and somehow I am strapped into PX-7708 listening to officers argue over approach vectors.

We have been running close to the storms for weeks now. First it was because the corridor was "temporarily congested." Then because some governor wanted relief supplies yesterday. Now the story is that our numbers are so clean we would be wasting fuel not using them. Funny how necessity always starts sounding like habit.

The crew talks in half-whispers when the duty lights dim. Someone mentioned settlers out along a narrow lane near Akila who swear a ghost pilot threads their shipments through dust like it is nothing. Another swears they saw the same signature buried in our course corrections, just a flicker in the logs. I do not know what scares me more, that they might be right or that I am starting to hope we have someone like that watching over us.

I keep thinking about that abandoned lab we passed weeks back, the one we were told not to log hull-side. Beacons spitting lies into the sky, ships following numbers they never meant to trust. Maybe that is all any of us are doing now, inch by inch. We did not set out to cut this close. We just kept shaving the margin until there was nothing left between us and whatever waits in those storms.

I am putting this down on a throwaway slate because saying it out loud in the bar would get me laughed at, or worse, remembered.

Couple days back I took a short-haul contract out past the usual freight spine, nothing fancy, just hauling nutrient and polymer to a LIST outpost. Midway through, the ship chirped with a course correction that did not come from my filed plan. No beacon ID, just a quiet nudge, like the autopilot suddenly remembered a better idea. I checked the math. It was good. Too good. Shaved six minutes off the run, slid us between a clutter of old traffic like it had been choreographed.

At the outpost they swore my arrival time matched their manifest exactly. No surprise. No delay. Like somebody had pre-written the coincidence.

Since then I have heard similar stories in Gagarin and Neon: freighters that arrive early with no one willing to swear to why, convoys that drop off scans entirely and then show up clean two jumps later. Every time someone starts to say it out loud, you can see them tap the brakes on their own words, make a joke, change the subject. Out here, anyone who sounds too certain about invisible hands on the lanes suddenly finds themselves short on work and long on scrutiny.

I do not know if there is really a man behind those corrections or just a pattern we are all leaning into because it is easier than admitting we fly half-blind. I just know the vectors are not random, and whoever is drawing them understands my routes better than I ever did.

I thought this posting would be quiet. A place to age out my contract with bad coffee and routine patrol schedules, maybe write up a few spacer disputes and call it duty. Instead I am drowning in other people's weather.

They come in waves. Farmhands with sunburned faces, freighter captains still smelling of coolant, one LIST rep who looked like she had not slept in a week. They argue about what they saw out there, always starting with something small. A storm that arrived hours early. A squall that parted just wide enough for one ship and then slammed shut on the escorts. A transponder that winked out precisely when the ion readings spiked.

I string their accounts up on the wall because there is nowhere else to put them. At first it was just to keep them straight in my head, a way to prove to myself it was all coincidence. But the pins kept landing in the same rough arc, across different systems, different months, different insurance forms that all said the same thing in nicer language: unavoidable conditions.

What no one mentions unless they forget I am listening is the pilot. Always the same shape of her, even when the details change. Quiet. Watches the sky more than the room. Talks like she learned Standard late and still thinks in another tongue. Pays in full, but leaves as soon as the clouds start building.

Looking at this wall now, I cannot tell if we missed her for years because the pattern was too small, or because none of us really wanted to admit the storms might have a favorite.

I am recording this while the hum of the relay is still in my teeth, before the story warps again.

When Division Garrison pulled us out here, they said it was a dead node, just a sweep and seal. First version. By the time we docked, it had become "possible contraband routing." After we stepped over old dust and fresh bootprints both, it shifted again into "nothing to see, finish up and forget it." Funny how orders keep changing after the fact.

I saw the core myself. Half the decks choked for power, security locks thrown together like someone ran out of nerve before they ran out of code. The buffers were supposed to be wiped, but there were still echoes if you knew how to look: signal bursts aimed at some backwoods farm system nobody on the manifest would admit to knowing, a run of bloodwork flagged and then unfiled, traffic patterns that matched a smuggler route we once intercepted out of Neon. Every time I tell it in the bunks, someone swears the details are different, that I mentioned a clinic instead of a farm, or a pilgrimage ship instead of a smuggler. Under the Span they say it was UC black labs; in Gagarin the same story turns into Freestar cutting corners.

Truth is, I only know three things for sure. The air in that relay tasted faintly metallic even through the mask. The name Navarro kept popping up in places it should not. And whoever paid us to seal the door wanted the story to drift, to turn into a superstition whispered over drinks instead of a clean, sharp line someone could follow.

I have been watching the traffic boards here on the relay for three nights straight, pretending I care about fuel allotments while the haulers complain about overtime. The system is supposed to buffer manifests for a few hours, then hand everything off to Cydonia for proper archiving. That is the theory. Somewhere along the line, the buffer became the only record that tells the truth.

Most of the routes are boring. Ore in, machine parts out. But there is one chain of tankers that never clears correctly, always marked with "temporary hold", always routed through the same lane down to the mines. The copies that make it to Cydonia show food-grade cargo and maintenance solvents. The ones still cached here, half-buried in a forgotten subdirectory, say something else entirely.

Someone has been feeding this place falsified labels and letting the hub on Mars stamp them as permanent, trusting nobody would compare the layers. I scrubbed identifiers, traced packet jumps, and every time I peeled back a spoofed signature, the same pattern underneath. Same sender codes that showed up on that broken slate from the rock, same timing as those "emergency" shipments the haulers in Neon grumbled about.

I pushed a pull request to Cydonia's archive node tonight, flagged as routine sync work. Buried in it is a trace marker and the checksum for this altered chain. If anyone there is actually looking, they will see the gap between what leaves this relay and what their records swear arrived. That gap is where she is hiding.

I used to think studying a man's habits long enough made him predictable. Turns out, it just makes you arrogant.

We watched his work for months from this hole in the rock. Every convoy hit along those neat, three-forked corridors, every "accidental" drift into pirate teeth, I logged it. At first it was terrifying, like staring down a black hole made of math and bad luck. Then it got familiar. Same bends, same blind spots, same shift in escort patterns. I started to think I knew him better than his own captains.

That is when things slipped.

We built our ambush on those patterns, drew firing arcs on the walls, ran sims until even the green raiders were bored. The last night before we rolled, someone dumped fresh intel on my console: a GalBank hauler quietly reassigned onto one of his favorite lanes, claim flags tweaked just enough to smell sweet. I skimmed the manifest, saw the corridor match, and assumed it was just another victim waiting its turn. Did not notice the timing, the insurance notation, the missing redundancy in their beacon protocol.

He noticed.

Now I am sitting in a half-collapsed command post, listening to the wind whine through shattered bulkheads, and the only thing that still makes sense are the logs I pulled on that contract transport before everything went loud. Same signature lane, same quiet adjustments, but something different in how he bent it. Feels like he is not just feeding off the banks anymore; feels like he is moving something for himself, and that ship is the key.

I am recording this from the Dustlance because paper burns and people vanish, but ship logs have a way of drifting into the right hands.

When we took that encrypted packet three days ago, nobody said much. Just a few looks across the bridge, Caleb checking the seals on his harness twice, Mara frowning at the routing code like it smelled wrong. Lena passed it through like it was any other priority traffic, voice flat, eyes on her console. Nobody asked who authorized the channel. Nobody wanted to.

We are Freestar Security; we are supposed to keep haulers safe and pirates nervous. Yet lately our patrols keep bringing us near the same dead rock, same blind patch in the beacon grid. Every time we file the report, someone upstairs kicks it back with a neat little note about "reallocated oversight." Details trailing off right where the questions should start.

On the mess deck, when the lights dim and the coffee has gone sour, the talk turns to settlements that wake up debt-free and others that get hit with numbers they never signed. It is always secondhand, "friend of a cousin" stories, but the pattern is there if you listen. Credits moving like they have a mind of their own, freighters robbed on paper before a raider ever sights them.

What nobody mentions out loud is the name sitting in the margins of the rumors. The quiet auditor who walked off the job and kept the keys to the vault in his head. We keep circling the same chunk of space, chasing ghosts in the manifests, and I am starting to think the ghosts are chasing us back.

Among independent hauler circles, the term "Unity Specialists" does not refer to any registered outfit or licensed contractor, but to a loose-knit cadre of troubleshooters who drift from ship to ship along the busier midlane routes. They are most often brought in when a freighter's routing, manifests, and ownership history no longer align cleanly on GalBank ledgers and Trade Authority screens, yet no one wants the delays that come with a formal audit. Their work is described as "reconciling the record," a tidy phrase that can mean anything from untangling nested cargo agreements to quietly folding unexplained containers into a new, more believable paper trail.  \n\nIn the region surrounding the derelict Voyager AX-1329, dockworkers speak of these Specialists in low voices, recalling how a small team once spent an entire night cycle in the ship's cargo spine, washing down coveralls in a half-functioning recycler while sorting through stained registry tags and flaking hazard labels that still smelled of scorched lubricants. One rumor has them pausing over a torn patch of cloth snagged on a cargo net, its faded colors matching an old festival pattern common to outlying farmsteads, remarking that they should have been home for that celebration instead of breathing rust and coolant. Since that visit, a cluster of "minor discrepancies" has appeared on lane reports near the drifting hulk, small enough to ignore individually, yet numerous enough that station clerks now mark any ship recently "unified" by these Specialists for quiet observation.

I keep telling myself I am writing this down so I do not forget it, but that is a joke; forgetting is exactly what I am afraid of.

The missioner at this little retreat was a quiet man. Not the calm kind, the brittle kind, like a pane already cracked. He kept his records in neat lines, all those settlers who came for help sleeping through the night and never made it back to their farms. I only saw the pattern because he misfiled one page under supply invoices. Wrong column, wrong date. That mistake saved us.

Names, ship IDs, dates, then a symbol in the margin I recognized from a slate I pulled off a dead spacer near Gagarin Landing. Same hand, same looping stroke. Cross-referencing with the freighter schedules he had scribbled on the wall, the trail points to a Helium-3 plant that should not have this much off-book traffic. Another mistake: his note about a "routine screening team" arrived two days early, so he wrote the actual time in the corner. It all lines up if you assume someone needed reactor output and anonymity in the same place.

What worries me is how easily this could have gone unseen. One cleaner stacking the ledgers differently, one shuttle delay, one conversation we did not overhear in the common room, and the line would have broken. As it stands, all I know is this: a stray dataslate on a dead rock, altered logs in a back-room clinic, a chem runner in Neon who panics near certain doors, and a missioner who charted disappearances until his ink ran out. Every missed word and wrong stamp along the way nudged us here.

I am writing this down because if I say it out loud in the wrong bar, someone will tell me to stop asking questions and someone else will make sure I do. Out on the fringe run, the board sent me to check a dead relay everyone else had written off as a bad install. The shack was half-buried in dust, beacon barely humming, and the tech who signed the last maintenance log was a stiff in a suit that did not even get his name right on the sleeve. His slate was cracked, but I could still see enough to know the distress calls coming through that node did not behave like they were supposed to. Not late enough to trigger alarms, just late enough that a certain unregistered hull could always be first on scene.\n\nSince then, I keep hearing the same story from different mouths. A LIST crew swears an anonymous tender showed up out of nowhere, patched their drive, left food and Med Packs, then wiped their nav history clean. A Crimson captain grumbled about reaching a juicy wreck only to find it stripped down to the safety gear, all of it lined up by the airlock like an apology. A clerk I know in New Atlantis whispered about sealed orders and an old rescue callsign that kept popping up in restricted incident files. Nobody will say his name straight, they just call him the one who beats the forecast. I can not tell if people are more afraid of him or grateful he exists, and that is what unsettles me the most. It feels like the truth sits right in that space between fear and convenience, where everyone knows something is wrong and keeps using it anyway.

I am recording this in the dark, helmet lamps off, just the glow from the console bleeding into the air like a wound.

FX-1555 should be a tomb. Power stripped, crew long gone, registry marked as "honorably decommissioned." That is what the UC Navy file said when they sold me the partial salvage rights. I thought it was just another dead hull to pick clean.

But the logs are not dead. They are edited. Whole sections of convoy records scraped out, then stitched back with new timestamps that do not match the maintenance cycles. Combat engagements that never happened, escorts assigned to ships that never crossed their path. I dug deeper and found the cross-index: civilian haulers, survey craft, even one LIST transport flagged "resolved" days before their last distress calls were forwarded through a relay that has since gone conveniently silent.

Whoever did this knew the codes, knew what internal auditors look for and how to leave just enough noise to make it boring. They wanted this to sit here, rotting in orbit until the last person who remembered those names was dust.

Trouble is, spacers talk. A tug pilot in Gagarin Landing mentioned a Navy hull that paid too well for scrap. A dockmaster in New Atlantis let slip that certain claims were tied to a combat ship that "does not exist anymore." One Sanctum Universum traveler in a bar swore there is a place where lost ships go, not by accident, but by design.

Follow the patterns far enough, every false line bends toward one graveyard. And someone out there has decided those ruins belong to them.

I am recording this from the crew bunk because the bridge mic logs everything and I am tired of choosing my words. Out there, you mispronounce a route code, drop a digit on a transponder tag, and someone sends you a polite message about "clarification." In here, I can admit I am scared.

When we took that contract back in 2329, it sounded simple. Trade Authority pallets, standard lanes, nothing anyone would write songs about. Then the first course correction came down, no explanation. A few degrees off here, a slightly different approach there. The navigator blamed a typo in the orders; ops shrugged and said traffic control was a mess. No one wanted to be the one to tell them their system was wrong, so we just flew it.

Next job, same origin and destination, but the route slipped again, like somebody was nudging all of us around something only they could see. We asked if there had been a new debris warning; dispatch said no. One of the loaders muttered about ghost-yards and tugs that move ships like pieces on a board. Everyone laughed, then changed the subject.

A relay station we passed weeks later had partial logs that did not match our memory of the sky. A rock I stopped on for fuel, a man there talking about near-misses that never made it to the record. Each little mismatch felt harmless on its own, easy to blame on lag, on tired controllers, on us mishearing instructions over static.

Stack them up, though, and it feels like someone has been rewriting the lines between ports while we all nod along, too busy or too afraid to correct the course.

I am recording this from what is left of the main corridor, sitting on a crate that used to hold ammo and now only holds dust. The roof is open to the stars and the air still smells like burned propellant and lightning. Somebody thought they were clever, laying an ambush here for her, scribbling routes and timings over the bulkheads. Looking at the scorch marks, she was cleverer.

Their tactician left a slate wedged behind a cracked support strut, like they knew whoever came next would not trust a central terminal. Took me three tries to bypass their lockouts; the encryption was sloppy but the pattern underneath was not. Every line tags the same convergence: her ship never jumps directly to the outlying farms or the old lab, always stages near a belt rich in Helium-3, always within a narrow band of atmospheric readings. Cross-check that with the anomalies the Rangers flagged and the miner chatter about flickering skies, and the picture tightens around one mining operation at the edge of the grid.

The truth of it feels simple when you say it out loud, and still it slides sideways when you try to write it down, like the numbers do not want to line up. She goes where the rock is thin and the reactors are hot, chases something in the air no one else can see, leaves behind storms and redacted reports. Out in the boonies I found the first whispers, then the support post logs and a Helium-3 facility running ghost diagnostics. Now I have the dead raiders' projections pointing at this mine, and a bad sense that all these routes have been leading there from the start.

I told myself I would come back here with a full team and a proper warrant, not just a pocket full of bad hunches and a half-charged pistol. The outpost was supposed to be a footnote in the audit, one more dead UC box I could tick off before getting reassigned somewhere with windows. Instead I walked in alone, saw those half-scrubbed route tables humming under a century of dust, and felt that cold little hook in my ribs that says "this matters."

I tagged the worst of it for follow up, set a reminder, and shipped my report upstream with all the sharp edges sanded down. "Minor anomalies in archived traffic records." That is what I wrote. The sort of thing a bored clerk glances at and forgets. The sort of thing I was counting on forgetting too.

But the stories kept circling back. Dockside captains swearing their ships came out of grav slightly off where they should have, freight handlers complaining about pallets that "never existed" on paper. A retired controller in New Atlantis buying me a TerraBrew and sketching a familiar curve on the table with condensation, like his hand remembered a pattern his head refused to say out loud.

Every time I see another near-miss buried in a log, another ship that took a detour nobody ordered, I think about this place. I think about the way the air tasted in that server room, metallic and waiting. Someone meant to come back here after me, to tidy up or dig deeper. Neither happened.

If this recording turns up in the same cold racks, I guess that means I joined the list of things that never made it into the official story.

I logged this because I am tired of hearing my own voice bounce back off empty hangar walls. Out here, on this forgotten strip of concrete and rust, everything feels like it was meant to be temporary: prefab sheds, rented loaders, us. Then someone never turned the systems off, and the place just kept listening.

We came to cut scrap, nothing more. First day I stood under those dead cranes, I could hear a low hum in the guts of the old relay gear, like a heartbeat the shutdown crews missed. The foreman shrugged, said the diagnostics were probably still cycling from some past contract and there was no point paying to rip it all out. So the hum stayed. The scanners stayed. The side jobs hauling "redundant" comms modules to buyers who never gave names stayed.

Now the Derelict Claim Jumpers drink under that noise, trade stories about rescue calls that never hit the registry, about a woman who can bend beacons like copper wire. We all pretend the rumors are just spacer talk, but nobody stands too close to the old antenna stack when the sky is clear. The grid was supposed to route evac drills and traffic control for a few months, until the big stations came online.
