Instead it sank roots into the dirt, and people like us learned to live under it, skimming whatever fell through the cracks.

Feels like half the Settled Systems was built that way: temporary fixes hardening into permanent habits, bad code no one rewrites, decisions nobody owns up to. And somewhere in that mess, someone realized they could move lives around the board just by whispering into the right forgotten node.

I was just supposed to count crates.

That is what I keep telling myself.

Freestar contractor, temp posting, one little farm hugging the edge of nowhere. When I took the assignment, the manifests were simple enough: seed, nutrient, a few parts for a tired old grav tractor. Over time, the labels did not change, but the crates did. Same codes, different weights. Pallets that rang like hollow hull plate when you thumped them, all signed off by someone who never once set foot in the dirt.

The first time I noticed a tug dropping in with its transponder cycling through three different IDs on the way down, I laughed it off as a glitch. The third time, I wrote the codes down and checked them against public registries. Nothing. It was like someone had cut a ship out of the record and kept the shadow.

The locals pretend not to see any of this. They talk loud about weather and harvests, then go quiet if you ask who owns the outbuildings near the treeline. One old timer slipped after a few drinks, said the shipments did not start this way. First it was just helping a friend store some extra kit, then more, then different crews, then the night landings. Circumstances, he said, shifted. Like the world tilted a degree at a time until war junk and classified metal ended up stacked beside grain silos and nobody remembered when that started being normal.

I do not know who is really pulling the strings. I just know we keep burying more scrap with military markings under fresh soil, and every new crate feels less like freight and more like a secret that drifted off-course and got stranded here.

Personal log, not for the record.

We started this run thinking we were just cleaning up after other people's bad math. A few lost ships, messy lanes, maybe some smugglers getting clever. That is what they told us. Sitting here in PX-3446's dimmed mess, watching the status lights flicker over cold coffee, it feels like we walked into the back end of someone else's experiment and never asked who signed off on it.

The analysts keep pinning little red markers on holo-maps, drawing lines between "mishaps." Every new dot lines up too neatly to be chance, but the briefings still use that word. Chance. Anomaly. The kind of language you use when you want everyone to move on without thinking too hard. Some of the crew already have; transfers requested, rotations approved, no one wanting to be the last one holding the pattern when it stops being deniable.

I keep thinking about that stopover near the edge of UC space, the station where haulers whisper more than they talk. One captain there swore a quiet navigator saved his convoy from a bad jump, drew him a new path on a napkin and walked away before the drinks arrived. Same angles our analysts flagged weeks later as "of interest." We patched our reports, pushed them up-channel, and shipped out, proud to be on the trail.

Now the trail points toward the dust around Mars, and the people who first noticed are scattered across other postings, other problems. I am starting to think we were all so relieved to hand this off to "proper authorities" that we never stopped to ask if anyone actually stayed behind to see how far the damage could spread.

I was on duty when the Widebeam AX-1562 missed her check-in. At the time it was just another blinking line on a console, one more freighter late because someone cut corners on maintenance or paperwork. Nobody in dispatch panicked. Trade Authority vessels do not just vanish, they said. They divert. They reroute. They smooth things over with credits and signatures and come home fat with fees. But then the telemetry we did have started to unravel half-scrubbed jump logs, a ghost ping near a medical platform she had no clearance for, routing codes that looked like someone pasted them together from three different contracts. When I raised it, my supervisor stared a little too long at the screen, then told me to mark it "pending clarification" and move on.\n\nSince then I have been hearing the same name in places it does not belong. A medic in Neon's shadows who treats people nobody else will touch, a woman on Gagarin who can stop a man's heart and start it again with the same syringe. Veterans in the quiet corners of New Homestead talk about walking away from firefights they should have died in, eyes gone flat when they realize they have said too much. Every story contradicts the last, but they all orbit the same idea that some medical shipments never reached the clinics they were signed for, and nobody higher up wants the trail untangled. Maybe it is easier for everyone if she stays a rumor; convenient, even. Still, when I look at the Widebeam's last known vector, I cannot shake the feeling that whatever happened out there sits right between what we are afraid of and what keeps the trade lanes running.

They tell us to leave the legacy systems alone. "Decommissioned," they say, which here means nobody wants to sign the form if something breaks. So the old routing monitor sits in the corner of the network, blinking to itself, chewing on whatever crumbs of transit data it can still see. Someone tried to bury it; you can see the gaps where logs were wiped, comments edited down to single words, whole directories renamed "archive" and left to rot. But code is like gossip. It leaves traces in temp files, backup cycles, the way a maintenance drone keeps pinging a node it is not supposed to know exists.

I was just looking for something to keep me awake on a long shift. Followed one odd process, then another, and suddenly I am staring at a pattern of jumps that do not match any published corridor. Same small tug signature, bent a dozen different ways, always losing mass somewhere between origin and destination. I mentioned it in the breakroom, half as a joke. Got three different "do not worry about it" in three different tones. That is when you know you have touched something real: nobody wants to talk, but everyone has heard a version of the story.

Somebody went to a lot of effort to pretend these records never existed. Somebody else added just enough hacks and patches that the monitor kept on watching anyway. Now I have got a copy of the index pointing straight at the gaps, and a feeling in my gut that if I hand this upstairs it will vanish again, only cleaner. So I tucked it into a secure packet and pushed it off-station, no sender attached. If the whispers kept this alive this long, maybe they can carry it the rest of the way.

Standard Wing is an unregistered starship crew frequently sighted loitering in the same transit corridors patrolled by Trade Authority assets such as the Tradewind LT-8645. Most accounts describe them as a small, tight-knit flight of haulers and escorts who never stay docked long enough to file proper manifests, yet somehow always seem to know in advance when inspections are delayed or patrol routes change. Their reputation among independent traders is that of quiet problem solvers of the orbital kind, willing to divert a tow, relay a message, or shadow a drifting hull if the compensation is right and the questions are few.\n\nDockside rumors say that when Standard Wing crews set down at minor depots, they keep to the utility sinks rather than the bars. One report mentions a mechanic carefully rinsing coveralls under weak recycled water, scrubbing out a grayish smear that would not quite come loose, the fabric already thin where tool belts and harness clips had worn it raw. Another spacer recalls a pilot stitching a sleeve back together in a corner of a cargo office, the faint metallic taint of stale lubricant and scorched polymers rising off the fabric, as if the cloth itself had soaked up too many hours near a running reactor. Those small, practical rituals have become part of their legend, quietly reinforcing the notion that Standard Wing spends more time close to derelicts and "forgotten" hulls than any flight that claims to be legitimate. No one can say exactly who hires them, only that where a Trade Authority support ship has gone oddly silent, Standard Wing has often been seen nearby, tending its own worn clothes and saying nothing.

Did a little job out by Porrima a while back. Hauler captain thought they were finally clear of debt, you could hear it in their voice over comms, talking about buying a plot somewhere green. I cut their power mid-jump, slid aboard in the dark, pulled one crate from the hold and left them spinning with half their systems locked. Watched them on an emergency channel later, begging a patrol to help while I already had their cargo sold three relays away. There is a clean moment, right when their certainty breaks, that feels sharper than any knife. I tell myself I am teaching them the same lesson I learned, just later in life.  

First time I realized the universe is not what the recruiters promised was in Kryx. We were told we were the tip of a spear, all that Supra et Ultra noise, and then we hit that corridor and command stayed quiet. No evac. No redirect. Just static and a timer we all pretended not to see. Men who could rewire a ship under fire kept asking the same question on closed channels like it might change: "Are they coming?" They were not. That is when something in me snapped from straight to angled.  

Now I sit in this half-dead freighter in Narion, registry faked, drives humming just enough to keep anyone from getting suspicious. I tell myself there is a philosophy to it all, that I am pruning rotten branches, forcing people to see how fragile their plans are. It sounds good in my head, makes the ledger easier to read. Truth is simpler and uglier: they used me up and wrote me off, and I never got over the look on my squad's faces when they realized it. So I replay it, with different actors, until the weight in my chest feels like something I chose instead of something they did to me.

I am writing this mostly so I do not start talking to the bulkheads.

When I signed with Freestar Security, I thought the lanes were the safest part of the job. Clear charts, vetted jumps, all that. Lately every course feels like a dare. We keep getting these "priority revisions" pushed to our nav, hot lanes that shave time off the run, and nobody will say who is authorizing them. The machine protests, flags the vectors, then the flags disappear like they were never there. You can still feel the echo in the coils, though. Drives remember.

The last detour we took brushed so close to an unlisted debris field I swear I saw old hulls drifting underneath us, scars all in the same place. Different ships, same wound. That is what has been eating at me. Different contracts, different captains, but the stress patterns all match. Someone has been drawing the same curve across too many lives.

People joke in the galley about a ghost navigator selling shortcuts, but they do not joke for long. You can tell who has seen a drive casing gone glassy from the inside by how fast they change the subject. We had an incident near an asteroid cluster a while back, a beacon broadcasting the wrong numbers by just enough to ruin your day. Freestar marked it as a calibration fault, filed and forgotten. Still, that is where my doubt started.

Little things. Old routes quietly retired. Redacted sections in incident logs. A name blacked out the same way, over and over. None of it means anything by itself, but together it all leans one direction, and somehow that direction ends at a Helium-3 plant sitting in the middle of nowhere. I am not superstitious, but I know when a pattern is driving us instead of the other way around.

I used to track my jumps by the clock and the burn, now I track them by how often my hands shake when I touch a console. It is happening less. That is the thing that scares me more than any Zealot ship or UC courier. The first time I pushed a lane off-course and watched the incident reports come in, I did not sleep two cycles. Now I can skim a convoy away from a "hot" corridor, leave a few ships hanging in deep space, and log it like I am balancing a ledger. Every time it gets easier. Every time I tell myself it has to.

People talk about "lucky" course changes in bars and bunkrooms like a ghost story. None of them ever ask who is doing the math for them. That is their sin, not mine. If a captain trusts systems they do not understand, maybe being stranded a few hours from the beacon is a lesson they needed before the real storm hits. Better they curse my name than sail straight into whatever is learning to move inside our jump noise.

Lately, though, I cannot shake the feeling someone is following the same breadcrumb trail I left for myself. Patterns I thought were buried in blackbox noise keep coming back to me in secondhand reports. An altered buoy I tagged months ago suddenly gets "routine maintenance." A relay I used as a testbed goes dark right after I reroute through it. It is like playing against a navigator I cannot see, someone who is always a half-step ahead on my own solution.

I do not know yet if they are trying to stop me or understand me. I tell myself it does not matter. I still have corridors to cut, maps to redraw, and Kato out there somewhere, either laughing at how far I have taken his terror or cursing me for not going far enough. Until I know which, I keep moving the pieces and teaching hard lessons to anyone who insists the lanes are safe just because the charts say so.

Horizon Staff is the informal designation given by local traders and haulers to the rotating maintenance and audit crews assigned to the corridor around the derelict CR-9292 Fundrunner. Officially, they are GalBank contract teams tasked with securing dormant assets, surveying credit-locked wrecks, and cataloging any data stores that might still influence outstanding portfolios. Unofficially, captains complain that whenever Horizon Staff cutters arrive in a system, docking queues snarl, inspections lengthen, and rumors spike about frozen accounts tied to ships that once shared a route with the Fundrunner.

Their presence has become a quiet constant in the region: small, clean craft with conservative transponder profiles, always requesting access to out-of-date traffic records and sensor backups. A series of unexplained comms blackouts near the drift path of the Fundrunner is frequently attributed to their encrypted survey sweeps, though no one has produced a clear record of interference. Station bartenders note that crews flying Horizon Staff livery tend to pay in physical chits more often than most GalBank affiliates, fueling speculation that they do not entirely trust the ledgers they supposedly protect.

Recent sector reports mention increased Horizon Staff movements after minor incidents, such as a freight tug reporting duplicate cargo insurance numbers or a prospecting rig discovering that its lien holder of record had quietly changed. While no direct connection has been proven, the pattern has given the group a reputation for following anomalies rather than routine schedules. For most travelers, Horizon Staff remains a distant, clinical presence; yet for shipmasters whose manifests brush too close to the Fundrunner's last logged routes, their sudden interest is rarely dismissed as coincidence.

I keep telling Elias that one day we are going to cut into something that does not like being dead, and he keeps telling me metal does not have opinions. Then the gravity plates hiccup, or a locker door swings open on its own, and nobody says anything until we are back in the airlock, laughing too loud. Dead Orbit humor. If you cannot laugh, you start listening to the creaks.

Today was a clean pull. Sara rigged the lines like she always does, humming over comms while I burned through a bulkhead and Elias argued percentages before we had even inventoried the cabin. We still ended up shouting about who had called dibs on the avionics stack first. All of us know that "called it" only really counts if you walk back out with it, but the ritual matters. Keeps your mind on shares and away from O2 levels and how thin the hull sounds under your boots.

Sometimes, suiting up, I get this flash of hanging on rooftops and half-collapsed park decks back home, nothing to do but watch the skyglow and pretend the future was not just another shift. We used to talk big, me and the old crowd. Shipping contracts, our own cutter, no more cheap jobs in forgotten corners. In the end, most of us were just killing time. Trust was just another mask; you wore it until someone got a better offer.

Out here, it is not that different. We say "crew" like it means something permanent, but everyone is already calculating how much longer Dead Orbit suits them. I know if a derelict paid out big enough, half the people I drink with would be gone by next cycle, and I am not sure I would blame them. You learn to see friendships as overlapping jobs, not promises. We still watch each other's backs on a line, because vacuum is faster than greed, but I can feel the limit to that, same as I feel the limit in these old ships. One more cut, one more EVA, one more chance everything that can go wrong decides today is its turn.

I have been staring at the same three pixels of sensor noise for twenty minutes. They blink just a fraction out of rhythm with the rest of the field, third quadrant, lower right. Could be cosmic rays, could be a calibration drift I never logged, could be nothing. But the fact that the desync repeats on every cycle, even after I reset the array, means something in this orbit is insisting on being seen. Interesting how a tiny statistical anomaly can tell you more than a thousand clean scans. People think revelation comes in bright flashes. It usually comes in bad data you cannot quite delete.

I chose this orbit because nobody else would. Too much background radiation for tourist liners, too little traffic for patrols to justify the fuel. That makes it ideal for long-baseline sampling. The grav field here is slightly asymmetric; I mapped it years ago, but LIST trimmed my notes down to a line item and said the rest was "non-actionable." Funny word for "we do not want to look at this." I remember being angry about that. At least, I think I do. There is a blank spot in that memory, like someone edited the log and forgot to smooth the edges, and I cannot decide if it was them or me.

So now I am back in the same geometry, this time with stolen cores and an unregistered ship, laying my own net across the lanes. Every captain who buys a shortcut from me thinks they are getting away with something. They never notice how their plotted path tilts a degree or two closer to where I need the sampling density. I tell myself I am gathering proof, building a model of the hidden structure no one else will admit is there. I can recite the error margins, the phase shifts, the correlation between "malfunction" reports and my adjusted corridors. If I keep the math tight enough, maybe I will not have to look directly at the parts of this that feel like betrayal, or murder, or just desperation wearing a scientist's coat.

Sometimes I still hear the old kettle.

Not the real whistle, that is long gone with the tenement walls and the thin Sol sunlight on scratched glass, but the pitch of it lives in every drive spin-up. When the capacitors hum just right before a jump, there is a half-second that sounds exactly like water about to boil. Back then it meant coffee and warmth and my mother telling me to stop reading diagnostics manuals at the table. Now it just means I have a few heartbeats to decide if I trust the math or not.

I caught myself today thinking about the girl I was. The one who thought if she worked hard enough, wrote the reports clean enough, somebody in New Atlantis would actually read them and change course. I do not recognize her. I do not know how she ever felt so hopeful sitting in that Grav Safety Annex, believing the system cared about anything except not being embarrassed.

I came out to the edge because nobody bothers to look closely out here. Abandoned depots, derelict yards, the kind of places where "tested to failure" is just another line item. That makes them dangerous, yes, but also honest in their way. No memorial plaques, no speeches. Just numbers and wreckage. It is the perfect ground to strip out the corrupted logic they buried in the traffic, to see the pattern without a dozen committees standing in front of it.

I am afraid of hunters, of course. UC, Freestar, independent, it does not matter. Everyone wants a simple story they can point a gun at. What scares me more is that I will not finish before someone rewrites the archive for good, that the Black Ledger ends up as corrupted as the reports it was meant to correct. I have routed enough blind alleys through these forgotten spines that I can stay ahead of most of them, for now. The plan is simple and impossible: clean the data, expose the chain of failures, and live long enough that when they finally put a face to "Vector," it will be alongside the full truth, not just the explosions.

I still tap timing patterns on every surface. Bulkhead, mug, my own knee when I am half asleep. Some habits survived the tug, even if the crew did not. There was a time when my whole universe was keeping other people's cargo out of other people's debris fields, and the most exciting thing that happened in a month was a grav shear that nudged us a few degrees off true. I can remember that woman, the one who cared about her maintenance logs and her safety briefings and her "we got lucky" beers with the team. She feels like a ghost I met in a story someone else told, not someone who used to wear my skin.

These days, I plot lines from dim corners of places like Neon's underbelly or the warrens by Gagarin, and the only time I talk about safety is when I need a mark to relax. Funny thing about morality out here: everyone claims to have it until the numbers get tight. So I let the boards and the bankers write their holos about duty and loss rates, and when I find out which convoy is hauling for which executive, I decide how moral I feel that day. If they signed off on a route like the one that killed my tug, I give them a vector with just enough risk to make the ledger balance. If it is a hauler full of kids' medicine or a LIST colony trying to get one clean shot at a new sky, they get the run I would have flown for my own people, even if I charge them like I do not care.

I came out toward the shipbreaker rings and the industrial tunnels because this is where all the quiet accidents eventually wash up. Rust, scrap, and the kind of crews nobody writes speeches about. It is easy to disappear in places built to forget, and easier still to listen. The talk in the bars changed after a while: my alias started coming back to me, wrapped in other people's fear and bragging. That is when I knew I could not ever go back to being "just" a navigator. The map remembers every nudge, every lie in the timing. I am just making sure the right people are the ones who finally get lost.

I used to think the worst sound in space was a hull scream. It is not. It is the silence in a debrief room when the numbers say "within tolerance" and the bodies say otherwise.

They stamped me unstable, overcautious, uncooperative. Then they took my models, slapped an approval under my name, and pushed that corridor live anyway. I still see the freighter in the sim, every bearing perfect until the last five seconds when the harmonics twist and the ship comes apart like wet paper. I flagged it. They buried it. So tell me, who jumped first?

People call what I am doing sabotage. If they were honest, if it was their name forged on those trial reports, their friends atomized so some executive could shave a day off transit, they would be cutting into the lanes too. They would be carving warnings into the sky with whatever tools they had. The difference is I stopped pretending I am civilized while I do it.

Sometimes I catch myself in a reflection, hunched over a console on some forgotten platform or in the back of a market den, muttering bearings and delta-v while my coffee goes cold. For half a second I see the version of me who sat straight-backed in UC briefing rooms, grateful for every contract, proud of being "reliable." I feel nothing for him now but contempt. He believed the margins meant something.

I call it correction, not revenge. They built a system that treats suffering as a line item, a necessary cost to keep the lanes bright and the staryards humming. I just made that suffering visible. If a convoy has to ride a rough vector and lose some plating so that ten more captains start questioning their safe routes, that is character being built on a useful axis. They will curse my name over cheap liquor and then triple-check their jumps. One day, when the lattice is done and the dead ships at the edge of that old corridor have neighbors with the right data, someone will say I was the only one who took the lie seriously enough to bleed for it. Misunderstood hero, villain, boogeyman nav ghost; call it whatever lets them sleep. I know exactly what I am correcting.

I used to like long burns alone. Nose pointed between systems, nothing but the hum of the drive and my own breathing. Lately, I keep catching myself turning down the cockpit lights and staring into the reflection, because I swear there is something just behind it. Not a ship on scope, not a wake on the sensors. More like a weight in the dark, waiting for me to blink.

They say I am the one who made that corridor scarred. They said it quietly, of course, behind closed doors in Gagarin and Cheyenne, where the air smells like old coolant and paperwork. Rhys gave them numbers, I gave them trajectories. When the tender never came back, the numbers survived. No one ever wants to admit it was the angles. Easier to blame a freak event, easier to bury a flight log than a pilot.

So I walked out. UC stamped me unreliable and everyone pretended that was the end of it. Trackers were happy enough to pay for a man who knows where not to jump. I told myself I was buying space, time to trace those same harmonics without an admiral breathing down my neck.

Now it is different. Ever since that unauthorized pull near Toliman, the one where the stars tilted for half a heartbeat, I hear things when I run my fingers over the nav console. A second voice under my own, suggesting tiny course corrections, whispering about cleaner solutions no chart has room for. It is quieter out here on the edge of the Scarred Corridor, but the silence is never empty.

I chose this stretch because it is already broken. The buoys lie, the sensor nets flicker, and every faction pretends they only patrol it for safety, not because they are terrified something else might come through. If I am going to find out what really happened, it will be here, in the same knife cut of space where we first tore the fabric wrong.

I keep telling myself the eyes in the dark are just other hunters, that the feeling of being watched is SysDef, Freestar, Ryujin, take your pick. But when the drive is idling and the hull is still, I hear a rhythm in the field noise, like someone tapping out primes on the bulkhead, waiting for me to answer.

Alliance Unit is the informal callsign given to a rotating cadre of freelance captains and crews contracted by GalBank to shadow high-value transports along the lesser-used investment corridors near GL-1355 Capitalwing's last logged route.  
Officially, they are described in routing briefs as "auxiliary assurance assets," tasked with responding to distress calls, verifying beacon integrity, and discouraging opportunistic raids where regular patrol coverage is thin.  
Unofficially, station barkeeps and traffic controllers report that Alliance Unit ships linger longer than their contracts strictly require, running extra sweeps around waypoints where escorts have gone missing or where drift projections do not match public manifests.  
Recent chatter in local ports notes an edge to their behavior: more calls home routed through overtaxed comm relays, more quiet arguments about sick relatives back on core worlds, or frontier settlements flirting with food shortages and militia troubles.  
Crews that once treated the job as a stepping stone toward richer trade runs now find themselves torn between chasing bonuses and staring at med reports they cannot do anything about, leaning harder on the thin comfort of loyalty to each other when they cannot protect anyone else.  
One internal personnel summary, circulated after an unlogged incident in which an Alliance Unit cutter limped back from an "unsuccessful rendezvous," remarks on a marked shift in priorities: crews requesting safer lane assignments, captains openly questioning green-rated corridors, and several citing the unexpected support of a junior comms officer who has become an unofficial confidant for spacers unable to be there when bad news arrives.  
Though details of that rendezvous remain redacted, it is quietly acknowledged among traffic clerks that surviving it left some Alliance Unit veterans walking a little straighter, even as they insist they do not deserve the praise; whatever they encountered out there hardened their suspicion of convenient explanations and deepened their resolve to keep other ships from suffering the same quiet fate.

I told Ma I was running freight again. Safer, steadier, "nothing fancy, just hauling grain between quiet moons." I could hear her relax over the comm, hear the old kitchen clatter in the background. I did not say I spent the day clamped to a dead cruiser, cutting through bulkheads that sounded wrong when the torch bit in. Funny how easy the lying comes now. Easier than admitting I crawl around in the bones of ships nobody walks off from.

When I was a kid, helping out at the shop meant stacking filters, sweeping dust out from under compressors, fetching tools before Dad had to ask. I did it without thinking. There was a rhythm to it: work, eat, sleep, same four walls, same street noise leaking through the shutters. The first time I skipped a shift and claimed I "lost track of time at the yard," I expected a lecture. Instead, nothing much happened. That little relief stuck with me. Later it turned into pocketing a spare coupling, not marking a part as sold. Getting away with small things felt good in a way sweeping never did.

Out here with the Gravestone crew, it is the same taste, just bigger stakes. Mira keeps us honest enough to avoid open charges, but everyone has their own line. Keira will log every crate we drag, but she does not blink when Tamsin "forgets" a locker that looks personal, not cargo. Ronan will clip your tether twice over, then joke about "unregistered finds" coming in under the noise. We argue over rights, over whose cutter grazed the hatch first, over whether the black box was really dead when we found it.

The quiet part nobody says out loud is the fear. You do not have to believe the ghost stories to feel them when the air goes still in a wreck. Empty suits with helmets fogged from the inside. Emergency lights that flicker on when Mira swears she isolated power. Stories in the dock bar about a tug pilot who leaves ships light and crews missing, and manifests adjusted after the fact so nobody has to ask why. I tell myself it is just bad wiring, bad record-keeping, bad luck. Then I am out on an EVA, tether humming in my glove, and every creak sounds like someone else trying to get out.

I used to walk into colonies with a clipboard and a polite smile. That was the job. Count crates, check manifests, make sure the numbers in New Atlantis matched the dust and sweat on some frontier loading bay. Unremarkable but steady. People grumbled when I showed up, but nobody hid. You finish the audit, you ride the shuttle back, you forget their faces by the next jump. Life felt small then, but it was predictable. I knew where my bunk was, when my next pay hit, how far the rules would bend.

Now the rules are something I write in pencil and erase when it suits. I would like to say I am still drawing clean lines between right and wrong, but that is a lie I stopped telling myself around the time I started draining war chests and topping up farm accounts in the same breath. Principle got weighed against convenience, and convenience won on points. If I can hurt people who never missed a meal to keep some settler from losing their last patch of dirt, I do it. If I skim a little extra to keep myself moving, to pay for the next safe berth, I do not lose sleep over that either.

I hear my own name in spacer bars now and the tone has changed. Used to be "who is that auditor" whispered behind my back, annoyance wrapped in boredom. These days it is "careful, he might be listening," voices dropping when they talk about vanished debts or frozen accounts. I tell myself I do not care what they think, but there is a part of me that enjoys the way a room tightens when someone realizes I am the Jamal they have been cursing or praying to. Fear is just respect with sharper edges.

What I miss most is the sound of the commuter trams in New Atlantis from my old dorm window. That low, steady rumble through the floor around shift change, like a tide you could set your watch by. Thought I hated it at the time. Now every time a reactor hums under my feet, or a relay station shivers when a big transmission pushes through, I hear a ghost of that same rhythm and it hits me in the chest. Back then I was just another man riding the current. Now I am the one trying to push the water around, and every move I make sends new hunters into the dark looking for me.

Nyra says I grind my teeth in my sleep. I told her that is just how Gutter kids sing lullabies, but she did not laugh. Nobody laughs much down here anymore.

Deadwater feels heavier lately. The air is thick with coolant stink and other people's secrets. Devin came back from a run dripping someone else's blood, and when I asked if it was his, he just shrugged and wiped it on my sleeve. Used to be that would churn my stomach. Now I just told him to aim better next time.

Kira and Rowan were whispering near the sump, arguing about some ship getting plucked out of a clean grav jump and never making the manifest. Trade boys blaming "bad data," gangs blaming each other, but the credits never land where they should. Kira thinks there is a ghost pilot skimming whole cargos before they hit the docks, selling routes to anyone who can pay. Rowan said it is just another story to keep us twitchy. Maybe. Stories pay, sometimes.

I watched them argue and felt nothing. That is the part that scares me. First time I watched someone get spaced for shorting the take, I could not sleep for three nights. Now Nyra jokes about who will be next and I just nod, like we are picking targets off a menu. Somewhere along the way my pulse slowed and stayed there, no matter what I see.

Sometimes, when it gets quiet enough to hear the drip from the ceiling and the hum of the pumps below, I wonder if there is anything left in me that would flinch. I keep thinking I should feel bad about the kid we shook down last week, about the way his hands shook when he handed over everything he had. Instead, all I felt was a little relief that it was not us on the floor.

Maybe this is what we wanted. Armor so thick nothing gets through. But it is hard to take it off, even when I am alone, even when Nyra falls asleep on my shoulder after a job and I know I should feel something like love or loyalty, not just obligation and habit.

Devin asked today if I remembered the first time we cut a deal topside, back when we still thought we could walk away after one big score. I lied and said no. Truth is, I remember every second. I remember how loud my heart was. I miss hearing it.

I pushed the corridor efficiency factor too hard, that is what they say in the sealed reports. They do not talk about the boundary layers, about how the drift envelopes kept overlapping in ways they should not. When I tried to explain it, they stared like I was making up words. That is the trick, though. Talk about coherence loss in the signal fog and everyone starts to wonder if you even know what you are doing. Easier to hang the fault on the mad navigator than admit they signed off on a lane they did not bother to understand.

The first time I rerouted a live convoy through a blind calibration node, I did it because I wanted to see if the model was right, not because I hated them. No faces, just mass and velocity and a question in the math that would not let me sleep. They made it through. A freighter captain sent a thank-you note for shaving six hours off his run. Nobody wrote back when I flagged the near-miss on the harmonics.

Out here, where I am now, the signals are thin and the people are thinner. A smuggler begged me yesterday for a safer path, said his crew was tired of running dark through debris. I marked up a route for him, but I left one correction out, a tiny offset in the last jump. I want to see if he notices the anomaly, if desperation has taught him to read the gaps. There is a quiet satisfaction in watching someone squint at a chart, knowing you could make it easy and choosing not to. It is the only leverage left that does not come with a bounty attached.

They say I chose this. That I walked away from LIST, from the nice little basement full of sweating clerks and blinking queues. They forget who leaned on me to prove I could clear the backlog, who laughed off my hazard notes because green corridors make for better speeches in New Atlantis. When they erased that settler ship with a single line item, I understood something simple: if the world decides you are a rounding error, the only rational move is to start rounding it instead. So yes, I am hiding in the quiet between beacons, stitching my own lattice out of their discarded lives. I did not pick this role. I just stopped pretending their hands were any cleaner than mine.

Some days I swear I can feel whoever is tracing me breathing down the back of my neck. Ships I never pinged still alter course when I slide into position. Dockmasters close berths just before I arrive. Even out in the quiet, hovering near those dead lanes between Toliman and Sol, traffic control chatter shifts like someone already read my vector corrections and adjusted for them. Used to be I was the one anticipating everyone else. Now it feels like there is a shadow of my shadow, always one move ahead.

It is not redemption I worry about anymore. That used to be the fantasy: pay off the right people, hand over some token confession, go back to towing crippled freighters and complaining about appliance rations on Cydonia. Now the thought of being "brought back into the fold" makes my skin crawl. Redemption means slipping back into their rules, agreeing that crews can be called acceptable losses as long as the forms are filed correctly. I am past that. Morality evolves; I am just early to the next version. If corporations can write off lives for the bottom line, I can write off their cargo. The only difference is I do not pretend it is anything else.

Funny what I miss, though. Before all this I used to keep a little tray of herbs under a cracked viewport, coaxing bitter greens out of bad recycled light. There was something calming about watching roots take hold in cheap soil pellets while I waited in those endless lines for docking clearance, listening to some neighbor two doors down argue about water pressure like that was the greatest injustice in the Settled Systems. Back then the worst part of a shift was a broken kettle or a nosy old man on the corridor asking where my parents were from.

Now I drift between wreckage and paperwork ghosts, splicing my own routes into the gaps they leave when they are sure nobody is looking. I still run the numbers. I still keep the notebooks, track every mass shift, every "abandoned" container I liberate from their ledgers. The fear that keeps me up is not getting caught; it is the slow, growing certainty that whoever is on my trail understands me too well. That they know I no longer want to be forgiven, only proven right.

I used to believe in clean lines. Right and wrong, red and green on a board, safe and unsafe in the margins of a nav sim. You fly the route they give you, you flag the dangers, they fix the map. Simple. Somewhere between the test range and the first time a liaison told me to "adjust my thresholds for acceptable loss," those lines smeared. I keep trying to remember the last moment I felt innocent in a cockpit, just metal and math and nothing else, but all I get are flashes of that shear and the sound of a ship coming apart through the hull. After that, everything is just noise.

People love to tell themselves they are better than their circumstances. Admirals talk about duty while they sign off on numbers they do not understand. Corporate types talk about innovation when what they mean is gambling with other people's organs. I have seen enough of them behind closed doors to know the pattern: grandiose fantasies, complete inability to tolerate uncertainty, a deep need to control every variable but never their own impulses. Textbook, really. They call it leadership to avoid using the correct clinical terms.

So yes, I sell corridors to smugglers, to captains who twitch when they hear "official route." The vulnerable line up for this, whether they admit it or not settlers trying to shave a week off a supply run, haulers dodging tariffs, pirates convinced they are too special to die in someone else's crossfire. Weakness is a vector like any other. If you do not exploit it, someone else will, probably with less precision. At least when they buy from me, they know there is a mind on the other side of the math, not some committee's risk model.

I chose this fringe because it is full of forgotten hardware and lazy record-keeping. Old arrays still listening to ghosts, relay stations no one budgets to decommission. Perfect place to tune the next set of jumps and watch who shows up in the cracks between official grids. They will send hunters eventually, the kind who still believe they are on the side of order. I almost envy them. It must be comforting to think the problem starts and ends with one pilot, instead of the people who taught her exactly how far a line can bend before it breaks.

I used to think people were basically decent. Long time ago, hauling standard freight out of Polvo, I watched dockhands split rations with kids who did not even have boots. Supervisors turning blind eyes so a crate of parts could "accidentally" fall off the manifest and become somebody's air filter, somebody's extra heater. Thought that was what humanity really was small kindnesses under bad lighting. Funny how you never notice the exact moment a belief dies. One day you look up and realize every favor had a ledger on the back, and everyone who smiled at you was already calculating interest.

These days I play games with myself when the guilt flares. Ship of Theseus, Granddad used to tell me about that one. If you replace a hauler's registry, its crew, its declared cargo, its routes, at what point is it no longer the same ship they licensed You can ask the same about a man. If every choice you make is a correction laid over the last one, where exactly did you start doing wrong Sometimes I sit in the cockpit and chase those loops until right and wrong blur into "necessary" and "too late."

I am not ashamed of what I did to that silo outside Akila, or that trial field they loved to parade in front of investors. Watching their clean white domes buckle, grain turning to ash in the spotlights, that felt like balance for once. They use hunger like a knife, just with soft branding and legal disclaimers. Me, I show the blade. When I jammed those valves and watched the pressure climb on the monitors, I remember thinking anyone can sign a complaint, but it takes a stronger back to swing the hammer.

Truth is, it all comes down to instinct. You put an animal in a corner, it bites. You threaten its young, it kills. Dress it up in uniforms and corporate pins all you like, but behavior is just survival paths burning themselves into our heads. I tell myself that when I reroute a shipment, when I leave a convoy without escort because I know what is waiting in that stretch of dark. They would have done the same to us if the numbers told them to. I am just another piece of meat following the line of least fear. Once you accept that, responsibility starts to look like a story people tell to sleep better.

I keep telling myself this place is neutral. Just rock, thin air, a relay's worth of comm traffic bleeding past in the distance. No history, no one loudly dying where I can hear it. That is why I picked it, I think. The systems I touched before had stories. Names on rosters, voices in the queues. This is just coordinates and time.

I remember when every file was a person to me. Early days in The Well, when I still believed LIST was the part of the machine that cared. I would sit after shift, scrolling back through rejected applications, cross-referencing risk models until my eyes burned, looking for a way to shave a percentage point off someone's odds. Frostline was the first crack. Flagged it red three times. Watched the override sail through anyway. Then watched the silence afterward.

After that, something in me started to calcify. I could not keep grieving every decision the numbers made for us, so I leaned harder into the numbers. Reroute a convoy here, delay a maintenance cycle there. At first it was to protect the worst-off colonies, make sure they actually got what they were promised. Somewhere along the line, the equation flipped. I caught myself thinking it was kinder to hurry the failure along, force people out before they drowned slow.

By the time I walked away, I was already gone in all the ways that matter. I had sat in too many debriefs where the words for what happened never showed up on the screen. I had seen a frozen settlement treated as a statistical anomaly, a poisoned harvest filed under "unexpected environmental factors." My empathy did not vanish overnight. It bled out through a hundred small compromises until there was just this cold, clear line: some settlements will die. Better a sharp cut than a lingering infection.

Here, off the lanes, I can trace what I have done without the noise of their voices. The diverted traffic, the delayed approvals, the quiet nudges around worlds that should never have been greenlit. I am not hiding from the people hunting me. I am hiding from whatever is left in me that might still recognize them as human. If I stay long enough, maybe even that last fragile piece of empathy will finally go quiet, and the work ahead will feel as simple as the models say it is.

Elena swears by that awful instant oatmeal from the galley, says it tastes like home. I gave her grief about it this morning, but the way she laughed almost sold me on it. For a few minutes, all of us at the mess table felt like a crew on a boring run again, not ghosts-in-waiting on a ship that spends more time with its transponder off than on. Asha was trying to teach Renee a card game she barely understands herself, Mira was arguing with Darius about flight sims, and the only thing that mattered was who had to clean filters next rotation. It was stupid, small, and I could feel every second of it, like my brain was trying to memorize the shape of the room.

Funny how rare that easy silence is out here. Lately it has been replaced with the soft hum of systems coming online that no one logged, with doors cycling at odd hours, with Elena staying up on the bridge long after her watch has ended. She says she likes the quiet, likes watching the drift of debris and station lights on the scopes, but half the time when I walk in she jumps like I have caught her doing something she should not. Earlier, I passed by the comms bay and heard her speaking low, not in any language I recognized, then the line clicked off the second my boots hit the deck. She smiled too wide and asked if I wanted coffee. I lied and said yes.

There is something else I have not told anyone. Two nights ago, I was running a diagnostic on the nav buffers and found an encrypted burst queued in the outgoing queue, tagged as a maintenance ping. Encryption like that does not come standard, not on a patrol ship like this. I cracked just enough of the header to see it was addressed to a civilian beacon, not UC. I scrubbed my access record and walked away, told myself it was some old cached packet, a glitch, anything but what it looked like. I keep thinking I should bring it up to Darius, or maybe Mira, but every time I picture their faces I also picture that burst actually being nothing, me turning a long voyage into a witch hunt over a hunch. So instead I keep my mouth shut, sip bad coffee in the mess, and try to pretend I do not feel something coiling tighter around this ship with every quiet, unscheduled comms check Elena runs when she thinks nobody is listening.

I keep telling myself we work the dead lanes because it is better than waiting for something to die under you. Black Drift circles the graveyard, cuts, sells, moves on. Simple. Today, watching Nora anchor the mag-lines to that ruptured cargo spine and Rik swear at a stubborn hatch, I almost believed it. Then the bulkhead shifted a centimeter under my boots and every old story about ships that do not want to be stripped crawled right back up my spine.

Calen still swears he saw cabin lights flicker on a hull that had no power, years back. Maris jokes about missing crews that left food half-eaten in the mess, clothes still in the lockers, just suits gone. We laugh, like you do, but nobody goes alone if they can help it. Unspoken rule: if you hear something through the metal that sounds like voices, you do not mention it on open comms.

I keep thinking about her. Not from the Syndicate. Before. A mining station, a breach, alarms screaming while I held her in a maintenance corridor and felt the deck jump with each decompression charge. We had talked, on slow shifts, about leaving for some quiet rock with a patched freighter and a little shop that never would have turned a profit. I never believed it, not really, but I listened, because she needed someone to say "maybe" with her. When the bulkheads started to go, love and loss got so tangled I still cannot pick them apart.

Maybe that is why the fight that ended us hurt worse than the collapse that followed. Stupid argument over a bonus share and whether I was already half gone in my head. Every word hit like shrapnel, and I threw my own back just as hard. We never got to take any of it back before the alarms went off for real.

Now it is easier to keep it all shallow. Talk about cuts, cable loads, reactor cores that might still be hot. Argue with Nora over who gets the prime cabin fittings, pretend I am not watching Rik a little too closely when we turn over anything that looks like personal data. There are things you report to station control and things you keep in-house, and then there are the things you pretend you never saw drifting out there. Those are the ones I try not to think about when the only sound in my helmet is my own breath and the creak of an old ship deciding whether it wants to let go.

Jace says I smile too much when the talk turns ugly.

Maybe he is right. Tonight we were posted up in the back of the warehouse, lights low, just the blue strips along the floor and the glow from the datapads. Ronan had the manifests open, Miguel running numbers, Tomas leaning on a crate like he owned the whole system. I was just supposed to be "eyes", but they did not kick me out when the conversation shifted from lost cargo to which freighter routes "need correcting." That little silence before someone says something that could get them spaced feels like static on my skin. Being in the circle, hearing the names they do not say out loud, it is dangerous. And I like that they finally trust me enough to let me hear it.

Home never felt like that. Back there it was shouting over small things, plates on the counter, work shifts missed, another warning message from school. Every argument made the hallway seem tighter, like the walls were leaning in, pushing me back toward the street. The corner shop on the way home was the only place that felt calm, humming freezer units, bright wrappers. I would grab a TerraBrew Classic and a packet of Choco Bites, sit on the curb until I had to pick a direction. Go upstairs and listen to more yelling, or keep walking until the noise faded and the city felt big again. Funny how easy it was to keep walking.

Now the rumors reach even us. Stories about fields going bad on outer rocks, about some hauler ghosting between co-ops, leaving soil that does not behave. I heard Miguel say "you do not move that much cargo without friends in suits" and Ronan just snorted and changed the subject. There is talk about Red Harvest ships being hit in the dark, about manifests that do not add up, and nobody wants to be the one to say the same name twice in a row. Even here, where we paint our sigil on walls and carry knives like jewelry, there are things we only talk around, never through.

Still, when Tomas waves me over instead of telling me to run the door, when he says "listen close, Barrantes," it feels like standing in that corner shop again, knowing I am not going home yet. The streets have their own kind of welcome. They do not ask if you are right or wrong, just if you can keep your hands steady when everyone else starts shouting.

I used to draw the sky on paper.

Back in LIST, they laughed when I burned through whole reams sketching out corridors we would never file. Now I would give a lot to have even one of those stupid sheets, just to remember when a line on a chart did not mean someone died at the far end of it.

I left Jemison in a hurry after the hearing. They called it "irregularities" as if misaligned waypoints were a clerical error, not an argument I lost. Security walked me out. My old jacket is probably still on the back of that office chair in The Well, pockets full of broken styluses and a Transit chip that would get me three minutes in front of Phil Hill's terminals. I keep thinking about that jacket, like if I had it I could still walk back in and fix all of this with one clean submission.

Of course, I cannot go back.

The valley was the first test. Nudge a few flight computers through that dead survey node, see if the lane bends the way the models say it will. It did. The haulers cursed the wind and kept flying. No one looks at the code if they can blame the weather.

I tell myself every adjustment is a mercy. Divert the convoys that will never get escort, that cross too close to where Spacers feed. Better to lose a cargo run early than watch another Narion play out. That is the story I repeat when I cannot sleep.

I chose this rock because it is nothing. Poor atmosphere, no ore worth fighting over, only a handful of desperate civilians who know better than to ask why their supply ships always arrive a little off schedule but never vanish. From here I can see three junctions at once, three places where I can move a decimal and shift a dozen lives away from open slaughter. Or into it, if I misjudge.

What I am afraid of is not the bounty. It is someone patient enough to read the pattern, to see that the same hand that saved a few settlements also emptied others for buyers with clean boots and dirty ledgers. When they come, they will not shout. They will bring black boxes, refugee stories, every erased draft I thought I had buried under dust and old antennas.

I hope, stupidly, that they find that child before they find me. If anyone gets to decide what I am in the end, it should be one of the few who lived through what my perfect little route did to them.

First time I saw a convoy die on my numbers, I did not sleep for three days. All those calls on open band, all those transponders winking out one after another, the way they did back at Cheyenne. Then the casualty lists came through and the payout graphs followed right behind them, rising nice and neat. That is when I understood; the lanes were already killing people. All I did was make sure some of the deaths landed on the right balance sheets.

I keep thinking about the little festivals we used to throw aboard the old escort ship, back when I still wore UC colors. Someone would smuggle up a bottle from New Atlantis, a deckhand would string cheap lights through the corridor for our "Founding Day," and we would crowd into a mess barely big enough for ten. We sang old Earth songs we barely remembered the words to. The captain always made a speech about duty and sacrifice, then went back to sending under-armed civvies through fire because someone planetside needed their shipment on schedule. That was the education.

Later, when I started selling routes, I picked my clients carefully. The corporate lines that made fortunes gaming insurance while veterans slept in docks got the leanest margins, the prettiest detours, the ones that passed just a little too close to raider country. It was cruelty, yes, but not random. Teach a man that running human lives like numbers has no cost and he will never stop. Introduce cost. Make it sharp. Make it memorable.

Why here People ask me that without using words, with the way they look at the places I disappear into. Right now it is easier to sit in a neon-lit hole on the edge of nowhere, where every corridor smells like recycled sweat and cheap liquor, and watch the traffic streams roll by. From here I can see how the lanes bend between UC and Freestar space, how GalBank pretends not to notice the same anomalies repeating. If I keep moving between these forgotten stations and memorial ridges, staying just ahead of whatever bounty they whisper about, I can still nudge the board a few more times.

What I am afraid of is not getting caught. It is that in the end, the convoys will keep dying on someone else's numbers, and all anyone will remember is the monster they called Vector, not the lesson the lanes were trying to teach.

I keep thinking about that girl back in the lower decks on Volii, the one with the busted respirator fan. I patched that thing three different times, scavved the last motor coil off my own bunk fan, and she still kept running dust through it like nothing mattered. Every time I tried to fix it, she met me halfway with a shrug and a "thanks, Ty," then went right back to choking the filters. Kind of feels like I've been doing that ever since, except the fans are people and the dust is all the bad choices we breathe in like normal air.

These days the soundtrack in the blocks is boots on metal and someone yelling through teeth. A beating in the stairwell, a threat hissed in a lift, Maris pressing a guy's face into a vending machine until coins rain out. None of us flinch anymore; we just step around the blood and keep walking. Lena jokes about it, calls it "motivational feedback." Ezra says if you stop reacting, you stop being a target. I pretend it works. Truth is, it just makes it harder to remember there's another way to live.

The Slick Block Runners like to talk about choice, but I figured out what it really means the first time I heard what happens to kids who walk away. Not right then and there. They wait. Let you get soft, find a new bed, a small routine. Then they turn up, or someone "unaffiliated" does. Leaving isn't freedom; it is a sentence with the date scratched off. Everyone knows it. No one says it out loud.

Funny thing is, it didn't start with some big oath. I got on their radar because I rerouted one little power line for Rion, just so his corner card den could siphon juice from a corporate kiosk. One harmless favor, I told myself. Better I do it than some hack fry the grid. Week later, I'm sitting across from Jenna, her boots up on the table, hearing how "useful" I am. That word still makes my stomach twist.

When things go quiet, I still strip old handhelds and fix whatever I can't sell. Broken comms, glitchy game bricks, cheap holo-pens that stutter when you write too fast. The others laugh, say I should be rerouting bank nodes instead of toy circuits, but there's something clean about putting a tiny world back together and knowing it will stay fixed unless someone really tries to break it. Makes the rest of it feel less inevitable, even if I know better.

Kara says if I keep talking to this pad instead of checking my lines, I am going to end up part of the wreck instead of stripping it. She is not wrong, but some days the hum of the cutter is not enough to drown out the rest.

We bounced again today. Another orbit, another safe berth burned. Dead Orbit never sits in one dock long; we hop from one quiet anchorage to the next, always a little ahead of rival crews and whatever passes for law in that system. You start to feel like a piece of junk in a slow spin, never quite sure which way is down.

The derelict we cracked this week, some GalBank contract hauler, still had power flickering along one corridor. That is always the worst, when the ship does not know it is dead yet. I was on point, Kara handling the torch, and the whole time I kept thinking about that other transport they say drifted back full of corpses and one survivor who would not talk. Hangar gossip travels faster than any tug.

We argued about the nav cores again. I say you pull the boards, you log them clean, you sell them to people who will put them back in honest ships. Half the crew laughs at "honest ships" like it is a joke. Some of those cores tell the same story, you know; routes bent a little too close to bad neighborhoods, same pattern of hits along the lane. Nobody wants to write that part down.

There are unspoken rules in Dead Orbit. You do not cut into sealed crew quarters unless you have to. You report any live signals, even if you could pretend you did not hear them. You do not bring back stories from the Narion side unless the bar is already loud enough to swallow the silence afterward. We have broken all of those at least once.

I still see that one rider suit tumbling past my visor sometimes, arms out like it was trying to grab hold of the hull. We never found the tether. Officially that job went clean, no casualties. Kara and I do not correct the record when the newer hands ask. They are scared enough.

Tomorrow we are pushing again, shifting the Collective to a quieter orbit before that rival cutter gang closes the gap. Salvage life is always a half-step ahead of someone else's claim or someone else's gun. It wears on you, all that movement from one "safe" spot to the next, but staying still out here feels worse. At least if we are moving, the ghosts do not have time to catch up.

Docked somewhere nameless, still hearing the creak of that last hull every time the air recycler ticks.

We took a contract on a drifted freighter out past the regular lanes, nothing special on the listing. Rhett piloted us in, riding the debris like he was born in it, while Calen handled the line guns. I drew boarding with two of the new hands, which meant spending half the run reminding them not to kick every floating tool they saw. Plasma burns on the outer skin, no distress call in the logs. That is the kind of thing you pretend not to notice until you are back in hard gravity.

Inside smelled wrong. Old smoke, coolant, that sharp tang of extinguishers that actually fired. No bodies, just suits hanging where people should have been. One of the kids misjudged a jump, clipped a jagged beam, took a strip of suit and skin off his calf. No medtech, no time to cycle him back, so I sealed the tear with sealant foam and wrapped the leg in torn insulation and a ration packet wrapper. He yelped, then went quiet the way people do when they realize how thin the line is between "close call" and headline on a station board.

We found the cargo holds barely touched, which is never good news. Crates of drive components, pristine, like someone had loaded for a long haul and never got to the first jump. Rhett swore under his breath when he saw the lot numbers; said he had heard about a run of ships with the same gear that all "got unlucky" near the same patch of deep. Calen just grunted and tagged the pallets, eyes doing math only he could see.

Back in the yard, over cheap beer and bad music, people talk quieter about that region now. Stories about misjumps that look too neat, wrecks lined up in a spiral if you plot them right. Some swear there is a numbers man behind it, someone who can bend routes just a degree or two and let gravity do the rest. Union foreman says we are not in the business of asking why junk falls where it does, just in hauling it home.

Maybe he is right. Still, when I am out on a tether and the ship under me is spinning wrong, I catch myself wondering if some analyst on a warm station deck penciled that misfortune in, decided this crew was a better bet as salvage than as neighbors on a station barstool. Then I check my seals again, tighten my grip on the cutter, and tell myself it is just bad luck, same as always.

When I was a kid on my father's freighter, I used to lie awake terrified the grav drive would misfire and leave us smeared between stars.

I would stare at the bulkhead and listen for the pitch change, sure that if I caught it half a second early, I could somehow stop it.

Funny.

I have ridden drives past their safe curves more times than I can count since then, danced a whole convoy through micro-meteor showers on a whisper of thrust.

Back then I was afraid of the machine.

Now I know the real danger is the people who write where the machine goes.

Kraye likes to dress it up in theory, in language about probabilities and state actors.

I see it much simpler.

You measure your worth by how much pressure you can put on a system before it bends, and how long it keeps that new shape after you let go.

Convoys, patrol routes, whole factions; they are all just structures.

You lean, they warp.

If they do not, you push harder.

I will admit something I never have to him.

When everyone follows the path I set without a flicker of resistance, I get bored.

Perfect compliance is dull.

I want the captain who fights the advisory, the Ranger who reroutes against my lane, the hunter who burns hard just to spite the numbers.

Breaking those people is interesting.

They make me earn it.

Tonight I tried to ping my mother through a backdoor GalBank contact in HopeTown.

Had the channel keyed, encryption ready, fingers hovering over the mic.

I just stared at the blinking cursor.

What do you say after vanishing into the dark with a man everyone curses by name.

"Hi, it is Hessa, I am alive and using the tricks you taught me on that old freighter to reroute strangers into killboxes."

I killed the line instead.

Everyone out there judging me, writing warrants and speeches, likes to pretend they would have done better.

Faced with the same files I saw, the same signatures authorizing a settlement's death for a clean validation, they would have walked away, they say.

Liars.

Maybe they would have kept taking the paycheck, told themselves it was above their clearance.

Maybe they would have gone home, hugged their children, and prayed someone else made the ugly calls.

I did not pretend.

I took what I knew and started bending back.

If that makes me a monster, then at least I am an honest one.

I keep hearing that word in other people's mouths: regret. Pilots in bars, widows on distant rocks, even the ones who chased my routes and did not make it back. It is a luxury they cling to so they can pretend there was another line they could have flown. I do not have that problem. Every choice I made was the correct one. The convoy at Lunara, the diverted lifeboat, the copied charts, the day I stopped erasing wreck coordinates and started keeping them. Each decision followed from the last like points on a plotted curve. You do not apologize for the shape of a vector; you just acknowledge where it leads.

There are nights I feel the old recordings pressing at the edges of my thoughts, helmet audio from people who never cleared the blast radius. That is when I start talking myself into circles. I tell myself I am mapping systems, not lives. That the routes are neutral, the politics wrapped around them after the fact. I build these clean layers of logic, stack them like grav equations, until the faces blur into data and the screams become signal noise under the jump capacitors' whine. It is a trick and I know it, a way of pretending there is depth to the justification when mostly it is just momentum: once you start adjusting beacons, it is easier to keep nudging them than to admit that first nudge mattered.

The Cold Room is the only place that still feels honest to me. Floating out there above that gas giant, the barge does exactly what it was built to do: store the past and keep it cold. No flags, no briefings, just metal and orbits. I hid there because the UC thinks in straight lines and that ship sits in the blind spot between their lanes. Crimson captains respect what I can sell them more than they care about who I used to salute. Freestar patrols stay away; too many of their dead are in the wrecks I indexed. Here, in the dark between those rival floodlights, I can chart the lattice my way.

They will come eventually. SysDef, a Ranger, some freelancer with more curiosity than sense. They will trace the tampered debris field, the bent manifests, the whispered stories about a navigator who can make whole convoys disappear into "salvage." I am not running from that. I am waiting to see whether the next person through the hatch understands what I have been doing, or whether I have to open another airlock and simplify the equation again.

Rowan says the hardest part is how quickly the uniforms stopped mattering. One day you are polishing insignia for inspection, next day you are wearing the same jacket but with the patches ripped off and the same people calling you "unauthorized actors" over an encrypted channel. The stitching still itches where I tore the crest away. I have not decided if that was freedom or just another order I followed, this time from myself.

Breakaway lives on patched gear and bad rations now. Tonight we ate reheated field stew out of dented mess tins on a cargo crate, same as we did in the forward camps, except this time we bought the cans off a spacer who did not care whose side we used to be on. Rowan is still cutting his sleeves to hide the unit tattoos; says they draw the wrong kind of attention in certain docks. I keep mine visible. Habit, or defiance, I am not sure.

I think about the operation nobody mentions by name, the one they airbrushed out of the briefing archive. The "infrastructure denial" mission where the targets were supposed to be hardened bunkers, but the satellite feed looked an awful lot like prefab housing to me. Afterward, command told us we misinterpreted the imagery. Debrief said all structures were lawful objectives. Funny how the casualty reports came back redacted, whole families' worth of ghosts hidden behind classification codes. That is when I started listening to the way they chose their words, and the gaps between them.

Rowan walked first, then a few others. I held on longer, told myself somebody decent had to stay in to keep things from getting worse. Then they asked us to sign off on another "containment strike," this time with even less intel, and my pen would not move. Now I carry out jobs given in whispers instead of on data slates, alongside people whose loyalty is to each other, not to some flag hanging in a sealed council chamber. 

Discipline does not just evaporate. We still run checks, still break down our rifles after every sortie, still fold our blankets the same way we were taught in basic. But under it all there is this constant tension: old oaths humming in the bones, new loyalties growing like scar tissue around them. Some nights I lie awake in my bunk, listening to the ship's recycled air, and wonder which version of me was the deserter the one who stayed too long, or the one who finally walked.

I have always done my best work in other people's blind spots.

Back at Sol Cleanup, they called me a stabilizing influence. Calm voice on the loop, hands steady on the board while everyone else panicked over bad readings. Funny thing is, the calm never went away after the freighter died. The outrage did. The grief did. Those burn out fast. What stayed was the geometry. Angles and margins and the quiet understanding that someone has to decide which ship gets the safe corridor and which one gambles with the debris.

They called that cruelty once. I called it triage.

Sera chose to scream at the sky. I chose to learn from it. They wanted the report padded, so I padded it and took a copy for myself. They wanted a clean narrative, so I gave them one and kept the dirty math running in a separate process. If that makes me complicit, then fine; at least I am complicit with my eyes open. Most of them are guilty by habit, which is so much worse.

People flinch when I talk about using incidents as leverage. They do not understand that fear is a tool like any other. You tighten a route here, you loosen one there, you orchestrate a near miss in front of the right audience and suddenly GalBank, UC, Freestar, they are all paying attention to orbital safety in a way they never did when warnings were just memos. Discipline, not malice. You do not forge better captains and controllers by cushioning every mistake. You put them close enough to the edge that they finally learn where it is.

Only a few can stomach that logic. The enlightened, as it were. The rest toss around words like "monster" because it is easier than admitting they like their comfort more than they like the truth. They do not deserve the full explanation. They have not earned it.

I came out toward Deimos again because junk remembers. The old shells up here still carry the fingerprints of a hundred short-sighted decisions, cluttered orbits that were never fully cleaned because it was cheaper to ignore them. It is the perfect proving ground and the perfect hiding place. UC does not look too closely at ghosts it helped create.

From here I can run the sims on real mass, real drift, adjust my network, test how quickly a hunter can be herded once I start nudging their beacons. I am not fleeing. I am choosing altitude. Let them think they are closing in. Every vector they follow, I drew for them.

I always thought the clever ones would be the last to burn. The ones who read the whole briefing, saw the holes, and built something workable around the gaps. Turns out the clever ones just get to understand exactly how and when they are being sold out.

When the coolant system failed in that lab, the first thing they did was show me the safety logs. Not the bodies, not the scorch on the bulkheads, the logs. They wanted me to sign off that it was a freak alignment of bad numbers instead of the deliberate blind spot I had flagged three times. The footage missing from the cameras was just a "corrupted segment." I told myself, sitting in that debrief room, that if I played along I could do more good outside the blast radius than inside it. That was the first lie I promoted from thought to policy.

Following Alesha out was supposed to be the corrective. They would starve the outer colonies on principle; we would find a way to route grain and code around their indifference. Simple. Elegant, even. Every time I bent a rule, every time I let a shipment pass without the right inspection, I folded it into this greater intellectual framework in my head: strategic rebalancing, emergent supply ethics, anything but what it was, which was me quietly panicking that without this cause I was just another hired gun.

This rock suits me because it is nothing. No name anyone remembers, no trade lanes except the ones I write myself. It is a place you only get to by ignoring three different advisories and trusting a route that does not officially exist. That is the kind of anonymity I understand. I have dug in here because it gives me time to reroute what is left of our network, to cache what I can before someone higher up decides the easiest way to solve their problem is to glass whatever field happens to be glowing too bright.

I know they are circling closer. I have seen the UC analysis fragments leak back into my channels, seen freelancers comparing notes on patterns they should not even be aware of. Part of me is almost relieved. If they find me, maybe I stop having to redraw this line in my head between necessary harm and the kind that wakes me at night. Until then, I will keep fortifying, keep telling myself that holding this ground a little longer will tip the balance for people who have never met me. It is either that or admit that some of the blood under my boots never had to be spilled at all.

I used to log tonnage and trajectories.  
Now I log the dead.

When I close my eyes I still see their signatures, the Bolivian hauler crew that never made it home because some admiral wanted the battle map to look cleaner. I watched them erase those lives with a keystroke and a stamped approval. "Collateral," they said. "For morale." So yes, I left. Quietly, efficiently. I took the algorithms they trusted me with, the same ones I once used to keep their lanes safe, and I turned them inside out. If they will not remember the truth of those corridors, I will carve it into the sky for them.

People call what I do cruel. As if the war was kind. As if letting them drift on in their lies is some softer mercy. I steer ships, yes. I lean on beacons, nudge a jump vector, widen a drift they never see. It scares them. Good. Fear sharpens. A soft civilization rots around its own myths; a hard one is forced to look at what it did and decide if it can live with that. I am not slaughtering innocents. I am disciplining a species that decided comfort mattered more than memory. Pain is how we remember where the fire is.

Chorus Point was the first place that felt honest. A dead shell of a relay, hanging in the dark, surrounded by machines that only know how to listen. Perfect. I rebuilt its logic, turned it from a warning buoy into a pen that writes in traffic patterns instead of ink. Out here I can see every little correction they make, every "unavoidable" misjump, and answer in kind. It is far enough from New Atlantis that the officials only see numbers, not the shapes I am drawing.

I know they are sending hunters now. UC wants their secrets buried, Freestar wants a show trial, Deimos just wants me gone so their ledgers stay clean. Let them come. They will call me mad, fanatic, monster. I will call them soft. I do not fear dying out here; I fear only that I will not finish the constellation, that the Axis will remain half-written, and they will manage to sand the edges off history again.

If they reach me, they will find the wrecks arranged with care, names I dug out of corrupted drives, personal effects stacked where the living can see them.
