They will call it a shrine and miss the point. This is discipline. This is a lesson engraved in metal and vacuum. If the living will not carry the weight of what they have done, I will lash it to their routes until they either break or grow strong enough to face it.

Not sure why I still write these. Habit, I guess. Same reason I still tap bulkheads when I walk past them, counting out the weight like it matters in a station that barely moves.

There was a time I thought doing the right thing would count for something. I burned propellant we did not have trying to nudge that hauler out of the field, stayed on the line with them longer than the regs allowed, lied on three separate forms just to keep their case open another cycle. You know how that ended. The only numbers anyone cared about were loss projections and premiums. The crew became tonnage with signatures under it. That was the night I learned kindness is just another vector. Easy to push on. Easy to exploit.

After that, it was not a jump from "this is wrong" to "this is useful." Once you admit the universe does not pay out for good behavior, all the old rules start to look like ballast. There is this line in an old text they made us read once, about how there is no universal measure, only what men agree to pretend is true. Felt pretentious then. Sounds practical now. If morality is just consensus, and the consensus decided some people are acceptable loss, then shifting a few hulls off the books is not crime. It is correction.

I am not stupid enough to spell out routes or names in here. Assume every channel is dirty. Every buoy, every locker node, every "private" relay. Someone is always listening, even if they do not understand what they are hearing yet. So I write in fragments and weights and angles, things that only make sense if you already know the structure.

What I want is simple: take the dead mass they wrote off and use it like a lever until something important cracks. Frontier crews getting ships for scrap rates while insurers quietly eat the difference. Certain "untouchable" registries waking up to find their clean losses smeared with questions. If that makes me a villain in some clerk's training sim, fine. I am long past chasing their version of hero.

Still, every time I route a new job through a station that "never sees trouble," I feel the same weight in my gut I felt watching that first crew drift. Funny. Even after you decide the game is rigged, part of you still waits for someone kind to step in and change the rules. I stopped believing they would. Now I am just hoping they are slow enough that I can finish what I started before they finally learn how to read between their own lines.

Among independent captains plying the sparse lanes near KN-9575, the name Central Watch carries a peculiar weight. Officially, they are listed in a few aging registry entries as a civilian survey crew contracted to monitor navigation beacons and debris fields around former UC patrol routes. Unofficially, traders say Central Watch make a habit of arriving late to disasters and early to coverups, their patched hauler slipping in to catalog wreckage and quietly redirect any black box or flight log that might embarrass old connections in the Core.  

Their shipboard customs are the stuff of spacer gossip: new hands reportedly sit a "silent watch" on first shift, staring through the forward blister in total radio silence while the others review last year's incident reports, a ritual meant to remind them that every contact they ignore becomes someone else's cautionary tale. Crew slang reflects the same fatalism; to "central" a problem is to lock it in a private log and hope no one ever calls audit on it. More than one dockside teller notes that their captain flinches whenever a manifest lists certain surnames common in Sol-born communities, as if terrified that some forgotten cousin or sibling will surface in the wreckage they pick through.  

In recent cycles, their presence around KN-9575 has drawn quiet attention. They were seen orbiting the derelict longer than any salvage contract would justify, and local haulers whisper that Central Watch passed up easy scrap to chase encrypted fragments in the ship's dead comms array. Some say they are finally cleaning up "old family business," others that they are trying to keep a lineage shame from ever hitting a public docket. Whatever the truth, station clerks report a subtle change in their demeanor: fewer jokes in the mess, more time spent in front of open reports, and one terse comment overheard about "signing our names to the things we walked away from."  

Rumor has it that after a long, tense orbit of the derelict, Central Watch requested no hazard bump, no quiet stipend, and refused to falsify the incident time stamps, letting the record show exactly how long the region went unprotected. For crews that have traded with them for years, this marks a shift. The watchers who once specialized in looking away now seem determined to look straight at the uglier pieces of their own history, even if it means admitting they were part of why ships like KN-9575 were left to drift alone.

I used to write for committees and tribunals, not for myself. Cloud patterns, variance bands, confidence intervals. No one ever asked how it felt to stand under a sky you had bent with your own hands. Maybe that is why I am here, hiding between jumps and storm cells, talking into a recorder instead of to another human being.

They say I falsified the models. Easier to blame one overconfident specialist than admit the framework everyone signed off on had a blind spot big enough to swallow a settlement. I keep looping the data in my head, frame by frame. If I had raised the thresholds, delayed the deployment, ignored the pressure from above to hit the "viable" milestone, would the wind have still found that resonance. The numbers say no. The screaming says yes. I am tired of being the only one who hears it.

I picked these edges of space because they are noisy in the right ways. Lightning-rich grids, old regulator networks, mining reactors that cough out just enough interference to hide a few extra lines of code. A good storm is the perfect place to disappear. You slip your corrections into maintenance updates, ride along on power audits and sensor recalibrations. Nobody audits the auditors. Not really.

Tonight I almost pinged home. I even opened the channel, typed in an old ID. Thought about sending a simple "I am alive" to the one person who kept a mug on my desk long after I stopped drinking coffee. Stared at the cursor until my eyes hurt. What do you say after this long. "Sorry the newsfeeds turned me into a murderer." "By the way, the equations were right and everyone else is wrong." I closed the channel. It felt like hanging up on a stranger.

They are closing in. I can feel it in the way contracts are phrased now, in the sudden caution from the usual intermediaries. Ryujin's pets stop smiling when my name comes up. Frontier liaisons drop their voices when they talk about "that ship that outran the storm." Someone is finally reading the weather like I do, seeing the same arcs across different maps.

I am heading toward one more thin-atmosphere world on the fringe of a Helium-3 chain. The data there has the same fracture signature as the first disaster, just fainter, like an echo. If I can catch it in the act, isolate the interaction, maybe I prove this was never just me playing god with other people's crops. Maybe I die with cleaner math. Either way, the sky is going to do something interesting when I get there.

I used to sign my name at the bottom of forms and believe it meant something.

"Layla Al Mansoor, inspector of record." I would walk a ship from nose to tail with a tablet and a TerraBrew cooling in my hand, check the same junctions, listen to the same half-bored captains swear their drives had "never given them any trouble." We would argue over minor variances, I would win because the manual said so, and everyone went home. Unremarkable work. Steady. I slept then. I miss the boredom more than I miss the rank.

Now I sleep in crawlspaces and engine bays, because walls and windows feel like invitations. Node Gray hums to itself in the dark, a ring of metal in an empty rock, chewing space in millimeter bites. Every micro-jump we put through it adds a data point. Every data point inches the graph toward the threshold I calculated and then pretended I had not. If I am right, the Settled Systems have already stepped over it. If I am wrong, I am killing myself out here for a phantom.

I fled because they made it clear that the choice was silence or erasure. They shelved the reports, massaged the numbers, called the survivors "statistical anomalies" and me "over-attached to outliers." Then the long-haul freighter ripped itself open on a route I had personally cleared, and a cadet I had certified came back with eyes that did not quite track the same reality as mine. I started seeing that look everywhere after a chains of jumps. Once you see it, you cannot unsee it.

So I stole what I needed. Algorithms no one wanted used the way they were meant to be used. A regulator tuned past sanity. Telemetry from ships that were officially "lost to mechanical failure." I threaded my way out through places like Old Selene, where no one asks why your IDs do not match your face as long as your credits clear. Drift 7 proved the pattern was not local. The clinic on Gagarin proved it was not just in my head. The wreck out near Cheyenne proved it was not going away on its own.

Hunters will come. UC wants a neat story of a mad saboteur. Freestar will want to know if they can point that story at the core worlds. House Va'ruun will see omens where there are only equations. I chose this station because it sits exactly where the math says the universe is thinnest and because it was already forgotten by the people who built it. If they find me here, it will mean they have followed the same fractures I did, and then it is no longer just my nightmare to carry.

I do my best thinking where no one can see me. Right now that is a maintenance berth tucked just off a dusty approach lane, ship on low power, scopes listening harder than I am breathing. The good thing about parking near those weather-torn corridors is that everyone assumes you are either crazy or lost. No one imagines you chose the turbulence on purpose.

Why here? Because the models say this patch of sky is an oversight. Patrol routes bend around the worst of the dust scatter, commercial traffic hugs the cleared lanes. That leaves a thin sliver where transponder noise passes for background radiation. I can sit in that sliver and watch them all go by. Change a bearing here, adjust a safety margin there. They do not even know who is doing the nudging. They just call it bad luck or a clever contractor.

I used to believe people were better than that. Back when I was a kid on that cramped station, the teachers talked about cooperation and duty until one of the air recyclers failed and the adults quietly shut down half the hydro beds to keep the system from crashing. I watched my mother uproot plants she had tended for years, no ceremony, no speeches, just a fast, brutal choice. That was the first time I understood the universe does not care how gentle the story sounds in your primer. You save what you can reach. Everything else is numbers.

It is easier, now, to say human behavior is just instinct dressed up in uniforms and mission statements. Push survival hard enough and everyone reverts to pattern: protect your own, hoard information, sacrifice the distant. If that is true, then I am not a monster for doing what comes naturally. I am just better at reading the map.

Of course, that is the story I tell myself when I cannot sleep. That I only smoothed the data around the disaster because panic helps no one. That I only sell storm windows to captains who would run those routes anyway, with or without my equations. That hiding near this approach lane is not cowardice, just prudent use of my skills.

What I am really afraid of is someone patient enough to trace the same lines I do. To notice the ships that always come through the storms a little too clean, the logs that always lose a few seconds in the same band of interference. If they follow that pattern long enough, it leads here. To the man who keeps pretending his instincts are in charge, so he can avoid admitting each of these "natural" choices was something he calculated down to the decimal.

I used to worry about stupid things. Air filters in the bunk clogging, hydro lines dripping condensation on my cot, auto-debits hitting my GalBank account for a cabin I barely saw on Jemison. Even had a plant once, some hardy little vine I kept by the viewport in Gagarin. It browned out the month I forgot to reset the grow lamp after a long sim cycle. Always told myself I would fix it tomorrow. I never did.  

People talk about redemption like it is a port you can always divert to if the drive holds. I used to believe that. File the inquiry, push the data up the chain, trust that someone above you cares what you saw. Now the thought of being "cleared" twists my stomach. Not because I think it is out of reach, but because I do not want them to wash me clean and fold me back into their ledger. I have seen the math they call acceptable loss; I will not be one of their numbers again.  

Out here, with only my slates and the hum of the grav rings, it is easy to believe I am the only one willing to run the real calculations. Someone has to decide which route gets the families through and which one the pirates follow and which one never should have been drawn at all. Once, in a HopeTown bar, a young hauler sat across from me, hands shaking around a cheap drink. He was three payments behind, desperate for a shortcut that would make his next run in half the time. I watched the way he glanced at the debt notices on his slate, listened to the strain in his voice, and I knew exactly how far I could push him. I sold him a corridor I had tested only once, skirting a field I still do not fully understand. I added safety edits he could not read, warnings buried in notation only a trained cartographer would see. He never asked the right questions. I never offered them.  

I remember swearing to myself, after Echo-19, that I would never again let someone else push my hand on a route decision. No more following orders when the numbers were wrong. Somewhere along the way I broke that promise without noticing, telling myself that if I held the pen, it was different. That selling options was not the same as forcing a jump.  

Now I sit on the edge of nowhere, watching my own paths crisscross the dark, and the thing that keeps me awake is not the thought of a bounty hunter finding me. It is the possibility that someone, somewhere, might still offer me a way back, a uniform, a clean record. I am not afraid they will refuse me. I am afraid, in a weak moment, I might say yes.

I keep the ship's clock pinned to that timestamp. No matter where I jump, no matter what local time the port insists on, my chronometer is always set to the minute the lane folded and all those voices cut out mid-sentence. People think that is morbid. It is just reference. If I let them move that, they can move anything.

There was a junior controller once, back on station, who kept second-guessing my corrections. Fresh cert, bright eyes, still believed the numbers coming off the board were sacred. I remember taking his hand off my shoulder more sharply than I needed to, digging my fingers into the meat just above the elbow, watching his face as it went from surprise to pain to compliance. I did it to see if he would break or hold my stare. When he looked away first, I felt this cold, clean satisfaction settle in my chest. That is how you know who can be trusted with the mesh and who cannot. The sky does not have room for soft hands.

I left because I watched the mesh get used like a weapon and then watched the same people who armed it sit in judgment of the fallout. The inquiry room smelled like recycled air and fear-sweat, and every time I tried to show them what had been overwritten, the logs came back cleaner than before. That is when I knew the truth is not something you present to them; it is something you drag out into the open where they cannot quietly fix it.

Here, tucked out past the official lanes, I can see the traffic from a distance, like watching a spider web from the corner of the room instead of standing in the middle of it. Forgotten relays, retired listening posts, dead corridors the charts pretend are empty. Perfect places to splice in my own feeds, test how far I can bend a route before it snaps, measure how fast command Looks Away when the wrong ships go missing.

What I am afraid of is not dying. That part is inevitable, and probably loud. What I am afraid of is waking up one day and realizing I cannot tell which edits are mine and which are theirs anymore. That the sealed channel I heard in the middle of the disaster was just another voice in my own head. So I keep backing up the rawest data I can steal, scattering it across caches and hands I do not like but can at least predict. If they send someone competent to find me, they will follow the distortions I left behind. Maybe they will kill me. Maybe they will finally see what I have been trying to show them since the minute that lane collapsed. Either way, the mesh will remember.

I have been thinking about that old saying, the one they slapped over the academy doors back in New Atlantis. Some Greek, some Roman, I forget which. Stoics, maybe. The point was always the same: virtue is clear-eyed calculation, not flinching. They taught us that without meaning to. Numbers first, feelings later. I just took the lesson further than they were comfortable admitting.

Everyone keeps calling what I did "crimes." As if survival, scaled up to a systems model, becomes something else. The UC was doing the same math long before I walked into the MAST building. They called it strategic prioritization, acceptable attrition, risk-balanced deployment. I call it what it is: not dying quietly in someone else's spreadsheet. When I sell a forecast to a pirate captain or a frightened homesteader, I am giving them a chance to move from the wrong column to the right one.

I remember the first time I read a loss report that listed a settlement I had actually visited. Kids playing under a half-built dome, dust in their hair. When the raid came, my projection said "within tolerance." I could not sleep for three nights. Now I watch casualty curves update in real time and feel the same way I do watching a storm track: interested, professional. Once I would have called that decay. Lately I am leaning toward calling it enlightenment. Detachment lets you see the whole board; the people who break are the ones still clinging to individual pieces.

Guilt is just a conditioned response anyway, a reflex hammered into us by civics teachers and recruitment ads. A useful tool for keeping citizens docile, auditors obedient. I have dissected that feeling the way I have dissected budgets and routes, and I can see where it was stapled on. It still twitches sometimes, like a phantom limb, but it does not move my hand.

I chose this pattern of hiding in the in-between spaces because that is where no one thinks to look. Out here, at a dead node where patrol schedules used to be written, the old systems still recognize my credentials. I can see how they used to bend routes around "sensitive assets," how easy it is to shift that curve a few degrees, how quietly it all happens. Once, the idea of touching those lines myself would have shocked me. Now I trace them without hesitation, because if I do not, someone else will, and they will not even pretend to care about the balance.

Survival is not noble. It is just arithmetic. I am tired of being the only one honest enough to say so.

I keep thinking about the first time I cheated the numbers and watched a ship arrive early instead of late. Everyone else saw a glitch; I saw proof that reality flexes if you push it hard enough. They called it reckless, selfish, endangering crews for "theoretical gains." But what is selfish about seeing a storm on the horizon and stepping out of its path first? All I ever did was move myself and a few paying clients off the firing line before everyone else realized how rigged the charts were.

They like to whisper that I have blood on my hands, that some of the captains who took my cuts never docked again. Maybe. Space eats people. It always has. When a Crimson Fleet raider learns that shaving a day off a route also means flying blind through a gravity eddy, that is not murder; that is education. If you buy a miracle vector from a stranger in a Neon back room and never once ask how it works, whatever happens to you after that is a lesson the rest of the sector needs to see written in twisted hulls.

Anchorpoint is quiet tonight. Too quiet. Every time the bulkhead pops or the life-support fans spool down, it sounds like magnetic boots on the deck, like someone finally followed one of my old signatures home. I tell myself it is just old metal and cheap maintenance, but sleep does not stick. I lie there counting the cycles of the beacons outside, waiting for one of them to stutter in a way that says someone else is writing their own equations up here.

Once, back on Jemison, I believed in purpose. Exploration. Defense. All those neat words they put on recruitment posters. Then I watched committees massage casualty projections until they fit the budget, watched routes get cleared because they were politically convenient, not safe. After that, it is hard to pretend there is any grand meaning to cling to. If everything is just drift and spin dressed up in mission statements, then any move you make is as valid as any other. Stealing models, selling paths, vanishing ships all permissible rearrangements of matter in a universe that does not care.

So I sit here in this rock with its borrowed air and its quiet instruments, tweaking corridors at the edge of what the drives will tolerate. Is it redemption, making the math cleaner, more "efficient"? Is it just another way to stay ahead of whoever is hunting me? Does it matter? The currents are there to be found. Better in my hands than left to blind chance and bureaucrats. That is the closest thing to faith I have left.

I have been tracing circles in the same patch of sky for too long.

The storms here are good. Mean enough to scare off patrols, not so bad they tear my ship apart. The local settlers think it is cursed weather, but I see clean corridors buried in the noise, little veins of laminar flow where a careful hand can slide a hull through unseen. That is why I stayed. Not because it is safe. Because it is predictable in a way people are not.

I remember the first time I sat in a UC briefing room and realized the adults at the table were afraid. Not of the enemy, but of being wrong in front of each other. We had just brought a strike group through a plasma wall, tight timing, everyone still shaking. The recon showed more civilians in the target area than anyone expected. I still hear my own voice, suggesting we hold, re-evaluate. The room went quiet. Then they started talking about acceptable margins and strategic necessity. One of them quoted some old Terran philosopher about the greatest good for the greatest number, like that made the numbers on the surface less human.

Back then it shocked me, how quickly they folded the dead into a theorem and moved on. Now I plan routes that let smugglers slip past blockades and watch the escorts vanish in a bloom of interference, and it barely stirs my pulse. I tell myself I am choosing the lesser harm, that some thinker with a name I mispronounce would back my calculus. It is easier than counting each face.

I came here because the storms erase tracks. UC wants my silence, Freestar wants my skills, and everyone else wants a ghost who can make their problems disappear between lightning strikes. In this place, the sky is loud enough to drown out the accusations, and the only honest thing left is the line between stable flight and a smoking crater.

What am I afraid of now. Not death. The storm will take me someday; that has always been the bargain. I am afraid some young navigator will decode the paths I have carved, sit in a clean briefing room, and be told to use them for purposes I never chose. I am afraid they will look at me the way I once looked at my instructors, thinking experience equals wisdom, not realizing how quickly both curdle into cowardice.

So I keep flying, mapping, humming the old song under my breath. Pretending I am above the common morality of merchants and admirals, as if knowing a few names from old philosophy makes me something other than another pair of hands steering other people's lives through a storm.

Rin says I do not know how to sit still, and maybe she is right. Shift ended an hour ago, and instead of racking out I am hunched over the tiny sink in my bunk, working detergent into the cuff of my jacket. There is a black smear there from the docking clamps and a faint metallic stink of burned propellant that did not come out the last two times I rinsed it. Funny the things you notice when the ship finally goes quiet. I scrub until the fabric roughens under my fingers, then hang it by the vent and watch it sway in the recycled breeze. For a moment, with just the low thrum of Prairiefire's reactors and the distant click of someone moving in the corridor, it almost feels like the nights back in the yard on Titan, washing work clothes that all smelled of dust and cold metal, nothing more dangerous than a late invoice. I catch myself breathing slow, shoulders loose. It feels new, like a part of me that has been locked down since basic is starting to thaw.\n\nWe did a handover for that weather work contract earlier, the one everyone pretends is just routine escort between farm moons. Kade spent half the briefing tracing routes on the holo, frowning at the way the storms line up a little too neatly; Jonas cracked a joke about someone selling "premium sunshine" to the highest bidder, and Tessa gave him that small, tired smile of hers without saying a word. She has been like that a lot lately, hovering close to the walls, listening more than talking. Rin shrugs it off, says some people carry their ghosts quieter than others, but I have seen her watching Tessa when she thinks no one is looking. Trackers talk big about codes and clean bounties, yet I keep overhearing Alliance dispatchers mention names in low voices, ships that never make it to official logs, clients who want more than just someone brought in. There is scuttlebutt about a specialist who can bend fog and rain around cargo like a cloak, and about old UC hardware in dead orbits humming with someone else's code. None of it should touch us; we just follow pings, bring people back, cash the cred. Still, the last job out near that abandoned grid felt wrong somehow. The storms shifted ahead of us instead of behind, like we were being guided along a path somebody else had drawn. I am writing this down because tomorrow we burn for another run along the same line, and for the first time in a long time, I am not sure if the thing gnawing at my gut is just nerves or the part of me that has finally started to feel again trying to warn me.

I caught myself flinching again today.

Wasn't a gunshot, not even close. Just Kincaid barking at Varela over the comms about a bad firing solution, voice up half an octave. My hand twitched toward the sidearm before my brain caught up. Old habits. Years of briefings where volume meant someone's career was about to be spaced. Back then, you did not talk unless spoken to, and if you answered wrong, they did not just strip rank. They stripped time, air, sometimes names from records. You learn fast that honesty is a luxury; the truth was what the briefing officer wanted to hear, nothing else.

Funny thing is, the first place I ever paid for myself was cleaner than anything since. Tiny cube off a side corridor on some station whose registry I have tried to forget. Single cot, half-broken cooker, clothes in a pile by the door. No cameras, no inspection schedules, no mystery "wellness checks." Just me, my mess, and the kind of silence that did not feel weaponized. I did not realize that was freedom until much later.

Lost Legion is supposed to be different. No brass, no black-bag orders, no pretending collateral does not have faces. Draven says we are "choosing our own battles" now, like that wipes the slate. Some days I even believe him. Other days I watch how Mercer goes quiet whenever a job stinks of the old playbook, how Varela keeps his rifle too close even off-mission, and I feel that same knot in my gut as when an op got tagged "need-to-know."

We talk about brotherhood, but everyone is always counting how many guns are in the room and who they are pointed at. Darius keeps a second route plotted on every exfil, "in case command screws us again" he says, meaning whoever is paying us this week. Jonas will share a bottle, share a story, but never quite share what he saw on that last official deployment. I see it in his eyes when someone jokes about "acceptable losses." There is a ledger in his head, same as mine.

I want to ask them what orders they said yes to. I want to say out loud that the worst part was not what we did, but how fast the debriefs buried it. But the muscle memory kicks in. You do not speak plain. You do not poke at sealed files, even if they are sealed in people instead of servers. Raise your voice, raise your doubts, and you paint a target on your own back. So I swallow it, let the flinch pass, and act like the only thing that matters is the next contract, the next drop zone.

Truth got men punished before. Out here, truth might get you something worse.

I used to mark time by storms. Back home it was birthdays under sleet, the whole family jammed into one pressurized room eating cake that tasted faintly of iron, listening to the roof sing with ice pellets. On the first harvest after a good season we would hang broken sensor vanes above the table like charms, thanking the sky for not killing us that year. Even on the outstations, people found excuses. A TerraBrew cart dragged into a cargo bay, someone strumming an old guitar made of scrap, engineers taking turns telling lies about what the weather would do next. That was before anyone trusted me enough to let me touch the arrays, before they trusted me so much they ignored me when it mattered.

I chose this place because the sky is already wrong here. The old UC hardware above this dead world hums with code nobody bothers to maintain, and the official forecasts read it as noise. That gives me room to work. The distance from anything that matters is a comfort too; if I make a mistake, I only scar rock and vacuum, not fields and lungs. The hunters will come eventually. They always do, following threads of shipments that arrived too dry, storms that split neatly around paying clients. I am not hiding from them so much as buying time to finish the model, to prove that the grids can be made safe without burning another colony to the ground or handing everything to some board that will ignore the warnings again.

I still see their faces when I sleep, the ones who did not get offworld in time. I built my projections on their deaths, tuned the equations so no one would be able to say "we did not know" ever again. The irony is that the more I fix, the more the stories twist. Smugglers call me savior, bureaucrats call me terrorist, settlers just call me when the rain stops coming. Once, that would have gutted me. I thought I wanted to clear my name, drag the buried logs into the light, make the people who overruled me say my real one and choke on it.

But redemption implies going back, submitting to their courts, their committees, their "proper channels." It means letting them put their hands on the levers again. I am more afraid of that now than of any bullet a bounty hunter might send my way. I do not want to be cleaned up and folded back into the machine that broke me and the people I tried to protect. I want the model finished, the failsafes seeded into every array I can reach, and then I want to be done. If they call that justice or heresy afterward, I will not be around to correct them.

I remember the first time the world showed its teeth. I was still a student on Jemison, staring at a casualty report from some far-off skirmish that the lecturer brushed past like it was a rounding error. A whole transport gone, folded into "acceptable loss" on a slide full of neat graphs and confidence intervals. Everyone else copied the numbers. I sat there counting how many names fit inside "acceptable." That was the first time I understood the universe is cruel, and the people in charge just learned to speak its language without flinching.

Back then I thought if I just worked harder, mapped cleaner lanes, I could make them listen. Turns out "listen" meant "sign here to say it is safe." They love people like that: the ones who mistake compliance for competence. UC analysts who smooth their own doubts because promotion tastes better than truth. Freestar captains who pretend their "freedom" is anything but gambling with other peoples lives. Trade Authority fixers convinced every risk has a price, as long as they are the ones charging the fee. Everyone has their little story that makes them the hero, even as they line ships up over the edge.

And me. I am sitting in the dark, somewhere between official space and the junk-drift they pretend does not exist, rewriting other peoples chances with a few degrees of correction. I hear myself now on the comms clipped, cold, counting down burns like it is all just math. I used to flinch when a ship winked out of telemetry. Now I shrug and tell myself that lane was a lie to begin with, that I am just dragging their illusions into the light. That is what I tell myself, anyway.

The truth is I do not recognize the woman who can juggle LIST convoys and smuggler runs in the same breath, who can sell a corridor to a desperate hauler and then sabotage the buoy that made it necessary. I can watch the numbers climb in the black box logs and feel nothing but a thin, sour satisfaction that I was right. That is not who I was on Alpha Centauri, squinting at anomalies and losing sleep over simulations no one else read. I keep meaning to draw a line, say this is as far as I go. Then another recall notice gets buried, another "incident" gets renamed, and I move my own line a little further out where nobody, least of all me, can see it anymore.

People like to say I am dangerous now. They are not wrong. But I look around and all I see are children in uniforms, in suits, in captain's chairs, still pretending the universe will reward them for good intentions. I am just the one who stopped pretending.

There was a time when my whole universe was three blocks of Neon and the Transit line that sang underneath them.

I used to start my days in that cramped TerraBrew by the spaceport, the one with the flickering sign and the sticky counter that never quite lost the smell of burned beans and wet grav boots. Dockhands, haulers, security pulling off third shift, all lined up for caffeine and lies. I knew which barista would slip an extra shot if you paid in hard credits instead of chips, which corner booth you could sit in without getting drafted into someone's sob story.

Back then my job was simple, almost boring. Load schedules, berth assignments, keeping Xenofresh haulers and Trade Authority crates flowing through the right doors at the right times. I was the one the foreman yelled for when two ships tried to sit on the same pad in the system. Unremarkable work, steady. You learned the rhythm of the grid, the way the conduction spans would crackle before a big storm, the way the city sounded right before a big Aurora shipment hit the Trade Tower. I went home dog-tired, but my hands only shook from too much coffee.

That life ended the first time a UC man in a clean jacket asked if I wanted to earn more doing the same thing, just with less paperwork. "You already know which customs officers are lazy," he said. "Why not put it to use?" One decision. A new route here, a mislabeled crate there. You tell yourself you are still the same girl pouring over dock logs, just with better shoes.

Now I am crouched in borrowed shadows on some forgotten rock, counting the ways they might find me. I picked this place because it is everything Neon is not: no grid humming above, no constant traffic, no one stumbling in high and loud. Waystations, LIST farms, little clinics on the edge of nowhere; those were always my relay points. I know how they breathe. I know how to fold myself into their routines and vanish.

My plan, such as it is, is to strip my routes down to one last loop. Tie off loose ends, scrub the minds that remember my face, then disappear into whatever quiet is left. The fear is that I am chasing a clean exit that does not exist, that every crate I ever touched and every patient I ever helped move left fingerprints I cannot see. Somewhere out there, someone is doing what I used to do at that dock console, looking at timestamps that do not quite fit and feeling the hairs rise on their arms.

I used to be the girl who straightened stacks of cargo records so they lined up just right. Now I am the smudge on the page she cannot explain.

I used to write logs like this for MAST, clinical language and timestamped anomalies, no room for the part where your stomach drops. Old habits. New truths.

I keep replaying the numbers from that test range. The official packet said one thing, the raw sensor bleed said another. Latency shaved off, warning flags timestamped after the fact, entire blocks of jump telemetry "lost to corruption" that I know for a fact existed because I watched them stream in real time. Someone went back and edited physics. It took me a while to stop blaming my own calculations and start asking who had motive to cut out the pieces that made command look culpable.

Then came the civilian incidents. A freighter that should have skimmed safely past a debris field, arriving shredded; a tourist liner hitting turbulence nowhere near a recorded anomaly. Quiet settlements with no political value being routed through crowded, unstable corridors while well-connected interests got the cleaner lanes. The reports did not line up. Internal messages referencing "acceptable loss brackets" that were never mentioned in briefing rooms. Every discrepancy, every missing log, another nudge toward the same conclusion  someone wanted unpredictability, as long as it never splashed back on them.

So I left. Not some dramatic break, just stopped correcting my aliases, stopped attending the right meetings, started selling "better" nav-packs in the places the Navy pretends not to see. Neon for the credits and the deniability, HopeTown and those frontier outposts for the data. The Key for when pirates wanted faster runs and did not care about the fine print. They think I am just another clever criminal skimming off the inefficiencies. Let them.

Here, buried in the dark with The Semaphore and its little web of relays, I can finally see the whole pattern. I tune the routes, bleed traffic away from the knots I know are lethal, or toward them when I need to make a point. Every time I watch a convoy thread a hazard I have modeled down to the millisecond, I feel that old guilt loosen its grip for just a moment.

What scares me is how often I catch myself wondering how far I could push it before anyone truly notices. A coordinated stall of military traffic over one system. A "mistargeted" jump that strands a task force in dead space. A demonstration. The thought comes with a taste like copper and static, and instead of spitting it out, I roll it around, savor it, test the edges. That is the line they always said we would never cross.

They crossed it first. I am just re-drawing the map.

Ship night, somewhere between jobs

Elias says the hum of the recycler is comforting. To me it just sounds like all the things that can fail at once.

We put in on a gutted hauler today, one of those wide-bellied things that used to drag ore for some corporate name no one bothers remembering. Jonah worked the tether, Marcus rode shotgun on the hatch in case someone else had the same idea we did. Inside was quiet, the bad kind. No drift trash, no loose tools, just a long corridor with all the doors sealed and all the cameras dead. Riya muttered over comms that it looked like the crew stepped out for a smoke and never came back.

First time someone called me "reliable" was on a job like that. Elias needed a runner to cross a half-pressurized span and reset a jammed bulkhead so we could get to the cargo spine. Everyone else suddenly had cable checks and suit diagnostics to do. I went. Hands shaking, mag boots slipping on frost, seal alarms chirping. Came back with my suit intact and the hatch open. Elias clapped my shoulder and said, "Knew you would not spook." I pretended it was nothing. Spent the next hour grinning like a fool inside my helmet.

Funny thing is, it is not just rival outfits you watch out for. The crews that smile at you on the dock are the same ones that will cut your line if your claim marker threatens their bonus. Even on Black Drift, people go missing on jobs that were supposed to be routine. "Cable snapped," "thruster misfire," "bad read on pressure." We all nod like that is enough of an answer. Marcus keeps his back to the bulkhead whenever that other salvage union is in the same bay. Says it is not paranoia if you have seen someone vent a man for less than a container of targeting parts.

At shift's end I keep seeing the same scenes in my head. The bridge where the chairs were all empty but the straps still warm against my gloves. That one freighter outside Kessler's edge, its hull torn in a perfect spiral, no distress call ever sent. In the dreams, the corridors are brighter, every scratch on the walls sharp as a blade, every frozen face turned toward me like I am the one who left them there. I wake with the taste of stale air in my mouth and the echo of my own breathing in my ears.

Tomorrow we suit up again. Someone will call me "reliable" when they need a line run through a dead section or a panel popped on a live grid. I will go, because that is what I am good at now. And when the hatch seals behind me and the ship goes quiet, I will try not to think about how many of these ghosts fell exactly where somebody's math wanted them.

They say this contract is "light duty," but my boots do not agree. Three rotations now of running lookouts on half-dead stations, courier runs between people who refuse to say names on open channels, and then sitting in barracks air waiting for orders that might never come. Grid Warbrand calls it "maintaining readiness." Feels more like pacing in a cage.

Funny how control always dressed itself up as protection. Back when I signed on, the pitch was structure, clear chains, layers of oversight so no one got left behind. What it turned into was authorization codes for everything, movement logs, handlers "looking out" for our mental health while quietly flagging anyone who asked too many questions. Safe, they said. Mostly I remember feeling like I could not breathe without someone noting the time stamp.

Adrian takes it in stride. He likes lines on the ground, boxes to tick. Says the predictability is what keeps us alive. Naomi acts like none of it touches her; she slides through the checklists, smiles at the right officers, walks away with the good gear. Then there is Sara, who double-checks every op sheet like she is waiting to find her own name under collateral. I see myself somewhere between them. I know how to play along, but the part of me that believed in any of this is long gone.

Today I was on perimeter when a maintenance drone bled a line of hot lubricant and burned against the steel decking. The smell hit me sideways. Same acrid bite as that hangar we cleared years back, the one nobody officially wrote up. I saw it all over again for a second: bodies under tarps, officers saying it was "containment," that we were being shielded from the fallout. Protection again. We were not shielded; we were muzzled.

Leah cornered me in the mess later, said there is talk some of our "logistics escorts" are tied to cargo that officially never existed. She did not name clients, just raised an eyebrow toward the ops office and left it there. Rumor? Maybe. But we have been parked near too many ghost stories lately. Shipments gone light. Captains gone quiet. And somehow our manifests always reconcile after the fact.

Certain places, certain smells, they keep pulling at threads I would rather leave buried. But this outfit runs on unspoken rules. You keep your weapon clean, your mouth cleaner, and your eyes open enough to see trouble coming but not so wide you notice who is signing off on it. For now, I stand my watches, carry my parcels, and pretend the waiting is just another kind of safety, not the feeling that something is being decided about us in rooms we are never invited into.

I used to put dates on these, like that would make anything feel official. Old habit from claims work. Today is just "after another transfer," and that is precise enough.

People keep calling what I do betrayal. That is a nice, simple word for people who think lines on a ledger are sacred. Out here, morality is like gravity: different on every rock, still pulls you down in the end. What matters is conservation. Loss here, gain there. The sum has to balance. When I reassign a ship or a deed, I am not stealing; I am correcting an equation that was already distorted in someone else's favor.

Leaving GalBank was the first necessary correction. They were already erasing people with those "national security" clauses, just less efficiently and with better lighting. I tried to fix it from the inside, and they tried to file me under "reassigned" until I stopped existing anywhere that mattered. So yes, I walked. Took what I knew, what I had built for them, and put it someplace they could not audit.

Lysa calls what we do liberation. I am less romantic. I watch the drift, find dead accounts and half-forgotten registries, and give them to clients who will pay to inhabit them. Sometimes that means a freighter captain gets to keep flying under a new ID instead of rotting in some backwater dock. Sometimes it means a pirate walks away from a crime scene wrapped in a citizen's paperwork. I do not pretend those are equal outcomes. I just accept that both sides already cheat; I am selling better tools.

Why flee here? Because this place is built on the lie that the records are clean. Every console hums with the assumption that what it displays is truth. That makes it the safest mask. As long as I stay close to the heart of the system, I can hear the pulse, feel where the rhythm skips. If hunters come, they will look to the fringes first. They always expect the rot to be somewhere ugly and obvious, not tucked neatly under polished floors.

I am not afraid of being shot. That is just one line closing. I am afraid of losing control of the archive, of someone who does not understand the ratio between damage and repair getting their hands on my routines. I have spent years turning random cruelty into structured theft. Imagine what a true believer, or a frightened bureaucrat, would do if they could unmake anyone with a keystroke.

So I compartmentalize. Each shell company, each node in the dark, another cell in a larger organism that only I see whole. They call that paranoia; I call it architecture. If I cut off a limb now and then to stay ahead of the hunt, that is not betrayal. It is surgery.

I always thought the quiet would help. Out here it is just reactor hum, stale air, and the faint tick of relays in the bulkheads. No city noise, no flight control chatter, no executives pretending to understand what a misaligned well actually means. I told myself I came to this nowhere dock to think. Truth is, I came because no one sane routes through this sector anymore unless I tell them to. That is the only kind of safety I believe in now.  

I keep replaying the convoy incident in my head, the pilgrim ship that should have skimmed the edge of the anomaly and instead slid right into its teeth. They will say it was my vector, my signature tucked into the corridor data, and they are not wrong. But they forget the memos I wrote, the warnings about unstable mass readings that got marked "low priority" and buried under schedules and profit forecasts. They chose their fate when they stamped those routes as safe and sent civilians along them. I just stopped correcting for their complacency.  

At some point I stopped asking if what I was doing was right and only asked if it was necessary. The first time a Trade Authority broker begged for a clean lane to save a shipment that was already late, I watched him sweat and decided he had not earned it. I gave him a corridor that worked, eventually, but not before he burned extra fuel and nearly cooked his drive. I liked seeing him wobble, seeing someone on that side of the table feel the uncertainty I live in every day. It scared me how satisfying that was, and I did it again anyway.  

The problem now is I cannot tell where the enemies end and the allies begin. GalBank paid me to optimize and then pretended they had no idea how my tweaks kept wiping their competitors off the lanes. UC survey teams nodded along in briefings, then looked surprised when I asked to put my objections in writing. Even the smugglers play at honesty, swearing they will keep my name off their manifests while they whisper it to anyone waving enough credits. Someone close has already sold a fragment of my archive; I can hear it in the way certain captains hail me on encrypted channels, using phrases I only ever used in private logs.  

So I sit here with my brass sextant and my encrypted slates, running simulations of a corridor that cuts through the dark like a knife, a ghost path no patrol can follow. If I finish it, I decide who gets to move safely between the stars and who spends their last minutes watching their instruments spin. Maybe that used to feel like a responsibility. Now, if I am honest, it feels like leverage. And leverage is the only morality left that makes any sense.

Sometimes I still tap the countdown on the bulkhead before I sleep. Old habit from the Navy days, when every burn had a schedule and every mistake had a name attached. Out here, the only schedule is how long I can keep ahead of people who want me caged, or quiet, or dead, depending on whose seal is on the order.

I picked this orbit because no one sensible comes here. Old engagement zone, sensor ghosts everywhere, everyone agrees on the charts to just call it "clutter" and look away. That suits me. The drift hides my test burns, the static covers my messages, and every time I cut a new window through the wrecks I feel that old certainty in my hands again. The math is cleaner than the stories about me.

Funny thing about betrayal. The Fleet quartermaster called me that when I fed his timing to a different buyer, like his plans mattered more than the lives stuck in the crossfire. He thought I had turned on him; I prefer to think I freed him from the illusion he was in control. Same with the UC suits, the Trade Authority broker, the ones at MAST who smiled at the projections and pretended not to see the civilian lanes braided through their "acceptable risk." I did not betray them. I just stopped playing along with their lies about what those numbers meant.

There is a point, right before a person breaks, where you see who they really are. I learned that watching captains read route changes mid-jump, hearing the edge in their voices when they realized the corridor was not what they were promised. At first I hated that sound. Lately, I have been curious how far the line can be pushed before the mask comes off. Where they will route their anger when they realize someone sold them comfort instead of truth. It is a kind of experiment, I suppose.

I remember one Trident officer on a secure channel, sobbing about families and vacations and anniversaries missed. I replayed that clip a few times, not out of sympathy. The way his voice cracked on the word "safe" was instructional. He still believed anyone could guarantee that. That kind of faith is a weakness, a structural flaw. You do not build lattices on it.

The logs I stole are safe for now, nested where the grav noise is thickest. UC, Crimson captains, the brokers, they all want different pieces of the story buried. They will send hunters, of course. Some will say they are after justice, some just want the bounty. I almost hope one of them reaches this orbit; anyone who comes this far deserves to see how the lanes really look when you strip away the lies. And if they break along the way, well. Better they crack out here than go on believing someone else is steering their life.

I keep coming back to the pumps.

When I close my eyes I still see the first one I ever helped install, out on a dusty strip so far from Akila you could barely pick the city out of the sky. We opened the valve, water came up clean, and for about six months those people believed the universe was fair. Then a new contract was signed three systems away, and a stroke of a pen dropped their pressure until their fields cracked.

That was the first time I told myself the old line about flows following gradients. Nature does not care if a child drinks or a refinery runs. It only cares about pressure, resistance, equilibrium. We are the ones who paint stories over it afterward and call that morality.

So if I increase the resistance where the hoarders sit and lower it out on the fringe, am I corrupting anything, or just correcting the math?

The Ark Cask helps me think. Most people would call it a tank in an asteroid nest, but to me it is a control volume. Up here, away from cities and their pretty fountains, water is numbers. Inputs, outputs, contamination coefficients. I can label one chamber "control" and another "catalyzed" and pretend that makes me a scientist, not a criminal.

I left HopeTown because they proved how quickly a "trusted partner" will turn land and lives into line items. I left LIST because they kept pretending their hands were clean as long as the paperwork said "advisory" and not "command." Out here, there is no one left to sign off on what I do. That frightens me more than any bounty.

I know SysDef has my name in a file somewhere in New Atlantis, probably pinned to Tamsin's like some kind of genealogy chart of bad decisions. I know the Freestar governors curse me over their private drinks while their aides quietly read my models to check how vulnerable their own intakes are. They will all call me terrorist until the day they copy my charters and claim they invented the idea.

Sometimes, when I am very tired, I taste a cup of water and it is perfect and cold and I think, you could stop now. But then I remember Polvo's reports being buried, the way Neon's underlevels cough rust whenever corporate guests are not listening, and I hear that whisper in the pipes again: flows seek balance. Right now the system's "morality" is just whoever owns the valves.

If right and wrong are just stories we attach after the fact, then I will write mine as cleanly as I can: every line annotated, every sabotage logged, every pressure drop matched to a name that earned it. They can hang me for it later. The archive will still be there, humming quietly in the dark, waiting for whoever finally admits the equations were on my side.

I can still hear the kettle from my old apartment in New Atlantis. Thin walls, cheap element, that shrill whistle every morning before another day of reconciling other people's mistakes. I used to hate it almost as much as the commuter traffic outside, the queues at the bank lobby, the neighbor who always asked what I did for a living but never listened to the answer. Now I would give a great deal to stand in that line again, bored and anonymous, instead of counting the seconds between sensor sweeps in a place that officially does not exist.

It is fashionable to call what I did "crimes." As if the system I walked away from was anything but slow murder by spreadsheet. I watched a farmer on a frontier rock lay every deed, every family heirloom, on my desk while I explained, calmly, that the compounding left them no way out. I could have been kind. I could have buried the review, moved the numbers, pretended not to see the trap. Instead I tightened it, because that was the job and I told myself they should never have signed what they did not understand. When he asked me, voice shaking, if there was any mercy in the model, I said no and felt a kind of clarity I had never felt before. Power. Not over life and death directly, but over whether anyone noticed when those lives were taken.

That was the day I understood the rules. Mercy is a cost center. Kindness is a liability. When I finally turned the machine back on its owners, redirected their hidden routes to my own shells, it was not malice. It was survival. They would have fed me to the wolves eventually; I simply moved first, with better math and fewer illusions.

This current bolt-hole a vaulted chamber buried in rock, insulated lines, no official name suits me. No neighbors, no broken appliances, no one knocking to ask if I am "still at the bank." Just the hum of zero-wire cabling and the faint, regular click of my own fingers drumming interest tables into the desk when I cannot sleep. I know there are hunters working back along the trail dead slates, ghost berths, nervous managers with suddenly expensive tastes. I built enough redundancies that losing one node will not kill me, but the thought of someone patient enough to walk the whole chain unsettles me more than any pirate captain ever did.

Could I have walked away quietly, lived small somewhere under someone else's debt? Perhaps. But the minute I understood how much of the galaxy runs on signatures no one reads, it became impossible to sit in those lines again and pretend I was not already marked for sacrifice. So I chose the only path that left the decisions in my hands. They call that villainy. I still call it staying alive.

I picked this rock because the charts call it "unremarkable" and the dust storms do half my sterilization for free. Low ambient bio-load, stable gravity, just enough atmosphere to keep the lab modules from whining. No one stations a patrol where the only indigenous life is extremophile mold and veterans too tired to move again. Perfect place to vanish, or to be found by only the kind of people desperate enough to ignore the warnings.

The last Ranger unit that came sniffing around, I knew them before they opened their mouths. Posture, trigger discipline, the way their medic kept scanning the horizon instead of the locals. When I told them the villagers' cytokine profiles were stabilizing, I used the right words, the dense ones. "Subclinical sequelae." "Nonlinear dose response." You watch their eyes glaze and you can see it, the precise moment they stop being sure they are angry at the right person. Fear does this narrowing thing to the pupils, and I would be lying if I said I did not enjoy it a little. Proof the situation is still in my hands, not theirs.

I go in circles in my head, drafting defenses like old exam essays. If you model supply chains as a triage tree, I tell myself, then every diverted shipment is just resource optimization. I rehearse it in more complicated language until the words sound almost noble, hoping if I stack enough qualifiers on top of each other, the image of that boy in Restline coughing blood into a dirty cloth will blur at the edges. It works for an hour. Then the TerraBrew cools, and the silence crawls back in.

I did not flee the UC because I "snapped." I did the math. Freighters full of chems parked in orbit while we bled on the ground. Command chose asset preservation over human beings, and when my formulations started making them money instead of saving my patients, I realized the system was using my work as a weapon either way. So I walked, and I took the only things that were really mine formulas, field notes, a portable rig.

Now I talk to veterans in bars that used to be habitat rings, and they keep asking me if they are the bad ones for taking what I offer. I hear the same question behind it: Am I. I give them the nuanced speech about dependencies, neuroplasticity, systemic neglect, and they nod like they understand. Complexity is a good sedative for conscience theirs and mine. But I still wake up before dawn, checking the vents, hand on the Trauma Pack, knowing that somewhere a clerk, a Ranger, maybe some ambitious bounty hunter is threading together the mislabelled manifests and ghost routes and deciding that the person worth blaming is the one who actually stayed when the official channels broke.

I keep thinking about Jaro.

Back when we were still patching colony freighters and scrap tugs over Gagarin, before the war junk got uglier and the contracts got sealed, he was the one who believed in rules. Safety lines, lockout tags, all that. We lost touch long before I started carving into the wrong hulls. Last I heard, he shipped off to some clean UC station where the forms always match the truth. I sometimes wonder what he would say if he saw the map I am drawing now. Probably call it madness. I call it gravity. You do not blame a grav well for what falls into it.

There was a time I thought consequences were fair. You follow procedure, you live. You skip a step, you get hurt, and that is on you. Then they handed me a scuttle order with living names still on the roster and called it necessary. Same signatures, same calm voices in my ear, just a different column to write the bodies into. That was the day I realized the ledger is rigged. After that, telling myself I am serving something higher than their morality got easier. Call it fate, call it destiny, whatever word makes it palatable. But I did not choose to see what was on those grav logs. It found me. Once you know the pattern is there, you either follow it or drown in somebody else's lie.

I would like to say I am still gentle underneath, but that is not honest. I have learned there is a certain satisfaction in withholding. Information, mostly. Core coordinates, escape routes, exactly how long a patched life support loop will really hold. You watch a man who has been bullying cutters his whole career realize the air is going faster than you said it would, and you do not quite rush to hand him the spare canister. Not lethal, not usually. Just enough struggle to remind him he is not holding the controls anymore. People never question a little extra vacuum burn in this line of work.

As for why here, why these forgotten yards and half-finished homesteads and silent garrisons: they are the places nobody expects to matter. Freight records get sloppy, patrols relax, locals learn to look away. Perfect spots to test a theory, move a pallet that should not exist, bolt another stray hull into the scaffold I am building out in the dark. Every new wreck that light touches wrong tells me the same story: something bent the jump, something left a fingerprint in the drives, and I am the only one bothering to collect them.

They will call it crime because that is the only language they have for anyone who steps outside their tidy columns. Let them. I am past ordinary morality. The only question that matters now is whether I finish tracing this signal before the people who still believe in fair consequences finally catch up.

I keep running my hand along the bulkhead even when I am not in a suit. Old habit. Check the welds, feel the seams, trust the metal more than the people who paid for it. Out here, tucked into this half-gutted hull in a field of dead ships, the structure talks to me better than any living mouth ever did. Every groan is honest.

They say I ran. Wrong word. I stepped sideways, out of a game that was already rigged. When a courier that was supposed to be dead turns up on your cutting schedule with the wrong power traces and the right signatures, and then your crew dies in a perfect sequence of "malfunctions," that is not an accident. That is someone cleaning up. Sticking around to be part of the clean-up was never enlightenment. Leaving was.

This graveyard made sense. No patrols worth a damn, too much old Deimos steel rusting in orbit for anyone to watch every plate. I know these bones; I have cut cousins of this wreck apart piece by piece. Easy to wire in bracing, weave deadman charges into the cranes, rig a thousand ways to make anyone following me regret stepping wrong. Paranoia, they would call it. I call it staying alive long enough to decide who to hurt with what I know.

People keep mistaking what I am for broken. They look at the way I can talk about my crew's last breaths like I am describing a clogged filter and call it decay. Truth is, you have to sand the feeling down or it will chew through you. Shedding that noise, seeing the pattern beneath, that is clarity. Emotional detachment is just not letting their script use you twice. You watch the system, not your own tears.

Nights are the worst, when the power draw drops and the only light is whatever leaks in from a distant star. I hear things in the dark parts of the ship. Knocks that do not line up with thermal expansion, footsteps where there is no gravity, a breath over my shoulder inside a sealed helmet. Sometimes I hear them whisper my name in the clipped cadence of a UC brief, like the handler from the debrief room found a way into the ducting. I sweep with a lamp, weapon ready, and there is never anyone there. But the feeling of someone watching from the shadows, taking notes, never goes.

Next step is simple on paper. Trade a sliver of what I pulled out of that crate to someone loud enough to make the right people sweat, while I keep the rest locked down as insurance. Maybe a LIST settler with nothing to lose, maybe some Ecliptic fool who thinks they can out-blackmail the UC. I do not need to win. I just need them all equally afraid of what happens if my heart stops and that final deadman key trips. Then maybe I can stop counting my steps in every corridor and sleep without waiting for the next "accident."

They keep calling it fleeing. As if I ran without a map.

I did not run. I re-routed.

The moment I saw the preliminary findings from that so-called inquiry, with my name highlighted and the override logs conspicuously missing, the shape of the network changed for me. Every node they trusted became a liability, every forgotten relay a potential lifeboat. So I left, yes, but I left along paths no one was watching. That is not panic. That is design.

Out here, far from New Atlantis, the traffic is thinner. Fewer eyes on the console, more gaps between official coverage. Perfect conditions for controlled trials. That is what these are, no matter what names they are throwing around in committee rooms. Trials in how people behave when the system falters. If you nudge one distress call thirty seconds down the queue, who lives. If you prioritize the ship with children visible on thermal over the freighter carrying munitions, who notices. When you quietly correct for the registrar's bias, does anyone thank you, or just complain the reports do not add up anymore.

They say I am harming people. I am measuring harm they already decided was acceptable as long as it was buried in averages. I am just moving the decimal point where everyone can see it.

I chose these fringe nodes because they are the ones I built to be redundant, the ones they never paid to fully decommission. Old telemetry stations, LIST relay shacks, the bones of an evac grid no one had the courage to maintain properly. They left them to rot, but the hardware listens if you speak its language. I can stand in a rusted-out control room and feel the faint rhythm of traffic passing through on unauthorized routes, like a distant heartbeat under the floor.

Do I fear what is following me. Of course. UC SysDef does not like ghosts in its machines, and bounty hunters like simple stories. But what I fear more is going back to pretending the casualty models were theoretical, that the drill did not show us exactly how many bodies the budget could tolerate.

So yes, I am testing things now. How quickly rumors propagate when a pirate ambush coincides with a misrouted medevac. How frontier settlements react when a warning comes from an unregistered band, not a shiny official channel. Whether a Freestar patrol will trust coordinates signed with a familiar hash even when they know I am behind it.

If my experiments work, fewer people will die in the long term, and the ones who signed off on those shortcuts will finally have to admit what they did. If they fail, I already watched the worst-case scenario unfold once on that industrial rock. Nothing I do from here will ever match the negligence they wrote into policy and called inevitable.

I used to write numbers, not words. Material coefficients, stress curves, neat little tables that told you when steel bent and when it broke. Lately, all I see when I close my eyes is that liner coming apart along lines I never signed off on, and my own name stamped under the wreckage.

They said take the deal, sign the statement, accept that I "missed something." Quiet hearing, sealed file, family keeps the lease. I ran my hand along a bulkhead outside the office, tapped it, heard the hollowness right through their lies. Someone shaved the margins after my approval. Somebody had to be the fault line. They picked me.

Gagarin was the first place that made sense. Old shipbreak yard, rust in the air, cutters whining day and night. Nobody looks twice at a man crawling through a dead freighter with a scanner there. I started tearing into retired frames, recording every bad weld and cheap brace stamped with the same logos. Then I started finding ships still in service with the same sickness, flying anyway.

I told myself I was only disabling "flying coffins," buying time for crews that did not even know they were already dead on paper. Strip a mount here, overstress a truss there, force an inspection, force a recall. Noble work, I called it, while I sold what I pulled to pay for tools and off grid time. Somewhere along the line, the line between saving ships and sabotaging them blurred.

The scrapyards suit me. Deimos dumps what it wants forgotten out here, whole skeletons of designs they would swear never left the simulation. I brace some of them, overbuild them until my hands stop shaking, and I leave those afloat as proof to myself that I still know how to do the job right. Others, I gut for parts and data, then lace the corridors with "lessons" so the next fool who comes sniffing understands what lazy greed costs.

There is a hull I keep coming back to in my head, a frame I have not built yet. Something clean, uncompromised, running a drive the way it was meant to be mounted, with every brace where it should have been on that liner. If I can build it, show it holds under stress they said was impossible, maybe the story finally shifts off my shoulders. Maybe.

Then I catch my reflection in a warped panel, tools laid out in perfect symmetry, explosives wired into access ladders "just in case," and I do not recognize the man staring back. I was supposed to be a quiet dock rat with a head for numbers, not some ghost haunting scrap rings and teaching with traps. I am afraid it is too late to turn back; the only way out now runs straight through the people who made me into this. And I am not sure, anymore, whether I am chasing justice or just looking for an excuse to bring their whole rotten framework down with me.

I used to think in quarters, not years. Quarters were cleaner. Predictable. You could tell yourself that if you just survived to the next reporting cycle, the graph would bend your way.

Before everything tilted, I had a table in a cramped little TerraBrew near the spaceport, the one where the recycler rattles every time a shuttle comes in too hot. Third booth from the back, under the flickering panel, good sightlines to both exits. I would sit there with a notebook, Tranquilitea steeping in a paper cup, watching suits and dockhands queue together and pretending that meant the system worked.

Outside, the same kid always tried to sell tourists fake UC citizenship badges. Inside, the same barista asked if my "late nights down in Risk" were worth the overtime. I used to tap interest curves into the tabletop while I waited for the line to move, thinking about how many of the people in front of me would ever qualify for a real loan.

The day I knew I had to run, I walked that same street and every storefront felt wrong. TerraBrew had a new security cam pointed straight at my booth. UC Security uniforms lingered too long in line, not talking, just listening. A GalBank courier I knew pretended not to recognize me. The air tasted like recycled fear and cheap espresso.

I did the math on staying. On trusting internal channels. On letting another "amended" report bury the projections that kept me awake. The curve always ended the same way: debts consolidating at the top, small accounts evaporating on the fringe, and me as a convenient variable to remove once my code had been properly nationalized.

So I stopped thinking in quarters and started thinking in flows. Places where power and credits move but the overseers do not look too closely. Neon, with its underbelly of unpaid favors and forgotten conduits. Old work camps no one wants to admit are still drawing maintenance budgets. Blind spots around certain relays that even UC SysDef only checks when something catches fire.

I fled because the line between "analyst" and "asset" dissolved the moment my drill proved it could move real money. I picked the shadows between districts and decks because they feel like the Well did, before the UC decided we were part of the view. If I can rewrite the ledger from there, even a little, maybe the next girl hunched over tea and spreadsheets in that TerraBrew will have more options than obedience or disappearance.

What I am afraid of now is not death. Death is a clean ending. I am afraid of waking up back in a brightly lit office, my code stamped classified, listening to some smiling supervisor explain how my work has "stabilized" things while the same people still stand in the same line outside, wondering why their accounts froze overnight.

Lost track of ship time again. You sleep when the grav plates hum soft and you work when they scream, that is about the only clock that matters out here.

We cleared a freighter carcass today, hull buckled like a crushed can, heat long gone. Kade took point, of course, swaggering through the breach with his torch like the void owed him rent. Mira followed, checking our tethers twice like she always does, muttering about microfractures no one else can see. I came last, watching my own breath fog the visor and counting all the ways this could kill us before we even touched cargo.

We found a hold with pallets still shrink-wrapped, too pristine for a wreck that dead. The beacon data did not match the manifests and I saw that quiet look pass between Kade and the Union overseer on the comms. That is when paranoia starts chewing at the back of your skull. Out here, betrayal is not some dramatic thing; it is just a man forgetting to mention a crate, shaving a few minutes off your air, misreporting who went in first.

I have not forgotten the day I realized I could lean into that. We were arguing salvage shares with a green crew on the dock at Gagarin, and one of them grabbed my rigging to make a point. I stepped in close, explained in a calm voice how long it takes for a suit breach to bleed a man out. Watched his eyes go wide. He backed off, whole gang did. Disturbing part was not that it worked. Disturbing part was that it felt good.

Recognition started after that. Other crews nodding when I passed, whispering my name under their breath like I was some kind of hazard marker. Pride, sure, but also this cold thread in my spine: once people know your face, you stop being anonymous. You become a story, and stories have a way of drawing knives in the dark.

I think that is why my last partner twisted me up so badly. She had this way of replaying old conversations, changing little details until I was not sure if I had misheard or if she was lying. "You agreed to this cut," she would say, "remember?" And I would stand there in the locker bay, trying to recall the exact words under the stench of burnt sealant and old sweat. After a while you start doubting your own memory more than anyone else's greed.

Tonight, Kade is laughing with some yard bosses over Erdebrau cans and Mira is down in the tool locker, rewrapping cables, complaining about how our patchwork gear is a deathtrap. I am sitting on a cargo brace, listening to the ship creak, wondering which is going to get us first: a failed weld, a bad call, or someone deciding that one less cut of the haul makes their life easier.

Salvage Crown Union calls us a family when the ledgers are healthy. Thing about families is, they know exactly where to cut when it is time to make someone disappear into the wrecks.

Lena keeps saying the suit tape is a bad sign, that once you start using it on the same patch more than twice you are basically asking the void to take a bite. Today I caught myself adding a third layer over my left thigh seal anyway. Out there, drifting between a cracked cargo spine and a freighter that looks like it tried to fold through itself, you stop pretending you are not already held together by scraps.

We shared reheated stew again in the locker bay, same dented tins balanced on an upside-down crate. Miles complained about the taste, but he still scraped the bottom, same as the rest of us. Calen traded a handful of loose connectors to a dock rat for a bag of half-stale bread, and for five minutes we were kings, passing it around, grease and metal dust on our fingers. It is funny what feels like luxury when your clothes are all patched canvas and heat-warped zips.

The run today was a quiet one, mostly. No bodies, at least. Just the echo of alarms that had long since given up. Even so, when the hull groaned and the lights on my wrist-fix flickered, I got that flash again, same as always: holding her in that collapsing corridor back on the station, bulkheads screaming, the air going thin. I remember her fingers in my suit gloves, clutching so hard it hurt, both of us breathing each other's fear through the comm, love and loss tangled so tight I could not tell where one stopped. I walked out. She did not. Everything since has been bargaining with that fact.

Lena says there is a new pattern in the graveyards, that some wrecks look like they were put there on purpose, lined up on the edge of certain lanes. Calen swears he found a nav-core last week that would not let go of its last plotted vector, like the route itself was holding on.
