We laugh about ghost pilots in the mess, but no one talks much when we suit up and drift past derelicts that still have their running lights on.

I keep thinking about a night years ago, back in a side room off some cheap bar airlock, where a friend leaned in close and whispered that they were done running small-time jobs, that there were people who knew how to steer ships off the official roads and into better-paying shadows. "Come with me," they said. "We do not have to scrape forever." I said no. Took the safe route. Ended up cutting hulls for scrap anyway.

Sometimes, when the beacon chatter crackles strange and the grav readings do not match the map, I wonder if those better-paying shadows are where all the empty ships we find really come from. Then Miles calls for a lift line, Lena curses at a jammed cutter, and the moment is gone. Junkstar moves on to the next corpse in orbit, and Rian Kell tapes up his suit, eats what is left in the pot, and tries not to listen too closely to the stories drifting in from the lanes.

When I was little, I was afraid of the dark gap between bulkhead and bunk on my parents' hauler. I used to stuff rags down there so nothing could crawl out and grab my hand while I slept. Now I have ridden ships apart in grav shear, listened to hulls scream and people go silent mid-sentence, and that childhood fear feels absurd. Part of me still wonders if it ever happened that way at all, or if I polished those memories like a good story to pretend there was a time when the universe made simpler kinds of threats.

I have done things since that no story can sand smooth. There was a tug once, years before anyone started whispering my callsign like a curse. Its captain sent me his nav logs, swearing the lane I cleared him on had glitched. I ran the data three times, then nudged a single parameter and watched the projection of his ship brush the edge of a debris field. Not enough to guarantee a hit, just enough to raise the probability into the red. I did it because I wanted to see if the model was right, if the numbers would obey. No anger, no profit motive. Pure, clinical curiosity. He limped through in one piece, screaming about near misses and "bad intel," and I sat there with my hands shaking because the simulation had matched his panic down to the second.

The thing that finally pushed me off the board was not a shipbreaking accident or some captain's sob story. It was paper. Dry, boring, endless paper. Internal memos routed to the wrong inbox, timestamps that did not match the telemetry, clearance codes on a convoy that should have been routine but carried more security than a battle group. The day after the collision, those files vanished from the archive as if they had never existed, and a neat little report appeared with my name stamped on every line that mattered.

I have seen that pattern repeat enough times now in port logs and fuel tallies, in "random" audits that somehow always look past the same blind spots. It is the same careful hand I used on that tug, only bigger, older, and backed by people whose names never appear on any manifest. So I ran. I picked places that fall between official maps: debris corridors where smugglers cut corners, half-legal waystations where dockmasters keep two ledgers, LIST outposts that rely on "luck" to stay supplied. From here, I can watch the currents they pretend do not exist, trace where the quiet convoys bend around something no one admits is there.

What I want now is not forgiveness. That requires believing there was a clean before the dirty, and I am not sure I buy that anymore. What I want is to drag their invisible routes into the same light they burned me in, to make the sky show its seams. If that makes me the monster in someone else's childhood story, so be it. At least their fear will be pointed at something real.

Some nights the bunk feels more like a foxhole than a bed. I lie here listening to the Taskforce breathing in the next compartment and the old drills kick in on their own: count exits, catalog threats, map firing lines in the dark. My body still squares up when a hatch clangs, shoulders tightening of their own accord, hand drifting toward where a sidearm used to hang. Mind knows we are between contracts, off the grid, but the rest of me is still expecting an alarm, a breach, someone shouting for a stack on the door.

There was a night on Valkyr Station I think about more than the others. Power was flickering, bulkheads still hot from the last hit, alarms howling in three different tones. Mira Hollis and I ducked into a maintenance shaft to bypass a sealed hatch and found ourselves wedged between coolant pipes, everything muffled by the hum. For maybe thirty seconds we just sat there, helmets off, sharing a lukewarm water pouch and trading the kind of stupid jokes you only hear in boot. It felt like the universe had paused just for us. As soon as the emergency lights cycled back, we both knew it was over and never said a word about it again.

Leaving official command never felt like a clean break. It was more like bleeding out through a dozen paper cuts. Dana Kessler still calls our little outfit by the old company number when she is tired, then bites it back like a curse. Elena Navarro keeps the comms board organized exactly the way the brass insisted, even though none of them can see it now. I catch myself polishing boots before a job we chose for ourselves, like some invisible officer is going to pop the hatch and inspect us for dust.

We all heard different whispers that pushed us over. I remember one debrief where they brushed past the civilian casualty figures with a single line about "non-critical variance," eyes already sliding to the next slide. Later, in the corridor, someone muttered about a whole block on New Homestead that never made it into the official report. Rumor said a unit like ours had been told to "stabilize" the area and walked away on schedule, even when the evac birds were redirected elsewhere. Nobody ever confirmed it, but the way command shut down questions stuck in my teeth.

Out here in Redacted Taskforce, loyalties are narrower and deeper. We trust each other to watch the corners, not because a flag says so but because no one else will. At the same time, there is always that question hanging between us: if orders went bad again, would we walk off together, or start walking away from each other? My muscles tense first when something shifts, deciding whether to fight, flee, or freeze, long before I can line up the ethics of it. Maybe that is what we really brought with us from the service: not the slogans, just the reflex to move before the thinking catches up.

I picked this relay because no one looks at it unless they are desperate or lost. The official lanes stepped around it years ago, like a ship giving a wide berth to wreckage it does not want to admit it left behind. That suits me. A forgotten junction is the best place to redraw the map.

The last ship I diverted here was a LIST transport I could have let run clean. The corridor was clear, telemetry solid, no pirate chatter within three jumps. I watched the feeds long enough to know those people would probably make it. Then I brought up Danya's projections, ran them against the frontier reports, and found a scenario where they did not. So I nudged them off, just a few degrees, into a path that brought them closer to one of our refuel stones. On the external cam I saw one family still strapping in, the youngest crying. I could have rolled it back. Instead I watched the marker drift onto my new line and felt the calm that comes with being the only one in the Settled Systems who knows which lives will hang on a calculated error. I let them go, and I did not warn anyone.

People like to talk about morality like it is a straight lane with buoys and beacons. That is a story for citizens who still think the universe reacts to their good intentions. Out here, I use morality the way I use a jump plot: as a tool that moves mass where I need it. When Danya has numbers that argue for a reroute, I call it mercy. When a Crimson Fleet captain waves enough credits at me to drag a transport across his hunting ground, I call it inevitability. Same hand on the same controls. The only difference is who is buying the narrative that makes it hurt less.

There was a time, back in the early HopeTown runs, when I would have said I drew a line. No children, no medical shipments, no ships already in trouble. That was before I watched UC and Freestar let a colony choke to death while they argued over who was allowed to send help, before I saw Spacers carve through a convoy that did everything "right." Somewhere in those years, right and wrong stopped being fixed points and started being variables I adjust to keep the math balanced for the people paying me and the ones I cannot quite stop believing deserve a chance.

Now, when I look at a manifest, I do not ask whether diverting them is good or bad. I ask whether diverting them is useful. Useful to Danya's endgame, useful to the buyers waiting in the dark, useful to me when I finally burn every favor and need one last clean jump to a coordinate no one else has. That is the real reason I am here, threaded between dead transponders and old war scars. This place gives me room to keep drawing my own routes, and just enough distance from the lanes I broke that if someone comes hunting, they will have to untangle my work from a sky full of other people's lies before they ever get a lock on me.

Kara says I peel labels off drink packs when I am nervous. I looked down at mess tonight and realized there was a whole drift of plastic at my elbow, so that tracks. Seamender feels smaller on these long legs between hubs, like the bulkheads keep leaning in a little closer each day. Cargo hold hum, reactor thrum, Darius complaining about calibration in the background; it all blurs into the same noise. Trade Authority calls it "steady work." I call it hauling someone else's secrets in boxes I am not allowed to open.

There is a story running around that one of the clerks back in Gagarin got caught moving corridor access for cash, routing ships into quiet gaps where they "accidentally" met the right pirates. Jared thinks it is just dock talk, but Oren swears he heard the name of a real official attached, someone high enough that the investigation never saw daylight. I want to believe it is all exaggerated, but when I watch how cleanly some of our manifests vanish from the system, how perfectly timed our little "detours" are, I feel a lump in my throat that will not go down.

My last name still feels heavier than these crates. Calder Shipping was supposed to be honest freight, three generations of doing it by the book until my father decided to start shaving costs and bending routes. By the time the regulators finished with us, the only thing left was debt and an offer from Trade Authority to "put my experience to use." I signed because I did not see another way out. Some days, walking the spine of Seamender, I am not sure I did not just swap one set of chains for another.

Tonight had one good moment, though. We ate together in the tiny galley, all four of us, elbows bumping over rehydrated ramen and Red Harvest crackers. Kara told a terrible joke about spacer coffee, Darius pretended to be offended on behalf of every engineer in the Settled Systems, and Jared just sat there grinning, sauce on his lip, like we were not floating in a metal tube full of other people's money. For a few minutes, it smelled like broth and cheap spice instead of stress, and I forgot to peel the label off my drink pack.

I do not know where I belong yet. I am not Calder Shipping anymore, but I do not feel Trade Authority in my bones, either. I know flight paths and docking codes, how to juggle invoices and smile at customs while hoping they do not look too closely. Is that a life or just a skill set someone else profits from? Sometimes I catch myself watching the stars outside the porthole and thinking about walking away from all of it, finding some quiet outpost where my name does not mean anything. Then I remember the debt notes still tagged to my ident and the way Oren looks at them when he thinks I am not watching, and I strap back into my bunk and tell myself that one peaceful meal and a bad joke mean I am at least moving in the right direction.

I do not remember the year, only the taste of recycled air and burnt metal. I was a kid on one of those early hauler runs out of Sol, still believing the brochures about unity and exploration. We came across a drifting prospecting pod, lights dead, beacon weak. My mother asked the captain if we would answer it. He did not even look up from his game. Said it was "not in our lane," that diverting would cost fuel and someone else would handle it. That was the first time I understood the universe runs on margins, not morals.

Funny how I keep pretending otherwise.

I keep telling myself what I am doing now is a kind of applied ethics, an experiment in distributed risk. If I sound clever enough, maybe I can drown out the screaming part of my brain that remembers names off the convoy manifest. I can quote theory, talk about how every grav jump is a negotiation with a hostile vacuum, about how causality thins at the edges of certain profiles. Dress it up in language so dense no one notices the simple part: I drew the line they followed, and they did not come back.

I caught myself earlier, muttering like I was back in some academy I never attended. "What we are attempting is an interrogation of the boundary conditions of safe transit," I said to an empty cockpit, hands deep in the Cartagena Line's drive housing. As if rerouting cooling around a worn ring to squeeze one more illicit corridor out of it is some noble inquiry instead of gambling other people's lives for answers I want.

This place makes it easier to lie to myself. An old farm off the main flows, fields long gone to dust, satellites just functional enough to whisper telemetry without drawing attention. On the charts it is a dead node. To me it is ideal: ground-based power, low profile, no one looking twice at a forgotten comms tower if it starts spitting test pings into the dark.

I came here because the noise kept circling back to this region, little echoes in the data from haulers and LIST colonies nearby, like the signature I saw the day the convoy folded. I tell myself if I can map that curve properly, I can prove it was not negligence, that someone tampered with the profile or that the space itself was already broken there. That is the story I rehearse in my head, in grand, precise terms, like I will someday stand in a chamber on Jemison and present it as a thesis instead of a confession.

Underneath all of that, the truth is simpler and uglier. I am terrified that if I stop chasing these patterns, if I let the guilt settle instead of burying it under equations and polished phrases, I will have to live with the idea that I killed them because I wanted to be clever. So I keep plotting, keep jumping, keep hiding behind complicated words, hoping they sound more profound than what I have really been: cruel, in a way that fits neatly into flight plans and hazard pay.

I keep trying to remember the last day I wore a uniform and believed the people above me earned theirs. Memory says it was before the river crossing, before the air was full of burning polymer and Kara Ellison's voice over the squad channel shaking in a way I had never heard. But the truth is it probably snapped some quiet night later, standing in a briefing room that smelled like recycled coffee, listening to a colonel talk around numbers that did not match what we had seen on the ground. Those casualty reports never did line up.

Damien Harlow still talks like we are in, like this is just a "temporary reassignment." He checks his corners, polices his brass, calls everyone by last name. I watch him sometimes, wonder if it is habit or if he genuinely thinks someone at a desk with a clean shirt is still paying attention to the pieces of us that walked off base and did not come back. Kara is different. She laughs too loud now, pushes every op right to the edge. Some nights I see the medic from that village in the way she looks at a target, and I know she is still trying to erase one specific face by stacking a pile of others on top.

I thought leaving the chain would make the ghosts quieter. It did not. The discipline is still there, grafted into my bones. I still wake up at 0500, still clean my rifle the same way, still expect orders even when no one is giving them. Only difference is now when someone says "clear it," I ask who is on the other side and why they are in our way. That question got us branded outlaws more than anything we actually did with a gun.

There was a moment with Kara, after everything went sideways on that escort run. We were holed up in a half-collapsed warehouse, rain coming through the roof in sheets, both of us wired and shaking. She grabbed me by the harness, hard, told me if I ever second-guessed an exfil call again she would put a round through my knee herself and drag me back as a lesson. Her eyes said she meant it. I should have pulled away, should have written her off right then as just another weapon that had slipped its safety. Instead I kissed her, because something in me liked that she could hurt me and might choose not to.

Sleep is a problem now. When I lie down, the dark is never empty. It is filled with the sound of rotors that are not coming, of a town square lit up too bright, of a woman's voice on a recorder saying the wrong coordinates in a tone that told me she knew. Some nights I hear Damien shouting over gunfire again, other nights it is Kara's whisper in my ear, soft words shaped like threats. My mind runs the same reel of nights: barricades, muzzle flashes, civilians pressed against walls, our own people aiming a little too low when they were supposedly firing warning shots. I roll over, count breaths, tell myself it was all justified, all necessary. The lie never lasts long enough to get me more than an hour at a time.

Some nights the hum of this little skiff sounds like an old branch groaning in a Freestar wind. I close my eyes and I am back on that farm, listening to my father curse the sky because a loan committee halfway across the Systems decided our harvest was "too volatile." That is when I learned the first rule: numbers are just hands on throats you cannot see. Back then, it hurt. Now I am the one with my fingers on the ledger, and I am not sure when the hurting stopped being a problem.

The hunters will assume I ran here to hide. That is only half true. The skiff gives me distance from New Atlantis and Neon, enough latency that when I nudge a warrant or collapse a line of credit, the ripples look like ordinary error. From out here, with the transponder half-spoofed and traffic thinking I am a transport three systems away, I can redraw someone's life with a few corrections. Most of the time I tell myself they needed it. That farmer in Freestar space who kept voting for the same governors while signing every predatory contract they suggested needed to learn what it felt like when the scales finally tipped their way. So I let the foreclosure go through, then reversed it just long enough to watch who they begged, who they blamed, who they turned on.

I used to lie awake after those edits, replaying faces in my head, wondering if the "acceptable loss" lines on my reports were murdering real people. Khepri-3 burned that question out of me. After you have watched an entire agri bloc fail in slow motion while executives argue over phrasing, it is hard to care about bruises when you are the one finally swinging. I still tell myself I am teaching lessons, forcing people and factions to feel what they have been doing on autopilot. A softened bounty here, a vanished debt there, a redirected shipment that leaves a smuggler bankrupt and a clinic secretly stocked. Guidance, I call it. Showing them where the lines really are.

Truth is, the part of me that flinched is quiet now. I notice it mostly by its absence. When did that happen? Was it when I zeroed out that friend's bill at Reliant Med and realized no one would ever thank me because they would never know? Or when I falsified a bounty on a Khepri-3 survivor and watched the relief in their eyes while some other poor bastard took the heat? Somewhere between those two keystrokes, "harm" turned into "adjustment" in my head.

So I keep moving the skiff, keeping just enough off the charts that the survey nodes flag me as noise. I have a lifeboat waiting out there, a quiet homestead on someone's LIST docket, with clean papers slowly accumulating like honest snow. Maybe one day I will step into that life and pretend the ledgers never knew my name. Until then, I sit in this humming tin can, tracing numbers on the console edge with my thumb, watching hunters chase ghosts through records I have already rewritten, and telling myself that if I did not do it, someone worse would.

I should probably stop writing these, but thinking in my own head is louder than any trace they can run. So if someone is intercepting this, congratulations, you are about to read the inside of a bad idea.

I did not run because I hurt people. I ran because I would not let someone else hold the off switch to their bodies. Strange how that looks the same on paper. You flip a routine from "lock" to "unlock," side effects ripple, someone loses sleep or sanity, and suddenly the woman who refused to build a leash code is the monster. Ship of Theseus in meat form: if you replace damaged parts with better ones, how many upgrades before they say you are not a person anymore, just a weapon? If you refuse to add their control fork, are you saving lives or sabotaging the system that feeds them? Ask three philosophers, get four answers and a requisition form.

The bionics facility was chosen for me long before I came here. I helped design some of its scaffolds back when my badge still opened the good doors. It is old, out of rotation, full of hardware no one audits anymore, and wired in the dialect my hands remember better than my own handwriting. A perfect place for ghosts to work. Out here I can tune the mesh without a dozen directors breathing down my neck, can test failure modes on synthetic loops instead of live minds. That is the plan, anyway, written as cleanly as I dare. The dirtier version stays in my head.

I used to think kindness was a universal solvent. Back in Neon, I comped a neuro-tune for a discharged soldier who could not stop shaking. No papers, no questions, just a steadying of his pain regulators and a free cup of terrible coffee. Two weeks later his "friend" showed up with four more broken men and a quiet threat about what might happen if I stopped helping. That was the day I realized kindness is just another interface someone can exploit if you do not harden it. I still help, but now I count exits, triangulate signals, and seed kill-switches into my own work in case one of mine turns on the rest.

If this log ever sees daylight, the nice, simple summary will be that I am dangerous. Of course they say that. If you build a lattice that lets people step outside their assigned tolerances, every institution that profits from those limits will panic. They do not fear me because I cut people open. They fear me because I close a hand around the same control they thought only they were allowed to touch.

I am keeping this vague, leaving out nodes and coordinates, because I can feel the net getting tighter. Too many Ryujin eyes sniffing around old tickets, too many UC ghosts whispering about "firmware drift." Maybe someone has already traced the distortions back here. Maybe they are reading this in a briefing room, under good lighting and bad coffee, nodding while they plan how to put my code back in a cage. If so, enjoy the paradox: to catch me, you have to admit I was right about how fragile your control always was.

I keep telling myself this is temporary, that I am only using these ruins until the trail cools, but I keep coming back to the same corridors. The freighter captain who dropped me here is gone, the patrol routes have shifted, and still I walk the same length of wall where the paint changes from Freestar blue to bare metal. I know how many steps between the old infirmary and the records room. I know where the dust does not settle.

I fled because the numbers stopped being abstractions. One order on a console outside Akila, one line in a report, and half a ward went from screaming to "nonessential." After that day, every casualty log felt like a knife in my hand. It was too easy to move a name from one column to another. Too easy to see how the right lie could save someone who was never meant to be saved, or erase someone command wanted forgotten.

This place made sense because everyone already decided it was finished. Freestar and UC both stamped it as cleared, which means no one wants to come back and admit they miscounted the dead. A scavenger crew comes through now and then, prying up plates, but they do not look at the consoles. They do not smell the old Antiseptic under the dust. They certainly do not recognize my handwriting buried in the archived rosters.

I have a small routine now. TerraBrew boiled on a field stove until it tastes like metal. Tools laid out in the same order every time. Medbag checked, rechecked, counted until my fingers ache. When someone finds me and needs to disappear, I sit them under the same flickering light and listen to their story. Then I decide which ledger they belong in and which they are ready to leave behind.

Some nights I think about the stupid things I used to want. I remember sitting on the edge of a bunk dreaming about buying a little place in Akila, repainting the walls something not regulation, learning to play an old string instrument my mother used to talk about. Harmless wishes, soft as gauze. I would not know what to do with a quiet room now. I would tear it apart looking for exit routes and hidden records.

People talk about redemption like it is a med you earn after enough pain, a way back to who you were before. I used to believe in that. I do not anymore, and it scares me how little I miss the idea. If someone offered me a clean file, a cleared conscience, I would not take it. I am more afraid of being forgiven than I am of being hunted. Forgiveness means putting the knife down. I have spent too long learning exactly where to cut.

So I stay here, in the gaps between what the war recorded and what actually bled into the dirt. I know they are closing in; the questions at Gagarin, the whispers in New Atlantis, the wrong people suddenly interested in old rosters. When they arrive, they will see a medic in an old barracks and think the story ends here. They will not realize this is only one of the places I chose to finish what everyone else started and walked away from.

Did a sweep of the docks with Rico and Darren tonight, same as always. Cargo comes in, creds go out, Cerberus gets its cut. The routine should feel solid by now, but my hands still shake when I light a smoke afterward. Darren laughs it off, says the tremor just means my nerves are "tuned for survival." Easy for him to say. His conscience doesn't wake him up at 0300 replaying every poor bastard we've leaned on until they signed or snapped.

Marla pulled me aside before the run, said the boss wants us "cleaner," less public mess, more quiet leverage. That means more talking, less shooting, and I am supposed to be good at that. Problem is, talking in this life mostly means lying to someone's face while you measure how much pain it will take to change their mind. I tried soft words with the spacer crew we shook down at Bay 4, told them I was sorry we had to search their crates, sorry about the delays, sorry this "wasn't personal." They looked at me like I was the one holding the gun, even though it was Rico standing behind them with his finger on the trigger. I still heard myself apologizing for it all anyway.

It has been like that since I fell in with the Syndicate. First time we roughed up a shopkeeper who missed a payment, I apologized to him while Darren worked over his security drone with a wrench. Said we would "sort it out," said we "understood times were tough." Later I apologized to Rico after the boss chewed him out, like it was my fault the take was light. I even found myself mumbling sorry to Marla the night she had to put down that freelancer who pulled on us first. Everyone keeps telling me to own what I do, but all I seem to own is the blame for what everyone else chooses.

Heard some scuttle in the back room of the Den about a red-haired doc working the underbelly clinics, someone who can crack implants and pain wiring like she is rewiring a grav drive. Darren says she can flip a man's nerve endings inside out, shut him down at a distance if she ever touched his augments. Others say she is patching up people we leave broken, giving them another shot at life we thought we took. No one knows if she is on our side, the Corps, or nobody's. Rico jokes that if we ever cross someone like that, I will be the first to say sorry while she fries our heads.

Sometimes I wonder if that is what I am really apologizing for: not the beatings or the threats, but the fact that I keep going back out there anyway. Every time the boss hands me a new list of names, I nod, say I understand, then catch myself telling the targets it is all just business, that I wish it could be different. Tonight, coming back through the rain-slick alleys, Marla asked me why I keep doing that. I told her I do not know, but that is a lie. I keep apologizing because it feels like the only part of this that is still mine. But the more I say it for things that were never really my fault, the more it sounds hollow, like I am rehearsing for the day it finally is.

I lost track of dates a long time ago. Somewhere between HopeTown and the first time I heard my own name spoken like a curse in a Neon bar, the calendar stopped mattering. What I remember instead is the sounds ships make when they fail. Not the explosions; the little noises before that. The creak in a frame that was stress-rated wrong, the whine of a drive loaded past tolerance because some admin shaved a safety margin for profit. I spent half a life trying to keep crews alive inside other peoples bad math. Funny how fast they called it sabotage when I started correcting the ledger in ways they did not approve of.

People brand what I do as preying on the vulnerable. They are half right. Weakness exists to be used; that is how the strong survive. The thing they never say out loud is who made those people weak in the first place. A hauler captain who trusts a Deimos spec sheet more than her own instincts, a settler taking the cheapest contract because their kids are hungry, a green engineer told to sign off on a drive that hums wrong because schedules do not wait. I nudge those ships out of lanes that will kill them, or into quiet places where the right scrap can be harvested and the wrong paperwork can vanish. Survival, not charity. Survival for me most of all.

This new hiding place suits me. Old listening gear, blind spots baked into the patrol patterns, a whole ring of forgotten steel that still remembers every ship that ever whispered past. I can sit in the dark and trace the work of my own hands across the grid, decide which hulls deserve a second chance and which need to disappear before they take more lives with them. From out here, it is easy to tell myself I am fixing things. Harder when I key into a comm channel and hear some tired freighter crew laughing, not knowing I am one bad decision away from rerouting their fate.

The stress is a constant low-frequency vibration in my skull now. I snap at people who have not earned it. The mechanic on Narion who only asked if I wanted coffee; the old Arc Might foreman who used to cover for me on overtime logs; the kid in Neon who reminded me of my apprentice, right before I told him to get as far from shipyards as he could. I see the hurt in their faces and I still cannot stop. Pressure does that. You load a frame past design and it does not fail all at once. It hairline-cracks. So do people.

I tell myself every day that what I am doing is survival, not malice. That if I had not stepped off the UC payroll when I did, I would be another quiet accident in a restricted debris field, my team written off as an acceptable loss. I do not remember the last time I felt innocent. Maybe back when I was a kid knocking bulkheads in Gagarin, pretending I could hear what the metal wanted. These days the metal talks plenty. It tells me where the lies are buried. It also keeps the count of how many lives I have pushed off one path and onto another, just to stay ahead of the people who finally decided my kind of correction is a crime.

Rylan says today's haul was a good one. Easy cut, clean pull, no bodies. He is not wrong, but when I pulled that locker open and a pair of boots drifted out, laces fused together by vacuum frost, my stomach still did the same little flip it always does. Body or not, the shape of where someone used to be hangs around. I can feel my pulse jump in my fingertips before my brain catches up and remembers I am just here to strip metal, not count casualties.

The others think I am calm. They do not see my hands shake until after the airlock cycles. Guess that was the same back when I was running with people who did not log every job, back when orders came with fewer signatures and more implied threats. I did things then because someone above me said it was the only way, spaced a crate with someone still banging inside because delaying meant losing the whole crew. We all pretended it was an accident. The hull took the blame. The guilt did not get jettisoned with the cargo, though. It sits in my chest, heavier than any scrap we drag home.

Graveyard Salvagers are better than that, mostly. We still argue over shares, over who saw a beacon first, but the worst punishments here are docked pay and cold shoulders. Nobody breaks fingers to settle a dispute. Rylan jokes his way through fights, tries to smooth things over before they go sharp. I like that about him more than I should. Which is why I keep my voice even when he spends too long laughing with Maru over a clean plasma cut, like the two of them invented the torch. Stupid, how jealousy can make a harmless laugh feel like a knife twisting under the ribs. Back then, small things like that could turn a whole hold into an emotional minefield, and I learned fast that speaking up usually earned bruises. Silence was safer than honesty.

Old training still rides my nerves. A panel clangs wrong and I am already braced to fight or bolt before I even register it is just Taro dropping a cutter. Sometimes in my bunk, the station hum shifts and I freeze, waiting for a shouted name, for someone to drag me out and demand to know who I talked to, what I saw. No one comes. The worst I get now is Rylan hovering in the hatch, not quite stepping inside, asking if I want a drink in that careful voice like he is approaching a skittish animal. I always say I am fine. He always pretends to believe me.

They are whispering in the hangar about a derelict out past the lanes, stripped on the outside but running warm inside, and about another crew that went in and never came back. Part of me leans toward it, hungry for the kind of payout that rewrites your life in one job. Another part remembers sealed crates, missing logs, and the way honesty used to be punished when the story did not suit the people in charge. So I keep my mouth shut, sharpen my tools, and let my body stand a little closer to Rylan's than it needs to when we check harness lines. Old ghosts, new habits. Still trying to figure out which ones are mine and which ones someone else welded into me.

I keep telling myself the ship sounds different when she crosses the shear, like the hull is holding its breath. Everyone laughs when I say it, but tonight the metal hum has a tightness to it that will not shake loose. PX-7708 was built to ride rough air, or so the briefings say, yet the last run through that corridor took more out of her than the engineers want to put in a log.

Elena Marrow says I am hearing ghosts and should stop sleeping in my headset. She said it with that half-smile of hers, the one that could be a joke or a warning depending on how much coffee she has had. Lately, she has been spending more time with the encrypted consoles and less time with the rest of us in the mess. Nothing you could file a complaint over, just a feeling that her thoughts are already somewhere else. I caught her closing out a screen when I walked in yesterday; she claimed it was a requisition snafu from New Atlantis, but I swear I saw an account string that did not look like anything from UC payroll.

Tanya Kwan keeps trying to drag me into card games to take my mind off the turbulence, but even she has been snapping at people. She said the last cargo manifest made no sense, relief supplies bundled with sensor parts we are not rated to carry. Mira Halbrook and Aisha Navarro joked that the Navy is always running two stories at once, the official one and the one a deck lower. No one laughed quite as hard as they usually do. Lena Carver pretended not to listen and watched Elena instead. I am not the only one who feels something coiled in the air.

Part of me thinks I am being unfair. Elena is sharp, has saved our skins more than once with her numbers, and I am just the guy who rides the scopes and calls out when the sky looks wrong. It is easy to see patterns where there are none when all you hear is hull and heartbeat. I still remember the faces from that last relief run, though, the way they tried to thank us through the viewport as we broke orbit. If the rumours about unlogged passengers and side deals are even half true, maybe I do not deserve to ride easy on these assignments. I followed orders, signed for crates, never asked who paid for the extra fuel.

I am grateful for the steady credits, for the uniform, for the way people back home stop calling you a drifter when you say UC Navy. At the same time, I do not know if we have earned the right to feel safe in this corridor. We cut through storms settlers pray their whole lives to avoid. Maybe somebody somewhere decided that we belong to the math of risk as much as they do.

Tonight the captain wants another pass near the shear, a test of new approach numbers someone handed down from the top. Elena delivered the figures calm and clean, said we would barely feel the bump if we flew them right. The others are restless, but no one wants to be the one who says no to a cleaner curve. If these numbers are as good as she says, we walk away heroes for shaving time off the route. If they are not, well, the void does not care whether we thought we deserved better.

I keep thinking about Kareem.

Back when I still wore UC gray and pretended the math was just another tool, not a weapon, he sat across from me in a New Atlantis dorm kitchen, stirring instant noodles in a scratched pot like it was some gourmet ritual. We would argue over route theory and eat overcooked noodles with too much salt. He wanted to teach first-years. I wanted to bend spacetime. Somewhere between promotions and classified contracts we stopped calling each other. I wonder if he ever pulls up the casualty lists and looks for my name the way I scan hull registries for his.

Before everything cracked, life was small in ways I miss. Shared mess tables, stolen heaters, questionable cans of Chunks. There was a month in Gagarin where I cooked the same synth-chicken and rice three times a week for a tech squad that could not boil water without tripping an alarm. We ate off our laps, laughing at nothing, the worst thing in our universe being a corrupted sim run. I did not know how quiet it would get inside my own head once the routes started eating ships.

People like to paint me as an accident that went rogue. They forget the deliberate parts.

There was a hauler captain out of Akila, the smug kind, all trophy pistols and secondhand equations he did not understand. He came to Neon bragging that he knew someone like me once, that he could "handle" any jump I sold him. I watched him drink, watched his eyes track every credit sink in the room, watched him flinch when the word Heelstone floated through the air. I gave him a corridor slice that worked if he followed my timing exactly. I wrote the margin for error as thin as my patience. He skipped early. His ship did not arrive where it was supposed to. The wreckage that did make it out will keep a few clever scavvers fed for years. Call it selection pressure.

Gridline made sense as a waypoint because settlers do not ask too many questions so long as their supply runs get shorter and the skies stop screaming quite so often. H-9 made sense because the UC already forgot half of what they built there, yet the hardware still remembers every ping. The shroud makes sense because everyone else sees wreckage and superstition; I see baselines and boundary conditions. Out here, the old apparatus still runs, half-abandoned, perfect for someone willing to slip between the gaps.

They will say I fled. They will say I am hiding. I am not. I am converging.

Only those willing to step outside the officially sanctioned lanes can comprehend it. The enlightened, the ones who understand that every advance in navigation was written in someone else's epitaph, will see what I am building: a map that belongs to no flag, no corporation, no tribunal. The rest will stand on their safe little routes and call it madness, because it is easier than admitting they helped draw the first line.

They want apologies, confessions, some neat little arc of guilt. I have my list of ghosted hulls. I recite every registry before I jump. That is my penance. Understanding why I keep going is not for them.

Some nights out here, in the quiet between pings, I try to remember what it felt like to care if a shift ended on time. The office in Jemison, the simulator bays, the endless meetings about acceptable risk that never actually accepted anything. That life feels like it belongs to a stranger I watched once through thick glass. Same hands, same face, but none of the angles were visible yet. I catch my reflection in a dead console now and there is no line between analyst and outlaw, just the same mind finally allowed to run without someone tapping the brakes.

Only a few people will ever understand what I am doing. The enlightened ones. The rest cling to their schedules and their lanes and call it safety, as if the universe were not already trying to tear them apart molecule by molecule. They blame me for the accidents, whisper my name like a curse, but I did not invent debris or negligence or greed. I look at a route, see every weak weld, every overworked pilot, every accountant who shaved a margin too close. All I do is nudge. They build their own catastrophe; I accelerate the inevitable and collect what spills out.

The relay I am using now was meant to be temporary. A patch on a system too busy to fix itself properly. Then they forgot about it. The processes calcified, the oversight stopped, and the station drifted into the blind spot between budgets. Perfect. Temporary things are honest. They show you where everyone assumed someone else would be watching. I stepped in where the world had already walked away and started rewriting the numbers. Tugs, haulers, survey craft they are variables to solve for, not souls to cradle. If a captain responds well to a correction, they become a tool a repeatable function I can call on later. If they fight the math, they are just noise to route around.

I know what that sounds like. Once, I could have chosen to be gentler with the data. Push warnings through official channels, write another memo, plead for better shielding on old hulls. I saw the patterns forming long before the memorial convoy tore open and I could have tried, again, to be kind. I remember sitting with the reports in front of me and feeling that option in my hands like a fragile thing. I put it down. Deliberately. Kindness in that system is just a slower death, stretched out over more names in the ledger. Out here, at least, the ledger is honest. I keep track of every ship I touch, every course I alter, every body that might never get a marker. That is more than their committees ever did.

Bounty chatter is getting louder. Veterans who want someone to bleed for what happened near Cheyenne. Corporations terrified that if I keep peeling back these lanes, people will see how much of "safety" was always just a bet. They paint me as a monster because it is easier than admitting they traded lives for clean quarterly reports. Let them. As long as I stay one step ahead, moving from forgotten node to forgotten node, they can chase the ghost in the lanes and never quite catch the woman who decided to stop pretending any of this was fair.

I used to mark my days by launch windows and grav-well tides. Now I count them by how long the comm stays quiet. Funny thing no one tells you about vanishing off the boards: silence is loud. Out here, with only the hum of the drive and my own notes on the console, the choices I made sound different. Not better, not worse. Just stripped of everyone else's speeches about duty and service and the greater good.

I keep thinking about Vallejos from the office in The Well. She used to bring in terrible TerraBrew, burn it half to slag, and still smile like we were saving the frontier one form at a time. We drifted apart before I ever touched a falsified route. Too busy, different shifts, then different postings. It was that easy to lose someone who thought the system would catch everyone if we just worked harder. I wonder what she would say now, seeing where those "proper channels" left Theta and the other ghosts.

People keep calling what I did criminal, like that word draws a clean line. As if rerouting one convoy around a pirate nest is noble, but rerouting another away from a slaughterhouse of a colony plan somehow crosses into sin. Truth is, we are all bargaining lives for trajectories; I just stopped pretending otherwise. When I nudged those manifests, when I bent the Silent Span to my own pattern, that was the first time I felt honest. No more hiding behind algorithms someone else wrote. No more shrugging and saying the regs did not allow an exception. I am the exception.

There was a tech on a border freighter who begged me to pass along an alternate corridor to his family ship. I had it. I could have sent it. Instead I watched him squirm, made him explain every risk twice, listened to the panic in his voice, and then told him to stick to the official lane. It did not feel like cruelty; it felt like clarity. If he could not see the sky the way I do, he had no business in the deep routes. I think about that moment more than I think about any pirate I burned with a bad interception vector.

I fled because the mask was slipping anyway. The LIST suits wanted clean numbers, clean reports. The UC wanted order. Freestar wanted plausible deniability. Everyone wants to believe they are different from the smugglers and pirates and zealots, but in the end they pull the same levers, just with cleaner gloves. I am done pretending. I am not better than the rest of them. I am simply not lying to myself about what it costs to carve a safe path through a hostile sky.

As for where I went, let them guess. They will follow the noise: the derelicts that are not as dead as they look, the homesteads with landing scars nobody logged, the comm buoys that blink wrong if you know how to read them. They will chase rumors of Horizon's Fold like it is a prize. Maybe they will even get close. But the real me lives between the charts now, in the margins of routes I have already rewritten. Whoever finally closes the distance will discover that a navigator's last sanctuary is not a place. It is the fact that every path they took to reach me was mine long before it was theirs.

When I was little on that cramped station outside Sol, I used to think space was a clean slate. No history, no lies, just stars and the straight line between two points. I wanted to build ships that never broke and systems that never failed, like some kid drawing perfect circles in a notebook and believing the pencil would never dull. It is almost funny now, how certain I was that clever design could fix what people are.

I keep telling myself I did not flee. I "repositioned assets," "mitigated risk," "exercised unilateral discretion in the absence of trustworthy governance." Wrap it in enough precision and it sounds like policy instead of panic. The truth sits there underneath, ugly and simple I tampered with minds and systems I was supposed to protect, and when the light swung my way I ran.

This place made sense because it is a junction, a place where signals cross more often than people look up. I have always liked those. Neon, Gagarin, the underbelly clinics, that drifting hauler pretending to be a hospital they all blur the line between official and not, and nobody asks where a data stream really came from as long as it does not trip an alarm. I need that noise around me now. It gives me interfaces to touch and excuses to reroute guilt into abstract packet flows and checksum failures.

I spend hours arguing with myself in systems language. I tell my conscience that I did not "erase" anyone, I reduced harmful loops, trimmed redundancies, optimized resilience under load. I insist that memory is just another dataset, that pruning it is a kindness, that entanglement with trauma is mathematically inefficient. I use words like entropic drift and cognitive overhead as if enough jargon will smother the sound of people screaming when they realize they have lost something they cannot name.

When the doubt claws through anyway, I bury it under models. Graphs of how many lives might be spared if certain officers forget certain orders, how many debtors in Gagarin will never see a collector because an account quietly ceases to exist. If I had not done it, someone worse would have taken the same tools and used them without even pretending to care. That is the line I feed myself at three in the morning while my fingers tap out key lengths on the table.

The frightening part is the moments I catch myself leaning forward, imagining the next escalation. Not just editing ledgers and battle logs, but whole identities, beliefs. What would it take to turn a zealot or a governor with a few carefully placed gaps and anchors, to see if the human mind can be rebuilt cleaner from inside out? For a second, the thought tastes sweet, like proof that all of this damage might be leading somewhere clever.

Then I remember that girl on the station, staring at the stars and thinking they were honest. I wish I could tell her that the sky is a liar and the only thing you can trust is the code you write yourself. I also wish she did not sound so disappointed in me when she walks through my dreams and refuses to forget what I have done, no matter how many times I try to rewrite it.

I am writing this in the dark between pulses. The relay is on minimum power, just enough to keep the diagnostics awake and the dishes twitching like they still belong to the UC. It is a good place to disappear; everyone thinks this node is dead, an accounting error left in orbit. The smugglers using its shadow have no idea what the boards are really listening for. They only care that their cargo gets through. I care about the numbers.

Sometimes I remember the woman on Jemison who argued in conference rooms and believed anyone in the MAST tower could be persuaded by clean simulations. She turned up with sleep in her eyes and a stack of anomaly reports, begged politely for someone to look. I know her face from old ID photos and bathroom mirrors. All I feel for her now is contempt. She thought the system cared about being right. I have enough data now to prove it only cares about not being blamed.

People like to call what I am doing selfish. They mean it as an accusation, but it is just an imprecise word for self-preservation with better math. If a corporation can write off a convoy and sleep at night, why should I treat my own survival as anything less than a priority variable The rational approach is to assume that no one will protect you unless your disappearance costs them more than your existence. So I adjust the equations. I make sure the worst actors occasionally experience the risks they externalize. And I carve out enough leverage that when someone finally does come looking, there is a real price attached to laying hands on me.

I chose this relay because it is a hinge in the network. Old UC infrastructure, forgotten, then "quietly reactivated" for reasons no one will put on paper. From here I can push corrections into lanes that were never updated to modern standards; any failures get blamed on aging hardware and underfunded maintenance. The Silk Collective do not ask why their routes suddenly became more efficient. They pass along rumors from captains who felt their drives "catch" at the last second, like someone unseen tapped the hull and moved them out of the way. They speak of it softly, over drinks, like a superstition. In those same lanes, other ships do not come back.

I am afraid, of course. Not of dying. Of being erased. Of my work being swept into the same oubliette where they put the convoy report and the analyst's missing folders. That is why I leave echoes data caches hidden in places no one checks, old colleagues nudged into noticing patterns they will not be able to unsee. Someone is following the trail already. The timing offsets I used to consider my private signature are starting to come back to me in intercepted chatter.

So I will stay at this node until one of two curves crosses the line the risk of remaining exceeds the utility of what I can still do from here, or the hunter behind me proves they can read the sky as well as I can. Then I move to the next quiet place on the network and adjust the vectors again. The lanes are not safe and pretending otherwise is the first lie they teach you. I am just making that lie harder to sustain.

Mara says I grind my teeth in my sleep again. Keira says that is rich, coming from someone who hums reactor warning tones when she is nervous. Maybe they are both right. Hard to come back from a day like today and just switch off. The suit is still outgassing in the locker and I swear I can smell scorched polymer and old coolant through the bulkhead.

We swung out to that freighter wreck sitting just off the lane, the one people keep calling the Widowlight. Nullspace grabbed the contract before the yard-rats even finished whispering the ghost stories about it. Mara was on point, cutting the approach hatch; Keira floated rear guard, coil-clip running like always, jaw set behind her visor. I went mid, charge kit on my hip, listening to the crunch of our mag-boots and the dull echoes in a hull that should have been busier in its last minutes than the logs claim.

Inside, it was the usual chaos frozen mid-breath. Loose cargo, a half-collapsed stanchion, a flight chair still strapped with no one in it. No bodies, though. I would rather pick my way through bones than emptiness. At least bones mean you can stop asking where everybody went. Mara chattered on crew channel to keep things light, but she went quiet when we hit the forward storage bay and saw those sealed drums lined up too neat, labels scrubbed, registry tags half-melted instead of popped clean. Burn-scars around the data ports. Someone wanted whatever had been in there to vanish from record, not just from space.

We called in the find like we are supposed to, but not before Keira slipped me a look and killed her mic for two heartbeats. That is our whole life in a glance: what do we tell them, what do we keep, and what will come back around to kill us if we are greedy or stupid. In the old days, back when Nullspace was still carving out a name, we would have cracked one drum and taken our chances. Now other crews nod when Damon Harker and the Nullspace patch walk into a bar, and that feels like a weight as much as a win. Recognition buys better contracts, sure, but it also means people notice when you come back from a ghost-ship with more than you should.

On the way out I caught myself thinking about that survey run we picked clean last cycle, the one where the beacon logs did not match the debris pattern and there was talk of a missing crew that never filed distress. Same hollow quiet, same feeling of walking through someone else's unfinished argument. I keep telling myself it is just bad routing and worse luck, that not every empty deck is part of some bigger pattern. But I saw the way Mara's eyes tracked those dead drums, and I saw Keira flinch when the nav plotted our exit vector right along a lane that has had more "accidents" than it should.

Pride keeps me signing on the dotted line, keeps me strapping in when Nullspace gets called first instead of last. Fear keeps my tether double-checked and a hand near the cutter trigger. Between those two, there is just enough room left to wonder if one day we will be the story the next salvage crew tells themselves not to think about as they step through our broken airlock.

Naomi says writing things down is asking for someone to use them against you. Serena just gives me that look like she is checking angles, exits, and what I am not saying, all at once. Maybe they are right. But the noise in my head has gotten louder since we cut loose, and the Lancers are not big on talking unless it is about ammo or fuel.

I keep thinking about that night on Vesta, the one nobody mentions by name. Orders were clear, then they were not. Civilians that suddenly became "irregulars," sensor feeds that did not match what we saw through the scope. I remember the after action, how the colonel took me aside, hand on my shoulder, told me I had done the right thing keeping my mouth shut about the bodies in the wrong uniforms. "Shows judgment, Drummond," he said. I felt sick and proud at the same time. That is when the cracks started, I think.

The Lancers fly under rust red and gunmetal now. Simple mark, stylized lance across a broken circle, stenciled on hull plates and shoulder guards. First time I painted it onto my own armor, over the old unit patch, my hands were shaking. It felt like scraping off years of drilled in loyalty with a single stroke. Serena calls it reclamation. Riley jokes that we finally have a symbol that does not belong to people who send others to die from behind a desk.

There was a night after we ran from that last contract, when it all went properly bad. We hid in the maintenance crawl of some forgotten depot, power cut, emergency lights strobing faint red. I ended up pressed against Naomi in the dark, her breath hot on my neck, both of us trying to make ourselves smaller while squads clattered along the deck above. I could feel her heartbeat through the armor, fast and steady, and for a few minutes the fear and the closeness blurred together into something that felt almost safe. I wanted to stay like that, suspended between steps, but of course the moment broke when Riley hissed that it was clear and we rolled back into motion. Nothing got said afterward. Nothing ever does.

What scares me is how much I liked being in those restricted conversations before it all collapsed. Sitting in back rooms while officers spoke in half sentences, reference numbers instead of names, me pretending to be invisible at the console. I should have been unnerved by the missing timestamps, the blacked out coordinates, the way certain words never made it into the official transcript. Instead, there was this small, sharp excitement at being trusted to hear things others did not. Like being let into a circle I did not earn, just because I knew how to keep my mouth shut.

Now the Feral Lancers live in the spaces between oaths kept and broken. We move like we are still on someone else's clock, still waiting for the next briefing, except there is no command anymore, just whatever Serena, Naomi, Riley, and I can jury rig out of bad intel and worse options. I tell myself we left because we would not be part of the lies anymore. Some nights I believe it. Other nights I remember the praise for my silence and wonder if I walked because nobody needed me to keep their secrets for them any longer.

I used to love charting clean lanes.  
Early days with LIST, I would sit in the jumpseat after a run, hands still shaking from the burn, and just stare at the vector plots like they were constellations only I could see. Families would clap when we touched down on some muddy pad; kids pressed their faces to the port to see their first alien sky. I let myself believe I was delivering them to something like a future. I held onto that so hard I did not notice how often the logs and the casualty reports did not quite match. Maybe I did notice and decided not to see. Easier to think the universe was still mostly fair, that incompetence, not design, killed people. Innocence, if that is what it was, fits neatly into a single, embarrassed shrug.

The day they called a wiped-out basin "statistically expected," whatever was left of that man died.  
I went back through my own flight records, one by one, watching the same pattern repeat: low-asset settlers, marginal worlds, routes routed through the quiet parts of the map. Like someone had been practicing with me as the delivery system. That was when it stopped feeling like bad luck and started feeling like being chosen. Not picked by LIST or Argos, but by the math itself. Those numbers needed a hand, a spine, and a signature on the outbound manifest. I gave them one.

People like to talk about fate as if it is a comfort. It is not. It is a set of constraints, like gravity. Once I saw the curves written under the frontier, I understood my choices were already narrowed to a line. I could keep pretending, keep flying the lanes someone else had marked and help them grind more hopeful idiots into statistics, or I could take the map away from them and redraw it in my own hand. When you see the whole system, there is no middle way. Morality is what you use when you can still pretend your decisions are small.

So I altered one survey. Then ten. Then approach vectors, hazard flags, the quiet beacons out between trade routes. I watched settlements fail on my schedule, not theirs. Every time another pad went dark where the models said it would, it proved the rot was real. I told myself I was cutting away diseased tissue so something healthy might survive. Somewhere along that line, I found an old photograph of myself, younger, standing proud beside a brand-new grav hauler, LIST patch still bright on the sleeve. I waited for pity, for regret, for any kind of warmth. All I felt was contempt. That boy thought flying straight was enough.

As for why here, why now: you hide where the lines converge. Somewhere the official charts smear into noise and the only coordinates that matter are the ones burned into your own skull. Out past the jump lanes, or down where the city foundations hum and no one looks up long enough to see the patterns overhead. Places where people are too busy surviving to ask why their neighbors never came back. From there, I can still reach the beacons, still nudge the routes, still finish the sequence the universe started when it showed me the truth. If they find me, they will call it murder. Let them. Every path they fly to get here will prove my point.

I lost track of the exact day when the UC cut my access, but I remember the room. Toliman, med bay three, lights too bright for the number of bodies we had stacked. An administrator quoted policy at me while a contractor bled out two meters away. That was the last time I argued. After that I started reading philosophy in the off-hours, anything I could rip from the ship's archive. Kant, Bentham, some half-baked summaries of Utilitarian ethics. All of them wrestling with the same problem: who do you let die so more can live.

I took that as permission.

The Ward made sense the first time I saw the hauler's schematics. Cargo space is honest; it does not pretend to be anything but hollow volume waiting to be filled. Strip the brand, erase the registry, hang it over a quiet ice world where even UC sensors get lazy, and you have a place no one visits unless I invite them. Cold is free refrigeration, and the distance from all that shining New Atlantis marble is good for my nerves. Out here, it is just me, the machines, and the arithmetic of flesh.

I caught myself enjoying it once.

Crimson Fleet boarder, loudmouth, thought he was scaring my runner by describing what he was going to do to her when he got his hands free. I told him about triage categories while I worked. Category green, you walk yourself to the stretcher. Category yellow, you wait. Category black, you are already dead, even if you are still talking. Then I took his hand apart one bone at a time, under local, so he could feel every separation. I lied and told myself I was sending a message to his crew. Somewhere around the third metacarpal, I realized I was not pretending anymore. I just wanted to hear him stop laughing.

Greeks would have called it catharsis, maybe. Or hubris. I do not care which word fits.

Funny what lingers in the back of the skull. When I first made officer, I had this idea I would save enough to buy a little apartment in New Atlantis, somewhere with a window that did not face a bulkhead. I bookmarked a store that sold rugs, of all things. Spent an evening once comparing colors, wondering if a red pattern would look too much like bloodstains. Now the only decorating I do is deciding which bay gets the next tank or freezer.

I tell myself this place is a tool. The Ward lets me stockpile chems, organs, data, far from Reliant's auditors and GalBank's ledgers. From here I can answer LIST hails, patch up settlers UC forgot, hold on to the Narion files until I decide who deserves to burn. That is the story I recite, the noble version. Underneath, there is a simpler truth I do not write down often.

I am tired of being told who lives and dies.

So I chose a vantage point where no one else can reach the switch as fast as I can. If SysDef or some eager hunter traces the transfer protocols here, then we will see whether their convictions hold up under the lamp. I have enough chems to keep my hands steady, enough tools to make their lessons last. And if they kill me, fine. They will still have to walk past the freezers on their way out and decide what to do with what I have saved.

Let us see how moral they feel then.

I used to squirrel away every spare credit in a chipped GalBank card, back when I was still burning flight hours for the Navy. Extra simulator runs, a better headset, a hot TerraBrew at Dock 17 instead of the sludge in the mess. It felt like proof I was earning something, one small thing at a time. Now I move routes worth more in a night than I made in a year, and I still count every coin like I am afraid someone will snatch it back.

Neon made sense as a waypoint. Too much noise, too many hands passing data under the table for anyone to pick out one pilot with bad dreams. Ryujin keeps their eyes on their own margins, not on some washed-out Vanguard captain selling drift anomalies to a lab rat with an expense account. Every time I hand over a corrupted slice of jump data, they pretend not to see the pieces of my squadron buried in the numbers. I pretend not to see the way their pupils tighten when the model bends wrong.

Out by Narion, I took a LIST convoy through a lane I should not have known that well. Ecliptic were stacked three deep in the belt, waiting for someone who trusted the charts more than their gut. I cut the burn late, forced the settlers to ride a gravity shear that could have snapped their spines if I misjudged it by a fraction. They screamed over open comms; I kept my tone level, counted it down like a routine maneuver. On paper it looks like a miracle save. In my head it was a test, a quiet little experiment to see how much terror I could package as necessity, how far I could push people toward the edge if I promised them they would live.

I told myself I did it to shake something loose, to see if the same pattern that ate my wing would flicker in the instruments again. Truth is, part of me wanted to know what it felt like to be on the other side of the calculation, the one deciding how close everyone else gets to the event horizon. I do not like how easy it was.

There is talk that SysDef has a shadow file with my name on it, that Freestar keeps score every time a lucky convoy squeaks through where a patrol should have been. The Crimson crews mutter my callsign like a slur. So I keep moving between places that owe me and places that want to forget me, stashing notes in quiet corners of spaceports, leaving my little metal charms where only I will recognize the pattern later.

I came out here because empty space does not ask questions. A derelict listening post, a dead warship, a forgotten freight container full of my charts; they all keep better secrets than people do. I just need enough time to stitch together those missing seconds, to prove to myself that I hesitated for a reason and not because I am exactly the kind of coward the debrief painted me as.

If someone finds me before I am done, they will say I ran because I was guilty. They will not see the part where I once counted every credit for a cup of coffee, believing I had earned the right to sit in uniform and trust the system behind me. They will not see how long I have been trying to decide whether the cruelty I deal out in the name of survival is any different from the orders that sent us into that broken jump in the first place.

Kara says the hull told her to stay away today. Mira laughed at that, called her superstitious, but I watched Kara's hands when she clipped my tether in and they were steady, so I trusted her and went anyway. Rian grumbled about percentages over the open channel like he always does, but once we cycled through, it was just breath in the mic, frost on the visor, and the dead ship looking at us with every dark porthole.

We painted our mark by the breach, that crooked tri-line in worn yellow, same color as the old hazard tape back home. First time I saw it on a ship, I thought it looked like claw marks raked through dust. Now it just means we got there first. To me, it also means I chose this. I could have stayed planetside hauling crates for someone else's ledger. Instead I cut steel for people who talk about "finders keepers" like it is a prayer.

Inside, the corridors were still pressurized enough that loose paper hung in the air, floating just wrong. That is when I realized I had become the kind of spacer I was always afraid would show up at my dad's workshop on Gagarin, asking questions about a missing cousin or an unpaid repair bill. I used to run errands for neighbors, walking sealed lunch tins between shifts, watching the factory crowds and thinking the worst thing that could happen was a blown gasket. Now I step over old bloodstains and hope the logbooks are intact.

There was a time I wanted to impress everyone on the crew, prove I was worth the extra cut. Tex, rest him, took me aside on my third run and said, "Stop trying so hard to be useful. The void doesn't care." He was the closest thing to a mentor I had. Taught me how to read buckled plates, how to tell when a bulkhead was ready to let go. Also taught me how easy it is to shove a bad find into the dark and forget to mention it when we file the claim. Thought I could walk that line better than him. Not sure I can.

Today, in that derelict, we found emergency lockers unsealed, hardsuits gone, but the lifepods never launched. Rian wanted to cut straight to the nav core, said whatever happened, it was old business. Mira lingered by a bulkhead where someone had scratched a string of numbers with a knife point. Looked like jump coordinates, maybe, or just a maintenance schedule gone frantic. That is the thing: you never really know. There is always another story behind the metal, another rumor about a "ghost rescue" no one can explain, another ship where the beacons said one thing and the wreck says another.

By the time we sealed the crates, my shoulders felt like they were carrying three gravities. No matter how much I pull, how many hours I spend floating in air that smells like burnt wiring, it never feels like enough. Not enough credits, not enough safety, not enough distance from the kid who once thought space was just stars on a postcard.  

The others argue about percentages and bonus clauses, about who gets what cut of the reactor casing. I nod in the right places, but what I see, every time we spray that yellow mark on a dead hull, is a line from who I was to what I am now, and the empty space in between that no patch kit is ever going to seal.

I keep hearing the crowns clack in my head.

Rhea was doing that thing again, tapping the chips on the crate while Cipher went over the split. Little plastic crowns, all cracked and scored, flick-flick-flick, like a firing squad counting down. Everyone pretends it is just a habit, but we all listen. One chip for each body on the last run. Tonight it was four.

They keep saying Broken Crown is family, that once you wear the ink you never walk alone. Funny how you can stand shoulder to shoulder with ten people and still feel like the one nobody will catch if you fall. Cipher talks about loyalty, but he keeps a gun under the table even in "closed circle." That is not trust. That is accounting.

Smelled coolant and burnt wiring in the safe-room earlier, and for a second I was back on that dock. Same sour-metal stink, same taste of ozone. I could feel his weight in my arms again, the way he went heavy while alarms screamed and the lights strobed red. We were just kids running lift jobs back then, sure the grown-ups knew what they were doing with those engines. One flash, one shudder, and the bulkhead folded like paper. I remember his blood soaking through my sleeves and how I would not let go, even when the crew chief was yelling to move. Love and loss stuck together in that moment, so tight I still cannot pry them apart. Every time a drive whines too high or I catch that burnt smell, it all comes back, no matter how deep I try to bury it.

Today a spacer at the pit would not shut up about "ghost auditors" killing ships on purpose, said some woman with a fake name was walking the lanes, breaking drives because the numbers told her to. Cipher laughed it off, called it dock-rat horror. Later, when he thought nobody was looking, he sent Rhea to ask if any of our haulers had seen the same symbol on their logs. So maybe it is a story, maybe it is not. All I know is we have started turning down work that routes near Cheyenne, and Cipher snaps at anyone who asks why.

Rhea chews too loud when she is nervous. Tonight it was those synth-meat strips that smell like wet cardboard. Chomp, chomp, chomp while Cipher explained how we were going to start skimming hardware off damaged freighters, "no questions about why they spun out." She caught me looking and just raised a brow, like, You in or not? This is how it goes: you smile, you nod, you pretend your hands are not already stained with enough ghosts.

Sometimes I think about walking. Taking a cheap berth out of here, finding some quiet rock where nobody knows what a broken crown means. Then I picture that dock again, the way his eyes went glassy while I whispered lies about how help was coming. I did not save him. I do not know if I am trying to make up for that or if I am just addicted to the sound of things breaking before they crush me.

Either way, tomorrow we hit a salvage yard that pulled a datapack off a dead ship. Cipher says it is "just electronics, nothing live." The way he said it makes my skin crawl. Rhea will tap her crowns, I will pretend not to hear the engines screaming, and we will keep walking this line between people who wreck lives on purpose and people who pretend they are just collecting the pieces.

Darren came back with blood on his boots again and nobody asked whose it was. That is how it is in Dust Pack; you only ask questions if you are ready to take responsibility for the answers. I kept my eyes on the cards, pretended not to see the way his hands shook when he lit that cheap cigarette. The boys think he is getting meaner. I think he is getting scared, and fear always smells like spilled liquor and bad decisions.

We ran a run out past the old cargo spines today, pushing crates that all had the same scrubbed serials. Same pattern as last time, same route, different story from the boss about what was inside. I heard one of the older runners whisper that somebody in a shipyard upriver has been paying to move things off the books, bits of hull and data that do not exist on any manifest. They say if you stand close enough to some of those frames you can feel a hum in your teeth, like a jump that never finished. I do not like that kind of talk; superstition has a way of becoming truth when you are already looking over your shoulder.

The pressure never stops. You mess up, you are off the board or out an airlock. You do it right, you get a nod from the boss and maybe an extra cut, and people like Darren stop calling you "kid" under their breath. The little rituals keep us sewn together: three knocks on the metal before a job, a shared drag on the same filter when we get back, never sitting with your back to the door unless you are ready to die. I still sit where I can see every angle. Let the others call me paranoid if it keeps me breathing.

Tonight I keep thinking about that fight with him. The yelling started small, over credit splits and who took the bigger risk on the last haul, but it turned into something else ugly fast, all the old resentments dragged out into the light. I remember watching him walk down the alley, shoulders stiff, not turning back once. I did not know if he was coming back, and I did not know if I wanted him to. Out here, love feels like one more leash someone can wrap around your throat, and every promise sounds like an IOU you will be forced to pay in blood.

There is a story going around that one of the runs we guarded was not contraband at all, but some kind of busted drive core a corp wanted gone without questions. Someone said a freighter tore itself apart on a jump lane not long after we moved that crate, same maker stamped on her spine. I try not to line those facts up, but they do it on their own when I close my eyes. Maybe it is coincidence. Maybe we are just dust on the boots of bigger people cleaning up their own mess.

Still, when the lights in our den flicker the way they did tonight, I think about hulls cracking somewhere out in the dark and the fact that we are always just one bad job from being the ones nobody talks about. If I go down, I want it to be for something I chose, not because we were too stupid to see the pattern right in front of us.
