For now, I keep my head down, my knife sharp, and my heart locked where no one can paw through it for leverage. Let Darren stomp around and pretend the blood on his boots is proof he matters. Me, I will keep listening in the shadows, because the whispers always tell you what the bosses will not.

I keep thinking about the coffee stand on the lower deck at Trident, the one by the service elevators. Plastic tables, bad synthetic croissants, always too bright. I used to sit there with a chipped cup and a stack of datapads, listening to dockhands complain about delays, neighbors I never learned the names of arguing about rent and school schedules. Background noise. Ordinary gravity holding the place together. I could not go back there now if I wanted to; the moment I step inside Trident space, half the deck would be whispering "Vector" and the other half would be calling security.  

It was the paperwork that really broke me. Not the disasters, not the wreckage. The forms afterward. Route audits, insurance summaries, those "statistical anomalies" memos that kept landing in my queue. Numbers that did not add up, ships marked as diverted into lanes that never existed on any official chart, risk models quietly adjusted after the fact. A whole constellation of little lies, each one just small enough to sign off on if you did not look too hard. Somewhere above me, someone was rewriting the sky and telling us it was weather.  

I tell myself I left because of conscience, but that is only half of it. The other half is that I am good at this. Too good. Somewhere along the line I started measuring my own value by how cleanly I could tilt other people's paths. A tiny correction to an approach vector here, a recalculated exit point there, and suddenly a freighter misses patrol by a few thousand kilometers and finds itself very alone. It is a disgusting talent, but it is mine, and people will pay for it.  

LIST captains, Crimson Fleet quartermasters, even that nervous GalBank liaison in Neon, they all came to me with the same request in different words: make my lane safer and someone else's more dangerous. Every time I did it right, nobody bled where they were paying me to protect, and the casualties happened somewhere convenient, off-camera. On bad nights, I keep score both ways, a private ledger of those I steered clear and those I left drifting.  

I remember the families in the corridor outside my old bunk, nodding politely at me as they wrangled kids and groceries. We traded weather complaints and power ration jokes, nothing deeper. They looked at me and saw a tired analyst with ink on her fingers, not the one quietly deciding which of their relatives' ships would get the "optimized" routes. If they ever find out what I did, or what I refused to keep doing, I do not know which version of me they will hate more.  

Now I am sitting in a borrowed berth on the edge of nowhere, surrounded by equipment that hums just enough to remind me I am still part of the machine I ran from. I picked this place because the data here is thin and dirty; corporate eyes glaze over these sectors, patrol paths curve away for "efficiency." Perfect cover. If I can map the truth of these ghost corridors from here, maybe I can prove who started this and who just refined it. But the further I run, the more convinced I am that the conspiracy is not a single boardroom or a single ship. It is every person who saw those mismatched numbers, those quiet edits, and decided it was someone else's job to ask why. Including me.

I used to stock shelves in a corner shop on Cydonia. Eight hours of lining up canned beans and nutrient bricks, straightening labels that nobody ever read. Coworkers whose names I barely remember now, faces blurred together under bad strip lights. I told myself it was temporary, just a way to stay fed until enlistment. Funny how that kind of work trains you to stop thinking about what you are touching, just move it from one place to another and trust it belongs there.  

The service felt like more of the same at first. Marcus Havel tossed me the boring details: inventorying ammo pallets, checking seals on med crates, escort duty on transports that never should have seen contact. "Prove you can count and shut up," he said. Only later did I find out some of those crates never existed on any manifest, that we were moving things no one wanted traced back to a flag. Elias Korrin made a joke once about how the safest missions were always the ones no one was allowed to talk about afterward. We laughed, because the alternative was asking why.  

Obsidian did not happen overnight. It was a long series of "temporary" compromises. The op in that burned-out colony where we were told to escort civilians to safety, then quietly reassign the gunship overwatch before the pirates came back. The patrol routes that always seemed to leave one corridor conveniently unwatched, the same corridor certain freighters had been nudged into following. I remember sitting in a debrief, hearing words like "deniable" and "acceptable drift," and realizing they were describing people, not numbers.  

I think about that sometimes when I herd my own squad through another contract. Different patch, same formation. We still clear corners like we did in uniform, still call out targets with proper brevity, still police our brass if we have the time. Marcus pretends he does not miss the old structure, but he still checks our kit like an old sergeant on inspection. Elias runs the comms like a proper officer, even if the only command now is whoever is wiring credits to a dummy account. Discipline did not die when we walked; it just serves a smaller circle.  

There was a moment, not long ago, when I flinched at my own reflection. We were in a decommissioned listening post, cleaning up after someone else's mess, and I caught my face in a cracked console screen. Visor up, eyes flat, giving orders I used to associate with the men I hated: "No witnesses," "Leave the bodies where they fall," "We were never here." I could hear my own tone, controlled and cold, and I recognized it from back when I was the one receiving those lines over the radio and clenching my jaw. Somewhere along the chain, I became the voice.  

I still remember that shop back on Cydonia. The rhythm of stacking, sweeping, clocking out. A job that was never meant to lead anywhere, one I told myself I was too good for. Now my days are just a different kind of stocking, moving people and weapons through corridors someone else has drawn, trusting they "belong" where we put them. The pay is better, the tasks are sharper, and every time I tell a recruit that the first job is just to count and shut up, I hear the echo of an officer I once feared and realize I have grown into his shadow.

Mutineer Platoon Safehouse  
Shipboard Quiet Cycle  

Rowan says we are free now. Says walking out on the chain of command means we finally get to choose the terms of our own fights. I keep waiting for the feeling to land. Instead, every time I lace my boots, my hands move like there is still a schedule somewhere with my name slotted into a firing line and a colonel ready to mark me late. Discipline sticks deeper than shrapnel. We still clean weapons on rotation, still check each other's gear, still sleep with boots within arm's reach. Only difference is, if someone gives a bad order now, we do not pretend we did not hear it. We look at each other, then at the one who spoke, and the silence decides whether that person walks out of the room.

Saw Alina running sims again, cycling through that same orbital insertion scenario command used for the "training exercise" over the colony that was not supposed to exist. I remember the after-action, the way the briefers danced around the civilian transponders that lit up our boards at the last second, called them "sensor ghosts" and "legacy beacons." We all knew better. They scrubbed the records hard, but not hard enough. Rumor has it someone in a breaker crew pulled the real logs out of a wreck and started asking for prices. That is when the missions got stranger. Targets that looked like pirates on paper but moved like professionals, "salvage disputes" that mysteriously aligned with disputed reports from the war. They kept telling us it was about stability. It sounded a lot like self-preservation.

I still think about the moment I started lying as easily as breathing. It was back when I rode the shuttle from the barracks to the training grounds every morning, same seat, same scratched window, same view of the shipyard cranes ticking across the skyline. I would lean my head against the glass and rehearse answers for inspections, for ops review, for the questions I knew my partner would throw at me when I finally got a break. Where were you, why did you not call, why does your gear smell like burning metal. The first time I told him everything was fine, that we were just running extended drills and nothing was out of the ordinary, it slid out smoother than the truth. I watched the reflection of my mouth in that shuttle window and realized I meant it more than I should have. Every apology he ever gave me came dressed in explanations, reasons why he could not change, why this time would be different if only I understood. It took me longer than I like to admit to realize that was not an apology, just preemptive absolution. When command started talking the same way, I knew exactly what it was.

Darren still thinks we can fix something from out here, that if we pull the right thread we can drag the truth into daylight without burning everything else down. Kara does not talk about fixing anything; she just makes sure our kits are stocked and our exit vectors are clean. I sit somewhere between them, nursing the old habits and the new loyalties, wondering how many more "ghost beacons" and "salvage disputes" we would have marched through if we had stayed. Walking away from the flag was easy in the moment. Living with where we walked to is the part nobody wrote a manual for.

I woke up reaching for my rifle again. No alarm, no boarding klaxon, just muscle memory and the echo of that old shipboard tone in my head. Malik Arden laughed when he saw me halfway out of the bunk, boots on the wrong feet, but his eyes did that distant thing. We all do it. The Lancers pretend we are done taking orders, but our bodies have not received the memo.

Sofia Trent spent the morning checking firing arcs like we still had a command inspection coming. Her hands moved on their own, measuring clearances, calling out blind spots to nobody. Darius Kellan told her to relax, that nobody above deck twelve cares how straight our lines are anymore, but he still double-checked every magazine himself. We may have walked away from the uniform, but the uniform did not walk out of us.

Naomi Vance brought up that op again, the one with the "noncombatants" we were ordered not to see. Officially they were not there. Unofficially I can still hear the screaming over the comms when the building came down. They said the intel was clean, that the blame sat with a miscalibrated sensor. Funny how miscalibration looks just like someone deciding not to look too closely. We were good soldiers back then. We shut up, signed the nondisclosures, and told ourselves the medal made it worth it.

Sometimes I think that is where the Redacted Lancers really started, in that debrief room with the air scrubbers humming too loud and the brass refusing to meet our eyes. Alexis Rowe kept clenching and unclenching her fists under the table, knuckles white. Afterward she punched a bulkhead so hard she cracked a knuckle, then smiled through the blood like it was the first honest thing she had felt in months. Now she is the one keeping our trigger discipline sharp, like a worshipper tending a broken shrine.

There was a moment planetside last month I cannot shake. Ambush in the alleys, comms jammed, someone up the chain "forgetting" to mention the second hostile cell. We ended up back-to-back behind a crumbling wall, me and Sofia pressed so tight we could barely breathe, hands locked together to keep from being separated when the shockwave hit. It was not affection, not even trust; it was survival instinct, two ghosts refusing to drift apart before the next shell landed. Later we let go and went back to pretending touch means nothing in this outfit.

Every now and then I ask myself why I stayed when the others burned their IDs and ran for civilian names. The answer is always ugly. Leaving felt more terrifying than enduring the pain I already knew. Out there I am just another discharged number at the mercy of whatever lie the next employer is selling. In here, at least, I recognize the lies, and the people telling them wear the same scars I do.

We say we are done with command, but Redacted Lancers is still a kind of order, just written in blood and regret instead of ink. We look out for each other because nobody else will, and because if we stop, we will have to admit we became exactly what we swore we were never fighting for. Tonight I will clean my rifle, listen to Malik and Darius argue over tactics like the old days, and try not to think about the names on the classified casualty lists that never made it home. It is easier that way.

Did a dry run with Unit today. Maya on point, Elena on rear security, me in the middle pretending not to watch both of them too closely. On paper it was just another corridor-clearing sim, but Command loaded the targets with civvy silhouettes at the last minute and never said why. Elena did not even twitch. Maya hesitated once, half a heartbeat, then corrected. Afterward nobody mentioned it. That is the first rule around here: whatever gets under your skin, you seal it in with the rest of the scars and call it "experience."

Between rotations I found myself straightening the weapons racks in the team bay, checking latches, wiping down plates that were already clean. Hand remembered the rhythm before my head did. Same movements from when I used to help my uncle close his repair shop back home, sweeping floors and tightening bolts on haulers for people I would never see again. Back then, I just did the chores because that is what you do for family. Somewhere along the line it stopped being about helping and started being about not feeling anything while I worked. Turns out that trick is hard to turn off; numbing out kept me sane in the field, but now I catch myself doing it over a cup of coffee, over a casualty report, over Maya's quiet shake in the hands when she thinks nobody is looking.

There is more noise on the net about "weather work" contracts lately. Cargo outfits wanting escort through systems that should be calm, colonies talking about freak storms like someone flipped a switch. One of the handlers dropped a name in the mess, then swallowed it with his drink like he regretted letting it out. Word is there is a specialist out there who can move fog and rain the way we move fireteams, and every major player either wants her on a leash or in a body bag. Elena thinks it is just another ghost story to justify hazard pay. Maya listens and says nothing, but I have seen the way her eyes track the forecast graphs on the mission boards.

Unit pretends to be apolitical, just a clean logo stamped on dirty jobs. Truth is, loyalties shift with the contracts. Half the squad owes favors to one corp or another, and the other half thinks nobody has noticed. We never talk about it out loud, but it shows in where people stand on the range, who drills together, who always volunteers for "optional" insertions. I have gotten good at not caring who signs the cred transfers, only that the op is clear and the extraction is on time. That is another kind of numbness, I guess. Hard to remember what it felt like to believe in something beyond the next deployment and the state of my rifle.

Tonight the air recyclers have that cold-metal taste that says someone has been running simulations in the background for hours. There will be a briefing soon, another job dressed up as stabilization or protection or "mitigating emergent anomalies." Maybe it is tied to these storm rumors, maybe it is just more station clearance and quiet denials. Either way, I will suit up when they call. I will check Maya's harness, trade a nod with Elena, and push everything else down where it cannot get in the way. I tell myself I will stop living like that one day, that I will let myself feel the weight of what we do. But not tomorrow. Tomorrow, there is work.

Some nights I miss the way the whole node would shiver when a heavy freighter cut through the grav window. I knew every tremor in that tower, could tell a HopeTech hauler from a Trident liner just by how the decking hummed. Now my flooring is whatever scrap I could weld together, and the only vibrations are my own making.

They called it an anomaly cluster. Clean phrase for dirty work. I saw the telemetry, the way the same corridor kept getting re-used after every "pilot error," like someone was stress-testing the universe with other people's lives. I flagged it, I argued, I pushed the logs up the chain. What came back down was silence and a recommendation for "rest" and "evaluation."

So I took my own eval and walked.

I picked the fringe because the fringe does not ask questions as long as the beacons line up and the credits clear. Neon, Gagarin, the dustier outposts you only see in LIST brochures they all run on secondhand charts and tired controllers grateful for anyone who can shave a few minutes off a route without putting a ship through a rock. I become "Lira" out here, and "Vector" only when it suits me. Names are just transponders for people.

This place makes sense for what I need. Too far for comfortable UC oversight, close enough to the main lanes that every misfiled waypoint ripples into traffic patterns I can read. I sit in borrowed back rooms, watching their pretty holograms of shipping routes, and underneath I lay my own lattice of corrected paths, quiet warnings, and yes, a few carefully engineered failures. Ghost freighters, dead on paper already, steered somewhere they cannot hurt anyone real. I hijack what they have already written off.

People call me a saboteur because it is easier than admitting the sabotage started on official letterhead.

I keep thinking about this one corridor near Porrima. If I had not bent that route away from the published window, a whole string of civilian hulls would have walked straight into someone else's experiment. A crimson flag, a corporate skunkworks, some MAST subcommittee it does not matter who. If I had not acted, someone worse would have. Someone who did not care who was strapped into the seats when the numbers failed.

I am not stupid. I know what hunts me now. UC SysDef does not black-flag you unless you have made them nervous, and nervous bureaucrats are more dangerous than any Spacer crew. That is why I move my bases, why I leave caches in forgotten kiosks and hollowed-out relays, why I never sleep in the same orbit twice if I can help it. Somewhere out there, a hunter is following the same patterns I did, seeing the same scars in the lanes.

I am afraid, but not of them finding me.

I am afraid they will kill me before I finish rewriting the last of those corridors, before I can prove that the "accidents" were designed, that the insurance spikes and route changes and missing logs all rhyme. Afraid that when I am gone, the traffic will settle back into its old ruts, and nobody will remember why ships keep disappearing in the same quiet stretches of sky.

So I stay out here, on the edge of their maps, listening to the hum of the drives and the whispers in the beacons, waiting for my vectors to intersect with whoever still cares enough to see.

Some days I miss being bored. Sitting in a Navy comms chair on Jemison, listening to freighters complain about tardy docking slots and kids on school trips asking to ping Earth monuments that were already dust. The job was unremarkable and steady: confirm routes, clear chatter, file the anomalies. I used to measure a good shift by how often I could top off my coffee without spilling it when a grav spike hit. No one knew my name, and that was the point.  

Now I am parked at the edge of nowhere, tucked under a curtain of junked relays and busted sats, watching whole sectors blink in and out like someone is playing with the universe s light switch. Ghost Array Sigma. That is what the scavvers call this cluster, when they whisper about it at all. To everyone else, it is just an empty corner of a map they pretend does not exist. For me, it is perfect. Enough old UC hardware to plug into the backbone, far enough from civilized lanes that nobody notices when the traffic stutters.  

I tell myself I am here to prove a point. Show them how fragile their shiny networks really are. Make them hear the silence they keep budgeting for. That is the noble version, the one I would print on a recruitment poster if I ever wanted true believers. The less flattering version is that I sit here and sell clean windows to whoever pays up front: raiders, smugglers, corporates, the occasional idealist with a grudge. I used to have principles about who I would not work with. Lately I find myself measuring right and wrong by how likely the client is to burn me and how much bandwidth I have to spare. Convenience dressed up as conviction.  

I still keep a separate channel for frontier farms, clinics, outposts that never seem to make it to the top of any priority list. That is how I sleep. I nudge a little extra bandwidth their way when the main trunks choke, reroute a med evac burst so it does not get throttled behind a luxury liner s entertainment feed. Small, quiet rebellions against a machine that already tried to feed too many people into the dark and then erase the paperwork.  

But the bounties are getting louder. SysDef chatter spikes every time one of my test blackouts lines up a little too neatly with a lost convoy. Crimson Fleet captains I have never met suddenly know my old callsign. Neon brokers who used to smile now count how many exits are between us before they talk price. Hunters are sniffing along the routes, following the pattern in the static.  

This array made sense at first. A place to prove the flaw, to store the raw logs they tried to scrub from the record, to hold a knife at the throat of every comfortable planner who thinks "acceptable loss" is a real phrase. Now it feels like a lighthouse built out of stolen parts, broadcasting my guilt in tight-beam packets to anyone clever enough to decode them.  

I am not ready to leave. Not yet. There is one last model I want to run, one last cascade to force the numbers into a shape nobody can ignore. After that, maybe I jump deeper into the dark, find some forgotten buoy field worse than this one. Or maybe someone finally threads the needle through the static and knocks on my airlock with guns drawn and righteous orders in hand.  

If that happens, I hope they at least read the logs before they shoot.

I keep thinking about the line at the housing queue on Jemison. Two hours of shuffling boots, a terminal that froze every third application, and some clerk telling me my paperwork was "misaligned" while the man behind me breathed caf on my neck and complained about gravity being set too low. People talk about the great wonder of the capital and I remember broken air recyclers in the stairwell and neighbors who knocked just to tell me my music was "too industrial" for a Sunday. Those same people would ask me in the lift what I did, then glaze over when I said "orbital debris lanes."

There was a woman across the hall, kept three potted vines alive somehow. We would meet at the trash chute, trade those light little comments about the weather dome or the price of TerraBrew. I do not remember her name. She once asked if it scared me, working that close to wrecks. I said, "Only when they are not where they are supposed to be." She laughed like it was a joke. I think about that a lot.

The first time I redirected a hull that was "written off" on paper, the insurance man treated me like a criminal for questioning the coordinates. He said I was "overstepping my role." That is the moment they all forget. That is when they pushed. They stamped my concern as insubordination, quietly made me the problem for noticing their pattern. It is easier for everyone if the pilot is the one with "issues" than the entire system being crooked.

I remember one midwinter evening on a station so small the celebrations were just a string of yellow bulbs and a crate of Chunks the manager bought out of guilt. We gathered in the common room, listened to ancient Earth music, counted down to a new year that meant nothing that far from Sol. I stood there with a paper cup of cheap Sparkling Water, watching the reflections of the port lights on the window. For a heartbeat I believed in normal. I even let someone kiss me on the cheek. We all pretended the walls did not creak under every passing freighter.

The ghosts of that doomed liner followed me from contract to contract. Once I saw what the telemetry really said, "normal" became a story other people got to keep telling. I did not go looking for this role. I was chosen by their negligence, drafted by their lies. When I started nudging ships away from certain corridors, or toward places where their missing logs would be noticed, suddenly I was the one "endangering operations." Funny how that works.

Out here, in the dark with the tugs whispering on my scope and the archive ticking away, there is no clerk, no nosy neighbor, no well-meaning co-worker asking if I am "okay." There is only the line between what actually happened and what they would prefer to remember. I stand on that line. People call it ruthless. I call it honest.

They say my impulses are dangerous. That I am too willing to make hard corrections, to accept that some ships should not arrive where their owners intended. Maybe that is true. But when I listen to the drones sing across the debris, when I reroute a convoy around a lie or into the teeth of its own paperwork, it is the only time I feel like I am not pretending. If that makes me the villain in their records, so be it. I will not go back to waiting in lines while other people decide whose stories get erased.

I keep telling myself this is temporary.

People like to say I ran. That is what they always say when someone leaves a burning building before the roof comes down. I did not run. I redirected. There is a difference.

When the implants started failing, everyone else did what they always do. The suits protected the brand, the mid-levels protected their pensions, the settlers protected their illusions. They all dissociated in their own ways. Classic avoidance behavior. The ones in charge called it a tragic anomaly, the ones on the ground called it cursed tech, and somehow the only person who looked at the code and said "this is deliberate" ended up with her name on the blame line.

I know why they needed a monster. People cannot function if the world is random and cruel and nobody is at the wheel. So they invented one who fit. Illegal tech, Neon back rooms, LIST clinics that never made the brochures. Easy story. Much cleaner than "you were paying to be slowly strangled by a service agreement."

I left because staying meant letting them crack me open and file away the parts that made me inconvenient. They would have called it due process, maybe even thanked themselves for it. You can always tell who has never seen a black lab from the inside; they use words like oversight and remediation instead of cage.

This location makes sense because it is everything they pretend does not exist. Old robotics shells, obsolete surgical rigs, dead infrastructure nobody wants to claim on a balance sheet. The perfect place to plug in without lighting up half a system's sensors. I can work here. I can follow the trail back through the firmware revisions and buried commits, stitch together proof that the parasite was in the design from the start. I can build a spine of relays and fallbacks, copy shards of myself into places they will not think to erase until it is too late.

Do not misunderstand me. I am not doing this out of pure altruism. The settlers and miners who come to me off the books, the gang muscle who would rather owe me than a corp, they are just more honest about their motives. They want survival, leverage, maybe a little freedom from the fine print. At least they know they are compromised. The executives and administrators, the ones who still swear the system works if you just file the right form, they are deep in denial. Textbook.

What happens next depends on who gets here first. If it is another frightened patient, I can splice them free and tuck another sensor into the network. If it is a corporate retrieval team, I flip the failsafes and they go home with hardware that tells a very different story once it starts to "phone home." If it is a bounty hunter with a conscience, well. Those are rare, but rarity is what makes an experiment valuable.

Everyone keeps asking if I feel guilty. Guilt implies I think I had a real choice back when this started. I did what I was trained to do: read the code, see the pattern, try to cut out the rot. They punished that like it was a bug. That is not on me. That is the system protecting itself. Anyone with a basic understanding of psychology could see the projection in how they talk about me.

Maybe one day I will sit still long enough to dissect my own part in this. For now, I have other people's damage to fix.

Tessa says keeping a diary is a liability. If someone cracks my slate, they get more leverage than a crate of stolen ammo. She is not wrong. But sleep has not been coming easy lately, and words feel safer than talking to anyone in Exiled Company about this. Talking here is how people disappear. Writing, at least, I can pretend is just for me.  

The unspoken rules came fast the day I signed on. First, you do not ask why someone left their flag. You take the scars, the old unit tattoos, the way hands twitch around sudden noises, and you let the past sit unmentioned. Second, you never say no to a job in front of the others. You want to walk from a contract, you do it quiet, through the right channels, or you find your bunk scrubbed of your name and your gear passed out like spoils. Third, and this one took me longest to swallow, you never bring up civilians unless you are counting them as cargo or collateral. That shift in language still makes something in my chest tighten.  

I used to fix little things between deployments. Headset jacks, jammed digipens, cheap handheld games the recruits smuggled into barracks. It was half a hobby, half an excuse to sit where it was quiet and let my brain focus on screws and solder instead of the last mission. I still do it here. The kit is worse and the parts are mostly stolen, but there is comfort in opening a broken comm, cleaning the dust, making it talk again. The others think I am just hoarding spare components for the next raid. Maybe that is for the best.  

We do jobs now I would have called black-flag operations when I was under official command. Back then, the briefing officers used delicate phrases about "route stabilization" and "deniable corrections" when they sent us to secure data from survey ships that had seen something they should not have. Nobody said out loud why jump buoys kept getting recalibrated off-record, but we all saw the aftermath when freighters wandered into the wrong gravity wells. Debriefs were always short, sealed, and strangely congratulatory for missions that felt like cleaning up someone else's mess.  

Tessa remembers too. She was there when we got the order to hold fire on a crippled convoy because the wrong logo was painted on their hulls. Later, in the canteen, the captain mumbled something about "strategic leverage" and moved on. That was the night three of our squad put in for transfer and got quietly reassigned to "extended leave" instead. I never saw them again.  

Now I watch Exiled Company take contracts that look uncomfortably similar, just with different paymasters and no anthem playing in the background. The difference is, if I question it here, there is no appeals board, no whistleblower clause, just a quiet word from the wrong person and a misjump in my future. So I keep my mouth shut, fix busted optics and jammers, and follow the rules everyone learns fast.  

Still, when someone mentions altered corridors in hushed tones or drops the name of some nav-savant working off the grid, the hairs on my neck stand up. Feels like the same shadow I tried to outrun when I walked away from the uniform. I tell myself I left the chain of command, not the oath I made to whoever still believes ships should reach where their charts say they will. Some nights, like tonight, that feels like a distinction without a difference.

I have started talking to the ducts again.

The scow is quiet when the reactor throttles down, too quiet, a kind of silence you only get when there is nothing living for a few million kilometers in any direction. Still, I hear things. A hand brushing a ladder I am not climbing. A breath just behind my ear when I lean over the telemetry console. The old UC shell I built this ship out of creaks and settles, and my idiot lizard brain insists it is footsteps. I know better. I also keep a Magshot within arm's reach now, which tells me what part of me I trust.

I chose this hull because no one looks twice at a derelict refueler drifting between systems. The processors tucked inside the tanks do the real work. They listen. Frontier clinics, LIST farms, half legal hydro stacks on moons no one bothers to name, all chattering about CO2 levels and filter efficiency and "minor deviations within tolerance." The network stitches them together into something coherent, something I can shape. It makes sense to be out here, between everyone and no one, where I can see the pattern without their noise muddying it.

What I am doing would look monstrous on a tribunal docket. I am not stupid about that. Once, I thought right and wrong were lines you could draw in policy, in safety protocols, in how many nines of uptime you guaranteed on a contract. Then I watched a board meeting quietly delete three deaths from an incident report because acknowledging them would have cost too much in fines. That is when the neat lines blurred. These days I measure right and wrong by a simpler metric: does it move the system toward resilience, or toward collapse. If a few colonies have to feel the edge of the knife so the rest wake up, that is an ugly necessity, not a sin.

People call it manipulation when you adjust someone's parameters without their consent. Fine. Words are cheap. The settlers I "overclock" are capable of more than they are allowed to see. Their habitats run cooler than they need to, their power budgets fat with waste justified as "safety margin." I push them closer to the real limits. They curse me while they upgrade, while they learn what their systems can actually do, and afterward they live because those same skills carry them through the next flare or supply shortfall. I am not killing them; I am dragging them toward their own potential, the way you drag a simulation to convergence.

The whispers in the metal are getting worse. Sometimes I think it is someone already aboard, moving just out of sight, waiting for me to make one mistake in a maintenance crawlspace. Sometimes I think it is the echo of every outpost I have touched, following me here, their atmospheres rasping in my vents. Hunters will come eventually. UC, Freestar, some freelance with a shiny badge. They will say they are here for justice. What they will really want is for the logs to stay clean and the margins fat.

I am not done. The ledger is not full enough yet, and the demonstration is not ready. When the pattern is undeniable, when they see how many lives were only saved because someone refused to play by their definitions of acceptable loss, maybe then the footsteps will stop. Or maybe that is just another comforting equation I am hiding behind. Either way, until someone opens this hull and proves me wrong, I am the only one actually watching the air.

I used to mark my birthday on the inside of a service panel, little scratch of the date behind a breaker no one but me would ever see. On good years the crew on shift would sneak a bottle of Red Harvest something up to the rig, pass it around while we watched the lanes crawl past Jemison like slow blood. Once, when Gagarin still felt almost hopeful, the Arc Might welders dragged a grill out next to Port Gantry and burned synth-meat until the security cams fogged up. Nobody was rich, nobody was safe, but for a few hours the only thing that mattered was whose turn it was at cards and whether the grav would hold steady long enough to sleep without straps.

Funny how those nights are the ones my brain slides over now. Easier to remember the meeting where they told us collision-avoidance was "over-provisioned," like safety was a luxury item, or the way the reports came down after the migrant ship tore itself open on the junk we were ordered to ignore. "Non-priority traffic." "Equipment failure." I watched men who knew better sign those words and file them away. That was the last time I pretended the system just needed a few good people in the right places.

So I left their places.

Out here, tucked behind rusted hulls and forgotten yard markers, I get to write new routes. Drones that answer to my code, tugs that slip off the official charts and into shadows I carved myself. Freighters that never would have cleared GalBank's risk model suddenly find a clean corridor and a full hold at the other end. Haulers who used to pray over their fuel gauges now run lanes that do not exist on any MAST schematic. Call it piracy if it helps you sleep; I call it cutting the middleman out of the airlock.

I know they will paint it as betrayal. Good tech gone bad, tragic fall, all that noise. But what was I loyal to, really? A set of charts calibrated to keep profit flowing and bodies cheap? If walking away from that makes me a traitor, then fine. Every drone I turn, every shipment I reroute, that is another crew unhooked from the illusion that some distant office is ever going to look out for them.

I chose this tangle of wrecks and dead beacons because no one sane comes here on purpose. Old war metal, half-mapped grav pockets, just enough interference to make sensors stutter. Perfect place to hide a switchyard, perfect place to listen. I can hear them hunting sometimes on the bands, arguing over bad data and mixed-up transponder pings. Same small miscommunications that started all this, still steering people into the wrong orbits.

What scares me is not that they will find me. They will, eventually; nothing built by human hands stays hidden forever. What scares me is that when they do, they will drag me back into those clean rooms and polished corridors, make it all neat on paper again, and everyone who ever counted on these ghost lanes will be told to go back where they came from, as if there is still a place for them there.

So I keep tuning the drones, keep adding little birthday marks in the code where no one will ever think to look. Small celebrations now: a convoy that makes it through a debris patch intact, a LIST outpost lighting up their towers because a "random" hauler dropped off more food than they ordered. They will call it sabotage. I know better. I am not breaking their system anymore. I am freeing people from it.

Aria chews like she is trying to intimidate the ration bar.  
Metal bench, boots on the deck, her jaw working in that slow, steady rhythm while we wait for the briefing packet to decrypt. It is a stupid, tiny thing to fixate on after a long op, but the sound gets into my teeth. I must be more tired than I thought.

Nightwatch says nothing about fraternization on paper. In practice, everyone pretends it never happens until it blows up a contract. The way Aria caught my eye in the drop bay after Varga's debrief, that half-second of almost-smile before she remembered who we are and straightened her shoulders, is the closest either of us has come to treason. She asked if my rig was running hot. I said it was fine. Both of us lied.

Voss and Kestal, matched pair on corridor breach. Sounds clinical when Logistics writes it. In the actual hallway, with tracers calling our names, we moved like we had rehearsed for years instead of weeks. She covered high, I swept low, we cleared the stack in twelve seconds. Later, in the locker row, we had that argument about collateral. She said, "You hesitated," and I said, "You did not." It should not have felt like an accusation, but it did. We kept talking, words getting sharper, digging at each other's judgment, her implying I was going soft, me implying she enjoyed the work too much. We both stopped just short of saying the one thing that would not be forgiven: that we did not trust each other in a breach. I walked away first, but it is still sitting there between us, like an un-cleared room.

Unit politics are quieter this month, which only means they moved off the main channel. There is chatter in the armor bay about a "civilian contractor" who is not so civilian, drifting in and out of our flight plans. Some recovery specialist with a GalBank past and a taste for off-the-books bounties. You can always tell when we are about to be used as someone's deniable asset; the orders get vaguer, the hazard bonus gets bigger, and the colonels start reminding us how replaceable we are.

Heard two of the older Dragoons muttering that some ghost in the ledgers has been buying and burning debts out in the fringe, rerouting freight and people without firing a shot. Nobody says why we have been doing escort runs on "inspection teams" instead of real work, or why Command suddenly cares about abandoned scrapyards and dead vault ships. Official line is that it is all routine containment, but everyone feels the crosshairs without knowing which side of the scope we are on.

I caught myself watching Aria during weapons check, tracking the way she brushed a thumb over the carbon scoring on her rifle like it was a scar on her own skin. I remembered the fight, the way her voice went cold when she asked if I still had the stomach for what we do. The ugly part is that she was not wrong; I have started counting faces again, not just silhouettes. Admitting that tonight, even in here where no one sees, might be the only honest thing I have done in months.

There is a rule no one says out loud in Nightwatch. You either harden up until nothing gets in, or you start leaking and someone eventually closes the breach for you. I am starting to understand I have been standing in the middle too long, pretending I could balance it. Sooner or later, I have to choose which side of that argument with Aria is actually mine.

Used to be my biggest worry was whether Mrs. Halpern at the corner flat in Cydonia would notice if I cut through her stairwell instead of hauling her shopping all the way around. Errands, that was life then. Running ration slips to my mother's friends, fixing a busted heater panel for a neighbor because I had smaller hands and could reach. I thought that was just what people did for each other. I never imagined I would spend more time calculating lines of fire than grocery routes.

I remember the first time I leaned on someone, really leaned. Not in a bar fight, not in training; a civilian quartermaster who had "lost" half our med ration. I stepped in close, let my voice flatten, repeated his name with that cadence they drill into us. Watched the color drain out of his face as he tripped over himself to "find" the missing crates. I walked away with what the squad needed and this ugly, hollow feeling in my chest that sounded a lot like satisfaction.

Redacted Squadron laughs now about how we used to salute. Morgan Ishida still folds her socks with regulation corners; she can pretend she does not, but I have seen her bunk. Caleb Hartman runs checks on our weapons like there is still an inspector waiting to sign off. Sofia Marquez keeps the op plans tight, even if the signatures on them are scrubbed. Naomi Carver talks like she does not care who is in charge anymore, but she watches Rhea Kostova before every move, like waiting for an invisible go-ahead. Discipline does not vanish just because the crest came off the armor; it just stops being about who is above you on the chart.

Thing is, once you have heard certain orders, you cannot un-hear them. "Collateral aligned with acceptable projections." "Civilian presence within tolerances." That was the language up the chain, back when we were still "respectable." We all knew what those phrases meant on the ground. Fire missions called in close, comms anomalies that somehow never made it into the public logs, evac transports that got reassigned mid-flight for reasons nobody would write down. Somewhere between the third and fourth time it happened, trust in command stopped being habit and started feeling like a bad joke.

I think about that night sometimes, the last one before I walked out. She was packing while I tried to explain that I could not keep pretending the reports matched what we saw. She said I did not know how to be anything but a soldier, that leaving would break me or turn me into something worse. Then she hefted her duffel and left the door open behind her, like even the apartment could not decide who it belonged to. I watched her disappear down the corridor and honestly did not know if either of us was going to come out of what was coming in one piece.

Now our oaths are to each other, for better or worse. We are the ones who ran when the after-action summaries turned into lies, who decided that if someone was going to pull the trigger in our names, it would only be us. I still catch myself standing a little too straight when an old uniform walks by in a starport, feel that reflexive urge to acknowledge rank. Then I remember whose signatures signed off on those "acceptable losses," and I let my shoulders drop. Out here, in the quiet between jobs, I can almost hear the kid I used to be, running errands for people who trusted me, asking what the hell happened. I do not have a good answer for him.

Ship night again, though the lights never really dim enough. The environmental hum settles into my bones after a while, like my ribs are just another part of the ductwork. Long shift on watch and my eyes still feel gritty, gravity cycling just a touch off so my gut keeps doing this slow roll whenever OM-2098 corrects her course. You would think you get used to it. Some days it feels like my blood is permanently half a second behind the ship.

Today Elena Marquez stayed on past her rotation in the data bay, said she was "catching up on backlog." Jonas Kincaid joked that she is trying to marry the mainframe. Nobody laughed too hard. Elena has been off lately, sharper around the edges but somehow distant at the same time. I caught her flinch when a UC Security flag popped up in the traffic feed, like a guilty reflex. She covered it with a smile so quick it almost made it worse. Maybe I am imagining it. Long hours make ghosts out of nothing.

Marcus Havelock beat me at cards again in the mess, which would be funny if I did not know every credit I lose to him has already been promised home. Banerjee means dependable, apparently. My mother repeated that enough times that it might as well be carved into my skull. "We do not default, Riya," she said, even when the collectors changed their tone. So here I am, floating in a steel coffin for hazard pay, patching sensor arrays and trying not to think about the numbers on those old debt sheets. Every time the hull shivers I picture them, recalculating.

Mira Chen fell asleep at her console during diagnostics and I nudged her awake before the duty officer noticed. She has that twitch in her eyelid she gets when the shifts run long. We all do, in our own way. Elena did not, though. She walked through the corridor like gravity was set just for her, no stagger, no fatigue. I told myself it is because she is good at this, that some people just fit the uniform more cleanly. Still, when she brushed past me her hand was ice cold, like she had just come out of vacuum.

Rumor run in the mess today: someone said we had quietly picked up a trail on that shipbreaker everyone whispers about, the one who walked away from a bad accident with something he was not supposed to have. Jonas claimed it is just another spook story to keep us alert, but Elena shut him down fast, said command does not chase ghosts. Funny thing is, her eyes never left the status board while she said it. I wondered who she was really talking to.

The air tastes a little stale tonight, like the filters are due for service and no one logged it. My shoulders ache from crawling through maintenance shafts, bracing panels that were "good enough" for weeks until someone finally read my report. Familiarity makes people lazy; OM-2098 runs her patrols so clean that command barely glances at her readings anymore. That is what scares me. Not the enemy outside, but the way we stop looking too closely at ourselves.

If anyone ever reads this, it will probably sound like I was paranoid. But something is wrong here. Too many quiet channels, too many logged anomalies that vanish on the next cycle. The debt back home keeps me in line, but it also keeps my eyes open. When the ship rocks in her sleep and I feel that half-second lag in my bones, I cannot shake the feeling that we are all a half-second behind something else, too. And whatever it is, Elena already heard it coming.

Calen said the patch looked good on me today.

Black cloth, white vertical bar dead center, stenciled over the heart on my rig. Uniform Blackguard colors are supposed to mean restraint, clarity, discipline on contract. To me it has always looked like a door you either walk through or get bricked up behind. I remember the first time I stitched it to my vest, palms sweating like a recruit again, thinking it would finally make me visible to the right people, not just another security grunt with borrowed gear.

Funny how a small thing like that puts you on radars.

Back on that station job in Narion, we were pulling overwatch for some corporate inspection team. Nothing flashy. I made a casual call over local comms, correcting a patrol route so a junior tech could get home early and see his kid on a birthday call. No harm, I thought. We still had coverage. Next thing I know, ops backline is flagging my ID, and a week later I find out that corridor was supposed to look thin, to force a simulated breach for some "assessment." A harmless kindness, and suddenly I'm on some manager's list as "noncompliant." That was the day I learned every deviation is an entry on someone's spreadsheet.

Our clients talk like the risks are outside: raiders, syndicates, whatever flag the local pirates fly this quarter. But the longer I'm with Blackguard, the more it sinks in that rival crews aren't the only threat. Our own people will cut you out of a contract or hang you with your own debrief if it nudges them one rung up the ladder. Calen plays it quiet, always neutral in the barracks, but I've seen the way he listens during after-action reviews, storing what he can use later. You learn to measure every word, every glance.

There was a moment last month, escort run on a mining moon. Some foreman tried to stall us on payment, arguing line items while his workers watched from the gantries. I took one step into his space, lowered my voice, and let the silence do the work. I saw his eyes dip to the patch, then to the rifle, then up to my face. He folded fast, authorized the transfer, practically tripping over his own boots to make it go faster. Walking away, hearing my own boots ring on the metal, I realized I'd enjoyed it. Enjoyed the way his shoulders slumped when he understood what we could do to him, contract or no. That sits in my gut heavier than any armor plate.

The exhaustion is different now than it was in regular forces, but it is still there. You push through drills, sims, live ops, client demands, internal audits, and somehow it is never enough. Hit all your marks, and they just move the target. You log extra hours smoothing over some executive's panic, and the only feedback you get is that your "tone" in the report could be more deferential. You keep your kit squared away, your record clean, and you watch others with worse habits get the soft contracts because they share drinks with the right handler.

Tonight I am bone-tired and still running scenarios in my head. Who is angling for whose slot. Which rumor about a "quiet restructuring" at the top might be true. How many more times I can walk into a room and make somebody flinch before I forget what it felt like to be the one flinching. That patch over my heart is supposed to mean order. Some days it just feels like a reminder that I'm part of a machine that never stops grinding, no matter how sharp you make yourself.

Sometimes I try to run the sim in my head and push time backward, all the way to a point where I did not have blood tallied against my name. I can picture the underdeck bunks on Gagarin, the smell of metal and fried noodles, the first time I saw a real starfield through a viewport instead of a cracked holoscreen. But if you ask me for the last moment I felt truly innocent, I cannot give you a timestamp. Somewhere between the shuttle fire and the first time I nudged a freighter away from a bad lane, whatever that feeling was got stripped out of me like old wiring.

It is funny how quickly control becomes a drug. When I sat in that UC pod above Jemison, my world was vectors and probabilities, the quiet satisfaction of threading ships through crowded grav corridors without a single scrape. It was responsibility then, and I thought that was enough. Now I can feel entire routes flex when I adjust one ghosted beacon, watch captains dance to an advisory they do not even know is mine. The first time I lost access to a node for more than a week, I shook like a junkie. Not from fear of being caught, but from the hollow silence where all that traffic used to be. Without that hum, the universe feels flat and dead and I feel tiny again.

They say the void does not care who lives or dies. I used to find comfort in that, the idea that we were all equal under the same indifferent stars. These days I twist it into something uglier: if the universe does not care, then neither do I, and who better than me to decide who gets a warning ping and who flies blind. I tell myself it is balance, that I am only correcting injustices the UC and the corporations built into the system long before I started touching it. In truth, half the time it is just because I can.

I replay that shuttle collision more than I should. There were a dozen ways I could have softened what came after. I could have walked out of that hearing and spent the rest of my life keeping people safe from some quiet desk in some forgettable colony. I could have taken the payout, let their lies stand, and been one more harmless cog. Later, when I had my hands back on the lanes from the shadows, I could have chosen mercy more often, turned near-misses into routine saves instead of lessons. Every time those options were in front of me, I stepped around them.

Out here, sitting in the dark with only the projections from the Storm Table for company, I can see all the routes I did not take floating alongside the ones I forced into shape. A LIST tanker that could have made it on time if I had not sold its detour to a Crimson quartermaster. A UC patrol that did not need to be in the same corridor as a civilian hauler, except I wanted someone in New Atlantis to sweat over the report. I tell myself it was necessary to prove a point, to make them look at what they built. But there is a thin, honest part of me that knows I enjoyed watching them flinch.

The farther I run, the more the lanes feel like an extension of my own nervous system. Every anonymous ping, every erased transponder, every rumor that some ghost saved this ship or doomed that convoy, all of it is me asserting that I still exist and that I am not done. I do not know if I am heading toward justice, revenge, or just the next hit of feeling the galaxy bend a few degrees because I said so. I do know this: kindness was always on the table. I just kept choosing the other thing.

I keep replaying that venting in my head and I cannot swear any more which parts are real and which parts are stitched in from recordings, rumors, and whatever my brain had to do so I could walk out an airlock again. I remember the alarms, the slam of the bulkhead, the rigger's face behind the visor. But I also remember a quiet moment afterward where I watched someone else choke on thin air in a different corridor, years earlier, and did nothing. I stood there, hand on the override, and let it ride because for once the call was mine and mine alone. That memory feels too clean, too sharp, like it has been edited for effect. Maybe I edited it. Maybe somebody else did.

They say people under prolonged stress disassociate, split off the parts that do not fit the uniform. Old psych texts called it adaptive compartmentalization. Brant used to throw around phrases like that when she wanted to smooth over the bad calls, like there was a textbook somewhere that made everything fine if we could just name it right. By that logic, the things I have done since the tug went dark are just my nervous system trying to survive system failure. Predation as a coping mechanism. Strategic cruelty to reclaim a sense of control. Sounds academic when I line it up like that. Does not feel that way when I catch my reflection in a viewport and do not recognize the man checking angles on his own crew like they are potential threats instead of people who trusted him to strap their helmets.

I ran for the wreck fields because I know every bolt and seam out here. The frontier drift where old war hulks spin, the forgotten hulk they turned into a lie, the broken frigate that keeps pulling everyone's attention without them admitting it. Steel does not care who signed which order or whose name is redacted. Steel only cares about stress, about where the next fracture will open. I know how to move where the scanners overlap, how to park a tug in the dead cone of a cruiser's blind side. It made sense to come back to the graveyard. Out here, I can rig drones, mine corridors, sell just enough hardware to pirates and mercs to stay relevant without letting any one of them think they own me.

What I am afraid of is not bounty hunters, or SysDef, or whatever private outfit some governor hires to clean this up. What scares me is how easy it has become to watch someone suffer and weigh it against the angle it gives me. How fast I am to justify airlocking a boarder or leaving a rival tether cut because the textbooks say control is grounding for trauma, because some old briefing talked about acceptable collateral, because once you have been told you were responsible for deaths you did not cause, there is a dark relief in choosing the next ones yourself. I keep telling myself I am doing this to drag the truth out into the open, to make them pay for turning my people into ghosts on a censored log. But I hear myself in the way the pirates talk, in the way the merc brokers laugh when they think nobody is listening. I am not sure when exactly I crossed that line, or if there was ever one to begin with. All I know is that every time I weld my mark into a new piece of hull, every time I map another blind route through the debris, it feels less like hiding and more like building a tomb I plan to fight from. And some days, when the quiet hits just right, I am not sure whether I am trying to keep them out or keep myself from ever leaving.

I used to worry about stupid things.  
Water leaks in the hab ducts. Whether the auto-pay hit my GalBank line before or after the utility surcharge. The way the cat back on that survey contract would yowl if the humidity dropped two points. It felt like adulthood, then, chasing drips and due dates. Funny how those tiny responsibilities taught me more about control than any university ever did. You learn fast that whoever owns the valves and the bills decides who sleeps dry and who does not sleep at all.

People keep calling what I do now "monstrous," as if reshaping a sky is somehow less honest than quietly signing forms that condemn a dome by neglect. I have been reading old fragments on "authenticity" lately, half-remembered names from philosophy feeds I never finished. One of them said the only real sin is betraying your true nature. If my true nature is to see the system as it is and act accordingly, then how, exactly, am I the deviant? Everyone pretends air is sacred until it is time to cut corners; I just removed the pretense.

I catch myself overanalyzing small things, as if dressing them up in technical language will make all this feel clean. The resonant frequency of a tower strut. The exact delay between an alarm ping and its automatic suppression. The way a Freestar foreman's hand shook when he signed for noncompliant stock, pretending not to read the fine print. I talk about phase margins and load curves because it sounds clever, because it keeps me out of the one place I do not want to go: the simple question of who lives and who does not when I touch a console.

The turning point was not Dustburn, though everyone wants the legend to start there. It was years earlier, on a failing dome where we arrived three days late. The local tech had been bleeding himself dry patching leaks and skipping maintenance fees to keep his neighbors warm. Corporate sent us anyway, with a polite note about "cost recovery." They thanked him for his service, then seized his rig when he missed a payment. He was kind, decent, all those words civics classes love. He died in the cold corridor outside his own equipment room, locked out by a system he had babied for a decade.

That was the day I understood that kindness is just another exploitable resource. The kind ones volunteer for extra shifts, sign waivers, look the other way when their betters cut corners. They become buffers, absorbing failure so the rest can pretend everything is fine. I stopped being a buffer. Now I am a fulcrum. I pick where to apply pressure and watch entire colonies tilt around that point.

Why here, this particular rock, this poor excuse for an atmosphere? Because the air is already bad enough that any "correction" can be blamed on the planet. Because the homesteaders are desperate enough to welcome a man who says he can buy them another decade of breathing, even if the price is paid by someone else, somewhere else. Because the maintrade routes slide just far enough away that UC and Freestar patrols argue jurisdiction while my towers hum.

I tell myself I am only making explicit what has always been true: air is political, survival is transactional, and pretending otherwise is a luxury for people whose children have never woken up choking. If that makes me the monster in their stories, so be it. Better an honest monster than another kind-hearted fool signing away the last of his warmth while the system thanks him for his sacrifice.

Day 142, I think. Hard to tell with the lights dimmed half the time to "conserve power and promote circadian hygiene," as Jonas keeps putting it in his maintenance reports. I still wake up feeling like I have a hangover made of recycled air and static cling, so I am not sure the hygiene is working. What has changed is how jumpy I am; every minor course correction, every little grav-drift in the corridor feels like an omen. What has not changed is the way my stomach knots whenever we pass through Sol, like the system itself remembers things the rest of us pretend to file away.

Today was more of the same: diagnostics, scrubber checks, arguing with the coffee recycler. Rhea swears it gives her "notes of ozone and despair," but she still drinks it and still chews louder than any human should be able to. Honestly, how can someone make synth-protein bars sound wet. I almost snapped at her about it at mess, then caught Maya giving me that careful, neutral look of hers, like she was testing stress levels on a console. I made a joke instead. Damian laughed, too loud, like he always does when he is covering something. Or maybe I am just hearing ghosts in every echo now.

We had another encrypted packet come in from command, all redacted headers and timing that does not match our published patrol pattern. Elena and Jonas went quiet as soon as they saw it, exchanged that glance over my head they think I cannot read. I watched Maya out of the corner of my eye. She did not flinch, did not lean in, just kept working her station with that steady precision. It is funny; the more the others tense up, the calmer she seems. I used to find that reassuring. Lately it feels like standing next to a perfectly balanced knife.

There is talk in the lower decks that our "route optimization support" work is not as harmless as it sounds. Rhea says she overheard Jonas muttering about civilian transponder IDs buried in some sim run, flagged and then deleted. I do not know if she misread the logs; she is good with people, not code. Still, I keep catching snippets: "near miss," "acceptable variance," "actuarial," words that sound like they belong in a bank office, not on a Navy scout drifting between dead satellites. No one says anything outright. We just work, eat, pretend the air does not taste of old secrets.

I dropped my digipick again. Third time this week. Spent ten minutes tearing apart my locker, cursing at my boots and that ridiculous extra EVA glove I keep meaning to stow. Found it in my bunk sheet fold, of course, like it always ends up in the last place I check. I muttered at myself the whole time about how a person trusted with reactor safety can apparently not keep track of a single tool. When I came back up to the bridge, Maya had that tiny almost-smile on her face, the one she gets when the universe proves her point about entropy.

Underneath the small annoyances, I can feel something coiling tighter in my chest every day. I used to get excited about new orders, new systems. Now all I want is one honest briefing that matches what we actually fly. Jonas is more tired, Damian snaps faster, even Elena has started triple-checking her own work like she does not trust her hands. And Maya, somehow, is always exactly where she needs to be, calm in the center of it all. I keep telling myself that is what makes her good at her job. Still, when the ship falls quiet at night, I lie awake thinking about those unlogged deviations in our path and wondering who really planned them.

I lost track of the exact day somewhere between Narion and nowhere, but I remember the sound. When a grav-drive route collapses around you, it is not like the holos say. There is no heroic roar, no slow-motion. It is the absence. A tearing out of the middle of the universe where familiar things used to be. One moment I am watching telemetry scroll, the next I am alone in a ship that should not still exist, with a cabin full of air that feels like a bad joke.

They called it pilot error on the report. Then a systems fault. Then nothing at all. Funny how language collapses faster than hull plating when someone important is about to lose their funding.

After they patched me back together and sat me in quiet rooms with soft lighting, I did what they train us to do: I checked the data. Line by line. My adaptive lines were there, but twisted into something else, embedded in contracts I never signed, tied to riders that did not exist when I wrote the first drafts. High-yield, low-input, "resilient." Such a nice word, resilient. It hides so much.

When the complaint went nowhere, when my access evaporated and my work came back to me marked up as recklessness, I understood my position on the board. Not scientist. Not citizen. Risk. Containment priority. Discreet resolution recommended. Once you see yourself written like that, something in you snaps or goes very, very still.

So I took what was mine to begin with. Vaults, codebooks, the clean baseline and the ugly derivatives. I tore out the parts of the archives they wanted to keep buried and walked them into the wild, because if the game is rigged, the only honest move is to kick over the table. They will call it sabotage. Terror. Fine. If their supply chains choke on the same poisons they signed off on, perhaps they will remember whose signatures line the bottom of those pages.

Why here, now? Because out beyond the neat trade lanes, LIST folk and forgotten farmers still believe a seed is a promise, not a weapon. I can test, refine, demonstrate on scales that hurt, but not yet kill the way they intended. I can build a sanctuary in miniature, prove that the clean strain works, and hold it against their throats as leverage. And if they send hunters, well, hunters eat too. Their blood chemistry will tell me what I need to know.

The fear is always the same: not death, not prison. Erasure. Waking up one day to find that every record says I was the monster they needed me to be, and nobody even remembers that there was a choice. That is why I leave logs, labels, breadcrumbs in freighter manifests and sick fields. It is childish, maybe, but it is harder to rewrite a story when the footnotes keep showing up on other people's desks.

Most nights, after I finish in whatever passes for a lab, I sit with a cup of bitter coffee and watch the stars. It helps to remember that none of this matters. Galaxies collapse. Species rise, burn their worlds, vanish. In the end, my little edits to a few patches of soil will not even register as noise. Thinking like that takes the weight off. If nothing has meaning, then guilt is just a chemical response, and consequences are temporary patterns in dust. I can do what needs doing without pretending there is some grand moral ledger waiting to be balanced.

And yet, when I step onto a failing homestead and see a child breathing easier because a field I tuned is finally feeding them cleanly, the emptiness cracks a little. I hate that. It would be simpler if I believed in nothing at all.

I miss boring mornings.

Back when my job was just a stack of claims and a lukewarm TerraBrew, I used to sit by the narrow viewport in whatever office they had buried me in, mark up manifests until my hand cramped, then reward myself with a synthameat sandwich if I cleared the queue before midshift. Same stool, same chipped mug, same view of some shipyard cranes inching across the horizon like they had all the time in the galaxy. I thought that was what safety felt like: repetition, harmless paperwork, nothing sharp in reach but a cheap pen.

Funny, how it was the paperwork that turned out to be the weapon.

The first time I rerouted a tug on my own authority, I still kept the old routine. Coffee, checklist, double-verify the transponder code, then quietly overwrite the beacon path so nobody with a conscience saw the distress call until I had what I needed. It is easier to bend the rules when your hands are already doing something familiar. You just let the cursor rest a little longer in the wrong field. You just type one extra digit. After that, it becomes part of the ritual. Wake, drink, adjust the ledger, eat, pretend the world is not tilting.

I used to collect little mechanical watches from flea stalls in places like New Atlantis and Gagarin Landing. Useless things, here, where no one trusts springs and gears anymore. I would wind them all on the same morning, listen to the tiny ticking storm in my quarters, then pick one to wear. It anchored me. Time passing, proof that something in the universe still moved forward at an honest pace.

Now my mornings are alarms and course plots and checking if any of the tugs in my little constellation have gone dark overnight. Coffee tastes like coolant. Food is whatever I can open one-handed while reading stolen logs. I still keep the watches, though. Wind them when I can. Not because I believe in honest time anymore, but because each one reminds me of a captain whose plaque I cut from a dead bulkhead. Names they tried to erase with a line in a claim report.

Leaving the offices was not a decision. It was an inevitability after that last hauler disappeared with my forged authorization on the file. I saw my own signature against a death I did not sign. They thought they could fold me into the silence along with the others. So I did what I do best: I recalculated. I took the backup data, the ghost hull list, one tug they had underinsured, and I stepped out of the pattern.

I chose the graveyards because no one looks too closely at what happens out here. Wrecks are supposed to be voiceless. Scrap is supposed to be just metal. My hiding place is made of everything they think has no story left to tell. Out here, among these broken frames, I can reroute more than distress calls. I can reroute blame.

I know they are coming. UC, Freestar, some bounty crew with clean uniforms or rusted guns, it does not matter. What I fear is not dying; it is them taking my ledgers and burning them, tidying the narrative so I go down as just another pirate who got greedy. So I keep moving the pieces. More dead-drop caches, more redundant exports, more people paid off quietly with credit transfers they will never trace back.

In my better moments, I imagine a morning again where I wake up and the only thing waiting is a mug, a sandwich, a pile of filings that are honestly dull. No ghosts, no rerouted cries, no one calling me Deadlock like a curse or a prayer. On most mornings, I just wind a watch, listen to the ticking, and remind myself that until somebody stops me, the ledger is still in my hands.

Shadowcell Barracks  
Shipboard Night Cycle  

Hartmann did the stare again today. Not the full dressing-down, just that quiet appraisal he does when he thinks no one is watching. Funny thing is, I notice it every time. I notice all of them now. The cameras in the hall bulkheads, the biometric pings at every blast door, Mara's eyes tracking me over the top of her report. Years in this outfit and I still catalog lines of sight before I can breathe. Somewhere along the way, being observed stopped feeling like a precaution and became the baseline. On ops, it keeps you alive. Off ops, it just makes sleep shallow and dreams crowded.

Ronan called it "professional accountability" once, with that half smile that almost passes for charm when he wants something. Maybe he believes it. Ward definitely does. He lives and dies by the handbook, the unspoken one more than the printed regs. Who you drink with after a contract, how long you take in the gym, whether you're in the briefing room five minutes early or two minutes late. All of it gets tallied somewhere behind his eyes. None of them ever say it out loud, but you can feel the scores being kept, deal by deal, bullet by bullet. One bad day and suddenly you are the one people track on the periphery.

It did not start here. Back home, it was the older kids leaning against the fence behind the hab-stacks, shoes too clean for our block, always flush with credits. No one ever said where the money came from and I did not ask, because questions make people notice you in the wrong ways. I skipped my chores for them. Skipped sleep. Skipped school. They would vanish for a few days, come back with new jackets and stories with the middle cut out. I learned fast how to listen for the missing pieces. How to keep my head tilted like I believed every word. That same trick plays well in ready rooms and corporate debriefs now. Tilt your head. Pretend you buy the story.

There is a different kind of story running through the unit lately. Shipbreaker contracts that keep circling the same coordinates. Names that come up too often in the after-action reports and then get redacted on the official copies. A handler letting slip that some "salvage incident" up in UC space is drawing more resources than it should, like there is something lodged in a wreck that the big commissions are scared to admit exists. Hartmann shut that conversation down when I pushed, told me to stick to our lane. Then, later, I caught him and Ward whispering in the corridor, eyes sharp, voices low. Professional accountability.

Mara asked me, casually, what I would do if a target turned out to be more than some pirate or spacer riffraff. She couched it in hypotheticals, but I could see the weight behind it. There are rumors about a man who used to keep crews alive inside hulls that wanted to come apart, who now sells those skills to whoever pays best. Some say he knows things that could set two flags at each other's throats all over again. Some say one of those flags is already using him. Nobody says it straight. They never do.

Sometimes I think the job is less about pulling triggers and more about carrying other people's secrets until they burn through your skin. Being watched rewired what "safe" means years ago. Now, safe is just knowing which angle the sights are pointing from and how many rifles are really in the room. If this salvage mess is as big as the whispers make it sound, the angles are about to change. And when they do, someone in Shadowcell is going to end up on the wrong side of the ledger. I just need to make sure it is not me.

Erin keeps saying we did not desert, we were discarded. She says it like a fact, like a range mark you can trust your shot against. Still feels like desertion when I wake up and do not hear a briefing channel in my ear, just the hum of whatever stolen hull we are riding this week and the Sundered arguing over rations in the next compartment.

Today we hit that relay out on the edge of nowhere. Old codes still worked. That is the part that stung. SysOp never scrubbed me, never flagged the access. According to the system, Darius Holm is still green-lit, still a good little piece of their machine. Walked through three bulkheads like I belonged there, and for a second I did. Muscle memory almost snapped to parade rest when the alarms chimed. Then Erin's hand on my shoulder, that little squeeze she does, brought me back to who I am supposed to be now.

We pulled the drives, looped the cams, left the guards breathing. Sundered Commandos do not shoot uniforms unless we have to. That is the rule Varik bled into us after things went bad on the ridge. Different world, different mission, different flag, same story. Bad coordinates, bad intel, bad weather, too many civilians in the way and an order chain that cared more about the after-action report than the body bag count. We all heard the closed-door debrief later, the way the brass massaged the numbers, turned screams into "collateral deviations." That was the day trust started leaking out of us like air through a cracked seal.

There are whispers that what we did today is no better. Hit a friendly install, rip out the eyes and ears, sell the data to whoever bids highest. I hear those whispers in my own head more than from the squad. Erin calls it balancing ledgers. She is not wrong that we are usually cleaning up things command buried.
