Half the time the targets we hit are side projects someone was running off the books, the kind that get people "reassigned" if too many questions get asked. You do three tours watching that pattern and it is hard not to think we are the only ones still following the original oath, even if we tore the patches off.

Funny thing is, back in barracks we used to talk about dreams. Not the sleep kind. The "after this is over" kind. Buy a hauler. Open a bar. Go back home and pretend we never learned how to clear a room in under three seconds. I never believed a word of it, not from myself, not from the others. You do not walk away from what we did and start counting crop yields. But the talking mattered. It was a way of pretending we had futures that were not written in operations orders and casualty lists. Now the only dreams anyone admits to are about better armor, cleaner bolt cycles, and a cut of credits big enough that no one can buy our names back into a briefing slide.

Today, standing in that relay, I caught a glimpse of another branch. Could have stayed. Could have locked my rifle, sat down, waited for Security to swarm in and put me in a box. Let them decide whether to court-martial me, interrogate me, or just erase me from the system like they did those villages we never officially entered. But I walked out with the others, drives in a pack, field discipline still tight, hearts still half-turned toward the flag we left behind.

We keep telling ourselves we are not running. We are repositioning. Tactical withdrawal in the face of compromised leadership. Erin believes it. Most days, I can almost believe it too. Then night rotation comes, the ship's lights dim, and in the quiet between engine pulses I can hear the old command channel that is not there anymore, waiting for an order that will never come.

I keep forgetting this slate autosyncs. One bad habit from the service I cannot shake; write it down, lock it away, pretend someone is not always reading over your shoulder. Old conditioning. Back then, honesty on a debrief got you reassigned, flagged, or worse. You learned to answer the question you were asked, not the one that might get someone important burned. Truth was a live grenade; you only pulled the pin once.

Deadline is supposed to be different. That is what Cole keeps saying, anyway. "No more lies, Rena. We call it like it is." Easy words from a man who still sleeps with his boots on and checks corners in the mess. I watch how fast his eyes go glassy when anyone mentions our last op under formal command, the one where the civvy convoy just happened to drift into an active fire lane. The report said "unexpected resistance." We all signed it. Marcus pretended his hand did not shake.

I tell myself I left because I was tired of being told which ghosts counted and which ones did not. That is cleaner than admitting I was afraid of what would happen if I started speaking plainly in a briefing room with a recording light on. You learn early that saying "this corridor is wrong, this target is wrong, this order is wrong" only ends two ways: you get moved somewhere quiet, or somewhere loud enough you do not come back. So I shut up. We all did, until Elias walked out first and proved there was a third option.

Gavin still calls him a coward when he has had too much Red Harvest whiskey, but I have seen the way he looks at the empty bunk like it is a mirror. Gavin is the loudest in the unit, the first to crack that hard, ugly laughter that passes for humor around here. There is no warmth in it. Just sharp edges, mocking and mean, as if every joke is a weapon test and we are all waiting to see who flinches. Deadline laughs like that a lot. Joy does not live here; only relief that, for the moment, the barrel is pointed at someone else.

Sometimes I catch myself almost saying what I actually think. When Marcus outlines another interdiction plan that looks too much like the old sabotage jobs they swore were clean. When Cole talks about "acceptable losses" in that same tone our former CO used before a drop. The words rise in my throat: this is the same game with a different patch on the armor. But my tongue remembers years of biting down until I tasted blood, and the fear that honesty is still a punishable offense keeps the sentences half-formed and sour.

Smell is the worst betrayer. I can walk past a fuel spill in a hangar and suddenly I am back on that orbital, breathing in scorched plating and burned sealant after the airlock breach they called a "structural failure." Or I catch a whiff of cheap Terrabrew from a cracked thermos and my hands think they are wrapping around a field mug while intel whispers through a cramped briefing room about a target colony we were not supposed to know had children in it. Even dust has a sound, the way it hisses against a visor in thin atmosphere, and sometimes the corridors here echo just enough that my chest tightens and I have to count steps like I am back on patrol.

Deadline says we have no commander now, that we are all accountable to each other. I want to believe that. But tonight, listening to Gavin's mirthless bark from the common room and hearing Marcus quietly adjust the lie of our latest op into something he can write down, I realize command never needed a rank. It lived in our fear of speaking plainly, in the way we trained ourselves to flinch from our own thoughts. We traded one set of orders for another, and the only difference is who signs the after-action report.

I keep thinking one of these mornings I will wake up and not feel that half-second of inventory: lungs working, weapon still within reach, no new shadows in the corner. It has not happened yet. Every day starts with the same question in my head before I even open my eyes: is this when someone in Cipher Blackfire decides I have outlived my usefulness.  

We all pretend it is just operational paranoia, part of the job. Darin calls it "staying sharp." Kellan says if you are not worried, you are already dead. But that is not what I mean. I mean the way conversations stop when I enter a room. The way Amira's gaze lingers a beat too long on my hands when I sign off on an after-action report.  

I remember the stupid, harmless thing that first put me on someone's radar. A card game in the ready bay, months ago. Stakes were low, I was just bored. I corrected the odds on a side bet, could not resist showing my math. I saw the look Darin gave me then, weighing what it meant that I run numbers in my head faster than the deck can shuffle. Two weeks later Cipher started routing me the contracts that never make the public ledger, the ones where pay and casualty estimates do not match.  

You do not say no when the handlers notice you. Not if you want to keep breathing. We all saw what happened to Mikal when he pushed back on the last redirect. No debrief, no tribunal, just a sealed airlock and a "training incident" notice pinned to the board. They left his bunk untouched for a week, boots still under the rack, as if the ghost of his gear would keep the rest of us compliant. It worked.  

Somewhere along the way I sanded down every sharp edge of feeling just to get through the days. The first time I watched a target bleed out because the contract said "no exfil," I told myself it was logistics, not cruelty. The fifteenth time, I did not have to tell myself anything. I just logged the rounds expended and checked my gear. That numbness is useful when your job is to walk into other people's endings. It is less useful when you are trying to remember what your own life is supposed to feel like.  

The worst part is I am not sure I want to lose it. The little I let in hurts more now, like thawing frostbite. A few months back, on a long haul between systems, I let myself fall into something that looked like affection. Long conversations in the dark with someone who knew exactly how far they could lean toward me without crossing the line. Their hand on my shoulder after a bad op, the way they stayed an extra second too long when everyone else had already turned away. Warmth, or the practiced pressure of someone making sure I stayed pointed where the unit wanted me. Love and fear felt the same in that moment, like standing too close to a reactor: you are not sure if it is keeping you alive or burning you from the inside.  

Lately there are whispers about lanes shifting, contracts tied to "route security" that read more like cleanup than protection. Someone is paying a lot of credits to erase particular jumps from the record, and we keep getting pulled in right after something goes wrong and before anyone asks why. I hear the techs talking about cargo haulers drifting wrong, relay stations feeding bad numbers. I pretend I am not listening.  

Discipline keeps my hands steady, keeps my name off the wall. The unspoken rule is simple: do the work, do not ask who moved the pieces before you got there. Still, every time I sign another encrypted brief, I wonder if somewhere in the small print there is a line assigning Cipher Blackfire to tidy up after someone else's invisible war. And if, when the math is finally done, my number is on the wrong side of the equation.

I am writing this strapped into a crash couch in a ship that is barely moving, but my stomach still feels like it is falling.

Today the nav officers ran another sim of the corridor, the one no one admits we are actually flying. They call it a "stress test," say it is all just contingency work for the academy archives, but everyone knows academy sims do not get their own sealed briefings. Jonah tried to joke his way through it, said if the grav shear did not pulp us, the paperwork would, but his hands kept hovering just above the console like he was afraid to leave prints.

Caleb spent half the shift buried in the sensor bay, muttering about ion density and noise profiles that do not match any public charts. When I brought him a TerraBrew, he just looked at me and asked if I had ever seen space look "tired." I laughed, but I knew what he meant. Out the port, the stars at that range smear into a faint halo when the tests spin up, and it feels like the ship is balanced on a wire instead of a lane.

Darius and Mira spent the mess break throwing cards at each other and pretending not to listen to the officers at the next table. They were arguing over whether command would ever actually authorize a live run. One of them said it already happened, off the record, and that is why half the senior charts are redacted. The other said that was just Spacer bar talk. The way they kept their voices low made it sound like they believed both at once.

Elias was quiet again. He has been like that for weeks now, watching people more than instruments, like he is measuring something softer and stranger than grav pull. He asked me, out of nowhere, if I would ever take a posting planetside if the pay was good enough. I told him no, that I like the way the ship hums when the lanes catch, that I sleep better with bulkheads around me than sky. He nodded, but his eyes were somewhere else, as if he was already measuring distances I could not see.

It is funny, thinking about sleep. Back when I first signed on, I was terrified of drifting off in the black. I told Mira about it once, in the dark of an off-shift corridor, and she said, "You do not have to trust the void, just trust the people who keep you between it and the hull." That stuck. On bad nights I repeat it to myself, and it settles my breathing. It worked again this afternoon, just long enough to get me through another round of drills where the instructors pretended we were not all one bad calculation away from becoming a classified entry in someone else's log.

Still, there is a different kind of quiet moving through the ship now. It lives between conversations, a half-second where people decide what not to say. In the liaison's reports from the frontier, there were whispers about convoys disappearing into storms and reappearing where no scanner caught them, about a pilot who rides the edge of the weather like it is a road only she can see. Officially, we are here to test instruments, to make sure nothing like that can ever happen without us knowing. Unofficially, no one wants to admit we might already be following in someone else's wake.  

If I am being honest, that is what makes my hands shake more than the grav surges: the sense that the charts are lying to us, and that someone on this ship knows exactly how. Elias watched me re-secure my harness at the end of shift and told me, very gently, to double-check my mag boots before the next cycle, "just in case things get rough." It was kind, and for a moment it calmed me the way Mira's words did, like the crew itself could be enough to keep the dark at bay. But I keep hearing that "just in case" long after the lights went to night mode, and I cannot tell if it was concern or a farewell I did not recognize at the time.

Ship's running cool tonight. I can feel it in the deck plates, that steady hum pulled back just a notch, like the whole hull is holding its breath. Environmental cut the ambient temp by a couple of degrees to save power on this patrol loop, and now the air in my bunk smells like metal and old filters instead of recycled coffee. Makes the hairs on my arms stand up. Funny how a small change in the background noise and climate can make it feel like the walls are listening.

We had another drill this morning. Leah Okafor barked us through breach protocols like she was auditioning for a MAST training sim. Marcus Llewellyn showed up late, again, with that half-apology smile that gets him out of everything. Leah just glared at him and marked something down on her slate. She pretends not to care, but I saw how tight she was gripping the bulkhead when the alarm cut off, knuckles white. This ship eats that kind of stress and spits it back as ulcers.

The mess was quieter than usual afterward. Jonah Mercer kept fiddling with the holoscreen, cycling through news channels then killing the sound every time they mentioned anything about drive incidents or "ongoing investigations." Elias Navarro tried to lighten the mood with some story about his last shore leave in New Atlantis, but it fell flat. Nobody wants to talk about home when you are strapped to a gunship pointed at nowhere in particular. Even the TerraBrew machine sounded tired, hissing out lukewarm sludge instead of coffee.

I ended up on hull watch for most of the afternoon, staring at nothing while the sensor board threw up clean readings. Out there, it is all black and pinholes. In here, you start noticing the little things instead. Like how Marcus has been spending more time near the secure terminals, joking with the comms techs and leaving with his pockets a little too heavy. Or how Leah's been sleeping in her boots lately, as if she expects the alarm to hit mid-dream. Or the way command keeps forwarding encrypted orders down the line without bothering to brief us, just "course adjustment, acknowledge and comply."

I am not supposed to see routing data, but you hear things when you float between duty stations. Gagarin, Cheyenne, some dead stretch of nowhere between flagged sectors. Never the same path twice, always skirting around the places people actually live. Feels less like patrol and more like we are drawing a pattern no one wants us to understand. I caught Jonah and Elias whispering about it in the armory, voices low. They shut up when I walked in, pretended they were arguing about weapons maintenance. If this ship could talk, it would laugh at how bad we are at lying to each other.

And then there are the rumors, the ones that slip in with encrypted traffic and off-the-record chatter. Talk of drives misfiring the same way on different hulls, of some tech everyone is blaming because it is easier than admitting hardware can be wrong by design. Leah says official channels cleared it all, "no systemic risk, nothing to see." But I have seen the way she lingers over the engineering logs when she thinks nobody is watching, tracing jump coordinates like she is trying to spot a ghost in the code. Marcus just shrugs it all off, says every generation gets its own campfire story.

Maybe it is nothing. Maybe I am just letting the cold air and the dimmed lights get under my skin. But tonight, walking back from watch, I passed Marcus in the corridor outside the secure bay. He was alone, no reason to be there, eyes a little too bright in the half-light. He flashed that same easy grin, clapped me on the shoulder, asked if I was "ready for another boring jump." His hand was warm through the fabric of my uniform, but I swear the metal under our feet felt colder than ever.

I keep thinking about how loud that neighbor used to be back in the stack housing on Volii. Guy in the next unit blasting cheap synth-rock at all hours, arguing with whoever he was bedding that week, faucets that never stopped dripping rust in the walls. At the time I swore it was the worst thing in my life, like if I could just get some quiet, everything else would line up. Funny, looking back from here, with blood under my nails and gun oil in my lungs, that noise feels almost gentle.

Executioner Ash runs on ritual and pressure. You do the work, you watch, you keep your mouth shut. Rhea Vargan and Dane Corvo act like they were born breathing syndicate air, like this is all just gravity to them. Me, I came in later, when things were already burning. Lena Kade told me first day, "Smile less, listen more," and I have been clenching my jaw ever since. The bosses talk about loyalty like it is oxygen, but we all know it is a currency. You spend a little to stay alive, and if you are lucky, you do not go bankrupt overnight.

There was a night in one of our backrooms on Neon, lights half-dead, fans barely moving the smoke. Maris Calder sat across from me, eyes rimmed red from more than just Aurora, and she said, barely above a whisper, "I tipped them off, Kade. That convoy you were on, it was never supposed to leave port." Threads of sound only just carried it over the hum of the old generator. That one sentence bent my life sideways. After that, every job, every smile from the lieutenants felt like it might be the last thing I saw. I did not tell anyone. Not Sera Mallin, not Rhea, no one. Some confessions are landmines. You do not share them, you just learn to step around where they are buried.

Being around Rhea feels like walking on broken glass most days. Careful, silent, and always afraid. One wrong word and those eyes of hers go flat, like you just became a name on a cleanup list. She jokes, sometimes, about who might be "next ash for the burners," and everyone laughs that strangled laugh we do when we are not sure if something is a joke. That is our culture in a line: everything half a threat, half a test, no way to tell which is which until you are already bleeding.

I tell myself I stayed because the payout was better than any dock job, better than hauling crates for HopeTech scraps or running legal hops for Trade Authority crumbs. Truth is, I stayed because the idea of walking away felt more terrifying than enduring the pain. Out there, you are just another face at a port, no backup when someone decides your ship looks soft. In here, at least the knives are mostly in front of you, and when they are not, you know you misread the room and that is on you.

Lately, the whispers have shifted. Neon bars go quiet when someone mentions grav lanes shuddering, jumps that feel wrong. Sera swears she heard a UC officer in The Den say there is a man tracing cracks in the routes, making ships disappear to prove a point. Rhea called it spacer superstition, but I saw the way she gripped her glass a little tighter. Executioner Ash loves rumors like that, stories about invisible wars nobody admits are happening. They make good cover for our movements, good shadows to slip through when authorities are staring at the wrong monsters.

Still, I catch myself listening harder when someone mentions drives that hum off-key, or a convoy that jumped and never showed at the other end. Maybe it is nothing. Maybe it is everything. All I know is, I traded a noisy neighbor and a leaky faucet for this life, and back then I thought I understood what a bad decision sounded like. Turns out, it was not the shouting through the thin walls I should have worried about. It was the quiet voices in the dark, the ones that never needed to raise themselves to tear my world apart.

I remember the first time I saw someone break the law and felt something other than fear. I was a kid, back on the docks, watching a pair of loaders skim crates off a freight pallet while the foreman pretended not to notice. Everyone else averted their eyes. I just stood there, fascinated by how smoothly it all moved, how a little tilt of the scanner and a bent signature could turn company property into someone else's payday. Later that week, the foreman pulled me aside, pressed a few crisp bills into my hand, and told me I was "a good lad" for keeping my mouth shut. I did not have the words for it then, but that was the first time silence felt like currency.

Funny how that same lesson scales up in uniform. Years later, suited and braced behind a barricade, I watched a squad from another unit go beyond the ROE on a cleanup op. Nothing dramatic from a distance: an extra burst of fire here, someone taking their time with a prisoner there. Erin Lockwood caught my eye as it happened, the way she always did when she wanted to know if I was going to be a problem. I said nothing in the debrief, signed where they told me to sign. The colonel shook my hand afterward, commended my "clarity and focus under stress." That same old warmth in the gut: praise for keeping quiet, for letting the machine grind the way it wanted to.

The Regiment was born out of that kind of praise. Enough of us pushed through enough dirty orders until one day the command chain snapped and we realized we were taking fire from both directions. Officially, we broke. Unofficially, we just stopped pretending. I still hear the old oaths in my head sometimes, the part about protecting people who never signed up for any of this. But then I see the reports they buried, the bodies they reclassified as "equipment losses," and my hands clench on a rifle that no longer belongs to any flag.

When my enlistment started to sour, I found myself leaving the barracks more often, slipping into the parts of town the MPs told us to avoid. Back alleys where smog eats the neon, corner bars where mercs and dock rats make side deals over cheap liquor and contraband. I would sit alone and listen to the way people talked when they did not think regulations applied, how orders turned into favors and favors into debts. At first I told myself I was just blowing off steam, learning the terrain. Truth was, I felt more at home in those half-lit rooms than I ever did in the sanitized briefing halls.

Erin says we are not criminals; we are soldiers without a country. Maybe she believes that. Maybe Jonas Recker still does, on the better days. On the worse ones, I think about how easily I slipped from sanctioned silence to paid silence, from being rewarded for ignoring a quiet theft on a loading dock to being commended for overlooking civilians caught in a crossfire they did not start. There was a time when I thought healing meant the nightmares would stop, that the faces would blur and fade. I know better now. Healing does not erase what happened. It just teaches you where to put the weight so you can keep walking without limping.

Tonight the Regiment is gearing up for another contract, another target someone else decided deserved to disappear. Erin is already running drills in the hangar, barking orders that sound just like the ones we used to get from the brass, only without the polished lies wrapped around them. I can feel that old fascination creeping back in as I watch the pieces come together: the false manifests, the scrubbed comms, the way we slide into the blind spots we helped design. Somewhere along the way, the line between watching a small crime and orchestrating a larger one blurred. I am not sure when it happened. I just know that I am still here, still quiet, and people are still very pleased about that.

I do not remember when exactly I stopped thinking of myself as a pilot and started thinking of myself as a system. Somewhere between the last time I filed an honest approach plan and the first time I watched a freighter arrive early, perfectly threaded through debris I never told control about. My old life, the shift rotations at Gagarin and the petty arguments with dispatch over fuel margins, feels like a story I heard about a stranger. A careful man who believed numbers were neutral and the people above him were merely inefficient, not malicious.

I know better now.

They say I wrecked good people. They say I turned traffic into a weapon. What they never write in the charges is what those people did first. They cut safety margins to shave minutes. They buried near-collisions and blamed the crew. They took my warnings, my math, and filed them under "cost overrun." Every one of them had a choice. They chose to stand in the way of better routes, safer corridors, because those routes did not line anyone's pocket fast enough. My fate, such as it is, is only the echo of theirs.

I still see the face of the first dispatcher whose day I ruined on purpose. I knew exactly when his convoy would hit the cloud of old traffic. Nothing fatal, nothing even reportable, just enough unmodeled junk that he had to scrub the schedule and eat the penalties. I gave his captains a quiet correction on a side channel and watched his whole neat timetable collapse. The pleasure was not in the chaos; it was in the moment he realized he was not in control, that someone else knew his lanes better than he did. I held that look in my mind when people tried to talk me back into taking orders.

Once, a long time ago, I trusted someone completely. She was another controller, steady hands, clean voice on comms. We traded songs and coffee and flight plans, built little redundancies into each other's shifts so no one died because a supervisor fell asleep at their desk. When the near-disaster came, when the defense convoy and that civilian stack nearly became a single smear of light, she signed the paper that said my vector math was at fault. I watched her do it. Could not forget the way she would not meet my eyes. After that, trust became something I retired like an obsolete beacon.

Now I live in the margins of traffic, in the spaces between where the registries think ships are and where they actually drift. This place made sense because no one looks at it anymore, yet it still sits wired into the old network. I can hear the hum of lanes from here, the faint pings of freighters that have no idea someone is watching their every correction. From here, I can clear a path for those who deserve it and twist the road under those who do not, without any committee telling me what an acceptable casualty rate is.

The nights are the worst, when the power draw drops and the station skin cools and every thermal pop sounds like a boot on the deck. I lie in the dark listening to the creaks and the soft whine of aging gyros and imagine footsteps outside the hatch, gloved fists testing welds I thought were invisible. Sleep comes in snatches, broken by the certainty that someone has finally followed the breadcrumbs I could not resist leaving.

Still, I do not regret choosing this over going quietly into whatever tribunal they had planned. They would have carved me up for data and hung me on a wall as a warning. Here, at least, I am still the one drawing the lines. If they ever reach me, it will be because I let one pattern repeat too often, or because I underestimated how much pain I caused someone by ruining their tidy little plans. I have seen that look before, on the dispatcher, on the officers who thought their convoys were safe. People do not forget the moment they realize the road betrayed them.

Neither do I.

Shift log: personal, encrypted  
Victor H.

Bravo Razorpoint, forward billet  

I used to think control meant safety. Parents said it, recruiters sold it, handlers wrapped it in words like protocol and overwatch. Turns out it just means every move graded, every silence noted, every instinct second-guessed until you stop trusting your own hands. Control packaged as protection, layer on layer, until you realize the armor is a cage and you are whatever they need you to be that week. Somewhere along the line it stopped feeling like someone watching my back and started feeling like someone counting my breaths.

Funny thing is, once that clicks, the guilt does not stick the way it used to. First couple of ops with Bravo, I went back to my bunk after cleanup and felt that little twist in the gut. What did we just do, who was really holding the leash, did they deserve it. After a while it all filed under accepted losses. You learn to turn it into checklists instead of questions. Clear angles. Police brass. Police traces. Wipe cams. The guilt gets replaced by a numb tick in the jaw and an early wake-up. Efficient.

Caleb still pretends it eats at him. He stares at his hands like they will turn on him one day. Riya prays when she thinks no one is looking, lips moving behind a chipped mug of coffee. Jonas just gets quieter. Marcus makes jokes too loud in the briefing room, like volume can distract from the smell of burnt composite. Elias moves like a ghost through it all, clockwork-clean, never a missed step, never a stray word in debrief. We are all supposed to be interchangeable parts, but the cracks show if you lean in.

The housekeeping is what gets me. That is what I call it now, so it sits lighter in my head. End of a hot room, ears ringing, and then the ritual unrolls. Gloves, solvent, bag the casings. Field-wipe the rifles, tape off blood tracks, kick loose concrete over drag marks. Swap in a new ID token on the dead drop, rewrite headers so nothing traces upstream. It is like cleaning a kitchen after a messy dinner, only the stains push back for a minute before they fade. You focus on the work, not the shapes you are erasing.

I remember when the worst part of my day was waiting in line at a food stall on Gagarin. Thirty people, one bored cook, steam everywhere, boots sticking to the floor. Same at the clinic after a dock accident, standing for an hour under flickering lights while some kid coughed his lungs out beside me. Lines for the shuttle, lines at GalBank, lines outside a Union office when I thought that was my way out. Back then it felt like the universe holding me in place just to spite me. Now I miss how harmless that kind of stuck could be.

There was a noisy neighbor in the first bunkhouse they put me in. Guy played some ancient rock ballads through a busted speaker, late, every night. I fantasized about kicking his door in more than once. Thought that was pressure. Thought that was being pushed to the edge. One leaky faucet in the shared washroom, too, that drip that never stopped. I used to lie awake and swear I could time my heartbeat to it, wondering if that is how I would die, drowning in drip, not in gunfire. Petty, small, stupid problems. Felt huge at the time.

Now the rumors coming down the chain are about firmware ghosts and people with rewired heads, about contracts that are not on any official slate. Caleb says someone off the books has been paying for clean-up crews around certain clinics and robotics plants, and Bravo keeps getting circled in red for the follow-on slots. Command calls it risk-managed, necessary, contained. Protecting the client, protecting the public. Same old story, control dressed up as safety. We nod, we load mags, we pretend there is still a line we would not cross.

Truth is, I am not sure I would see the line anymore if we did.

I keep telling myself the hum of PX-9199's reactor is comforting, but tonight it sounds like a warning I am too tired to decode.

Gamma watch was a mess again. Jonas Khatri fell asleep at the aft scopes, head bent at that angle that means he will complain about his neck for two days. Darian Holt covered for him, like he always does, fingers dancing over the console, muttering about "phantom echoes" on the long-range. He laughs it off, but his eyes never leave the readings. I swapped shifts with Marina Solanki so she could get a clean six hours before the next drill. She thanked me with a half-warm TerraBrew and that little crooked smile that makes this metal coffin feel less like a sentence.

I keep thinking I do not deserve small kindnesses like that. I coasted into the Vanguard on test scores and a scholarship speech about service and duty, while half this crew bled for their stripes. Some days it feels like I am just playing at the uniform, waiting for someone to call me out. When the captain barked about the nav discrepancy yesterday and Elias Mercer just stepped in, calm, precise, explaining away the mismatch before anyone could look my way, I felt equal parts relief and shame. He did not have to do that. I do not know if I earned that kind of cover.

Elias has been strange lately, though. Not in any dramatic way, just... off. He spends more time alone in the forward comms alcove after shift, claiming he is catching up on deferred reports. I passed by once and caught a glimpse of an encrypted channel handshake that did not look like standard traffic. Could be I misread it. Could be I am seeing ghosts because everyone whispers about shadow bounties and off-the-books contracts these days. Still, when I asked if he wanted to join a card game, he smiled the way you do when you have already made up your mind to say no.

Caleb Rios has theories, of course. He says our patrol route does not make sense, that we are skirting the same patch of nothing too often, like someone is waiting for the right moment to meet us out here where no one bothers to listen. He joked that we are bait. Then he lowered his voice and said if anyone on this ship is talking to the outside, it would be someone who knows which reports never see daylight. Someone like Elias. I told him he was being unfair. Elias is the one who makes sure our messages actually get through the bureaucratic sludge. If he is distant, maybe he just carries more than the rest of us on his shoulders.

I wonder if I am being naive, or if cynicism is just the luxury of people who are certain they belong. Maybe I do not get to judge. I have a bunk, a Vanguard patch, a paycheck that clears through GalBank on time, while settlers at the edge of nowhere bet their lives on pilots like the ones we used to fly with. I did not earn that safety so much as inherit it from a home that could afford tutors and simulator time. When PX-9199 swings through dead space, I sometimes feel the universe doing its calculus and deciding I have not paid enough yet.

Tonight, the corridors feel thinner. The air recyclers have a hitch I have never noticed before, like someone cleared their throat in the vents and then went silent. Holt says it is just age in the ducts. Jonas joked that if we vanish out here, no one would believe it was an accident. I laughed with them, but the idea stuck in my teeth. We are a handful of names on a manifest, circling the same coordinates, trusting a chain of orders none of us have seen in full.

If something does go wrong, I hope I faced it with more courage than I feel right now, writing in a dim bunk while PX-9199 hums around me. I hope the people I have been quietly judging for their secrets were at least trying to protect someone. And if I have been blind to what is coming, maybe that is what I deserve for thinking this ship's routine meant we were safe.

I have been thinking about drills and dishes tonight, which is not the combination anyone expects from Cipher Crossfire. Muscle memory is the throughline, I guess. Out here, I clear a corridor the same way I used to clear tables at my uncle's place back home, stacking plates without really looking, restocking shelves because that is just what you did when your shift ended. There was no decision to it. You saw a mess, you fixed it. Now I walk a perimeter with that same empty-headed efficiency and try not to think too hard about whose mess we are cleaning up for credits.

Riya gave me that look again in the armory. She has this way of measuring people against the ledger in her head, weighing what you cost against what you bring in. She did not say anything, but the pause before she signed off on my loadout felt longer than usual. Elena, on the other hand, keeps playing the calm older sister, asking about sleep schedules and hydration like we are not about to drop into another contract no one will ever officially admit happened. I trust her more than I should, which is probably a mistake. Tessa floats between us, always with a joke ready, always just a little too informed about who has been taking side offers. Jonas is the one who stays quiet and watches the corners; he is either the safest one to trust or the last one I should.

There is talk going around that some of our recent work is feeding into something bigger on the civ side. Patterns in atmospherics, orbital routes getting scrubbed from logs, clients who never show their faces in the briefings. Supposedly it is all coincidence, just the way jobs line up. But I have heard the pilots mutter about a handful of names that keep disappearing from manifests, and I have seen charts vanish from the ops table between one debrief and the next. We are not supposed to care who signs the wire transfers, as long as they clear. Still, when people start talking softer as you walk past, you notice.

I catch myself replaying old arguments with her, too. Back before I signed on here, when the worst firefights I saw were in our kitchen. She used to twist things so fluently that I would walk away wondering if I really had said what I thought I said. I remember bringing up how we never went anywhere I picked, and somehow by the end of it I was apologizing for not being "flexible enough." She would shake her head, tell me I was remembering it wrong, that I was too sensitive, too suspicious. It took a long time to realize that every time I raised a concern, the conversation ended with me doubting my own eyes. On bad days, I hear that same tone when certain clients say "trust me" and "minimal collateral."

Helping at the family store taught me to run on auto-pilot. Sweep the floor, restock the cans, check the seals on the freezers. You did it because it needed doing, not because anyone was watching. That made me good at following checklists here, at moving through the choreography without needing to be told twice. It also made it easy to stop asking why we are being sent to one refinery and not another, why this comms buoy has to go dark while that one stays bright. Routine blurs the questions.

Cipher Crossfire lives on that blur. Unspoken rule one: do not pry into contracts that pay on time. Rule two: never be the first to suggest the client is lying. Rule three: know who will cover you when the plan burns down. Elena will, if she can. Jonas probably will, if the angles make sense. Riya will, if the numbers justify it. Tessa might, if she is not halfway through cutting her own side deal. Me, I will do what I have always done: walk the line, check the seals, clear the corridor.

Lately, though, the line feels like it is painted over something we are not meant to see. And I am starting to hear my partner's old voice again whenever command tells us we are "just imagining patterns."

I keep telling myself the hum of the grav drive is comforting, but tonight it just sounds like someone grinding their teeth in the walls.

We ran another long-range sweep and came up with absolutely nothing. No pirates, no distress calls, no interesting anomalies, just cold stars and some old telemetry packets the brass wanted us to pick apart. I spent four straight hours at the console with Jared Whitlow in the next chair, both of us pretending not to be half-asleep. Marcus Bellamy walked by twice and smacked Jared on the shoulder the second time, muttering something about "falling asleep on state time." Jared laughed, but he did not really look at him.

Mess was quiet after that. Talia Serrano and Noah Calder claimed a corner table, as usual, talking in low voices about transfer postings and whether Cydonia is as awful as everyone says. Bellamy held court by the dispenser, telling some story about his last posting that had Kincaid rolling his eyes. Elias caught me watching and gave me that small, polite nod of his, the one that never quite reaches his eyes. I nodded back and kept moving. We are all very good at passing each other in tight corridors, trading thin smiles, pretending this ship is bigger than it is.

The unspoken lines are getting sharper, though. Bellamy and Talia have decided our orders are pointless busywork, and they are not shy about it. Jared sides with whoever he is standing closest to. Noah just wants his next leave, wherever that ends up being. Elias floats between them like he is allergic to taking a side, always "just following the route," always reminding us we are lucky to be on a quiet posting. Lucky. That word is starting to itch.

There was a moment on my last maint shift where absolutely nothing was happening. Sensors flat, comms dead quiet, even the circulation fans sounded tired. I checked the same diagnostics three times anyway, then stared at the viewport and daydreamed about being dirt-side somewhere with real gravity and bad coffee you cannot recycle. I imagined walking through some crowded spaceport on my day off, nobody looking twice, nobody expecting me to know which way to jump first. For ten whole minutes, I forgot the way this ship feels like it is holding its breath.

Then I remembered the way our current route bent off standard lanes. Kincaid had called it an "optimization," and the captain signed off because apparently he used to do routing work before this assignment. Marcus made a crack afterward about letting a glorified bus driver tinker with Navy paths. Everyone laughed except Kincaid, who just watched the star plot with that tight little focus of his. He has been spending more time alone on the bridge after lights-out, "reviewing jump curves." No one questions him; we are all happy enough to have someone else care about the numbers.

Still, I have caught odd looks between Elias and the captain when they think no one is watching. Short conversations cut off when I walk in, a file window slammed shut a little too quickly, that kind of thing. Nothing you can report, nothing that adds up to more than a feeling that there is a second briefing none of us are invited to. I overheard Noah mutter that the last set of orders we relayed were stamped with clearance well above this bucket's pay grade. Bellamy shrugged it off as politics, the sort that blows over and never reaches grunts like us.

Maybe he is right. Maybe it is just another forgotten errand in a forgotten corner of UC space. But the way our corridor dances around the usual beacons, the way Kincaid never seems surprised by last-minute course changes, the way the captain has started locking his terminal even for quick trips to the head all pull in the same direction. Something out there is expecting us. Or maybe I am just tired and hearing too much in the hum of the drive. Either way, the air feels heavier every time I strap in.

I nearly tore the hinge off my locker again this morning. Thing has been sticking since the last grav micro-spike, when half the ship shuddered and everybody pretended it was routine. I keep meaning to file a ticket, but there is always something more urgent than Malik Traynor s whining storage bin. So I did the usual dance: shoulder into the metal, curse under my breath, wiggle the latch until it finally gives with that ugly screech. Lena Moretti says it sounds like the ship complaining back at me. Maybe she is right. Maybe we are both one bad bump away from coming apart.  

Breakfast was powdered eggs and a long, slow line down the mess corridor. Standing there, tray in hand, listening to the same recycled jokes about rations and rotation schedules, I watched Naomi Kearns three people ahead of me. She kept checking the time on the wall display, fingers drumming against the tray, eyes doing that quick scan she gets when she is thinking in bandwidth instead of faces. Riley Sandoval nudged me and whispered that Naomi has been spending too much time in the comms bay after hours. Elias Monroe said that is just what you do when you want a transfer out of "graveyard escort duty." Everyone has a theory. Nobody actually asks her.  

I caught myself getting annoyed at how many times she has brushed past me without really seeing me lately. Used to be we would swap stories about Jemison, compare cafeteria coffee to the real stuff on shore leave. Now I get half-smiles and "sorry, busy," as she rushes off to babysit the array. Funny thing is, our routes have been getting quieter, not noisier. Fewer check-ins, fewer escorts overlapping. Feels like the void is opening up around us, one subtle schedule change at a time.  

Today, during equipment checks, the stuck locker set me off more than it should have. I pulled out the toolkit, finally, determined to fix the damned hinge. The screws were stripped from years of half-hearted repairs. Someone before me had jammed a bit of metal foil in to keep it from rattling. I sat there on the deck for ten minutes, trying to line everything up, hands shaking just enough to miss the groove again and again. In the end I bent the hinge back into "good enough" and left it. That seems to be our standard operating procedure lately. Nothing gets fixed properly, just nudged so it holds a little longer.  

While I was sitting there, legs going numb, an old memory came crawling back in, one I have spent years shoving into a mental airlock. The last convoy I crewed before this posting, the one that went dark in the middle of a routine jump and came back with half the calls logged as "equipment failure." I remember hearing the distress bursts on the monitor, cut off mid-sentence when someone killed the channel to avoid "panic." We never saw the aftermath, just signed the reports. I have told myself a hundred times that I did not have the authority to change it. Today I let myself replay the sound of that broken voice, let it dig in behind my ribs. It hurt, but in a way that felt cleaner than all the excuses I have been running on.  

Naomi walked past after midwatch, locker bag over her shoulder, that distant look in her eyes. She said we might be seeing some "planned outages" on upcoming runs, that command is trialing new protocols and not to worry if comms go strange. She tried to make it sound like a joke, but her smile did not reach her eyes. Lena rolled hers and muttered something about "bean-counters playing with our lives again." I laughed along, sharp and hollow, because that is what you do in a line, in a mess hall, on a ship where nothing ever really changes until one day it does and no one even remembers when it started.  

The hinge on my locker is going to fail sooner or later. I can feel it in the way the metal drags. Sometimes I wonder what else on this ship is hanging by the same thread, just waiting for the right nudge in the dark.

I always thought scout duty would feel bigger than this. Turns out most of it is the same three corridors, the same hum from life support, the same shift bells that Mason insists on tapping out on the bulkhead like the world's most annoying metronome. BL-6924 could be any other UC can in the dark if I did not know every scratch on these panels. I used to like the predictability; lately it feels like the ship is keeping time on me instead of the other way around.

Today I broke my own little superstition. First launch on any patrol, I always touch the edge of the nav console and count to five under my breath. Stupid, I know, but I have done it since academy. This time we were late cycling the Grav Drive tests, Elias barking about drift tolerances, Rhea asking for another round of diagnostics, and I just strapped in and answered roll call. I realized halfway through the jump I had not done it. Nothing happened. No alarms, no hard burn, we just rode the corridor clean. I told myself it was proof the ritual never mattered, but my hands still shook when I took my gloves off.

Rhea caught that, I think. She asked if I was cold, and it was the way she said it that got me. Too soft for a ship this small, where everyone can hear everyone else breathe. Sometimes when she leans over my station to check a plot, I forget what Elias is saying about error margins and just watch the reflection of the nav lights on her visor. That is a bad habit on a Navy paycheck. Worse when I catch Isabella watching the two of us with that little half-smile she hides behind "just teasing." I do not know if I am imagining the way she lingers when Rhea is on duty or if they have their own orbit I am trespassing on without realizing.

The rumor mill is running hotter than the Grav coils. Supposedly someone in Ops back in New Atlantis has been selling timing offsets to freelance captains. The way Mason tells it, it is all desperate haulers and unlucky smugglers trying to shave minutes, nothing we need to lose sleep over. Then Elias pointed out, very quietly, that our patrol routes keep getting "revised" at the last second, and that some of those revisions make no tactical sense at all. The whispers say a controller down in the Well is the one moving the pieces, and that certain UC ships get cleaner windows than others if the right credits move through the right Trade Authority hands.

Now there is this latest piece of gossip making the rounds in the mess: a MAST official and a Navy logistics officer supposedly scrubbed a whole incident record together, then went for drinks like nothing happened. The story has already grown three extra details in two days. Personally, I think half of it is spacer exaggeration and half of it is real, ugly truth. What bothers me is not the idea of some faceless bureaucrat cutting corners; it is watching Elias go very still and quiet when people joke about reports "going missing." He trusts the system more than anyone I know. Seeing doubt in his eyes makes the deck feel less solid under my boots.

I am caught between feeling guilty for breaking a meaningless little tradition and feeling oddly relieved that the universe did not punish me for it. If something that small can be let go and nothing changes, what else can we stop pretending about? Still, when I think about how easily our shifts get adjusted, how routes appear in the console with no explanation, and how no one questions it as long as the coffee is hot and the pay clears, it makes my stomach knot up. We shrug, we adapt, we stop touching the console and start trusting the timing some stranger sends us from a clean office.

Maybe that is the real superstition on this ship: that the people behind the schedules know what they are doing. Tonight the hull is quiet, the stars look exactly the same, and yet I can not shake the feeling that someone, somewhere, nudged our path a few degrees and none of us noticed in time.

I have spent most of my life pretending nothing rattles me. You cannot be the one who tunes convoy chains and admits you have not slept in three nights because every trajectory looks like a casualty estimate. So I learned to keep the jitter out of my voice, to hold the coffee cup steady, to trace neat little arcs in the air while my mind screamed about what happens if I am wrong by half a second. No one wants to see the cracks in the person telling them when and where to jump. I have been hiding that from everyone for years, terrified that if I ever said it out loud the thin layer of trust I still have would peel off and I would be left with nothing at all.

The day I walked out on them, all those neat uniforms and their comfortable certainties, I told myself I was the only one in the room honest enough to see what the numbers meant. They call it protective redundancy; I saw it for what it was, a blade wrapped in a safety manual. Convoys do not accidentally appear next to disputed farms at the exact moment a task force swings through. Somebody built that. I built that. So I broke it. Sabotaged their perfect timetable, tore a hole in their plan, and then I ran. And yes, I can hear the way they say traitor. From where I am standing, no one else had the spine to get their hands dirty.

I chose this kind of exile because it makes tactical sense. Out here, skirting refueling barges and forgotten traffic towers, the lanes are thinner, easier to bend. The UC cannot move a capital ship through these corridors without everyone noticing; I can slide a handful of hulls through and leave nothing but a timing anomaly behind. Smugglers, settlers, even the occasional idealist with more hope than fuel, they all come to me when they realize the official routes are killing them by degrees. They think I am saving them. In a way, I am. I am also using them as test cases, proof that my geometry works outside the clean simulations. Someone has to. None of the people still playing by the rules are going to redraw the map.

I keep telling myself that makes me necessary. That I am the one willing to make the hard decisions, to decide which convoys get the clean gaps and which patrols arrive five minutes too late to do any harm. It is an ugly calculus, but at least I admit I am doing it. The UC buries their equations in classified reports and calls it peacekeeping. The pirates dress theirs up as freedom. I sit here in borrowed chairs on Morrow's Folly or in the dark of an old tower, and I decide who gets to go unseen. If that does not make me better, it at least makes me honest.

There are moments, usually at the end of a long run, when the coffee has gone cold and the charts are all drifting into each other, that I remember I could have been kind. I could have slowed things down instead of shaving them razor-thin, could have told some scared captain to take the safe, sanctioned lane and live with the inspections. I could have refused to weaponize what I know. More than once I watched a junior tech flounder with a route and chose to correct them with a cutting remark instead of a gentle one, because it was faster to make them afraid of disappointing me. Efficiency as an excuse for cruelty. I knew what I was doing, and I did it anyway.

I tell myself I fled to these edges because they make sense for what I am building. That is true, but it is not the whole truth. Out here I can be indispensable without being seen too closely. If anyone ever really looked, really listened, they might realize I am just as scared as they are of being turned into a tool again. Better to keep moving from relay to relay, from underbelly dens to quiet buoys, leaving behind only the traces I intend: corrupted jump data, odd timing, stories. As long as they are chasing my shadow through the lanes, they are not close enough to see the person underneath it, still tracing paths in the air and hoping to pretend, one more day, that none of this is getting to her.

I used to keep field logs, not diaries. Funny how the habit comes back when the chain of command is just a name we burned off our armor.

Obsidian runs quiet tonight. Damon is stripping down rifles on the far bench like he is still in an armory, muttering about carbon scoring as if any of that matters when your real problem is which one of your own might put a round in your back. Rafael is on watch, eyes always a little too bright since that last black ops drop. And Elena, down in the cargo bay, pacing like a caged artillery shell.

It was easier when orders came from a clean voice over a secured channel, even if that voice sent us to do things no tribunal would ever admit happened. Flooded bunkers. "Unmarked combatants." The time they told us to erase a village that did not exist on any map because the satellites "malfunctioned." I remember the briefing room afterwards, how the senior staff smiled too tight and told us we had done the right thing for the flag. I also remember the smell of burned synth-wood and the way the medics avoided our eyes.

The worst part is how jealousy rots you from the inside and nobody trains you for that. I trusted Elena more than any officer I ever bled for. We were good together, in the cracks between deployments. Then the rumors started, stupid things about her and Rafael running off on side jobs, about special favors from command. I did not believe them at first. Then every small disagreement felt like a test I was failing, every joke at my expense sounded like a coded message I was not meant to hear. I started reading angles into where she stood in the ready room, who she chose for fireteam, how long she talked to Damon after drills. It turned the whole operation into an emotional minefield, and I laid half the charges myself.

There is one image I cannot scrub: Elena stumbling back into the evac zone, helmet off, face streaked with someone else's blood. I remember the surge of horror before the training kicked in, before I checked for holes in her armor, before the medic pushed past me. She laughed, said it was not hers, that I should see the other guy. I nodded, made some hardass comment about keeping her visor down. Later, alone, my hands would not stop shaking. I still do not know if I was more afraid of what had happened out there or of how badly I wanted to hold on to her in front of the whole squad.

Out here, away from official insignia, isolation is easier than letting anyone that close again. Outwardly, I talk like the rest of them: jokes about being ghosts, about how we answer to credits and survival now, not to some council on a distant rock. Inside, I still hear the old oaths. I feel the weight of every time we picked the "necessary" option because someone with a higher clearance said there was no other way.

You learn fast that any sign of softness is an invitation. In the Regiment, if you flinch, someone will use that to move you up the breach stack, or leave you with the worst sector of fire. When we broke from command, that did not change; it just got messier. Now the pressure to act tougher than I feel is constant. Show doubt and Damon will write you off as unreliable. Let your guard slip and Rafael, with his soft words and hard eyes, will start asking what you are really in this for. Elena just watches, waiting to see which way I jump.

Trust is the rarest commodity on this ship. Every briefing, every whispered side-deal, every off-the-books contract from some corporate ghost just twists the knife a little deeper. I know some of us are in this to expose what happened back then, to drag certain names into the light. I also know some would sell those secrets if the price was right. So we sleep in shifts, lock our gear, and swear we have each other's backs, even as the tension hums in the bulkheads. Some nights I lie awake, listening to the engines and wondering which comes first: the moment we finally turn on each other, or the moment the past catches up and saves us the trouble.

I keep telling myself that if the ship's humming, we're fine. That steady vibration in the soles of my boots means the grav ring is still spinning, the drive is still breathing, and nobody has opened us up like a can of Chunks. Still, tonight that hum feels more like a warning than a lullaby.

Routine was normal enough. Cargo checks, system diagnostics, another pass over those navigation updates from Command that no one can explain properly. Jonah Reyes grumbled through half of his shift about how the new route cuts tighter to restricted space than anything we trained for. He laughs it off in front of Marina Holt, but when he thought I was busy with the panel I saw his hands shaking a little on the console. He is not the type to spook easily.

Amira Chen caught me in the corridor and asked if I had heard anything about "an audit run" piggybacked on our orders. She said it casually, like gossip about rations, but her eyes flicked up to the camera dome and back down too fast. She mentioned someone in logistics bragging at a TerraBrew line about insurance payouts spiking along certain corridors. Pretended it was nothing, then changed the subject to GalBank loans and vacation plans on Paradiso. She does that when she's nervous runs two conversations at once so she does not have to finish either.

Lila Park has gone quiet. Used to be you could hear her laughing from two compartments away, especially when Elias Mercer was around. Lately, if he walks into the mess, she finds a reason to leave early or suddenly remembers a calibration she forgot. She told me at drill this morning that Elias has been "too lucky" with his off-duty assignments, always pulling the easy monitoring posts when we hit the tight lanes. Then she said she was being paranoid and laughed it off. It did not sound like her own laughter.

Elias himself is harder to read. He has that easy UC smile, the one they put on recruiting posters, but there is a distance in it now, like he is already gone somewhere else in his head. I caught him alone in the storage bay, staring at one of the external sensor housings like it had just spoken to him. When he noticed me he snapped right back, cracked a joke about the food, and walked off humming some old Earth tune. Maybe I am imagining it. Maybe the ship is just getting to me.

The corridor chatter has changed tone. People lower their voices when they talk about our route; they call it "threading the needle" like it is a brag, but no one asks why Command is so intent on shaving fuel and minutes through the same patch of space that keeps spitting out "navigation anomalies" in the reports. Marina said that if she were a Trident captain and saw our plotted corridor on a chart, she would pay extra to go the long way around. She was only half joking.

Today's mid-shift was one of those long, dull stretches where nothing happened at all. No alarms, no course corrections, no interesting pings on the scope. Just me, a console, and the faint smell of stale TerraBrew someone left in a cupholder. I found myself daydreaming about Akila City skies and even New Atlantis crowds, of all things. Imagined getting out, earning UC citizenship proper, maybe buying my father one of those overpriced Red Harvest bottles just to prove I made something of myself. Then I caught my reflection in the screen and remembered I am still here, in a metal shell chasing coordinates written by people who will never float this close to the dark.

I am not saying there is something wrong with Elias. I am just saying that when Marina asked me, quietly, if I trusted everyone on this crew with my life, his was the name that did not come to my tongue right away. Maybe it is nothing. Maybe tomorrow will be another hum-dull day, another safe pass through another corridor someone swears is fine on paper. But the way people speak lately half-sentences, unfinished questions, words swallowed when a door hisses open it feels like we are all standing one step too close to an airlock, hoping no one reaches for the control.

9th shift, station night-cycle

Got that ping from ops again today. Same clipped priority tone, same two-word summons. Every time it hits my slate my gut does the same slow roll, like I am waiting to see if it is a contract brief or a bullet with my name already engraved. Uniform Blacksteel likes to pretend there is a line between those two things. Out on the floor, most of us stopped believing that a long time ago.

I walked the long way to command. Old habit. Gives you time to read faces, see who is not at their post, who has been suddenly reassigned to "extended leave." Caleb Harker was on corridor security, stance tighter than usual. He nodded once but his eyes were on the mirrored bulkhead behind me, checking angles. He has the same dread when the boss calls; he is just better at burying it under procedure.

The briefing turned out to be another "discreet overwrite" job. High-orbit clean-up, logs to scrub, no questions to ask. The boss did his usual routine, all neat phrasing about risk mitigation and deniable presence. The more polite he gets, the more I wonder whose throat we are stepping on. There is a rumor going around that some shipwright has been turning disposal yards into crime scenes with a conscience, and now the contracts that land on our desk feel like we are sweeping his footprints off the deck before anyone else sees them. No names, just hull numbers that should not exist.

I asked once about rotation out. Told the boss I wanted ground-side work or a transfer to a lower-risk attachment. He fed me that gentle line about "one last tour" and "earning a cleaner slate." I even half believed him. A week later I was back on an airless corridor with my boots ringing off the decking, running escort on the very same kind of job I had tried to get away from. Second time I raised it, he brought up breach of contract penalties, repayment schedules, and how hard it is to find employers who will look past certain files. Every promise feels like a patch over cracked plating. Looks good till you put stress on it.

Day-to-day, it is the small, ugly comforts that keep us from drifting apart. Shared scavenged meals in the service bay after a run: whatever we can heat in a dented pot over a rerouted coolant line. Caleb has a hook-up for discount UC BattleMeals that "fell off" some cargo. We cut them with CAN-uck! Bacon or Synthameat scraps and pretend it tastes like real food. Our uniforms are on their third life, underarms re-stitched with cargo net twine, knees patched with offcuts from armor plates. Most of my gear is improvised. My side rig is held together with Zero Wire and adhesive from a crate that was supposed to go to some mining colony; my gloves have been re-palmed so many times the original fabric is a rumor.

In the quiet, you can hear the unit talking in code. Not in prep rooms, but in the way people skip topics when someone else walks in. Harker says there is a pattern to our deployments; every time we get sent anywhere near a wreck site or a disposal node, some other team has been there first, and their reports do not match what is on the ground. Too clean. Too consistent. One of the techs swears she found structural notes hidden in standard maintenance packets, like someone is trying to leave a trail for anyone stubborn enough to look. Might just be paranoia, but it fits the way ops keeps changing our kill-switch phrases.

I keep thinking about walking away again. Just not showing up after a cycle, slipping out with a free trader or LIST convoy. Then I remember the last time I tried to talk exit terms, how the room got colder even before the boss smiled, how the conversation turned to obligations, debts, favors already called in on my behalf. The unspoken point was clear: you do not just leave; you are allowed to be repurposed. So I keep my gear ready, keep my slate charged, pretend the summons are always about work and never about airlocks, and tell myself that as long as we are patching each other's armor and sharing stolen stew, we are still more crew than cargo.

I keep telling myself I am going to stop writing these, that it is childish for a grown man to keep a diary, but tonight the hum of the reactors feels louder than usual and I need something that is not numbers or manifests.

Day started with the usual: coolant flow a little off in bay three, so I spent the first two hours shuttling between engineering and cargo, logging temperatures, filing yet another maintenance note that GalBank will pretend to read. The ship feels slower this week, like the grav plates are half a beat behind our footsteps. Even the air feels thicker, stale from too many closed-cycle days. Funny how that alone can sour your mood before anything actually goes wrong.

We had a simple meal together between shifts, all of us cramped around that too-small table in the mess. Mara Ellison joked about the Synthameat ham being older than the ship, and Naomi Varga tried to class it up by slicing her potato into neat little cubes like some fancy restaurant plate. Riya Sengupta shared a packet of Red Harvest lentils she has been hoarding, turned it into something that almost tasted like home for her. Elena Khatri sat opposite me, quiet as usual, but she actually laughed when Gavin Moretti told that story about the captain with his suit stuck in zero-g because he forgot to lock the seal. For a few minutes it was all just clinking forks, bad coffee, and the comfortable sound of people complaining about the same dull things. Ordinary. Safe.

Of course, ordinary never lasts. The news ping came through about my brother back on Gagarin; lungs still bad, fever cycling again, doctors saying they are "monitoring." Monitoring what, exactly, from half a system away I cannot do anything but watch the updates scroll past while I tick off inventory of sealed crates and log insurance codes. I signed off on a shipment of emergency meds this afternoon, and all I could think was how none of it is headed toward him. There was a tightness in my chest all day, like the ship's grav was pressing down harder just on me.

Later, while I was running a slow errand to check ballast readings in the aft storage, I heard Naomi and Mara in the corridor, voices low. Insurance this, risk that, someone upstairs recalculating corridors as if our lives are just another line in a GalBank model. They hushed when they saw me. It is not like we have not all thought it; still, it is different hearing it said out loud. Gavin shrugged it off, said every route has its price and we signed up for the bonus pay. Elena just watched the discussion from the edge, eyes unreadable, then changed the subject to cargo stacking protocols like none of it mattered.

I spent an hour reorganizing supplies after that, lining up crates in perfect rows, labels all facing the same direction, just to bleed off the frustration. Somewhere between counting the third and fourth pallet of zero wire spools, something in me just snapped, quietly. I realized I have been carrying this constant anger at the people holding the charts, at the numbers that say my brother is not profitable enough to treat, at being trapped out here while others play their games. And for once, I let it go. Not because they deserve forgiveness, but because I am tired of giving them free rent in my head. The ship seemed to breathe easier afterward, or maybe that was just me.

The chatter in the routing den on Gagarin keeps coming back to me, those captains talking about "low-risk" corridors that somehow keep failing for the same kinds of ships. Here, aboard Stockwind, I can see the paper trail starting to match the whispers: altered flags on cargo, routes that bend closer to bad neighborhoods in space. Every time I look at our manifests, I find another little discrepancy that no one will admit noticing. People claim to know the lanes are safe, that the models do not lie, but what they say at the mess table never quite matches what they murmur in empty corridors. I am starting to think there is a pattern running under all of this, something we are all stepping around without daring to name.

Think my hands are still shaking.

Mira said it does not show, that I looked solid backing her play at the drop, but I can feel it in my bones. All day with the Squad Drifters and you keep your chin high, shoulders loose, act like you were born in a firefight. Then you get a moment alone and the truth leaks out through the cracks. We walked away with the crates and without any bodies that belonged to us, so by the only measure that matters it was a win. Does not feel like one.

Jace would laugh if he heard that. For him it is simple: job hits, gun goes up, someone falls, credit chip blinks green. He lives in that straight line. Maybe that is why Leena keeps him close, like a blunt instrument she can point at problems. Me, I overthink. I run every angle twice, check sightlines a third time, hear Rena muttering about how slow I am. She means it as a joke mostly, but the thing about jokes is they start near something true.

It is the same feeling every time we come back to the lot. Cargo parked, doors sealed, everyone circling up in that half-lit bay while Leena does the quiet rounds. Who did good, who almost cost them. She never says it that plain, but you can hear it in which shoulders she squeezes, which eyes she skip. Tonight she clapped Tomas on the back, told him his wheel work saved us a nasty tail. She gave Mira a nod for keeping the buyers smiling. When she got to me, all she said was "Next time, faster on the draw," before moving on.

I know what she meant. Second crate, top of the ramp, I hesitated. Saw the dock rat reach for something under his jacket, but I saw his eyes, too, and they looked more scared than mean. Turned out it was just a slate; Rena saw it first and smacked it out of his hand with the butt of her pistol. She did not look at me afterward, but the others did. That is the thing that sticks under my skin. You give everything, pull watch till your eyes blur, keep your weapon clean, run drills in the rain, and still you are the one who got "almost" attached to his name.

Back when it was just me and a maintenance crew on some forgotten pad, I thought if I worked hard enough, some boss would see it and I would stop being the kid everyone forgot about on rotation. Now I am in a gang with a name people whisper in bars, and it is the same story. You bleed for the colors and you are still one wrong move away from being the guy they do not bring next time. Exhausting. Like running a grav drive in the red, never quite burning out, just running hotter than you should.

Heard some interesting noise while we were waiting on the buyers, though. Mira was trading gossip with one of the dock bosses, did not notice I was close enough to catch the low parts. Someone out in the scrapyards has been pulling apart condemned ships and leaving their own notes in the bones. Not just stripping hardware either, more like rewriting whose fault certain "accidents" were. Freestar hauler captains muttering about it over drinks, UC patrols suddenly very interested in old wrecks. The name they kept circling was the same one Tomas mentioned last week after a run near Narion, said it like a ghost story.

I do not know why that sticks with me, either. Maybe because this life keeps teaching me that the story on the slate is never the whole thing. People disappear, jobs change destination mid-flight, and we are told not to ask why. Then some quiet engineer out in the dark starts scratching the truth into dead metal, and everyone starts getting jumpy. Could be just another rumor to scare jumpy crews into better insurance. But Leena has started asking a lot of questions about routes and registries lately, and that means this ghost, whoever he is, might end up crossing our path.

If that happens, I want to be more than the one who hesitated. I am tired down to the marrow of never quite being enough. But there is no space here to be tired, so I will clean my gun again, run the approach in my head until I can smell the oil, and tomorrow I will stand in that bay with the others like it all rolls off me. Maybe one day it actually will.

I keep telling myself I left the uniform behind, but my boots still line up heel to heel at the bunk edge and I still wake up ten minutes before alarm, listening for a sergeant's voice that will never come.

Today, it was Darin who woke me instead, banging on the bulkhead because someone used the last of the solvent and did not log it. Stupid thing to bark over, but the way he squared off with Jaro in the corridor, hand hovering over his sidearm, you would think someone had defected mid-firefight. That is what it is like out here now: tiny sparks over nothing, flaring because underneath we all know any argument could end with a body being spaced and a "training accident" written in the log.

The old days had rules, or at least the appearance of them. Fall in, follow orders, trust that someone behind the desk knew why you were kicking down the door. I still remember the day they hauled Kelnar and Ruiz out in front of the whole company after Londinion, made us watch while the provosts read out charges about "unauthorized engagement parameters." They stripped their patches, marched them off in cuffs, and left the rest of us standing there in full kit, understanding perfectly well the only thing they had done wrong was shoot the wrong people without the right signatures. That was the lesson: you are not punished for the act, you are punished for making the paperwork inconvenient.

Breakaway pretends we came out here because we will not be used like that again. Maybe some of them believe it. I thought I did, once. Then the first time our boss pulled the whole unit into that cramped briefing room, air thick with gun oil and recycled coffee, he smiled that calm little smile and laid out a contract that sounded exactly like the ones we used to run, just with the insignia filed off. I remember the dread in my gut as he spoke, not because of the target, but because I could not tell if he had called us in for a job or to thin the ranks. Every summons feels like that now, a coin toss between work and execution.

Rival crews nip at our flanks when we pass through the wrong fence's turf, but they are not the ones I watch most closely. We worked a corridor op with another outfit two months back, supposed to be a clean crossfire to drive a convoy into a killbox. Their leader smiled too wide, said all the right brother-in-arms lines, then quietly tried to reroute the payout to his own accounts. Darin caught it before it cleared. We fixed it, but only because it would have cost us. Next time it might be one of ours rerouting the credits, and then what.

And then there is Elen. If I had stayed in the Navy she would be the exemplary officer on the recruitment posters: sharp posture, cleaner record, the kind of eyes that see three moves ahead. Out here she runs logistics and target packages, but I have watched her flip from lover to executioner faster than I can chamber a round. Once, after a deal soured and a local broker tried to renegotiate at gunpoint, she did not flinch, did not even raise her voice. Just tilted her head, gave a quiet order, and watched as two of our own pinned him and broke his arm in three places. The look on her face never changed, and I felt something cold settle in my chest when I realized I understood exactly why she did it and that, given the same calculus, I would have done worse.

We argue about rations now, about bunk space, about who forgot to cycle the filters. Petty things. But under each snapped word is the memory of all the times someone "forgot" to raise a safety, or "miscalculated" a yield radius. The day we walked away from command we told ourselves we were done letting other people decide who lived and who got written off as collateral. Maybe that was a lie, or maybe we just traded one set of liars for another. The difference is that now, when I look at the people I fight beside, I no longer pretend they are safer than the ones shooting at us.
