And when the boss calls my name over the intercom, I still feel that old dread in my spine and have to decide, every single time, whether to walk into that room or start running.

I keep telling myself this thing is just for checking zero on my rifle grip, not for feelings, but here I am again scratching words into a pad instead of cleaning gear.

We ran drills today like we still wore the old colors. Marcus barking time checks, Noah counting rounds, Riley watching the angles like someone is always about to kick in the door. Damien handled overwatch, same as he did on the border stations, only now the only court-martial waiting for him is us. Elena watched all of it with that officer stare she never quite lost. Fractured Phalanx, the joke goes, but the muscle memory never really broke.

I keep thinking about the last time I stood in front of an actual tribunal. Not as a defendant, not officially. They needed someone to sit in the back and take notes while they made an example of three kids who tried to rotate off a meat-grinder posting on their own. They stripped their stripes, scrubbed their records, and shipped them to a penal garrison so remote the star maps came with warnings. They left the cell door open just long enough for the rest of us to see them go. One of the captains called it "reaffirming discipline."

Funny thing about examples. You look at them long enough, you start imagining yourself in their place. A bad toss of the dice, a question asked one layer too high. Or being the one locked in the room with a choice between calling out the lie in the op order or signing your name under it and pretending you didn't see what the sensors showed, what the medics muttered after.

Betrayal was always the word they used for going off-mission, never for what they did to us. Yet everyone knew there were eyes and ears in every squad that did not belong to the squad. Quiet types whose reports traveled faster than bullets. People disappeared for less than what we know now. They called it reassignment. We called it being buried alive. That is the part that still sits under my skin, even here. Even with a different patch.

Out here with the Phalanx, nobody pretends we are clean. Marcus still wakes up swinging some nights, like he is back in that corridor with the evac alarms and the sealed blast doors. Riley drinks just enough to sleep and not so much that her trigger finger shakes. Noah jokes too loud when anyone mentions "loyalty," as if volume can drown out the word. Damien and Elena do their arguing behind closed hatches, but the walls in this bucket are thin. I hear "lines we won't cross" and I hear "we crossed them already, remember?"

Me, I lie awake in whatever bunk or storeroom we are calling home that week, listening to the ship creak and the coolant cycle, counting my own breathing. Sleep comes in slices. Every time I close my eyes I see those nights pinned between civilian houses and incoming fire, orders to hold even when the feeds showed movement we weren't supposed to admit existed. The screaming in the distance, the way the brass congratulated themselves on "containment" while we hosed blood out of our armor. The threats were never written down, but we heard them clear enough: disobey and join the ghosts.

The paranoia never really left. Maybe it is earned, maybe it has crawled too far into us to dig out. Even now, when we are the ones off the leash, I watch Marcus's hands when he checks his comms, wonder if he is sending more than coordinates. I watch Elena when she takes a private call, remember the way she signed off on op plans that burned towns because someone higher up said the numbers were acceptable. I see the way Riley flinches at unexpected visitors on the scope. We all carry the memory of being used, and the knowledge that anyone can sell you out if the price or pressure is right.

So why stay with them? Because we all know exactly what the other has done and what was done to us, and there is a comfort, bitter as it is, in looking around a mess table and knowing there are no illusions left. Because out here we pick our own targets. Because if that tribunal ever comes back for us, I'd rather be standing next to these broken bastards than alone in some airless cell, listening to someone else talk about discipline.

I keep telling myself this ship sounds different lately.

Engines are steady, readings are clean, but there is this thin, nervous buzz in the deckplates that sets my teeth on edge. Maybe it is just me. Mira joked at mess that I am starting to hear ghosts in the grav drives, but the way she said it was too light, like she was keeping it from landing. Renee laughed, tapped her fork against my tray, but even she kept one eye on the duty rota display behind my head, like it might suddenly rearrange itself and send us somewhere we were not supposed to be.

We are flying tighter and quieter than the last tour, and nobody is saying why in plain words. Jonas tried to float something about a routine patrol, but he is a terrible liar when he cares about something. His jaw locks. His eyes slide past you. He did both, right before he cut himself off and said he needed to check a sensor calibration that was already green. Amara caught my eye and rolled hers after he left. Later, in the passageway, she muttered that if command wants us blind, they could at least have the honesty to admit it.

Elias has been different too, and that is what keeps sticking in my head when I am trying to sleep. He used to sit with us in the common room, share bad TerraBrew and worse stories from basic, losing every card game to Mira on purpose just to make her grin. Now he takes his coffee to go, spends most off-shift time in some quiet corner of the ship, "reviewing op orders." I found him on the upper catwalk above the hangar once, just leaning on the railing, staring at nothing. When I called up, he smiled, but it did not reach his eyes. Later I noticed his locker was a little too neat, like someone expecting to travel light.

The rumor mill has become its own kind of background radiation. Whispered fragments about "civilian lanes" and "nothing official" circulate in the air recirculation like dust. Nobody mentions names, but everyone has heard the story of the consultant who could bend routes like wire and the missions that did not make it to the after-action reports. Supposedly we are riding some leftover shadow of that, cleaning up something half-finished. I do not know if I believe it, but the way the nav plots update without the usual chatter from command makes my skin prickle.

I caught myself watching Elias again at dinner tonight, which is probably its own kind of problem. There was a time I would have admitted to myself that I liked the way he looks when he is not trying to look like anything, when his guard slips and the tired real him shows in the lines around his mouth. Now I just feel stupid for noticing. Renee nudged me under the table, followed my line of sight, and raised an eyebrow in that way she has that says, "So, are you going to do something about that or just keep pining over your rations?" I kicked her back and changed the subject, but she is not wrong.

It is funny, all the little rituals we still go through, like they are enough to hold the hull together. The card games, the shared coffee, the weekly check-in where we pretend we are still on some clean, named deployment and not half-erased on someone's terminal back in New Atlantis. We all stand for the same old speech about duty and citizens and how the lanes are safer because we are out here, even though half of us are thinking about the near-miss reports that never made it past our own console. I do not know if those words still fit what we are actually doing, or if we stand and nod because nobody wants to be the first one to sit down.

Amara said, offhand in the corridor, that the only real tradition that matters is watching each other's backs when the quiet gets too loud. I wanted to believe that. I still want to. But when I see Elias walking the ship alone, when I hear Jonas choke off mid-sentence, when I catch Mira triple-checking escape routes she will never admit she mapped, I start to wonder if we are all just going through motions we inherited from people who trusted the system a lot more than we do.

If I am wrong, I will feel stupid for writing any of this. If I am right, it is already too late for stupid.

I have been sleeping too close to old hulls again. You can taste the rust in the air here, tangling with the coolant stink. Funny thing is, these graveyards always felt like failures to me once: air I did not get to soon enough, hands I did not pull through the lock in time. Now I look at a stripped freighter and see clean numbers. Tonnage. Salvageable cores. Probability curves that landed exactly where someone decided they should.

The first time I understood the world did not care was back on that corridor between Alpha Centauri and Toliman. All those civilian ships drifting nose-to-nose, plenty of time to do something, and command holding us on a leash so the right people could argue about who would pay. I was still young enough then to think duty and urgency could outweigh signatures on a form. Listening to the silence in my headset while the collision warnings climbed was the day I realized nobody up there was ever going to choose lives over ledgers. Something cracked, and it never quite set right again.

There was a LIST convoy not long ago, small families, cheap freight. I bent their route just enough, introduced a fault I could fix on arrival. When I dropped in, one of the settlers had been hit by shrapnel from their own overworked drive, leg torn up, breathing like a punctured bellows. I could have ended the pain fast. Instead I stabilized him just enough, kept him on that edge while I walked the others through securing the cargo I wanted. I watched his eyes, the moment he understood what I was, and I felt nothing but a quiet, clinical interest in how long he would hold on. I do not tell myself stories about mercy anymore. I do not pretend it eats at me.

It did not happen overnight. At first, every line I crossed came with a speech about necessity. A few seconds shaved off a beacon relay here, a course correction there, always with the plausible excuse of "testing response times" or "compensating for interference." Then the first time I withheld a relay altogether, letting an independent hauler drift blind so I could beat the official teams there, I expected to wake up shaking. Instead I woke up checking my math, making sure the window between failure and my arrival stayed within acceptable limits. Each step after that was easier. Rescue. Sabotage. Rescue again. It is just calculus if you squint.

I remember when rerouting a convoy under false protocols would have horrified me. Now I sit with a TerraBrew cooling at my elbow, watching nav plots tilt under my fingers, and the only thought I have is whether the angles will keep the wreckage inside a corridor I can reach before anyone else smells blood. I used to think about the faces on those ships. Now I think about the manifests, the insurers, the specific underwriters who signed off on "acceptable risk." The ones who never had to scrub blood out of vacuum seals.

People like to imagine I made a choice somewhere, that I woke up and decided to become the villain in their little campfire tales. The truth is, the choice was made the day they taught me that delays and optics mattered more than breathing bodies. You feed someone a system where catastrophe is just another asset class, and you act surprised when they treat it like a market to be optimized. Gravity pulls where it pulls. Trajectories follow from the forces applied. I am just riding the lines they drew long before I ever sat in a cockpit.

So I came out here, to places nobody audits unless something explodes on the right channel. The scrapyards, the forgotten tenders still limping along in dead orbits, the corners of Neon and Gagarin where official eyes look away if the traffic stays profitable. From here I can watch the whole pattern: the memorial buoy that lies, the underwriters whose portfolios swell after every "tragedy," the way certain transponders always seem to be just out of position when it counts. They will send someone eventually. They always do, once a ghost starts costing them more than he saves. By then, I will have my logs in order. When I flip the switch and pour everything I have recorded into their channels, I want it to be undeniable who really bent the first beacon.

Talia says I have started checking exits the second we walk into a room again. She is not wrong. Old habits are the only thing between Mutineer Division and a bad headline, most days. We still stack on doors like we used to, clear corners, call our sectors. The difference now is that when it is over, there is no debrief, no commendation, just a split of whatever haul we took off some black ledger. Funny how the muscle memory stayed when the flag did not.

I keep thinking about that forward outpost on the rim, the one command insisted on calling a "stabilization mission." We all saw the footage before the feed got scrubbed: evac birds turning away, civvies still on the pad, some logistics officer on the line saying bandwidth was saturated and we were to secure "critical infrastructure" instead. We held perimeter while the sky burned and then got handed medals and told to stand tall. That was the first time I realized I liked the quiet thrill of signing off a falsified after-action, of tucking one inconvenient line into the margins and watching it slide right through.

Kincaid, the good soldier. I wore that like armor for years. Even when we were taping field dressings together out of ration wrappers and cut-up undershirts, stuffing coagulant into wounds because the official med crates never quite made it past the "priority units," I found a way to make it make sense. Patch them up with whatever is on hand, get them back in the line, salute the man who underfunded the mission. That was the job. The worst part is how much of me still misses the simplicity of that.

Talia did not walk away lightly. She was the one who kept the rest of us in line, the one who would still bark about proper sight pictures when half the squad was running on stim shakes and four hours' sleep a week. When she finally handed in her badge and left it on the table without a word, it shook me harder than any orbital strike. If she could not square the orders anymore, what did that say about the rest of us still pretending we could?

Then came the "containment action" that never happened, at least not on paper. We were told to secure a facility, no questions, and when it was done, the ground smelled like metal and burned soil for miles. Afterwards, I remember sitting on a crate with my hands still shaking and listening to the command channel cut in and out, words like "acceptable attrition" and "strategic ambiguity" floating through the static. Part of me knew we had crossed a line; another part could not look away from the fact that every op like that pulled us tighter together, a family forged out of things no one else wanted to admit existed.

That is the rotten core of it. I have always wanted to belong somewhere, no matter the cost. First it was the unit, the ritual of inspections and shared jokes in the barracks, the feeling that if we were monsters, at least we were the same kind of monster in the same uniform. Now it is Mutineer Division, patched-together armor and off-grid safehouses, but the itch is the same. Elias Kincaid, still chasing a banner, just with the insignia scratched off.

There was someone once, back when I still believed those deployments were for something greater. We met between rotations, snatching days out of borrowed time. She said I smelled like propellant and antiseptic; I said she smelled like the only place I did not have to look over my shoulder. We burned hot and fast, fought like we were clearing rooms, loved like we were laying charges. It took me too long to realize my presence in her life was breaking more than it was holding together, that every time I left, I tracked a little more of the war back through her door. Our love felt like ordnance: intoxicating to ignite, catastrophic on impact. I knew it, and I still could not stand down.

Elias Kincaid, honorable deserter. That is the joke Talia makes when the bottle is low and the lights are off. Whatever we are now, it is built on bones and redacted lines. I do not know if we are making anything better. I just know that walking away from lies I helped write felt like the first honest act I have taken in years, and that honesty terrifies me more than any firefight ever did.

I finally got the smell out of my jumpsuit. Mostly.  

Sat in the tiny wash alcove for half an hour, scrubbing at that rust-colored streak along the cuff where I slipped in Cargo Two last shift. It is not rust, and we all know it, but no one is calling it anything else. The detergent here always smells faintly metallic, like GalBank thought of "neutral" as a balance sheet instead of a scent. I stitched the torn seam along the hip while the spin cycle rattled the bulkheads, and every time I pushed the needle through, I kept thinking of how that fabric tore when I slammed into the deck as the ship shuddered out of its lane.  

Marcus Havel passed by while I was hunched over the sink. He hesitated in the doorway like he wanted to say something, then settled for a half-nod and a joke about "hazard pay for laundry duty." He has been trying to smooth everything over since the course logs went missing, pretending that if he keeps smiling, we will all forget our last jump was nowhere near what the manifest claimed. I used to trust him with anything that involved numbers. Now I watch where his eyes go when someone mentions route corrections.  

Elias Mercer, on the other hand, has stopped pretending. Today he snapped in the mess, slammed his tray down so hard that freeze-dried lentils flew everywhere. He all but accused Jared Holcomb of playing favorites with the reporting. Said Jared has been feeding New Atlantis what they want to see, not what the nav arrays actually show. Naomi Kwan tried to calm him down, but she got the worst of it when he turned on her, asking whose side she thought she was on. The silence afterward was colder than the hull. No one moved until Elias stormed out, muttering about "ghost corridors" and "sacrificial cargo."  

Since then, the ship has been split in ways that do not show on any roster. Marcus and Jared orbit each other, trading low-voiced updates and shutting down any questions with "GalBank will sort it." Naomi floats between groups, still trying to mediate, pretending she does not see the way conversations die when she walks in. I find myself drifting toward the quiet corners, listening, never quite belonging. There is a sort of soft power struggle now, where access codes and who gets to review which log matters more than anything written in the org chart. You can feel it in the way Jared casually locks down a console after someone else has used it, or how Marcus "forgets" to share the raw nav data, insisting the filtered output is "cleaner."  

I thought I could fix things with Naomi after the last argument, when I accused her of overlooking a discrepancy in the freight records. We talked, or maybe circled each other with words, but nothing settled. Tonight, folding my still-damp jumpsuit, I realized there are fractures that will not close, not out here, not on this ship. It hurts to admit that a friendship I counted on has drifted beyond retrieval. Strangely, there is a kind of relief in naming it. Loss acknowledged is easier to carry than doubt gnawing at you in the air ducts.  

Rumors keep leaking through the crew like condensation. Someone swears we were on a corridor not listed in any official registry, that the beacons we followed were running a pattern that does not match standard charts. Another swears they saw a contractor's ID buried in the diagnostic metadata, a name that has been floating around fleet whispers for all the wrong reasons. I do not know what to believe, only that our last jump left us too far from our assigned trade lane, and nobody filed a deviation. That is not an accident. That is a choice.  

I keep telling myself that time will dull this, that one day the tremor in my hands when the Grav Drive spins up will fade. Maybe it will. But healing is not forgetting. The stain on my cuff is mostly washed out now, yet I still see it, still remember the metallic taste in the air and the way the ship groaned like it wanted to shake us off. Some wounds stay sore even as the skin knits. Maybe the best I can hope for is to move forward with eyes open, knowing some things on this ship will never be set right, and deciding to live with that instead of pretending we are still on a clean, approved route.

Some nights the ship feels too quiet for the amount of credits she's supposed to be worth. Silverwake hums along, drive steady, lights at half to keep the systems boys happy, but the corridors feel hollow. Maybe it is just me. Ever since that mess hauling emergency stock out toward Freestar space, I have not slept right. I keep thinking about how fast air can go bad, how fast everything you think is guaranteed thins out around you. It puts a film over the world. Food tastes flat. Jokes land soft. Even the stars look a little further away.

I have learned to live with it, I guess. Suffering sands things down in places you do not see at first. I do not spark off as fast when Darion Cole starts in about route bonuses, and I do not bother arguing with Harlan Mendez when he insists the Trade Authority would never send us anywhere they would not go themselves. The marks are there all the same. I feel them when the bulkheads groan or when the ventilation coughs for half a second too long; my whole body tightens like it is waiting on a verdict. Still, I am here, still working the cargo checks, still putting one boot in front of the other.

Journaling like this turned into a habit when I was stuck on a rock with no decent comms, and it never quite left. Five minutes at the end of a shift, a couple of lines while the coffee goes from hot to lukewarm; it is the one place I can unspool everything without someone telling me to toughen up or keep it light. Sometimes I just count breaths between the ship's little shudders, matching my lungs to the Silverwake's rhythm until my shoulders drop. Watching the stars helps too, when I can steal a moment by an external port. They do not care if you are late on quotas or if someone is gaming the manifests again.

Day to day, things almost look normal. Maris Keller gives me that little nod when we pass in the main corridor, the kind that says, "I see you, but let us not make a scene." She sits with Rhea Solanki most meals, talking in low voices over reheated rations and pretending not to notice the way Jonas Verrick keeps one ear open from the next table. Harlan is louder, always has been; he slaps people on the back in the mess and talks about side deals a little too openly. Darion pretends not to listen, but his eyes track every crate that comes through the bay.

There is this unspoken scramble for favor whenever word filters down that a big client is involved. Trade Authority work is supposed to be clean, "apolitical," as the suits like to say, but out here it plays more like soft politics. Maris always seems to know which numbers to highlight when she briefs the bridge, and somehow she gets more face-time on priority calls than the rest of us. Darion tries to buddy up to her, laughs too loud at her dry jokes. Harlan nudges me afterwards and mutters that some of us still have to earn our keep the hard way.

We have built these tiny rituals to make the ship feel less like a floating ledger. Every third evening, if the schedule allows, a bunch of us drift into the mess just after lights dim. Jonas brings out whatever passable drink he has scavenged from port, Rhea scrolls through a library of old starmaps and picks a random system, and we go around the table trading one small story about the worst job we ever took. No heroics, just little disasters and narrow escapes. Maris never says much; she usually offers a short, careful anecdote, something where all the names are blurred. But she smiles more on those nights, and for an hour or two, we sound like a crew that might actually trust each other.

Even so, there is this murmur under everything now, like static behind a clean signal. I catch it in half-finished sentences when people think they are out of earshot. A mention of atmospherics gone strange on some farm moon. A joke that dies too quickly when someone notices me in the doorway. Stories about an engineer who can change the fate of a world and the way those stories get softer every time they are retold in back corners and cargo alcoves, as if the truth is too sharp to handle straight. I do not know what to believe yet, only that the pattern of our routes and the way people avoid certain topics share the same uneasy shape.

Jemison orbital night, shift-cycle unknown

Hands are still shaking, so I might as well use them for something other than dropping tools.

We cracked that old hauler outside Cheyenne today, one of those bulk tin cans with a registry so faded Jace had to scrape frost off the nameplate just to log it. No beacon, no heat, just a slow roll and a lot of quiet. Ronan swore it was a dead simple cut-and-strip, "milk run" in his words. Funny how often those are the ones that stick in your head.

Airlock fought us on the manual crank, but Darius got it breathing with that hydraulic crowbar he babies more than his suit. I took point inside. Standard drill: lights on low, atmosphere tester humming in my ear, tether giving that little tug every time I forgot how far I had floated. Jace behind me, grumbling about the cable snagging on every bolt. He always talks when he is nervous.

The cargo bay was wrong. Too neat. Netting still clipped, containers lined up in perfect rows, like someone had set them for inspection and just walked away. I have seen my share of derelicts, and time always leaves a mark. This one felt like it had been paused mid-breath.

We found the first suit in the crew commons. Helmet sealed, visor frosted from the inside. No breach, no burn marks, no blood. Just a person-shaped question, kneeling by a console that had been wiped clean. Darius wanted to check the data core, see if anything was left. Ronan called over comms, told us to stay off any black boxes. "We are here for hardware, not stories." That is Cinderfield in a sentence.

Later, back on our own deck, he caught me alone by the lockers. Clapped a hand on my shoulder, told me I had done "good work" not logging the frozen suits in the first sweep. Said it made life easier for everyone when people remembered what we are and what we are not. His smile never reached his eyes, but the praise did what it was supposed to do. I shut my mouth, scrubbed the bodies from my recollection of the run, and everyone got paid on time. That was that.

Tonight it is not that simple.

Word in the bay is there have been more ships like that one turning up near the routes no one admits are still in use. Same shallow burns on the hull, same gutted drives, same clean holds. Someone mentioned a pattern in the way they spin, like an invisible hand nudging them along. Mira said you can trace those wrecks on a map and get a neat little spiral pointing out into nowhere. She laughed when she said it, but Mira laughs when she is scared. Jace told her to shut up and pass the torque driver.

Couple cycles back, after we dragged in that "lucky" freighter with the untouched medical lockers, Ronan slipped me a pair of antique grav boots. Real leather, brass buckles, the kind of thing you see in museum vids. I asked him where he found them, and he just raised a brow. "Call it a bonus, Selene. You earned it." They did not have store tags, did not have serials that matched anything we had on the claim list, and they definitely did not belong to anyone who had walked off that ship under their own power.

I put them on anyway. Fit like they were made for me. Did not ask questions.

That is the thing about this life; the line between "find" and "theft" is just whatever everyone agrees not to see. We cut open silent hulls, strip out their guts, and pretend we are just cleaning the graveyard. We argue over who tags which panel, who gets first pick at reactor scrap, who is owed a cut for popping a stuck hatch. Under all of that noise sits the quiet fear: that one day we will open a door and find something staring back, or slip a saw into a bulkhead and set off whatever killed the crew.

Sometimes, floating through a corridor with only my lamp and my breathing for company, I think about the crews that never called for help. The ones whose manifests show up in the hands of nervous brokers on remote relays, pieces of their lives traded like ordinary contraband. I tell myself those stories are just hangar gossip, meant to keep rookies edgy and careful.

But then I remember frost on a visor, a ship that looked too fresh to be dead, and the way Ronan's hand felt heavy on my shoulder when he told me I did the right thing by keeping quiet.

I keep telling myself the suit smell will air out someday, but it never does. Old coolant, recycled sweat, a little scorched insulation from that time a cutter arced against a bulkhead. Smells like work, Jonas says. Smells like failure, if you ask me, but no one does.

We cracked a commuter hulk today, one of those mid-tier liners that never made it back to its hub. Dead in a Lagrange pocket, tumbling just slow enough you can pretend it is sleeping. Mara took point, as always, barking over comms about tether discipline and hull charges like she is the captain of a destroyer instead of foreman of five half-broke scrappers. Sienna rode her line right behind, checking the mag-clamps, never saying much, just tapping out confirmations. Delia stayed back on the tender, watching the boards, sounding calm while she counts every tick that means we are probably underinsured.

Funny how the hierarchy here feels solid even when the metal under our boots is crumbling. Mara barks; Sienna enforces, that quiet shove of her shoulder when someone drifts a little wide or ignores a safety call. Jonas plays the wise old spacer when it suits him, mostly to get out of the dirty jobs. Me, I am the one they kick down the narrow decks when they are pretty sure the ship is empty but not willing to bet their own lungs on it. Delia ignores half the orders that come over the line if they do not fit her numbers; she will cut power to a section even if Mara is still swearing about needing it. Somehow it works. Most days.

We found a crew locker on that hulk, still sealed. No bodies inside, just frozen air and personal junk. Sienna floated a little closer than she needed to, eyes on a dented metal flask that bobbed out. Red Harvest something, label half-peeled. I saw the way she palmed it, slipped it into her thigh pouch without a word. Later, as we cycled through the airlock back on the tug, she bumped my arm and passed it over, no eye contact. "For after shift," she said. I did not ask where she found it, or who it had belonged to, or why there were still scratch marks on the inside of that locker hatch. We just passed it around bunkside, pretending it tasted like victory instead of theft.

I remember when we used to talk about getting out. Back when I first signed on, Jonas would go on about buying a little hauler with our shares, running clean cargo between quiet moons, staying out of the lanes the big boys fight over. Mara pretended to humor him, said she would own a yard someday, have crews working for her while she sat inside somewhere warm and dry, counting credits. I said I would go dirtside, maybe New Atlantis if I could stand the gravity, fix local skiffs, drink TerraBrew that did not taste like someone rinsed a filter through the coolant line. We all knew it was talk. Nobody climbs out of dead orbit; you just drift a little longer.

The stories make it harder to sleep lately. Jonas swears he tore open a bulkhead once and found another crew's cutting lines still sunk into the ribs, torches floating where they should not be, no bodies, no suits, just tools. Mara says there are ships that keep showing up on scopes, same ID, never broadcasting distress, just there on the edge of a scan cone until you look straight at them and they are gone. Hangar gossip says some analyst out in the core is selling forecast maps of which routes are "safe to disappear on" and that is why we have been seeing more fresh wrecks with cargo intact and logs scrubbed clean. I tell myself that is just rumor made fat on boredom, but then we board another ship where everything looks staged and the fear crawls up under my helmet seal.

Out there in the dark, cutting through old logos and burned paint, you get time to think. I count welds, count pulses on the suit readout, count the seconds between Mara's check-ins, anything to drown out the hiss of the recycler and the echo of those old conversations about futures we never believed in. Every panel we pry up, every locker we crack, every unlogged trinket slipped into a pouch feels like another little choice nudging a big equation. Small decisions, Mara calls them when she signs off on a haul sheet that does not quite match what we pulled. Small enough that no one will notice, until they do.

Day 191 in the log, though it all feels like the same long shift with different hull numbers.

We burned out to the graveyard shelf over Toliman today, chasing a ping on an old passenger liner that never filed a distress. Sera rode shotgun on the tug while I checked suit seals and Dane pretended not to be hung over. Rylan kept fussing over the cutting torches like a nervous parent. Same ritual as always: argue on the approach, go quiet once the airlock's in sight.

The liner was wrong from the moment we mag-clamped. No scorch marks, no visible breach, transponder broadcasting a decade-old registry that should have been archived with the rest of the dead. Inside, the gravity was out of tune, half-strength and jittery, like the ship could not decide if it was really empty. We floated past drink packs and meal trays still strapped in, no bodies, no messages. Just a bridge console looping a route plan to nowhere.

Mara took point, like she always does when things smell off. Sera kept muttering on the line about how the manifest tags looked too clean, how the cargo list was scrubbed of anything worth hauling. Dane wanted to start cutting bulkheads anyway, mumbling about "hidden compartments" and "lucky nights." Typical. Rylan stayed on the threshold, watching our tethers, not the shadows. I watched both.

On the way back, with the hold half full of stripped panels and nothing that justified the risk, I had that old thought again: I walked out of the gang to be "free," and all it bought me was danger with paperwork. Back then there was a hierarchy, ugly as it was. Cass barked the orders, Jak enforced them with a shock baton and that dead-eyed stare, and I pretended not to hear the screams when someone asked the wrong question about a miscounted crate. Freedom meant no one could order me into a breach without a suit, but it also meant no one noticed if I got left spinning with a severed tether. Out here, the vacuum does not need a boss to be cruel.

Red Beacon is better, mostly. We argue instead of obey. Mara calls the shots because she has the best instincts, not because she owns the guns. Sera cross-checks every ID tag like a religion, making sure we do not walk onto something still under active claim. Dane is loud, full of half-bad jokes and full-bad decisions, but he has held my line more than once. Rylan is the quiet spine of the rig, the one who never cuts a corner on air mix or clamp checks. No one "enforces" anything, but if you keep putting the crew at risk, you just do not get invited on the next burn. That is our version of exile.

Still, the stories follow us. Dockside, people whisper about crews who latched onto the wrong derelict, the one with registry entries that keep changing every time someone looks. About a freighter that was repossessed on paper five times in three months, then found drifting with the transponder screaming two conflicting names at once. About a LIST outpost that called for tow and instead got boarded by two different "legal owners" who never came back out. Everyone swears they know someone who saw the ship logs before they were erased, but no one ever has the slates to prove it.

I tell myself I do not believe in ghost ships, just ghost numbers. Easier that way. You can cut through steel; you cannot cut through a contract written to make you vanish. But the way that liner looked today, like someone walked through and tidied up everything but the people, reminded me of those rumors about an auditor who can make a ship disappear without ever firing a shot. Sera swears she saw that same audit code on one of the shadow manifests the TA broker tried to sell us last month, before Mara shut the deal down and walked us out.

Tonight, the dock is quiet. The others have drifted off: Rylan checking valves, Dane chasing bad liquor, Mara locked in the office arguing with some distant station over salvage percentages. I am sitting on the edge of the tug bay, boots hooked under a ladder rung, watching the constellations smear slowly past the viewport. It hits me again that leaving the gang did not put me beyond reach of people who kill with ledgers instead of knives. It just traded the certainty of a short, loud ending for the slow uncertainty of working the graveyards, where a single wrong hull number or a forgotten suit check can flip the timer to zero without you even noticing.

I used to start these with the shift change time, like some kind of log, but I am late and I do not care. Maybe that is the first thing I have really let slide since we left Neon run six months ago. Every day bleeds into the next on this ship. Same rations, same hum of the drives, same smell of recycled TerraBrew in the galley that never quite goes away.

Breakfast was quiet today. Rhea sat opposite me, picking the raisins out of her cereal like she always does, piling them in a sad little mountain on the edge of the tray. We did the usual small talk: grav turbulence last jump, another delay on port clearance, some spacer pirate story Caleb swears is true. I laughed in the right places, but I kept watching the door, waiting to see who else would come in. Jared nodded at us on his way to engineering, already halfway to sleep on his feet. Maris just grabbed a drink and went back out without a word. She does that more and more lately.

Caleb cornered me in the cargo bay later, said there is another discrepancy in the manifests. "Nothing big," he said, which means just big enough to bother someone like me. Same origin, same destination, same dates, but different route code embedded deep in the file. It is like the paperwork knows we are making a detour no one wants to say out loud. He grinned like it was a game, told me if I kept my head down I would not have to answer questions if customs ever actually checked. I smiled back, but my stomach clenched so hard I thought I might be sick.

Rhea told me in passing that she heard the captain on a private call, arguing with someone who sounded very calm. Too calm. Words like "corridor adjustments" and "salvage rights" floated through the bulkhead, she said. I joked that she should stop listening at doors, but part of me was grateful she did. Trade Authority routes are not supposed to change on a whim, not for a ship like ours. We are the boring ones, the ones that do not get stories told about them. Lately, it feels like someone else has their hands on our course lines.

There is a rumor going around that we are running close to some graveyard of scrap and dead transponders, the kind of place tug pilots whisper about in dockside bars. Caleb says it is nonsense, just spacer tales, but his voice went thin when he said it. Maris will not talk about it at all; when I mentioned the pattern in our last three jumps, she just stared at her drink until I changed the subject. Everyone pretends they do not see the same tags reappearing in the nav buffer, the same odd little shifts that never make it into the official log.

I keep thinking about whether I deserve whatever is coming. I took this assignment because it was supposed to be safe. Steady credits, no guns, no blood on the cargo. I told myself I had earned something quiet after the last station contract fell apart, after watching everyone else scramble for work while I landed on my feet. Sometimes, when I pass the sealed containers with their mismatched labels, I wonder if I am just telling myself a nicer story than the one someone else is writing for us.

Today I broke my own rule. I have never snooped in the nav cache. Ever. Not even when I was sure someone was padding the mileage to skim fuel allowances. I always said if I did not look, I could honestly say I did not know. But after shift, when the corridor cams cycled and the bridge was empty, I slipped into the chair and pulled up a nonessential archive. Just enough to see that our last path had been overwritten three times, that there was a ghost vector sitting under the one we officially filed. I backed out so fast my hands shook, and I have not stopped feeling like I am standing on the wrong side of a thin line since.

Maybe I am making too much of it. Maybe it is just routing politics I am not paid to understand. That is what I tell myself as I share another quiet meal, as I nod to Jared when he brushes past me in the corridor talking about a "minor power draw anomaly" he is already fixing. But the way people avoid eye contact when the subject of our next stop comes up, the way conversations bend away from certain words, it all feels like the truth has been passed from mouth to mouth so many times it has lost its sharp edges. What is left is something soft, almost harmless, that everyone can swallow without choking.

And I am the one who finally looked behind it.

I always forget how loud a "quiet" ship can be. The YP-4360 has this constant undercurrent of reactor hum and coolant cycling through her bones, but it is the little sounds that get under my skin lately the relays ticking as they cool, the occasional stutter in the grav compensators when we cut too close to something the charts pretend is empty. Feels like the ship is grinding her teeth in her sleep. Ethan Kwan says I am getting jumpy, that after a few more long-haul patrols the noise fades into the background, but Ethan could probably sleep inside a Magstorm breech test and call it meditation.

We ran another simulation burn this morning, long chain of microjumps threaded tighter than I am used to seeing outside a war game. Havel plotted them, of course. Marcus sits in the nav pit like it is a chessboard only he understands and everyone else is just pushing pawns. I trust his math more than I trust my own balance lately, but there was a moment during the third jump where the vector overlay looked wrong to me, like it wanted to curl in on itself. When I mentioned it on the mess deck later, he just gave me that thin little almost-smile and said, "If it felt off and we are still here, it means the model works." I do not like being the test case that proves the point.

Amelia Cho has been spending more time down near the black box array, pretending she is just running diagnostics. She forgets I handle half the maintenance tags down there. She is pulling grav-response logs, marking segments where the drives complained, recording voice, too. We all say it is just best practice, ever since those convoy losses near Toliman, but the way she flinched when I came around the corner told me she is working off more than procedure. People have started lowering their voices when they talk about "shortcuts." Shortcuts usually mean some idiot spacer trying to shave a day off a haul. Lately, though, it sounds like they mean something else. Tighter, sharper, like the word has an edge.

There is a rumor making the rounds in the hangar that someone back in MAST is feeding new corridors directly to select units, and we are suddenly one of those units. No briefing, no commendation, just different numbers on the nav board and a quiet expectation we will not ask questions as long as the hull holds. Havel shrugs and says someone has to fly the hard lanes before they get certified. Ethan thinks if we do well enough, they will accelerate his citizenship application. Amelia does not say anything, but I notice she has started recording more crew chatter than before. I keep wondering who volunteered us, and what exactly we signed up for that was not spelled out in the oath.

Today I caught a fragment of conversation between two techs from engineering, something about an older test range and "data they said was lost." They shut up as soon as I stepped into the lift. That is become the new normal, people stopping mid-sentence if the subject drifts too close to how our vectors have been changing, or why our patrols keep grazing the edge of zones we used to give a much wider berth. Feels less like we are guarding the line and more like we are drawing it over again with our own lives as the pencil.

I keep thinking about the old Vanguard tradition whenever we cleared a rough run. First time I shipped out, every successful deployment ended with the crew gathering around the main table, passing a single bottle and retelling the ugliest moments of the flight until they turned into jokes. The idea was simple you look the fear in the face together, and you own it so it cannot own you. Lately that has gone away. Now, after we dock or power down from another tight set of jumps, everyone drifts off to their quarters, or clusters in twos and threes in the corners of the mess, voices low. Ethan tried to revive the old ritual last month brought a bottle, even got Havel to sit, but the stories never came, just long silences and the sound of cutlery on trays. I wanted to raise my cup and make it like it was on my first cruise, but forcing the laugh felt worse than saying nothing. So I sat there, holding on to the old shape of the thing, while the new version slipped past me a room full of people choosing quiet over honesty. I do not know yet if that means the tradition is dead, or if this is just what it looks like when it grows into something I do not recognize.

Not going to sleep until my hands stop shaking, so I might as well write.

Today was supposed to be easy metal. Old freighter, broken spine, no heat, no pressure. The kind of job Marek calls "lunch money with extra bolts." Everything looked clean from the tow line. No scorch, no obvious breach, just a ship that folded wrong on a bad jump and never called for help.

First pass was standard. Sienna on the winch, Marek and me on the cut, Naledi riding comms and sensor board because she still does not like vacuum. We clamped, burned the lock, and stepped into that corridor, and it was the quiet that got me. Not the usual thick silence, either. This was thin, like the air had never been there at all. No floating debris, no loose bits, nothing. Just the sound of my own breath punching my ears and Marek humming that stupid tune through his helmet.

We worked three decks before we found signs anyone had lived there. Two cups velcroed to a mess table. A jacket still clipped by the hatch. No bodies. No log beacons, even the emergency ones. Sienna said they probably got picked up, but none of us said "by who." Too many stories lately about crews stepping through a jump and never stepping out, and then months later their hulls drift in where they are not supposed to be, stripped of everything except the parts that talk.

We hit the bridge last. Naledi said we were good on air, but her voice had that tight edge it gets when the scanners are telling her more than she wants to pass along. Someone had already pulled the main nav core. Clean job, not drift cutter work. Data spines cut with the right tools, no mistakes, no hurry. Whoever did it got paid well, and did not feel like sharing coordinates. There was this smell in the insulation too, even through the suit. Not rot, not coolant. Just wrong. Made me think of that wreck we cut over by Gagarin last cycle, the one whose jump logs had holes big enough to fly a hauler through, like whole hours had decided not to exist.

On the way back to the rig, Marek started up again about the "grav ghosts," those voices some of the long-haul crews swear they hear bleeding into comms after a bad chain of jumps. I told him to shut it and watch his tether. He laughed, but I saw his boots drift a little wider than usual when we crossed the gap. We all know somebody who did not come back from an "easy" grab. You do this long enough and you stop believing in cursed ships and start believing in stupid, tired humans missing one latch.

Back aboard, Sienna and I were stripping our suits in the locker when the lights flickered. Just once, barely. She reached over and bumped her helmet against mine, a little knock like we used to do before long EVAs. For a second it felt like the old days when this was just a job and not a question mark hanging over every hull we touch. She smiled, eyes soft, and I thought about saying something dumb like "When we get a quiet run, let's burn some leave somewhere with real sky." Instead, I just squeezed her glove, and the power hum stuttered again, and the moment folded up between us. All I could think was, what if that is the last time we get to pretend we are not living in a graveyard.

Naledi swears she picked up a spike in background noise off the freighter's skin, right at the point its jump trail went sideways. Says it looked like interference from something that is not on any chart we use. Marek told her to stop reading backlogged incident reports in her off-shift, that she is starting to sound like the long-haulers who drink alone and talk to the bulkheads. No one said "maybe they are not wrong." We just signed the cargo manifest, logged only what we are required to log, and left the rest in that dead corridor.

Drift Cutters rule number one: report enough to get paid, never enough to invite questions that come with uniforms and sealed files.

Now the rig is quiet except for the occasional thump of cooling metal. Sienna is asleep two bunks over, one arm hanging out of the blanket, fingers curled like she is still gripping a tether. I want to reach across the aisle and catch her hand, just to feel something warm and real that is not welded steel or recycled air, but I do not. Part of me is afraid I will wake her. The other part is afraid that if I close my eyes after, I will open them to nothing but stars and a soft vibration in the hull that sounds too much like breathing.

I can hear the reactor hum through the bulkhead again tonight. Caleb says the Dustlance sings when she is happy, but to me it is more like teeth grinding in the dark. The air scrubbers are running hot, so the whole corridor smells faintly of metal and old boots, with that tang of recycled sweat no filter ever really gets out. Rhea propped the hatch to the galley open to "circulate" earlier, which mostly just gave the ship a nice undertone of burnt UC BattleMeal and whatever was left in Jonas's coffee mug from three shifts ago.

We ran another sweep on freight routes out by Toliman, nothing special on the docket, just the usual pinging of transponders and grumbling when paperwork does not match the cargo. Mara caught a manifest with a missing page and spent an hour muttering over it, tapping her stylus against her teeth the way she does when she smells a lie. Caleb joked it was just some farmer shaving a crate of Red Harvest Wheat off his taxes, but Mara's eyes did this narrow thing when she handed it to Lena, like she was testing her reaction. Lena just shrugged and said she would log it for follow-up, all easy smile and tired eyes.

The thing is, Lena has been off lately. Not in the obvious ways. She is still at her post on time, still running drills, still beating Jonas at cards in the mess like it is nothing. But she stopped joining us for the stupid late-night movie rotations, even when Rhea queued up that old cowboy serial she likes. Says she is tired, paperwork, headaches. She does not laugh properly anymore, either. It is like she pushes the sound out without letting it touch anything inside her.

Tonight at chow, while we were pretending the stew was not reconstituted from a bag, I caught Caleb watching Lena over his spoon. Really watching. When he noticed me noticing, he just shrugged and said, "People change, Tess," like that explained why she flinched when the comms crackled with an incoming encrypted burst. Mara said it was just GalBank being GalBank, another audit request nobody asked for, but she would not let me see the header, just told me to mind my own rations.

I keep thinking about that mining family we met on patrol last month, the ones who had their whole claim tied up over a loan they swear they never agreed to. The way their eldest kept asking if we could "fix the numbers" and Jonas had to be the one to say we are not bankers, we only make sure transports do not explode and pirates keep their distance. I have not stopped seeing the mother's face when we pulled away, all those years of work hanging on a ledger line someone else wrote. Healing does not mean forgetting; that kind of thing sticks in your chest, an ache that does not care how many jumps pass.

Maybe that is why the whispers about some ghost in the accounts bother me more than I admit. I hear Jonas and Caleb trading rumors in the corridor when they think I am asleep, about some ex-auditor who rearranges debts like airlock schedules, about settlements that suddenly owe nothing or owe everything overnight. Rhea thinks it is spacer bar talk, something to scare rookies. Mara does not say what she thinks, just keeps checking the routing codes twice, then a third time.

I wish this job was only clean patrol lines and the comfort of a ship that always brings you home. Truth is, the Dustlance feels more like a crossroads lately. Every ping on the scanner, every encrypted packet, every quiet glance between officers has started to feel like a test I do not know the rules to. I came out here for something simple: to earn my badge proper, pay off my father's old freighter debt, maybe one day put down roots on a piece of rock that has my name on the deed. Instead I am floating in a tin can that smells like metal and reheated stew, listening to secrets echo down the vents.

Still, there are small mercies. The ritual of strapping into my bunk, the scratch of this old pen on paper while the ship creaks around me, the way the stars smear into white lines on the other side of the port when we spin up the drive. Those are the moments that almost feel like healing, like the old burns on my hands from the farm are just pale lines instead of memories of everything we lost. But even as they fade, they still ache when the ship runs cold, reminding me that trust is just another kind of credit, and every day out here, we are adding interest without knowing who is going to come to collect.

I keep telling myself this is just another overnighter in deep orbit, a glorified spreadsheet wrapped in hull plating, but the air feels thinner tonight. The Securehaul hums like always, that low vibration under the soles that says GalBank is still counting. Yet every time the lights dip to emergency levels for power balancing, my chest tightens like we are already halfway to drifting dark.

Elena was on shift when the last cycle flickered. She laughed it off, said the generator AI was "sulking again." She has that way of making even a systems warning sound like a joke you are supposed to share. I caught myself watching her hands on the console, the little half-circle of nail she chews when she thinks nobody is looking. I do not know when I started cataloging details like that. Maybe back when she helped me correct that misfiled portfolio and did not make a big deal of it, just bumped her shoulder against mine and moved on.

Sabine rolled her eyes at both of us after, called Elena "the ship's mascot" under her breath in the break alcove. Sabine pretends she is pure cynic, but she stays late to balance risk forecasts nobody will ever read. You do not do that if you do not care. Mina ducked the whole conversation, buried in reclamation stats, just murmuring about how our air scrubbers are older than any of us and no one at central wants to pay for replacements. Priya keeps trying to organize "game nights" to stop us from talking about failure rates and liability exposure. I keep promising I will go, then stay here instead, spilling into these pages where nobody talks back.

There has been more traffic on the encrypted lines than usual. Darius mentioned it first, said some of the agritech riders on our mirrored contracts are marked with review flags but no one ever opens them. "Too big to fail, too ugly to look at," was how he put it. Sabine snapped at him to stop reading metadata he was not authorized for, but I saw her lingering on the terminal long after she told us to clear the room. Later, in the mess, I overheard Elena asking Mina, very casual, how hard it would be to isolate one node during a power shuffle. "Hypothetically," she said, but there is a heaviness under her hypotheticals lately.

Rumors trickle in with the portfolio updates. Quiet notes about colonies with record yields and rising sickness reports. Insurance riders that pay out more when things go wrong than when they go right. Phil in Compliance sent an internal memo asking if any of us had "concerns about exposure" tied to certain accounts. By the time it reached my queue, the message had been retracted, replaced with a bland clarification notice. Only Sabine admitted seeing the original. She did not want to talk about it.

Sometimes I wonder if Elena sees me at all, beyond another pair of hands punching in corrections. She jokes with everyone, but there is something in the way she stands a little closer when we are alone on the monitoring deck, how she points out oddities in the risk models just to see if I will catch the pattern. I want to believe that means something. Then she glances away the moment I try to answer seriously, as if I have stepped over some line she drew in her head. I am stuck between hoping there is more there and fearing I am just one more coworker she knows how to disarm.

This journal has become my little ritual. End of shift, I float one hand on the bulkhead, feel the thrum of the engines, and breathe in time with the noise until my pulse quits racing. Then I write until the day starts to make some kind of crooked sense. Mina watches stars on the external feed to calm down. Priya drinks too much TerraBrew. Darius plays the same card sim on loop. We are all finding ways to pretend this ship is a normal posting, that we are not strolling through a vault built on other people's disasters.

Still, the patterns on our ledgers itch at the back of my skull. Crops that fail where projections say they should thrive, payouts that clear faster than emergency aid arrives, contracts routed through shell accounts that lead nowhere. Gagarin taught me that scorch marks on a terminal are never just a hardware issue, and even from out here, I can smell the same discreet smoke curling off these numbers. I keep thinking if I can untangle just one chain cleanly, it will prove the truth is simple under all the obfuscation, but every time I pull a thread it loops back into another knot.

Think I've re-stitched these same knee panels a hundred times by now.  
Thread in, thread out, same old scuffed black canvas, same rust-green trim. Mira jokes I could have ditched them for new leathers cycles ago, but it is not about needing better gear. It is the habit. You patch what still works. You keep what remembers the hits.

Vermin Gravepack colors do not match, not really. We say they do. Rotten green over dead black, gray smear of paint or ragged scrap tied at the arm, and that little glyph we scratch where it matters three jagged lines crossing like claw marks over a circle. Used to mean something simple to me back when I was just running lookouts meant nest, meant we watch the spaces nobody else sees. Now it feels more like a warning label. Like we mark things the world will not get back.

Kara came back from a run tonight with that symbol smeared in oil across her knuckles, laughing about how some spacer captain started shaking the second he saw it on the bulkhead. Says word is going around that if you spot our mark on a hatch, you leave it closed. Rhett liked that. He has been walking around like he owns the whole damn underdeck, talking big about how Gravepack is moving up, how we are going to ride the new routes bleeding through the frontier. Jonas just listened, chewing his synth-stick, eyes doing that thing where he keeps measuring people like they are exits.

He has been doing that more since the stories started. Someone on the docks saying the lanes are changing. Accidents that do not feel like accidents. A tug nudged three degrees off course and suddenly there is scrap to pick that nobody filed a claim on. Rhett says there is a ghost-chart out there, someone who can bend traffic for the right creds. Mira says that is spacer superstition, a way to blame math for carelessness. Jonas just muttered that if someone really can steer whole convoys, Gravepack is late to the game.

We lost Rian over this kind of talk. Funny how everyone pretends not to remember his name now. He was the one who asked the wrong question in front of the wrong people.  
Why are we following marks that are too clean?  
Why do the hits line up with whatever routes that quiet Ecliptic handler slid us, like we are testing someone else's pattern?  
He did not say it that neat, but that was the gist.

Next day he rode out with a crew on a simple grab.  
Next day he did not ride back.

No one asked why. That is how it goes. You patch your clothes, you patch the story, you pretend the seams always looked like this. Rhett said they must have hit resistance, shrugged, moved on to lining up the next score. Kara started working Rian's old corner without missing a beat. Mira stitched Rian's green scrap into her own sleeve, said she was not letting good fabric go to waste. And me I just watched the symbol on the wall and tried not to count how many times I had painted it over doors that never opened again.

Exit routes have been on my mind more than usual. Not just the usual crawlspaces or maintenance shafts we keep mapped in our heads, but the big exits. The grav jumps. Whispers that there is a map somewhere that does not match the official charts, that some ex-UC number-runner knows how to slide a ship between patrol sweeps and debris like threading a needle. Rhett is hot for that lead. Says if we ride with whoever is bending those vectors, we stop picking bones and start choosing victims.

Part of me likes the sound of that. No more scrabbling in the vents, no more taking the scraps after Trade Authority and Ecliptic have eaten their fill. If there really is someone out there rewriting the lanes, that would be the kind of monster worth standing next to. Or the kind that erases our mark with one bad calculation and does not ever bother to learn our names.

Impossible to tell which from down here.

For now I just keep sewing. Same black knees, same green thread. I can still picture Rian hunched over his boots doing the same thing, muttering about how a good patch outlives its owner if you are not careful. That is the part that sticks with me the most not the way he vanished, but how fast the gap closed over him. Gang life is like that. You disappear, and the colors just shift to cover the hole. The glyph on my sleeve still means we see what others miss, but it also means this if you start looking too hard at who is pointing us where, there will be one less pair of eyes to worry about.

Rhea says only idiots write things down that can incriminate them, but Rhea still trusts people, so what does she know.

Quiet night in the bays. Generators whining like they are about to tear themselves apart, glow from the welding rigs leaking under the door. Smell of burnt polymer and cheap beer everywhere. Stray Rust home.

I keep thinking about that run to the outlying stacks last cycle. Sable shoved a cracked slate in my hand, said she needed someone "reliable" to ferry it through SysDef patrol routes without blinking. Reliable. I laughed it off, made a joke about her mistaking me for someone competent, but it stuck in my ribs like shrapnel. First time anyone ever called me that and actually meant it. I remember feeling this weird, hot pride in my chest, like I had been stamped with a mark that finally counted for something. Came back with the slate and an extra scorch mark on the hull, and Sable just grinned, slapped my shoulder, and never said the word again. Did not need to.

Funny how you can live your whole life trying to fix things that never wanted fixing. I did that back on the rock where I grew up. Always patching, smoothing, apologizing. Trying to mend a father who could only talk to a bottle, a mother who cared more about the next cargo drift than her own kid. No matter how many times I bit my tongue or picked up extra shifts, neither of them ever came even halfway. Felt like soldering a cracked beam that someone kept kicking out from under you. Different orbit now, same reflex. I am always the one tightening the bolts after a job, cleaning up the mess when deals go sideways, stitching cuts closed in the back room while Kyra curses and spits Aurora foam into a bucket.

Stray Rust runs on that kind of quiet work. The loud ones get the songs in the bar, but it is the people who sweep the blood off the deck who keep the floor from buckling. Sable understands that. Kyra pretends not to. Rhea acts like she could walk any time she wants, but I have seen the way she stares at the bulkheads when she thinks nobody is looking, like she is afraid they will vanish and she will be weightless again, nowhere to latch on.

There is talk in the bays tonight. Heard Sable and Rhea trading whispers about some shipbreaker out in the deeps, a ghost with a welding mask and a map no one is supposed to have. Someone who cuts up war hulks and vanishes the evidence, makes entire records go missing. They say he is been playing both sides, selling hardware to whatever flag pays, leaving bodies in rigging fields when people ask too many questions. Kyra claimed she saw a slate pass hands in Neon, stamped with a lattice of lines that did not match any trade lane she knew. She swears he is building something out there. Rhea just said some people cannot stand the idea of history being written without them.

I do not know what is worse. The idea that someone like that exists, or the way my gut twists with something too close to admiration. A person who decided the whole sky lied to them and then carved out their own truth with a cutting torch. Maybe it is all just bar talk, another story to scare the fresh runners. Or maybe those extra crates we have been parking in the shadow of the docks are not just scrap like they tell me.

Part of me does not care as long as the creds clear and the engines keep humming. The other part remembers that first time I walked into the Syndicate's bay, hands shaking, eyes fixed on the floor. I told myself I was just looking for a job, but really I was begging for someone to say stay. When Stray Rust took me in, gave me a bunk and a patch and a share so small it barely bought a drink, I told myself I could walk if things got ugly. Truth is, part of me has always wanted to belong somewhere, no matter the cost. That scares me more than any patrol ship.

So I keep fixing things. I patch the hulls, straighten the ledgers, calm Kyra down when her temper runs hot and she wants to solve everything with a pistol. I make sure Sable's dead drops are neat and the Syndicate's secrets are stacked where they will not crush us if someone kicks out the wrong support. Maybe one day I will find out what is really inside the containers marked "do not open" that Rhea pretends not to notice. Maybe I will not.

For now, I am still the one they call when a lock sticks or a plan starts to groan under its own weight. Reliable. I should hate that word. But it feels better than invisible.

I keep catching myself getting bored when people just nod and follow procedure. In the early days, back in New Atlantis, I thought compliance meant the system was working. Now it just feels like a dead signal. There is nothing to learn from someone who accepts the numbers at face value. The interesting ones are the captains who argue, the techs who double-check my models, the administrators who smile while they bury a report. They are the ones I want to crack open, to watch as their certainty fractures and they finally hear what the math has been screaming at them.

I remember the first time I realized the world was not what I had been promised. I was a child, standing in a resettlement line while some official with a perfect uniform told my mother there would be space for everyone, that the move from Earth was orderly, fair. Later I watched those same names get priority housing, priority schooling, priority everything. My father called it "weighting the equation." I pretended not to understand, but the truth is that was the day I stopped believing that any of this was neutral.

These days I can diagnose a person faster than a drive failure. The UC overseers at Calyx cannot tolerate uncertainty; they build whole careers on pretending probabilities are guarantees. Freestar haulers hide their fear under jokes and liquor, pushing their luck because if they slow down they have to admit how fragile their lives are. The frontier settlers who flirt with LIST want to believe in community but only if it costs them nothing. Everyone around me is just acting out their damage in different costumes. I see it so clearly in them. It is almost funny how none of them ever stop to examine why they need me to be the villain in this story.

I fled the lab because I did the one thing the system cannot forgive: I tried to pull the raw data out from under their thumb. The breach was an error in coolant tolerances, yes, but the pressure behind it was deliberate. They had already decided to lock away what we saw on that freighter, to treat a possible lattice-wide instability as a public relations problem. After that, staying would have meant nodding along until the day the lanes finally tore and we all pretended to be surprised. I chose exile instead.

The locations I move through now are not random. Dustfall Outpost, the old test hulls drifting in that graveyard belt, the hidden buoy the captains whisper about as if it is cursed; they all sit on top of soft spots in the lattice. I do not need full observatories. A few stolen diagnostics, a handful of custom sensors, and I can hear the hum shift. Each "test failure" I stage is not sabotage for its own sake. It is a forced admission, a glitch loud enough that even the most complacent administrator has to log it, patch it, or find an excuse creative enough to fool themselves.

People like to call me paranoid, unstable, traumatized. They whisper that I am projecting my own fractures onto the lanes. Maybe. I can sketch out their neuroses in a few lines and yet conveniently skip over my own. That is the luxury of being the one holding the models: I decide which variables matter. I am aware of the irony. I simply do not have time to indulge it.

I came out here, near what I have started to call the Scar, because the noise falls away and the anomaly stands almost alone in the readings. No planetary fields, no corporate interference, just the raw conversation between our drives and the dark. If I can map its shape, if I can prove this is not some one-off quirk but the logical end of how we jump, then it will not matter what they say about me in their hearings and backrooms. History will vindicate me, even if no one else ever does. They will write my name with curses, call me a murderer, a fanatic, a cautionary tale, but buried in their own records will be the quiet admission that I was right about the flaw.

What I am afraid of is not capture. It is that they will find some way to patch around the symptom again, to smooth the graphs and issue a software update, to declare the risk "within acceptable tolerances" and move on. That they will turn even this into just another footnote in a quarterly report. If that happens, then all the lives I have already spent in this campaign will have bought nothing. So I keep moving along the thin edges of the lanes, listening, adjusting, breaking what must be broken so someone, somewhere, will finally be forced to look at the truth.

Boss called us in again today. Same three taps on the bulkhead outside the berth, same weight in my gut like I swallowed a grav core. With command, you always knew what you were walking into: briefing room, objective, rules on paper. With Silent Fireteam, every summons feels like a coin toss. Darius shows up at your door, you do not know if you are getting a target package or a bullet behind the ear for knowing too much. Funny thing is, I trust him more than I ever trusted the brass. Fear is cleaner when it is honest.

Renee watched him the whole time during the brief, eyes like she was reading trajectories instead of faces. She believes in this more than any of us. Believes we are cutting out tumors, doing what the uniform never had the spine to admit needed doing. Jonas called it "course correction" once, in that dry way he has. We laughed, because the alternative was thinking about the list of names sitting on our dataslates, most of them people wearing the same colors we used to wear.

I keep trying to remember when I stopped being a soldier and became whatever this is. Maybe it was back when my partner decided our life was a two-person deployment and I was just an asset, not a person. Their needs were orders, every day: be here, say this, do not talk about that. Slowly learned to file my own thoughts away like classified annexes. After a while you forget what you actually want, you just respond to tasking. Leaving command should have felt like freedom, but all I did was swap chains. At least now the shackles fit better.

There is one op that will not leave me alone, no matter how many times I bury it under maintenance checks and weapons drills. We were sent into a settlement we were told was compromised, "soft collaborators" they called them. Our job was to make sure no one could help the other side when the push came through. Orders were clear, language intentionally vague. I remember the way the dust hung in the air after the first volley, thick as smoke, the way a kid's toy ship lay on its side in the doorway, still blinking a little cabin light. Renee pulled me out of that doorway by the collar, told me to keep moving, that we had to clear every house. Officially, we neutralized a logistics node. Unofficially, I still wake up hearing the echo of that empty toy hull hitting the floor as I kicked it aside.

We never saw the after-action on that one. Just a commendation that arrived late, unsigned, and a quiet reshuffle of our unit away from that sector. Later, in some mess on some station, I heard officers at the next table whispering about "collateral engagement ratios" like they were talking about fuel efficiency. I knew they were talking about us. About me. That was the first time I realized the reports were written long before we pulled triggers. The second time was worse; that was when I started to suspect some convoys were never meant to make it through, that the routes we were given and the windows we were told to hold were stacked against civilians from the start.

The guilt does not care that we were following orders. It settles in the seams of the armor, in the spaces between ribs, in the taste of recycled air. Every time I clean my rifle I see a reflection in the metal that looks a little less like the man who signed his enlistment and a little more like the man who walked through that settlement and did not say no. Darius tells me we are balancing the ledger now, taking down the ones who gave those orders and hid behind flags and legal phrases. Maybe he is right. But the numbers never quite work out when I run them at night.

What scares me most is how efficient we have become out here. No chain of command, no oversight, just four people who know how to break things quietly. When the boss knocks, when that dread rolls in, part of me is relieved it is another job and not the day he decides loose ends need trimming. Part of me thinks I would not even fight it. It would just be one more line item, signed off and filed.

I tell myself I stay because someone out here has to remember where the bodies are buried, which settlements were "nodes," which ships were "acceptable losses." Renee still believes in cutting out the rot. Jonas keeps the timelines, makes sure we never stay in one place long enough for the past to catch up. Darius carries the decisions on his shoulders and pretends it does not bend him. And me, Miguel Harran, I play my part, one more weapon turned off its target and never really disarmed.

Took a round in the plate tonight. Nothing serious, bruise spreading like a storm cloud under the ribs, but it was close enough that Elena made me sit on a crate while she checked the seal twice and told me I was an idiot for stepping wide on the third volley. She was right. Executioner culture says we don't talk about fear, so we call it "bad position" and argue angles instead. Mara just looked over from the weapons rack, shook her head once, and went back to scrubbing carbon from her rifle like she was polishing a conscience.

Caleb and Jonas are still snapping at each other over the Narion exfil. Caleb swears Jonas held the drop shuttle too long to milk the bonus, Jonas says Caleb tripped the sensor grid and forced his hand. Rhea plays mediator, but I see the way her eyes narrow when Jonas talks about "acceptable attrition." In Warbrand, trust is measured in how many times someone has had a shot at your back and didn't take it. By that metric, I trust Elena the most, Rhea enough, Caleb only when the odds are bad, and Jonas as far as the next payday.

There's a rumor working its way through the barracks that our next contract isn't just "asset recovery," that we're being hired to walk into the middle of some shipbuilder's dirty laundry and make sure the wrong person disappears. Heard it in fragments, mostly, over mess hall trays and in the hum between dropship checks. A designer gone rogue, ships failing in ways that don't look like accidents, corporate suits paying too fast and asking too few questions. It smells like politics with a body count. None of that hits the brief, of course. On the record, it will be clean words about liability and security.

Funny where life runs. Back home, I was the kid who ran errands for the old folks in the tower.
