Carry water filters up twelve flights, stand in line at the GalBank kiosk, carry back canned food with labels half peeled. We had our own little code, me and the other kids: three chalk slashes on a door meant "debt collector inside, come back later," a folded flyer tucked under the left corner of a mat meant "husband's on shift, safe to knock." We thought we were clever, playing messenger in a world we didn't understand. I never pictured myself in armor, selling my aim to the highest bidder.

Some of that old habit never left. Warbrand has its own codes now. A hand resting flat on a rifle stock in the staging bay means "eyes open, something in the op order smells wrong." An extra sugar packet dropped on your tray in the mess is Mara's way of saying "command is sitting on intel, check your blind spots." Jonas has his own language too; when he calls a job "straightforward," it means someone isn't walking back. We live in these signals because speaking plain carries consequences, and we all like our contracts renewed.

Got a few fresh scrapes tonight patching myself up after the plate strike. Med kit's locked in the quartermaster cage, so I did it the old way: strip down in the bunk, rinse the grit out with whatever distilled water I had left, press a ripped undershirt against the worst of it and tape it in place. Rhea walked past, tossed me a single dose of general painkiller without looking, then told me to log the injury as "minor impact during training" so the unit's numbers stay pretty on paper. She calls it managing optics. I call it bleeding quietly.

I thought about him again, like I always do when the pain flares. The one who said he'd wait, back before my first off world contract. His promises always came wrapped like gifts and felt more like knives; every "I'm proud of you" lined with "don't come back a failure," every "I'll be here" carrying the weight of "as long as you keep sending credits." It took me too long to understand that his love was just another contract, all sharp edges and penalties. Walking away from that felt harder than any extraction under fire. But at least out here, the terms are written down.

Tomorrow, command says we get a full briefing. Jonas slipped that the client's logo looks a lot like a certain staryard's, the one people in New Atlantis curse under their breath when transports fail inspection. Elena just sighed and checked her rifle torque again. They'll point us at some ghost in a scrapyard or dockyard, tell us it's a threat to stability, and expect us not to ask who built the conditions for that threat in the first place. Maybe I won't ask. Maybe I'll just read the angles, watch the codes, and make sure that this time, if someone is meant to vanish, it isn't me.

Day 173, LX-2547  

I keep telling myself the hum of the reactors is normal. Background music. Home. Tonight it sounds like it is thinking about something, like the ship knows more than it is saying. Maybe I am just tired. Jonas Mercer caught me zoning out by the viewport and asked if I was "listening for ghosts again." I laughed it off, but I think he meant it. The way people talk in the mess lately, you would think dead ships really can whisper.

We ran another mass-balance drill today, triple-checking cargo we have not touched in weeks. Elena Park had us cycling through the manifest like it was a final exam. She is cool about it, jokes just enough to keep everyone awake, but her eyes keep going back to those containers from Gravelight. Same numbers every time, same readings, yet she still frowns. I asked Mara Ellison if command had said anything; she just shrugged and said, "If they did, we are not cleared to know." Classic Mara, loyal to a fault, even when the deck feels like it is slanting under us.

Amira Cho tried to lighten the mood over dinner. We shared rehydrated UC BattleMeals in the mess, everyone pretending to enjoy them. She asked about a festival back where I grew up, on a little station that flew the flag like a letter from Earth. I told them about our old "First Light" night, when we would cut all non-essential lights and sit in the dark together, waiting for the star to rise over the hull. Just quiet. No screens, no announcements. Parents whispering stories about oceans none of us had seen.  

So tonight I tried to recreate it, just a little. Killed the lights in our berthing for five minutes on a maintenance pretext and pointed Jonas and Amira to the observation blister. Jonas grumbled about regs, but he came. Amira loved it, said the darkness made the stars feel closer, like we were inside them. Mara did not show. She said she was "too busy with diagnostics." That is the polite way to say she is not coming to anything I plan anymore.

I do not blame her. Not after the argument about the last derelict. I signed off on the structural report; she thought we should have flagged it unstable and pushed for a different tow. Command sided with me, and then the rumors started that some of those "abandoned" hulls were not as empty as the paperwork claimed. Now every time we pass in the corridor it is nods and clipped words, the kind of politeness that feels like a locked door. I have replayed that fight a dozen times, tried to think of a way back to how we were before, but I cannot find it. Maybe some breaks stay broken. Accepting that hurts less than pretending I can fix it.

Funny thing is, the First Light tradition back home changed too. Last time I visited, my little cousins streamed some old Earth sunrise on their slates instead of just sitting in the dark. They had playlists, branded snacks, even a sponsorship logo on the projection. "It is the modern version," my uncle said, like that made it better. I smiled, but inside it felt like someone had swapped out a load-bearing beam for plastic. I do not know if I am angry at them for moving on, or at myself for wanting the old version back. Maybe both.

That is how it feels on this ship now. Half the crew holds on to the idea that we are just doing the job, clearing wrecks, following orders. The other half has heard the same gossip I have, about registries getting "adjusted," about distress calls that mysteriously never make it into the log. No one says names, just vague talk of a rigger who can make mass disappear on paper, of cargo that is "too dense" for its label. It all stays just this side of unbelievable, because if we believe it, we have to admit we are part of it.

Earlier, in the corridor outside engineering, I passed Jonas and Mara mid-conversation. They went quiet when they saw me. Jonas gave me a quick nod, Mara stared past me at the bulkhead like it suddenly needed a detailed inspection. I swallowed whatever apology I was about to mumble and kept walking. Later, over a rushed cup of TerraBrew in the galley, Amira asked if I was ever going to talk to Mara properly again. I told her some things do not go back the way they were, and maybe that is how you know where your lines really are.

Still, the ship keeps humming, and we keep running drills, and the cargo keeps weighing exactly what the manifest says it should. On paper, everything balances. Out here, with the stars pressing in and the gossip curling through the air ducts, it feels like something is leaning, waiting for the smallest shove to tip.

The Widebeam smells like recycled air, stale coffee, and ion scorch from the last docking mishap someone will eventually admit to on the manifest. The coolant hum through the bulkheads is my bedtime lullaby and my morning alarm, depending on which shift Rafi leaves the engine tuning for. Tonight it feels louder than usual, or maybe it is just my nerves. I watched Jonas log that last cargo transfer under my code, and I did not stop him. I told myself it was just smoothing paperwork, a harmless favor in a maze of Trade Authority fine print. Then the routing discrepancy bounced back flagged, and suddenly it is my name on the audit trail. I could blame him, or the system, or those phantom "priority clients" that never have real IDs. But when I was sitting in the cargo bay, staring at the crate stamps under the strip lights, I knew the truth this was my line to draw and I stepped over it.

Kira tried to tell me it was not that serious, sitting across from me in the galley while the steamer coughed out that burnt-metal steam and someone reheated synthameat for the third time this week. She has a way of making everything sound survivable, like the worst that can happen is an angry supervisor and a pay cut. Elias was less gentle. He cornered me outside the avionics crawlspace, all low voice and clenched jaw, asking if I really understood who might be leaning on Jonas to reroute medical shipments in the first place. I hated him for that look, the one that says he expected better from me. I also hated that a part of me felt relieved someone finally said it out loud that I am the one who signed, that my hands are not clean just because I did not crack the seals myself.

I keep thinking about Adrien when my bunk is too small and the lights flicker in that way that tells you the capacitors are overdue for replacement. Back on New Homestead, he used to say we were going to be different, that we would take contracts without losing ourselves in the fine print and the bribes and the quiet looks the older traders gave each other. His promises always had a shine to them, pretty on the surface and razor-edged underneath. When he left for a better berth without saying goodbye, I told myself I would never be that naive again. Now, when Jonas leans too close over the console or Kira jokes about sharing a cabin someday planetside, I can feel that old reflex kick in pull back before someone walks away first. I wonder if I am turning into the kind of person who keeps everyone at arm's length, then signs off on things that make it easier to sleep alone.

The ship is cramped enough that you can never really avoid anyone; footsteps on the ladder rungs, the clink of metal mugs in the mess, Jonas humming off-key while he checks the seals is our version of weather. Tonight, the air in the corridor outside my berth smelled like spilled TerraBrew and ozone from a misaligned coupling. I stood there, hand on the hatch, listening to muffled voices from the next compartment Kira laughing too brightly, Elias speaking just low enough that I could not catch the words. For a second I wanted to barge in, demand they tell me exactly what they think of me now, let everything spill. Instead, I closed my eyes and let myself actually feel it the shame, the fear, and a thin thread of hope that maybe owning this mistake is the first right thing I have done in a long time. No jokes to soften it, no excuses about pressure from upstairs. Just the quiet acknowledgment that if I want to be the person I used to imagine on long nights under Titan's sky, I have to start with being honest about who I am in this steel box.

I do not know if I am getting closer to that version of myself or further away. Some days I am proud that I still flinch when someone suggests cutting corners with med shipments, that I still care who ends up on the other end of our manifests. Other days, like this one, I look at my initials under a reroute and wonder if that imagined Mina was just a story I told to get through the grind. Maybe growth is not as clean as I wanted it to be. Maybe it looks like admitting to Jonas tomorrow that I am not covering for him again, even if it means taking the heat now. Maybe it looks like letting Kira see that I am scared, really scared, without laughing it off. The Widebeam will keep humming along, trade lanes and credits and quiet little compromises. The only thing I get to change, in this cramped cabin that smells faintly of metal and my own tired sweat, is whether I keep pretending I am just a passenger on decisions I helped make.

Rhea says only idiots keep diaries, but I need somewhere to put the noise. The lot was quiet tonight, the kind of quiet where the dust hangs in the ship lights and you can hear every bad idea someone ever had. Jace was running his mouth again, talking about how the Backlot Boys used to mean something before we started hauling other people's secrets instead of our own. Rhea just watched him with that sideways look she has, the one that says she's adding up what he's worth if it comes down to it. I pretended not to see. Pretending is half of survival around here.

Funny what I remember, before all this. Long lines. Everywhere. Lines at ration kiosks, lines to see a clinic tech, lines wrapped around transit platforms that smelled like coolant and old sweat. Everyone holding a number and staring past each other, waiting for some overworked clerk to decide if they got medicine or just advice. Dust Backlot felt like freedom at first, like cutting to the front. You slip past the queue, use a code phrase at the right back door, and suddenly you're on the other side of the counter. Took me a while to realize you just traded one line for another, only this one ends in a shallow grave if you step out of place.

We had one of those hand-holding nights last week. Not the sweet kind. We were moving a crate for some suit who does not want his name spoken where cameras hear. Alley was bottled up, no clear sightlines, and that cold silence rolled in, the kind that means scopes are waking up somewhere you cannot see. Jace grabbed my hand, squeezed hard enough to grind the bones, like he could anchor me to the wall by grip alone. We moved as one body, shoulder to shoulder, eyes front, like just two lovers out for a walk between rusted containers. My pulse was sprinting, but my feet stayed slow. Rhea drifted a few meters behind, laughing too loud at nothing, making herself bait. If a shot came, it would go for the noise. Nothing came. That almost felt worse.

Paranoia is just oxygen here. We breathe it or we choke. Betrayal lives in the quiet gaps in conversation, in the way someone's eyes skip past you when they talk about a job that "just came in" and "needs a tight crew." The elders act like we are one big family, but their hands are always on different pockets when they hug you. I hear things when they think I'm not listening. Talk of off-lane routes and doctored traffic logs, of ships that never make it back but somehow keep paying their dues. There is this woman's name that drifts through it all, said with either respect or hatred depending who's drunk. Half the stories say she saves people from pirates. The other half say she feeds whole convoys into the fire for the right price. Either way, people lower their voices when the lanes come up.

We talk quiet too, just in different ways. Kids on the outside think it is all big speeches and blood oaths, but mostly it is small things. Rhea will say, "Weather's changing," if patrols are getting twitchy. Jace taps three times on the railing if a stranger's listening on a shared channel. We swap chip wrappers with certain corners folded when a run has gone bad but we cannot risk saying how. The phrase "left my boots by the vent" means someone's stiffed us and is about to learn what airless space feels like. All normal sentences, all loaded. Sometimes I wonder how many times I've heard my own death warrant wrapped in words about laundry and shift rotations.

The boys have a new ritual now. Before a risky job, everyone touches the same rusted support beam by the old shuttle husk, knuckles brushing the metal like it is blessed. First time I laughed, called it superstition. Then we lost three in a week and nobody skipped the beam after that. I still do not believe it does anything, but I touch it with the rest. It is easier than being the one who does not, easier than seeing their faces if I walk past and something goes wrong. There is comfort in shared lies.

Some nights, when the backlot finally goes dark and the haulers are just hulking silhouettes, I think about those lines again. Standing for hours, thinking my life would start as soon as it was my turn at some grimy little window. Joke's on me. Turns out the window was just another gate, and instead of a clerk I got Rhea, leaning against a crate, telling me the Boys could use someone who knows how to listen more than she talks. I said yes because anything felt better than waiting. Now I listen to the hum of ships and the whispered codes and I try to decide if I am moving forward or just in circles around someone else's hidden moon.

I keep telling myself the hum of the reactors is comforting, but tonight it just sounds like teeth grinding in the dark. PX-2395 feels wrong lately. Not dangerous in any clear way, just out of tune, like a grav ring a few RPMs off. Maybe it is just me. Maybe I am just tired.

We ran another inspection loop over the aft systems, Jonah Kincaid cracking the same bad jokes he always does about SysDef not paying him enough to climb into access trunks that smell like boiled suit liners. Marcus Hale laughed, but the sound caught halfway, like his throat had forgotten how. He snapped at Jonah later in the mess when the coffee ran out, slammed the mug so hard it chipped. Jonah went quiet, stared at the table. Nobody said anything until Sara Holloway changed the subject to a card game. Marcus apologized after, mumbled something about not sleeping. We all pretended that was enough.

Elena Marquez sat through all of it, that unreadable half-smile on her face. She has been like that more and more, hovering on the edge of conversations, not quite in them. When I asked if she was all right, she said she was just "processing the latest directive" and changed the topic to training rotations. That is the thing with Elena. She always has the right words, but lately they land a little too clean, like they were rehearsed.

Mira Chen stopped me in the corridor outside life support this morning, eyes red, hands shaking. Her brother on Jemison has some kind of respiratory issue, and the last comm burst from home said the waiting list for treatment is longer than the time his doctor says he can afford. Mira cried, really cried, chest-heaving, gasping sobs she kept trying to smother because "SysDef does not break." I held her till she stopped shaking. Later, Elena passed us and asked if there was "a situation." I said no, everything was fine. That was a lie and we all knew it.

I keep thinking about my mother back in New Atlantis, stuck in that tiny apartment looking at the same patch of sky where Earth used to matter. Her last message mentioned "a little stiffness" that she brushed off, but I saw the way she moved her hand, how slow it was. If it gets worse, I am half a system away locked on deployment. I tell myself I signed up to protect people like her, that this distance means something. Then I remember how long it took us to respond to the last piracy report and wonder if that is true or just what we need to believe so we can sleep.

There is talk in the lower decks that some of our "abandoned" targets are not accidents at all, that ships like this one get left to drift on purpose when the politics get messy. Jonah said he heard at Gagarin Landing that a whole refit line got written off because "the numbers had to look a certain way" for a board back on Jemison. He laughed when he said it, but it did not reach his eyes. I file all of that under rumor, but rumor has teeth out here.

I am starting to understand that if I wait for some perfect day to feel happy, it will never come. Between patrol logs and emergency drills and the soft, constant threat of being in the wrong place when somebody cuts a maintenance corner, there is not a lot of room for joy. Still, when Mira made a joke about us all retiring to a beach somewhere that does not exist, I laughed hard enough my stomach hurt. For a minute, I felt like I deserved to laugh, like all the nights cataloguing faults and double-checking seals might entitle me to something gentle someday. It felt strange, daring, almost wrong, to think I might deserve that.

Part of me also wonders if I deserve whatever is waiting out here, good or bad. I have moved my share of reports to the bottom of the stack when it was easier. I have looked away when an order felt more convenient than just. Maybe that is just how the system works, and I am complicit. Maybe the universe does not keep score. But when the lights flicker just a fraction too long, when the hull creaks like a tired joint, I catch myself thinking, if something happens, did we earn it.

Tomorrow I am running another calibration check with Elena. She requested me specifically, said she "trusted my eye for detail." I should feel flattered, I guess. Instead I feel that little murmur of unease you get when a bulkhead reads within spec but your fingertips swear the metal is too warm. I keep telling myself it is nothing. That the truth behind all of this is simple: long hours, thin nerves, too much space and not enough answers. But there is a part of me that wonders if we are all just making it convenient to ignore what is really cracking under the paint.

Could not sleep again, so I am burning power on this pad instead of staring at the ceiling of the berth and counting the weld seams.

Today was simple on paper. Perimeter sweep, sensor recalibration, live-fire drill in bay three. The usual Outpost Nightwatch routine, where everything is squared away, logged twice, and no one ever admits they are tired. Darius runs the line like he was born with a rifle welded to his shoulder. Elena moves through a room like a ghost, calls her shots before she takes them. Watching the two of them on the range, you would think this outfit is clean, sharp, uncomplicated.

Then you step off the firing line and everyone goes silent when the door to the briefing room opens.

We do not ask who paid for tonight's contracts. We just see the data packet, the route overlays, the "non-attributable" clause stamped in the corner. Marcus pretends he does not notice those seals, but I catch him flicking his eyes to them every time. Professional curiosity, he calls it. I call it a survival instinct. Men like us do not live long if we stop asking who benefits when the gun smoke clears.

Rumor in the mess is that one of our recent clients has their hands deep in frontier food shipments, moving more than manifests say they do. Darius says that is above our pay grade, to keep our noses in our own optics and out of corporate ledgers. Elena does not say anything, but she always takes her tray to the far table lately, back to the wall, eyes on the door. You can tell when a job brushes too close to something she has seen before. She gets that stillness, like she is waiting for an echo.

We ran escort last week on a convoy nobody wanted to talk about. Crates with the serials shaved down, cold-storage humming louder than it should, and a route that bent wide around any major hub. I asked the handler if we were hauling medical, he said "nutrients" and changed the subject. Since then, half the unit swears they saw dust signatures in the distance that did not match any of our own. Someone riding the weather, watching us without wanting to be seen. Might be nothing. Might be someone testing how close they can run alongside our paymasters without us noticing.

Outpost Nightwatch has unspoken rules. You do not ask where the money comes from. You do not freeze your teammate out, no matter how much you want to. You do not miss a shot that matters. Break the first two and the work stops coming. Break the last and men like Darius and Elena cannot trust you on their flank. Trust is rationed out here more carefully than air.

I keep thinking about that when the generators dim at night and the humming settles into something almost like quiet. About how much of what we do is built on the idea that the floor will stay under our feet as long as we follow orders and keep our optics clean.

But I have seen floors give way.

I keep coming back to that station, years ago, when I was still green. Alarms screaming, bulkheads shaking like they were alive and trying to tear free. I had her in my arms, the only calm point in a corridor full of panic. She was laughing and crying at the same time, blood on her teeth, insisting she could walk even as the deck pitched under us. We held on to each other while the lights went out and the world sounded like it was tearing apart around us. Love and loss, tangled so tight I still cannot pull them apart in my head. By the time the noise stopped, she was gone and the corridor was just another twisted passage on a casualty report.

Since then, every contract feels like a slow replay of that moment. Different walls, different clients, same question rattling around in my skull. How much of this is going to come down on our heads, and who am I going to be holding when it does.

Outpost Nightwatch likes to act like we are above the places we work. Private, disciplined, detached. The truth is we live in the same air as everyone else. If these whispers about shipments and scorched farm belts are true, then whatever is turning soil sour out there will not stop at a perimeter line. It will find its way into our vents, our water, our mess trays.

For now, the ops board is full, the pay hits on time, and the only things we are allowed to kill are what show up on the briefing slides. Darius trusts the numbers. Elena trusts her instincts. Marcus trusts patterns in the intel that nobody else has noticed yet.

Me I am trying to decide if I still trust the outpost more than I trust the feeling in my gut that we are walking the edge of another collapsing corridor, waiting to see who we will be holding when the lights go out.

I used to mark time in survey windows and burn limits. Thirty seven minutes over the pole, ninety to grab atmosphere reads, three hours to convince some overworked clerk on Queue Row that the numbers did not justify delaying a hundred people's lives another year. Now I mark it in how often I have to move the ship before someone notices the gaps I left in their records.

The first crack was not dramatic. No one fired a shot. I filed a risk assessment on a little rock with too much dust in the air and not enough water under the ground. The models said marginal, high failure chance with the prefab kit they were budgeting. I wrote all of that down. I watched the board stamp it "pending." Next month I saw the same coordinates come back through as "revised, approved" with my risk section overwritten by someone who had never set foot outside an office. Six months later I listened to the distress calls taper off from that place, the way the signal starts clean, then ragged, then just static. Officially, that outpost was "lost due to unforeseen conditions." Unforeseen, my ass.

People think I ran for profit. Some of it is credits, sure. Spacers will pay for a line that does not end in a waiting room. Settlers on their last shot will pay for a valley that has not already been promised to three different corporations. But the real reason I fled the nice clean desk was the day I realized I had become the excuse for other people's shortcuts. My name under approvals I did not write, my models cited to justify landings I would never have signed off on. Either I scrubbed myself out of that machine, or I let it keep eating people in my handwriting.

Hearthline was the one I cannot stop circling, even out here. Early job, early mistake. On paper it was my model that greenlit it. In my memory, I never cleared it. Somewhere between those two truths is a file someone erased and a radio log I still hear when I am too tired to keep the noise out. That is the day "safe enough" stopped sounding like anything but a lie.

So I built something else in the margins. A network of almost worlds and hidden valleys, places I had run numbers on and then watched get buried under "administrative complexity." I started selling what the queues would never reach. One family here, three ships there, coordinates slipped across a bar in Neon's Underbelly or whispered beside a rusted gantry in Akila. Every time it worked, it felt like stealing something back from the people who thought they owned the grid. Every time it failed, I added another waveform to the archive and told myself I would do better next time.

They say I am dying. Maybe. Radiation is not a rumor. Some days my hands shake when I draw a nav line, and the cough tastes metallic. Healing, if you can call it that, has started to feel like nothing at all. There are mornings I wake up and the guilt is not clawing at my ribs, and for a second I wonder if that is progress or if I have just gone numb enough to function. Numb enough to move the next group, adjust the next manifest, pretend the archive of lost signals is just data and not voices I knew by name.

This canyon I am in now was always supposed to be the last experiment. Kade's Pocket, they started calling it when I was not listening. The numbers are right water, shelter, decent soil, tight approach vectors easy to hide in shipment noise. I routed just enough cargo here to keep them alive without drawing a straight line any idiot could follow. It made sense as a final proof of concept a place the big powers could not revoke with a signature. If I can get this one truly self sustaining, truly off every chart, then maybe all the compromises and corpses in my wake add up to something other than a crime.

What I am afraid of is not the bounty hunters or the suits sniffing around my old logs. It is that someone will crack the pattern and decide to copy it without the hesitations. No risk models, no sleepless nights over weather anomalies, just raw throughput. I bent the grid to feed people I thought the system was throwing away. There is nothing stopping someone else from bending it to make themselves king of a valley they did not earn.

So I keep moving between the canyon and the junkyards, between the farmers who swear they owe me everything and the brokers who know exactly how much my head is worth. I keep hoarding transmission ghosts and half erased jump plans, telling myself that if I can just finish this one hidden settlement, just once get everyone in and stable and safe, then maybe I will have earned the right to lie still long enough to feel something other than this thin, dangerous calm.

The barracks are finally quiet, which means Caleb has stopped pacing his corner and Naomi is off somewhere pretending she sleeps more than three hours a night. Forward Shadowline breathes different after lights-out; the air cools, the hum of the recyclers gets louder, and all the unspoken rules settle in like an extra blanket. Keep your kit squared away. Keep your mouth shut. Never draw attention unless you are being paid to. We have written versions of that on paper, but it is the unwritten ones that bite. The ones you learn watching what happens to people who forget their place.

I keep thinking about the tap in my old rental on Cydonia, how the drip used to drive me insane. Thin metal walls, one noisy neighbor who blasted music through shift-change, and that idiot faucet that ticked every ten seconds like it was keeping time on my patience. Back then, I thought if I could fix the leak, get the neighbor to shut up, things would feel manageable again. It is ridiculous now, how big those problems felt when I still had a name that was just mine and not a line on a client roster.

My partner back then liked that version of me the one who organized bills, arranged appointments, smoothed over every rough edge so he did not have to. His needs filled whatever space was left in the day. Shift meals when he felt like it, calls when he felt like talking, long silences when he did not. I watched myself get small around that, turning down drinks with colleagues, skipping range time, telling myself I was being supportive. Little by little, whatever I wanted got filed under "later," and later never showed up. By the time I realized how much ground I had surrendered, there was not enough of me left to argue with.

Isolation sneaks up the same way. It started as "I am too tired for drama" and "I will see them next week," until eventually the only people I could stand being around were the ones I was fired at with. Easier to eat alone than to listen to friends tell me I worked too much, or that he did not deserve the way I bent my life to fit his. Easier to ghost them than fight about it. So the calls stopped, the messages thinned out, and one day my contact list was mostly logistics officers and armory techs. At least they only wanted signatures and serial numbers.

Funny thing is, one harmless decision did more to change my life than all the big, tortured ones. I stayed late one night to help a logistics clerk sort a misrouted weapons crate, because I was already there and it felt good to be needed for something that did not involve emotional triage. The crate had the wrong routing code, wrong destination, but everything else screamed someone important wanted it to vanish between depots. I flagged it as a simple error, wrote a short note, thought I was being thorough. A week later, a representative from Forward Shadowline "coincidentally" requested my transfer record. Turns out thoroughness is a good way to wind up on the radar of people who pay for that kind of thing.

We keep examples close in this line of work. The guy who double-billed a low-profile client for ammo and fuel, thought no one would notice. They did. He came back from a debrief with a busted jaw and a reassignment to a deep-space escort route nobody wanted, the kind that does not always log your return. The woman who kept asking why our last target list shifted mid-mission lost her next contract to a "performance review" and now works security for some mid-tier mining outfit. Discipline here is not all written reprimands and lost bonuses. Sometimes it is a quiet word in the right ear that your name no longer appears on shortlists.

Caleb plays the game better than I do. He knows when to nod, when to ask questions, when to pretend he did not hear the rumor about a rescue ship that never made it to a beacon it should have. Naomi carries the data in her head and pretends it is just numbers. I am still learning the balance walking the line between noticing too much and not enough, between being the kind of contractor they cannot do without and the kind they decide is thinking too hard for her own good.

Tonight I can hear the plumbing in the wall behind my bunk ticking in uneven bursts, almost like that old faucet. It is faint, but once you notice it, you cannot unhear it. That is what this work feels like: once you notice how the routes bend, how the accidents line up with the payouts, how certain names turn into vague gestures mid-sentence, you cannot go back to pretending it is just noise. So you either learn to live with the drip or you start taking things apart, piece by piece, hoping you can fix it before something important cracks.

Day 184, by my count  

The bunk smells like solvent and cold metal again. Jonas swears he can still smell propellant from the old days, but I think that is just memory clinging to the walls. Bloodied Unit rotates ships like other people change socks, yet somehow every hull feels like the same barracks they locked us into before they cut us loose.  

I spent half the evening stitching up that old field jacket. Same one I got issued before the last planetary siege, seams reinforced three times over, patches on patches. Not because I cannot requisition something new. Because my hands do not know what to do with downtime unless they are mending something that already survived. Caleb watched me at the table, boots up, pretending not to notice the way my fingers shook on the heavier thread. He offered me a new set of fatigues once, fresh from some depot we "reallocated" from. I told him broken things are honest, at least. New fabric lies about how long it plans to stay.  

Elena came back from a meet with our latest benefactors with that look again. Eyes too bright, jaw too still. She does not say much about what they want from us, only that it is "close enough" to what we used to do. Targets labeled "noncompliant," grid squares pre-approved for cleansing, rules of engagement phrased nicely so no one has to write the ugly words down. Orders used to come in that same polite language. We all remember how those ended.  

Mara has started laughing more. That should be good news. It is not. In the mess today she was doubled over at some joke Jonas made about an old op, something about losing count of bodies when the drones glitched and fired twice. Everyone joined in, but the sound was wrong, all sharp edges and teeth. No warmth in it, just the kind of laughter that says the only other option is screaming. That is how it has always been with us. Even before we walked out, nobody laughed because something was funny. We laughed to prove the horror had not cracked us yet.  

I keep thinking about that last classified strike they swore never left the briefing room. The one where the maps did not match the satellite feeds, and the civvie comms conveniently went quiet right before we dropped. I remember the colonel closing the door, telling us the blackout was a "routine safety measure," that collateral was "within tolerance." After, when the aerials leaked, someone somewhere just changed the numbers and signed off. Caleb says I should let it go, that we did the job we were built for, that the ones who signed the papers are the ones stained, not us. But they are not the ones waking up with dust in their teeth and the taste of burnt plastic in their mouths.  

We tell ourselves we left because command betrayed the oath first. Because they turned us into a clean-up crew for mistakes they intended to make. Because we were tired of the debriefs where every inconvenient fact was "reclassified" and every doubt was "operational stress." All true, in pieces. None of it explains why I still line my boots up by rank every night, or why I still check my locker three times before lights-out, like a sergeant is going to throw it open and scream about inspections.  

Sometimes I watch the others when they think no one is looking. Caleb still checks his rifle like a priest with a relic. Jonas paces deckplates counting under his breath, same cadence he used walking perimeter in the rain, waiting for artillery that never came. Elena folds and refolds her sleeves so her old unit tattoo just barely shows, then disappears again. Mara sits with her back to the wall, eyes on every exit, fingers working invisible triggers. We are all still in uniform, even stripped of patches and rank. Just changed who we answer to.  

Word around the crew is that tonight s run is not just another smash-and-grab. The way the brief was worded, the way our contact avoided looking anyone in the eye, the way the coordinates line up a little too neatly with an old restricted corridor. Feels like we are circling back to something they tried to bury under red tape and sealed files. We pretend we are in this for the pay, for the freedom, for the chance to choose our own targets. But every one of us heard the same thing in that briefing: the echo of an order we already disobeyed once, and the knowledge that this time, if we follow it, there is no court-martial waiting on the other side. Just us, and what we can live with.  

I patched the last rip in the jacket and ran my thumb over the crooked stitching, all the places I have had to pull it back together. It is ugly work, but the fabric holds. I wonder how many more times we can do the same thing to ourselves before something finally gives way for good.

I keep telling myself I will not write on duty days, that I will sleep instead, but sleep on this ship is a rumor like everything else.

FX-1555 feels emptier every week. The hum in the bulkheads is the same, the same flicker in corridor B7 where the lighting panel never got properly refit, the same stale coffee smell outside the mess, but the spaces between people are widening. Marcus Ellison has stopped lingering after shift change. He logs his reports, nods to whoever is at the console, and vanishes into the bow end of the ship like he is afraid someone will ask him what he has been doing in the data archives.

Today was inventory day again. I spent four hours in Storage 3A scanning crates that have not moved since before I transferred aboard. Structural, titanium, adhesive, microcells, all lined in their neat little slots while the tags on the manifests tell a different story. I had to correct three serials on cargo modules that were logged as "expended" but are very much still sitting on the rack. Paper ghosts, Julian Mercer calls them. He tried to make a joke about them forming a union and demanding better lighting. I laughed because it was easier than saying that paper ghosts do not misfile themselves.

Adrian Kovacs asked me to help re-sort the emergency med kits along the forward passage, said he trusted my eye for "fussy details." It was an excuse to walk the long route and feel the ship beneath our boots, I think. We checked expiry dates, counted trauma packs, made sure the digipicks in the secure box were still sealed. Mundane work, comforting in its own way. On the way back, he stopped by the observation port, stared at the scatter of debris outside, and asked if I believed in coincidences. I told him that on a ship like this, coincidences are just paperwork that has not learned how to confess yet.

In the mess, between shifts, I taught Lena Hartmann how to fold the little paper boats my grandfather taught me. He used to sit by the window on wet monsoon afternoons and make a fleet on the table, say every ship deserves someone who remembers the people before the metal. Lena's first few tries were crooked, edges not quite lined up, but she kept at it, tongue between her teeth, until one sat properly on its own. We floated it in a cup of water, just for a moment, then flattened it and tucked it behind one of the status panels on the mess wall. "A secret harbor," she called it. It felt ridiculous and sacred at the same time. Out here, someone has to remember the quiet, stupid human things.

And then there is the other secret, the one I wish I had not seen.

Yesterday, I was rerouting a minor power alarm near the auxiliary records room. The door was half-closed, the way it always sticks on the track, and I heard Marcus inside with someone on a secure line, voice low but clipped in that way he gets when he is pretending not to be angry. I know it is wrong to linger, but I did. He was reading out registry numbers, civilian hulls, and whoever was on the other end was confirming "resolution" dates that do not match what I have filed in our daily logs. I recognized one of the names, a hauler we escorted through a supposedly quiet corridor last month. In our system, it still shows as "en route." On the line, it was "closed."

When he came out, he almost walked into me. For a heartbeat his eyes were wide, like I was an airlock he had forgotten to seal. Then he smiled, asked if I had fixed the flickering panel yet. I said yes, even though I had not. After he left, I slipped into the room. The comm was closed, of course, but the auxiliary console still carried the residue of his access. There was a list of hull IDs with a watermark from an insurance consortium I do not recognize and a notation in the margin: "Claims synchronized with combat logs."

It is not my place to question fleet business. That is what Lena says when I bring up oddities. That is what Julian says, quieter, when he thinks I have pushed too far. But I keep stumbling into these little misalignments: crates that exist but do not, ships marked safe that whispers say never made port, beacons that pass through our lattice and then fall silent. If I put all of it together in the open, I would be accusing people I share air with of pretending metal is more valuable than the names attached to it.

So instead, I teach paper boats. I check inventory twice. I reroute minor alarms. I press my hand to the bulkhead sometimes and remind myself that FX-1555 is just a vessel, not a judge. The people making decisions sit behind screens somewhere else. Still, I cannot unhear those registry numbers in Marcus's voice, cannot unknow that in some other ledger, ships we were supposed to watch are already considered gone.

I keep telling myself I will not use the shipboard log as a diary, and yet here we are again, hiding a personal file in an auxiliary maintenance folder because the official channels feel too clean for real thoughts. The hum from the forward capacitors is running half a tone higher tonight and it is driving me mad; engineering says it is within tolerance, but when you sleep three meters from the bulkhead it is like someone whispering a question you cannot quite hear, over and over.

Dinner was the same lukewarm UC BattleMeal slurry they have been cycling all week. Darius tried to joke that it tastes better if you do not look at it, which is true of most things on SysDef deployments. Elena just shook her head, stabbed the packet once with her fork like she was arresting it, and ate in silence. We all pretend the rotating menu is still working, but the reality is the cook is as tired of the requisition system as the rest of us.

On my way back to quarters I almost tripped over someone's mislaid toolkit in the starboard corridor again. I am ninety percent sure it is Darius leaving it there when he goes chasing sensor ghosts, but he swears it is not his. The locker door beside it has started to squeak every time it opens, and nobody has logged a repair request because the noise has become a kind of roll call; if you hear it, you know someone is still moving around on this graveyard shift.

Rhea stopped by earlier, looking more wired than usual. She had that half-smile she uses when something is bothering her and she does not want to admit it. We ran another drill in CIC today, and she kept glancing at the boards long after the scenario ended, like she expected real contacts to start populating the tactical grid. When I asked, she said she had been reviewing some "old pattern analysis packages" the brass pushed down from a data vault on New Atlantis. Then she changed the subject, asked me about my coffee stash instead.

I taught her how my father used to make chai when I was a kid, or as close as you can get to it with shipboard supplies and a tolerance for improvisation. Heat the water until it just thinks about boiling, not a bubble more, then in go the spices, then the cheap tea last. She let me guide her hands on the pot so it would not scald, and for a moment it felt like something fragile and old was still alive out here, something not written in protocols or transfer orders. Funny, given how often I promised myself I would not be like him.

My father believed in uniforms with a kind of religious conviction. He used to say that if you wore the flag, you did not get to ask what the numbers meant, you just made sure the line held. We stopped talking after I questioned one of his deployments, asked too many whys and not enough yesses. Signing on with SysDef felt like both a rebellion and an apology, as if I could prove service did not have to mean blind obedience. Now I look at some of the models we are fed, the way resource flows and "acceptable losses" get packaged for us, and I hear his voice telling me this is just how things work.

There are whispers on ZT-7430 that someone has been blending financial data with our engagement sims, that some analyst from the core came up with a way to tell which routes can be "stressed" without anyone important noticing. No one says it out loud over comms, but I have caught Elena and Darius lowering their voices in the corridor when the topic veers too close to certain convoys, certain colonies whose names only show up in tiny print. It is all rumor and half-heard snippets, yet the pattern sits at the edge of my vision, like a contact you are almost sure is there but the scope will not lock.

I keep finding my thoughts circling around Rhea when they should be on duty rosters and diagnostics. She laughs at my bad jokes, lingers a second too long when we pass in the narrow ladderways, but she is also the one pulling double shifts in CIC, eyes flicking between threat indicators and those mysterious "analysis packages." Part of me wants to trust her with what I am starting to see, to ask if she thinks we are still just hunting pirates and smugglers. Another part is terrified that if I say it out loud, she will either report me up the chain or worse, agree completely.

So I nod at the right people, share polite small talk outside the mess, complain about the squeaky hatch and the cold meals, and pretend I do not notice how often our course brushes close to certain trade corridors that have been "flagged for observation." The ship keeps humming, slightly off-key, and everyone pretends not to hear it. I am still trying to decide which I fear more: that my father was right about what service demands, or that he was wrong and we are all just numbers in someone else's ledger.

I keep telling myself I am done apologizing for things that are not my fault. Airlock jams, bad coordinates, a cut line that fails because the cable was already half-rotted when we got there. Somehow it still comes out of my mouth on reflex, like sorry is just another tool hanging off the belt. Riya Calder calls me on it more than anyone. Says if I keep owning every mistake in the hullborn radius, the Collective will happily let me carry all their ghosts too.

Day-to-day is the same grind. Wake up to stale coffee and stale jokes, stand lookout on the scopes while someone else gets the fun of suiting up. Run courier runs between our tug and whatever station still lets us dock, shuttling parts, paperwork, and promises. Then back to waiting for orders that might never come, watching the job board flicker while the old hands mutter about how the graveyards are getting crowded with bigger, better-funded crews. Half the life is anticipation; the other half is pretending you are not counting the minutes until something breaks the monotony.

Last month twisted things more than I like to admit. That failed pull on the SysDef wreck left a crack in the crew you can feel in the air. We came back light on salvage and heavy on questions about who leaked coordinates, who cut corners on the mag clamps, who conveniently forgot to log the extra crate drifting off our stern. Now every argument over salvage rights feels like it has teeth. Folks who used to share a drink just share side-eye. You stand at the mess table and you can feel everyone running numbers on how much they trust you compared to how much you might be worth cutting loose.

Jealousy eats at people in small bites. I saw it with my last partner in the rigs. A few lucky finds with Riya, a few extra credits, and suddenly every routine difference of opinion turned into a minefield. Why did we choose that hulk and not this one Why was I always on the good runs These were questions I could not answer without sounding guilty, even when there was nothing to confess. When it finally blew up, we both said things we cannot take back. I caught myself apologizing again, out of habit if nothing else, and hated myself for it all the way back to the bunk. Isolation started to look simpler than trying to convince someone I was not stealing their future one job at a time.

Now I keep my circle small. Riya on the line when I can get her, because she has this way of laughing at the void that makes it feel less hungry. A couple of riggers I trust to double-check a weld without trying to knife me for the bonus. The rest I nod to and keep my stories polite. If I let them in, I hand them leverage. Out here, in orbit around rusting bones, that can be more dangerous than a bad seal.

Every time we hook a derelict, somebody brings up the ghost-ship tales. Crews vanishing mid-burn, freighters that left port on full tanks and never pinged a lane beacon, an old LIST convoy that arrived days early with fuel they should not have had. Lately there is this one story about a navigator who can thread ships through gaps nobody else sees. Some swear they found her mark on a chart on a dead hauler; others say she slipped a whole Crimson Fleet wing past SysDef and left their patrols swinging fists at empty space. You hear that enough times and start wondering how many of these so-called mysteries are just clever math you are on the wrong side of.

The paranoia after that botched job made everything worse. Someone swears they saw an extra route file in the nav cache. Someone else says the traffic control timings were wrong, like they had been nudged just enough to leave us hanging without cover. Nobody can prove anything, so we circle each other with forced smiles and inventories that never quite add up. It is hard to admit that what really scares me is not sabotage, but the idea that some invisible hand is rewriting the lanes and we are just crawling along behind with torches and cutting gear, picking over the leftovers of decisions made far above our heads.

There are nights, strapped into my rack, where the hum of the engines feels like it is pushing us toward something we never chose. I think about everything I have said sorry for, every time I let someone else frame me as the problem because it was easier than a fight. Out here, in the graveyards, the metal does not apologize. It just breaks, or it does not. Maybe that is the lesson I am supposed to drag out of all this; stop taking blame that is not mine, stop letting other people write the route for me. But then the klaxon sounds, and orders come down, and I find myself in the airlock again, one hand on the helmet, the other smoothing things over with a joke and a half-hearted apology for snapping earlier. Old habits cling tighter than vacuum.

I used to think the worst sound in the world was incoming fire on a bad approach vector. Turns out it is boots walking away down a metal corridor after you have run out of words and excuses. I can still hear her heels on the deck, sharp little taps fading into the hum of the recycler, back when the Guard was still pretending to be a "temporary regrouping." Riley never once looked over her shoulder. She did not need to. Every promise she ever made had an edge on it, like a blade you check with your thumb. Stay with me, she said. I will keep you alive, she said. There was always an unspoken or else hanging in the air between us, as clear as any mission brief.

Damon says that is what command does to people, grinds everything down to leverage and compliance. Maybe he is right. Maybe that is just who we were even before the uniforms. I do not know anymore. I remember the last real op before we bolted, smoke still hanging in the carrier bay, Kade tossing his helmet hard enough to crack the visor, Riley and the colonel trading those quiet, poisonous smiles. The official line was that the civilians we evac'd "succumbed to complications." Off the record, half the squad heard a different body count over the secure channel. I signed that after-action report anyway. I signed it knowing it was a lie, and I did it to protect Riley. That is the part that keeps me up some nights how easy my hand moved, how natural it felt to bend the truth around the one person I could not stand to lose.

Renegade Guard likes to talk about honor now, like we dragged it with us when we walked. We still run patrol drills, still clean weapons on rotation, still snap to Kade's hand signals without thinking. Same discipline, just with the serial numbers filed off. But there is a hum under everything, a quiet question: who is watching whom. Erin sleeps with her rifle mag'd and safety off, even inside the perimeter. Damon logs extra hours on comms "for security," which really means listening for whoever might be bargaining us away. I wake up each day with that half-second of blankness before the old training kicks in, and in that space, the thought is always there like a reflex someone in this outfit is already doing the math on whether I am worth more as a partner or as a problem solved.

I catch myself studying people the way I used to study threat boards. Riley taught me that, too. Check posture, check tone, check where their eyes go when they think no one is looking. I saw her flinch the first time talk of desertion stopped being hypothetical. Saw the way her jaw tightened when Kade mentioned the "incident" that never made it into our records, the one that turned a clean op into a burial detail. I knew then command had dirt on her, enough to pull her back if they wanted. Maybe that is why she walked away from me that night in the corridor. Maybe she decided I was a liability when my conscience started leaking through the cracks.

The rumor mill says our last unit still runs deniable work, same insignia, different colors. I hear they are using some of the same tactics we pioneered, but stripped of the restraint we used to cling to on the bad days. Every time I picture them in the field, I wonder if my name still sits on a list somewhere as "recover" or "neutralize." And then I look at the people around me Damon drafting contingency plans, Erin cleaning her rifle with that distant expression, Kade mapping extraction routes none of us asked for and I realize it does not matter where the bullet comes from: old command, or one of our own with a clearer idea of "acceptable risk."

I try not to think about the day I walked away from Riley. About the way she did not follow, did not call after me, just let the silence harden. We had just finished shouting at each other over whether to turn in the data chip that proved what really happened in that village. She wanted leverage. I wanted out. I told her I destroyed it. I did not. I hid it. I lied to the woman I loved to protect people I will never see again, and I did it like I had been doing it my whole life. Maybe that is what we are now liars with good aim, still pretending we are better than the ones who issued us our first rifles.

Some days I imagine finding her on some burned-out rock, both of us older, slower, pretending we do not have scopes trained on each other from the first moment. Other days I half expect her to step out of the shadows in our own camp, that same surgeon's gaze taking inventory of my weaknesses before she smiles. Until then, I keep my pistol within reach when I sleep. Not because I fear the next contract, or whatever ghosts of command might finally decide to clean house. I fear waking to the soft sound of familiar boots on metal, and realizing they did not come back to keep any of those sharp little promises they made.

Did a gear check twice tonight and still do not trust the rifle. Nothing wrong with it on paper, zeroed, clean, no carbon in the bolt. It is everything around it that feels off. New contract, partial brief, too many redactions for a "security support" op. Division Garrison likes to say we are not mushrooms, but they still keep us in the dark and feed us canned lines about "stability services" and "deniable presence."

Rios laughed when I said that in the armory. She always laughs too loud right before a bad deployment. Says if they are paying hazard rates, it is not our job to ask what is really in the crates or what those remote survey stations were really relaying. She is not wrong. Pay clears on time, armor upgrades show up when requested, med coverage is better than half the regular militaries out here. But even Rios got quiet when the handler mentioned "crowd behavior contingencies" and that we might encounter colonists "under chemical influence." Never heard them phrase it that way before.

There is a rumor moving through the bunks that some of the unrest we keep getting sent to "contain" is not natural at all. Tavi swears she saw blood panels on a tablet once, levels all wrong for any known stim, and the doc just turned the screen away and changed the subject. Someone else claimed a UC liaison had an off-the-books file open with our next AO circled, same AO that supposedly had a "farm accident" last quarter. Nobody admits they have seen the reports firsthand, but everyone has a cousin or a friend in some militia who has. Funny how that works.

The unit rule is simple: keep your eyes open, mouth shut, and questions strictly off record. You talk in the gym, under the noise of the old treadmills. You talk in the motor pool with the fans going. You do not talk in briefing rooms or near any console that looks newer than the paint on the walls. Division Garrison is professional, no question, but it has layers. The shooters and techs like me on the outer ring, logistics and intel on the next one in, and then that little hard core of handlers who never joke and always know three answers more than they will give.

Sometimes I wonder how I ended up here instead of back on Grav Street, leaning against a busted groundcar with friends, watching the sky flicker in a storm and doing absolutely nothing. We used to sit in that half-abandoned lot behind the old mall, passing a bottle, drawing futures in the dust with our boots. One of the rooftops nearby had a rusted-out air conditioner we used as a throne; you could see the whole block from there and it felt like a kingdom even though it smelled like hot metal and cheap beer. There was that dead park with the broken swing set too, where the lights never got fixed and the only thing moving after dark was us. No grav drives overhead, no non-disclosure clauses, just the sound of insects and somebody's old music bleeding through apartment walls.

Now my forgotten places are cargo bays between contracts, or the little maintenance catwalk above the firing range where nobody bothers to look up. I sit there while the others clear drills below, listening to the rhythm of automatic fire and trying to decide which of them I would actually trust if something went sideways. Rios, yes. She has that steady-center thing, knows when to push and when to duck. Our new comms specialist, I am not so sure. Too friendly with the liaison, too quick to shut down a conversation when it veers toward "why are they really paying us to stand between angry farmers and off-world suits."

There is talk that our next tasking involves a settlement that has not technically asked for help. "Preemptive stabilization," the handler called it. That is a nice phrase. Means someone with money is nervous and does not want official uniforms anywhere near the problems. We go in with soft IDs, "commercial security," patch a few leaks, make sure nobody looks too closely at air intake systems or the odd way tempers spike whenever the wind shifts. And when it is done, we stand down, debrief, and pretend we did not notice that the casualty lists never quite match the population numbers we were briefed on going in.

Part of me still likes the clarity of this work. Target, perimeter, fields of fire, clear communication. A simple math problem with variables you can influence. But more and more, the variables feel like people whose nerves were rewired by something no one is willing to name, and we are the ones paid to stand in that mess and call it order. Rios says do the job, take the credits, live long enough to walk away. She might be right. Still, on nights like this, I can almost smell those old parking lots again, hot asphalt and fried food, and I wonder what it would feel like to be bored on a rooftop instead of alert in a war I am not allowed to admit exists.

I used to think boredom was something you grew out of.

Back before contracts and hazard pay, it was just me and a couple of kids from my block, haunting forgotten places with nothing to do. We would sprawl over cracked concrete in an old parking lot, climb rooftops we had no business being on, kick gravel through dead parks where the swings only moved when the wind bothered. We had no credits, no plans, just cheap drinks and cheaper games on a shared hand-terminal. I remember thinking that if I ever got out, really out, life would stop feeling like waiting.

Turns out waiting just got better uniforms.

Hotel Hardstrike has its own vortex of dead time. Long stretches of lookouts, courier runs, standing in corridors that smell like cleaning solvent and recycled air, watching doors that never open. Today was one of those days: stand fast, stay dressed, weapons cold, comms on, orders "imminent" for twelve hours straight. Damian kept pacing the same five meters of corridor until Caleb threatened to weld his boots to the deck. Lena just sat on the crate stack, tuning her rifle like it was a stringed instrument, eyes somewhere far beyond the bulkhead.

I filled the gaps the same way I always have. Took apart an old comm beater from the equipment bin, scratched schematics on my forearm with a grease pen, tried to coax another few hours of life out of a board someone else had already written off. There is something calming about tiny screws and tracing burnt lines with the tip of a knife. Circuits at least make sense; they fail for reasons you can see.

People are different.

There is a moment I keep coming back to. Different ship, different job, thin corridor lit by emergency strips. Fire behind us, pressure doors not far enough ahead. We were moving in single file, smoke clawing down our throats, when the blast wave hit and dropped half the squad. The deck heaved, lights went dark, the world shrank to red status glyphs and the sound of someone screaming through a helmet. I felt a hand clamp around mine, iron-tight. No romance in it, no comfort. Just reflex and terror. I squeezed back so hard my knuckles hurt for a week afterward. Later I realized it had been Lena. We never talked about it. In this line of work you pretend you do not need anyone that close, even when your grip says otherwise.

I skipped my first real job to follow a man I barely knew. Should have been at a loading dock on some frozen rock, counting crates and pretending that was a future. Instead I watched this ex-military type a friend of my brother's walk into a bar, and on impulse I tailed him. Spent the whole day leaning in the shadow of a bulkhead, listening as he talked to a recruiter about what "contract work" meant: better pay, cleaner kit, risk you chose instead of risk handed down by people who would never bleed. That man never remembered my face, but he changed my trajectory more than any teacher I ever had.

Now that I am here, sitting under the Hotel emblem with a rifle that probably costs more than my entire childhood block, I see the seams he did not mention. The quiet politics in the mess who sits with who, whose contracts are up for renewal, which names get spoken soft because someone upstairs likes them. Caleb plays the loyal company man, but his eyes always track the exit routes like mine do. Damian talks about "career arcs" like this is something you retire from. Lena keeps a little mental wall around herself that even a blast charge would not breach.

And then there are the whispers.

Someone in Logistics swears one of our data escorts bounced through the same ghost traffic that has been wrecking haulers out on the frontier. A medic mentioned hushed orders to sign off injuries as "training accidents" after a job that was definitely not training. One of the comm techs thinks we have done at least one contract for people who caused the very incidents the news feeds paint as unavoidable. Nobody wants to chase those threads too hard. We live on those credits. We are the knife; we do not ask who drew the outline.

So the days blur: lookouts, courier runs, waiting for the ping that throws us into somebody else's crisis. I fix broken gadgets, sharpen blades that are already sharp enough, play stupid games on an old slate until the battery gasps. Sometimes we gather on the top level of whatever hab they have stuck us in and stare out at whatever passes for a skyline city lights, station traffic, or just a smear of stars. It feels just like those old rooftops and parking lots, the same empty hours, only now we are all pretending the next call will finally make it feel like it adds up.

Maybe that is why I write any of this down. Not for a record, not for anyone else. Just so there is something in here that is mine, that was not issued, contracted, or requisitioned.

Something that is not waiting.

I do not know why I still write these. Habit, I guess. Something about putting it down in words makes the day feel like it belonged to someone, even if that someone is just a name on a contract.

We rotated back from overwatch three hours ago. Alpha Warfrost standard: strip, scrub, log your ammo, sign the debrief, act like nothing under your skin is still shaking. Kade did his usual quiet sweep of the ready room, eyes on everyone's hands, not their faces. He trusts fingers more than smiles. Rhea was already running sims, chasing the last half-percent out of a breach route we might never use. That is how this unit breathes: always rehearsing for the thing that might not happen, so that when it does, nobody has an excuse.

No one said anything about what floated through on encrypted tonight, but you could feel it. Longer contracts. Deeper space. Someone rich enough to keep their name off the brief wants deniable assets near corridors that do not officially exist. The talk in the armory was all half-jokes: "escort duty," "routine security," like we do not all hear the way veterans say those words and then fall quiet. I heard Kade ask Rhea if she had ever flown close enough to see derelicts hanging in the dark, lined up like markers. She did not answer. Just checked her rifle latch again.

I remember the first time someone offered me protection in exchange for loyalty. Not here. Back in the low decks, when I was just another skinny kid who knew how to keep his head down. Boss man with perfect boots told me I could eat regular and sleep without watching the door if I ran errands and never asked questions. I said yes like I meant it, squared my shoulders and tried to stare back like I was made of metal. Inside, I felt like glass. I learned quick that if they smell fear, you stop being a person and start being inventory.

That lesson travels well. In this outfit, the armor is not just ceramic and plating, it is the way you walk into the ready line like you have never missed a shot. The way you pretend firing drills and live fire feel the same. Loud noises or sudden movements still flip something in me, even now. A dropped crate, a misfired test charge, somebody slamming a locker, and my hand is halfway to my sidearm before my brain catches up. Saw Rhea clock it the other day and look away like she had not. Courtesy, mercenary-style.

The unit talks a good game about brotherhood, but the unspoken rule is simpler: you are what you deliver. Protection is measured in how many times your fire keeps the others alive, how reliably you hit the mark and keep your mouth shut about the things you see on client ships you should not. There is a rumor that one of our upcoming contracts is not about guarding cargo, but about steering it off-course, making sure it never makes a scheduled stop. People pretend they do not believe it. People also clean their weapons more carefully these days.

Sometimes I catch myself wondering if I even deserve peace after everything I have done for other people's ledgers. Doors kicked in that did not need to be. Targets whose eyes said they were messengers, not monsters. There is a tally in my head and it is not written in numbers. Nights like this, when the barracks finally go quiet and the humming of the recycler is the loudest thing around, I do the math and come up short.

It does not help that off-mission, I have a bad habit of disappearing into whoever stands closest. Last partner taught me that lesson the hard way. She liked the idea of a soldier more than the man under the armor. Her needs were always louder, always urgent. What she wanted me to be, where she wanted us to live, who she wanted me to cut ties with. I said yes to all of it until one day I realized there was nothing left in the mirror but her choices wearing my face. When it ended, all I had left that felt like mine was the recoil of a rifle and the way my squad said my name on comms.

Kade tells me we are professionals, not heroes. Rhea says the only thing that matters is that when the hatch blows and the air turns to static, we do exactly what we trained to do. They are not wrong. Still, lying in my bunk with my ears tuned for the next alarm, I can almost feel the shape of something else I used to want before the contracts and the noise. Something softer, slower. Then somebody drops a tool two bays over, my heart jumps like a round just cracked past my head, and I remember who this life made me.

Morning rotation in four hours. Another briefing, another client who treats us like a line item with guns. Maybe this next run is just escort work out by some dead refueler, like the chatter says. Maybe it is something darker, a job where navigators do strange things with paths and certain ships just never check in again. Either way, Alpha Warfrost marches, and Jaxon Hale keeps his hands steady and his voice level, because around here you do not survive by being the one who blinks first.

I keep telling myself I am going to stop writing these on company time, but the ship never tells on anyone and the ship is the only one who ever really listens.

Starwharf feels wrong tonight. Not broken exactly just off, like a song half a beat out of time. The lights in the forward cargo spine keep dimming and brightening for no reason, and Jared swears it is just the regulator cycling but I have watched that panel long enough to know when something is talking through our systems. Marcus called it "phantom telemetry" with that Trade Authority shrug of his, like as long as the invoice clears, ghosts can have their own stateroom.

I went through the manifest again at mid shift. Half the crates are marked as obsolete medical equipment destined for some LIST rock and the rest are just as bland, all neat codes and dull words that should make me sleepy. Instead, every time I scroll past that one routing flag, my head aches in the same place behind my eyes. Leah says it is just fatigue from staring at screens but she winces the same way and thinks I do not notice. No one will say it out loud, but we all know there is something riding this ship that is not in the paperwork.

I have been thinking a lot about home. Back on Mars, my mother brewed coffee strong enough to peel hull paint and always kept a little extra for whoever came through the door last. I still make a tiny pot at the end of my shift, even if the beans come from some generic vacuum packed brick and taste like they passed through half the Settled Systems. I pour a cup for myself and leave an empty mug across the table, like she used to for my father when he ran late at the docks. It is a silly ritual, but it makes this rented galley feel less like a cargo container and more like a kitchen.

Last week would have been the festival back in our block, when everyone strung lights between the hab stacks and the kids lit sparklers so bright they wiped out the stars for a moment. We would write the worst parts of the year on scraps of paper, burn them in a metal bowl, and then stay up too late eating whatever our neighbors cooked. Out here, the only lights are status LEDs and warning strobes, and the worst parts of the year are all stored on drives we are paid not to read. I miss the noise most of all. A freighter hum is not the same as a crowd laughing.

Healing is a strange thing in space. We get patched up by med kits and stimulants and keep flying, but the things that hurt do not just vanish because the bruise fades. There are days I can talk about the accident on my last posting without shaking, which I suppose means I am healing, but whenever the ship shutters the same way, my stomach drops and my hands go cold. Healing does not mean forgetting. It just means the wound has learned how to ache quietly instead of screaming every second.

Small things grind at me more than they should. That one locker door in the port corridor that squeaks no matter how much lubricant I feed it. Jared leaving his tools scattered on the diagnostics bench so I have to hunt for a zero wire tester every single time. The galley warmers that somehow turn every UC BattleMeal into something lukewarm and soggy, no matter what the wrapper promises. Leah hums the same four notes when she is anxious, over and over, and tonight she caught herself and went quiet so fast it made me more nervous than the humming.

I heard Marcus arguing on the comm with someone from a Trade Authority office earlier, voice low and clipped. I caught words like "override" and "far edge route" before he noticed I was in the passageway and shut it down. Later, in the mess, he cracked jokes like always but kept checking the corridor cameras out of the corner of his eye. People say the Authority is neutral, apolitical, all that brochure talk. Maybe that used to be true. Lately it feels like we are the middlemen for things nobody wants to admit exist, ferrying debts, secrets, and data that can not be allowed to sit still long enough for anyone to look at it too closely.

Some of the spacers we hauled cargo for back at Neon spoke about a woman who could lift memories clean out of your head, neat as pulling a chip from a socket. At the time I laughed, said Aurora makes people see all kinds of things. Now, with our logs flickering and blank spots in the transit records where there should be nothing but routine, I catch myself wondering if I would even know if someone had taken a piece of me. Maybe that is what scares me most that you can be hurt and half healed and never entirely sure what was lost.

I am going to finish this cup, leave the other one untouched across the table, and pretend my mother is just late from the docks. Tomorrow I will tighten the squeaky hinge again, sort Marcus's tools into proper order, and argue with Leah about whether the flickering lights are a problem or just "atmosphere." The ship keeps moving, the crates stay sealed, and whatever rides in our data channels keeps humming under everything we do. Some wounds, personal or otherwise, are not done bleeding yet.

Didn't sleep again.

Lights are off in the berth, but my head's still lit like a targeting HUD. Every time I close my eyes I see corridors, breach foam, the haze after flashbangs. There is always someone shouting, even when it's quiet. Back in uniform, they used to call it "operational overstimulation." Out here with the Cohort, we just call it "another night."

I keep thinking about that night on Vesta's dark side, before everything finally broke. The evac never came, comms were jammed, and the temperature in that half-collapsed depot kept dropping. We stacked in close under a busted heat duct, helmets off, armor plates clacking every time someone shivered. Mara Kincaid ended up pressed against my shoulder, knees touching mine, Riya Salazar pinning the other side. We said we were conserving body heat, but we all knew the real reason was that none of us wanted an inch of empty space between us and the next breathing heartbeat. I remember feeling every stutter of Mara's breath, every time Riya's hand flexed near her sidearm. Tight little circle of warmth in a dead place, and all I could think was how connected and how damned exposed I felt at the same time. If a shell had come through that roof we'd all have died in a single, perfect cluster.
