Outcast Cohort started that night, we just didn't know it yet.

Elena Ward brought me a "gift" a week after we cut ties with command. We were docked at some forgotten transfer ring, flushing tags and burning serials. She walked up, dropped a brand-new sidearm in my lap, cleaner than anything we'd been issued in months. No requisition forms, no crate logs, no questions. The grip was still warm like she'd been holding it too tight. I knew it hadn't been bought. I also knew better than to ask which armory suddenly turned up short. I just racked the slide, checked the chamber, thanked her. Old discipline gets twisted like that; we still follow the rules, we just write our own now.

Sleep used to be a safe house. Lately it's another AO. I lie down and the mind runs drills I didn't approve. I'm back in that slum block after curfew, tracer fire painting the walls, some officer's voice in my ear saying "minimize collateral" while the targeting overlay paints half the neighborhood as threats. I hear the kid I didn't see soon enough. I hear the doors being kicked in two floors over that weren't on our op order. I remember the smell of burning insulation mixed with whatever passed for dinner in that place. Waking up doesn't make it stop. It just changes the color palette.

The Cohort pretends we're fine after a job. Last month, when we pulled that convoy job clean, the celebrations hit fast and hard. Someone tapped a hidden cache, someone else sliced power to a cargo lounge, and suddenly that concrete bunker turned into a riot. Loud music off a battered speaker, cheap liquor poured into ration tins, Mara dancing like she was trying to unlearn every parade-ground step she'd ever been drilled on. Elena laughed for the first time in months, Riya climbed onto a crate and tried to toast "new loyalties" before she forgot the words. I remember the sound of glasses slamming and boots pounding, voices climbing higher and higher until, just as it felt like maybe we'd burned the ghosts out of us, the power flicked back on and it all evaporated. Next morning the place looked like any other staging area: empty shells, spilled drink, a few blood drops no one remembered earning.

I keep going back further, to something smaller. Before desertion, before rogue orders. Shore leave on some backwater rock, walking patrol off-duty because I couldn't switch it off. I saw a dockworker pop open a sealed crate, palms shaking, slide a couple of high-grade components into his jacket, then reseal the lid like nothing happened. Tiny theft, nothing compared to what we were moving in and out of that system. He looked around once, twice, never saw me. I should've called it in. Instead I watched, fascinated, at how easy it was for him to rewrite his little corner of the universe. No reports, no debrief, just need and nerve. I told myself it was beneath my concern. Maybe it was the first time I realized the rulebook was optional for some people, and that the sky didn't fall when they broke it.

Outcast Cohort lives in that space now. Between the orders we were given and the ones we can live with. Between the warmth of a squad pressed together in the dark and the fear that the person closest to you might be the one to pull the trigger when the next impossible command comes down. We walked away from official command because we were done carrying their secrets. I tell myself that every night, while the threats and violence replay in my head like a briefing I can't dismiss.  

Tomorrow we ship out again. Maybe I'll sleep on the way. More likely I'll sit in the troop bay, watching Mara strip her rifle, listening to Elena argue with Riya over routes, feeling the weight of that "gift" on my hip, and wondering at what point a soldier stops being one, and just becomes another man who learned the wrong lessons a little too well.

I used to mark days by op numbers. Now I am measuring them in transport shifts and how long my shoulders ache after carrying crates that are supposed to be "non-military." Old habits say log the weight, the route, the risk. New reality says you are just a contractor hauling cargo between forgotten depots on the edge of nowhere. The funny part is, the muscle memory does not care which flag you work under. It only knows the heft.

Damian says we should be grateful. "Low profile keeps us breathing," he tells me, while he triple checks a manifest for serials he swears he has seen before on another front. It is still work, still a chain of command, just with fewer patches on the uniforms and more lies in the job brief. Marcus shrugs and calls it "staying in shape between real fights." Caleb treats every run like a rehearsal for the day someone finally comes to close the file on us and writes a different ending.

We do not talk much about that last campaign. Not properly. You hear it at the edges. The way Adrian flinches if someone says "collateral" too easily. The way Serena cannot sleep when a ship's engines hold at a certain pitch, because it sounds like the drones did when they circled that target we were assured was all enemy infrastructure, right up until those flashes on the feed did not move like heat signatures should. I remember the briefing room after, the captain's voice too smooth while the holo showed our fire pattern and the word "necessary" hanging in the air like bad smoke. I remember the explicit order: no private recordings, no external copies.

Somewhere between that and the tribunal that never happened, we became a rumor instead of a unit. Command did not discipline us, they just reassigned files, changed designations, and let us drift toward the planetside work no one else wanted. That is when "Blacklisted Unit" stopped being a joke spat in a barracks and turned into something written, quietly, on certain contracts if you knew where to look. We left because we knew what it meant to be given that much silence. Or that is the story we tell ourselves.

Truth is, I did not walk away clean. I edged out sideways. I kept taking part-time gigs on the side, the kind of things you tell yourself are temporary: delivering sealed packages between checkpoints, sweeping hangar bays after hours, stocking shelves in a supply depot that smelled like dust and solvent. Nothing heroic, nothing that should have meant anything. Just mindless work where nobody expected me to make life and death calls. For the first time since enlistment, I thought maybe I could be small and unimportant and that it would be enough.

My partner at the time did not agree. He liked me better when I was the one taking the hard deployments so he could have an excuse to play the worried soldier waiting at home, collecting sympathy and favors on my rank. His needs filled every room we ever slept in. If I had a bruise, he had three stories about worse wounds. If I was exhausted, he was more exhausted. Somewhere across those years, his narrative ate mine. I stopped having preferences that were not measured against his. Stopped saying no. Stopped noticing that every decision bent around what he wanted: the posting, the hours, the leave requests. When the unit finally splintered off, part of me followed just to see who I was when the mission did not already belong to him.

It turns out I am still someone who checks corners, runs mental contingencies, and counts exits. Flea-ridden cargo relay or luxury starport, does not matter. That discipline is wired too deep. I still line my boots up at night. I still wake up at the time reveille used to sound, even if there is no bugle, no sergeant, just the hum of some underfunded life support.

Blacklisted keeps us close without pretending we are a family. We are bound by things we do not say out loud. Damian tracks the money paths, muttering about contractors whose names pop up in both our old op orders and our current "civilian" manifests. Caleb returns from every side job with a fresh rumor about a black archive where our after-action reports went to die. Marcus spends his downtime maintaining weapons we are officially not supposed to own anymore. None of us ask why a simple freight route needs those contingencies. We already know.

What I do not know is how to reconcile the person I was trained to be with the one who pushes a mop across a hangar at 0300, knowing the same floor once saw medevac teams sprinting past. I used to believe in clarity: us, them, objective, extraction. Now the lines are layered like old scars, hard to tell which came first or what cut deepest. Maybe that is why I write this instead of sending another message I will regret to a command net that probably flags my name in red.

We may be off the books, but the war is still inside our heads. And on nights like this, when the cargo bay is quiet and the stars beyond the bulkhead do not care who we killed for whose orders, I am not sure if we left the chain of command or if it still has a hold on us, just without the courtesy of a uniform.

I keep thinking about the way the ship sounds when everyone else is asleep. The environmental fans settle into this low, even hum, and you can hear the tiny corrections from the thrusters come through the hull like someone tapping metal knuckles on a bulkhead far away. On nights like that, the corridors feel too long for a courier this small, like Ironkeel's been stretched out to make room for ghosts and overdue invoices.

Kellan was on watch when I walked past the bridge earlier. He snapped his datapad shut the second he heard my boots. Said he was recalibrating route updates from Trade Authority central, but the way he palmed that chip into his pocket looked more like a street dealer than a nav tech. Maybe I am just tired. Maybe everyone guards something on a ship like this. But the last time I saw anyone move that fast, it was a Crimson Fleet broker trying to hide a side agreement from his own captain.

Nadia caught me staring and gave me that look that says stop making trouble with your eyes, Roland. She trusts Kellan because he smooths our registry pings, makes sure the inspectors see what they expect to see, nothing more. She says a ship like ours only keeps flying by having someone who knows how to blur lines in the paperwork. Hard to argue when the Authority lets us run half-broken, hauling crates no one wants to ask about. Still, I swear I saw an extra destination flagged in the nav queue this morning, one that was there for a second and then just... wasn't.

Maris tried to laugh it off backstage in the commons, saying if Kellan is running a side hustle, she hopes he remembers who shares air with him. She has this way of making every bad idea sound like a joke until it is not. Elena, on the other hand, barely said a word at dinner. She kept glancing at the bulkhead where the route display sits behind the panel, like she expected it to start bleeding numbers onto the floor. When I asked what was wrong, she muttered something about hearing our transponder hiccup twice in a row while she was on maintenance. According to her, that only happens when someone is teaching the ship a new name.

Kellan asked me about home today. Not in the usual small-talk way either. He waited until Nadia was out of earshot and then just asked, dead middle of a cargo inventory, what I miss most. So I told him about lantern night back on my habitat. We would shut off every main light, even the corridor strips, and everyone lit these tiny, cheap paper lanterns with battery candles inside. You would line them up along the walls and floors, all the way down the spine of the station. The air scrubbers would push just enough current that they drifted very slowly, like they were walking on their own. The idea was simple: for one night a year, you let things move without course corrections, see where they end up.

The first time I talked about it here, Maris loved it. She tried to rig a version in the cargo bay with spare packing foam and little glow tags, but Nadia shut it down the moment she saw us. "No floating junk near my manifests," she said. Kellan just watched, leaning in the hatch, smiling that soft, distant smile of his. When I explained you were supposed to let go and not adjust anything once the lanterns were drifting, he chuckled and said, "Sounds like a good way to find out who cannot stand giving up control." Nobody else really understood why I went quiet after that.

These days, when I mention lantern night, most of the crew asks the same question: did people ever crash into each other in the dark, get hurt. That is what they worry about. Not the point of letting things be, but the liability forms afterward. I guess that is the Trade Authority mindset baked into bone. The funny thing is, Kellan seems more interested in the part where you shut off the main systems and trust the little lights to be enough. He keeps coming back to that, asking how long we left the corridors dark, how far the lanterns got before the rotation brought them drifting back.

Maybe he is just homesick in his own way, looking for some ritual to make this rustbucket feel less like a loan with engines. Or maybe he is mapping the idea onto something in his head, a way to let the ship slide for a while, unguided, while he watches from the shadows. I do not know. I tell myself I am imagining the way his fingers tap out neat little trajectories on the table when he thinks no one is watching. I tell myself a lot of things lately.

Anyway, tomorrow we cut closer to that dust-heavy corridor everyone keeps arguing about. Some say it is just a timing quirk in the traffic updates, others swear they saw ships vanish from scopes for minutes at a time and come back with fresh scorch marks they did not have before. Nadia says as long as the Authority stamps our route, it is not our problem. Maris rolled her eyes and said if the pay clears, we can drift through ash for all she cares. Me, I am going to double-check my suit seals before we hit that patch. Traditions are one thing. Letting go of control is another. And lately, it feels like someone else has been practicing both on our behalf.

Started the day polishing a rifle I do not officially own, for a unit that does not officially exist, in a war everyone swears is over.  
Funny how the hands still remember the drill even after the flag is gone. Safety check, breach, feed, sights. I could do it blind and half sedated. Some days I think I have.

Bloodied Platoon was not born; it just failed to die when the rest of the regiment did. They rotated us home, handed us discharge papers that still smelled of printer ink, and pretended nobody heard the screaming through the bulkheads on the way back. Elias Marrow tried to go straight for a while, last I heard. Took a contract with some corporate security outfit that promised him "structure" and "clear rules of engagement." Ronan Keats laughed himself sick when he told me, then went quiet in the same breath, like even the joke hurt to say out loud. Marcus Ellery never even bothered pretending; he walked off the shuttle, cashed his payout, and started recruiting us into this little ghost platoon before the ink dried.

I was the slow one. Thought I could live like a civilian. Rented a coffin stack in a "quiet" block, took a job watching doors for people who thought a Grendel on the wall made them invincible. I told myself I was just using the training, not breaking any oaths. The uniform went into a locker, but the nightmares did not. I started wandering at night, just to get away from my own head, drifting into the parts of town where the lights flicker and the law pretends the transit line just skips that stop. Bars where the music covers the sound of fists meeting bone. Alleys that smell like coolant leaks and cheap antiseptic. 

At first it was just walking. Then it was stepping in when a pack of dockside kids picked a fight with the wrong spacer. Then it was escorting a cardsharp home in exchange for a cut, backing down a couple of debt collectors who did not realize ex military were off their usual script. It felt good, in a twisted way. Simple problems. Visible threats. No intel briefings, no double speak in the orders. Just "those guys are trouble, stand between them and the soft targets." I stopped going back to my quiet block as much. The trouble districts felt more honest.

Of course, trouble sees you back. Rumors followed us from the old days. The op where civilian signatures vanished off the tactical map during a "localized kinetic adjustment." The patrol that walked into a village, walked out five bodies heavier, then got told the footage was "corrupted" and the after action report needed "edits for clarity." I remember a debrief room with no windows, a colonel who never removed his gloves, and a line about how sometimes "exposure to the full truth impairs operational efficiency." We all nodded. We all signed. Later, over contraband bottles, we pretended we had misheard. Time passes, but the way everyone avoids that one campaign patch tells the real story.

That is the trust that broke, not in some firefight but in a conference room under cold white light. When command starts rewriting history in front of the survivors, you either swallow it or you walk. Bloodied Platoon walks. We still keep discipline in our own way. We check each other's kit before a job. We run drills. We settle arguments with sparring, not bullets. Elias, if he comes back, will probably try to push us toward some code like we used to have. Marcus pretends we are just "professionals," but his eyes go dead whenever someone mentions the old insignia. Ronan masks everything with jokes until he has had too much to drink, then he gets real quiet and stares at doorways like an ambush is coming.

Me, I am stuck in the middle. I know I will never wear a sanctioned uniform again. I also know I still move like I am waiting for inspection. I do not kid myself that we are heroes now. Half what we do would have gotten us court martialed back then, if courts had been honest. We take contracts that keep the worst people in check and others that just pay us to look dangerous in the right direction. The streets where I spend my nights do not care about the difference. They just know that when things go loud, someone in a Bloodied Platoon harness steps in and makes sure only certain people walk away.

Sometimes, in those parts of town, I catch myself scanning faces like they are targets on a range. Evaluating lines of fire, cover, probabilities of escalation. It feels too natural. I tell myself I am maintaining readiness. That is what we called it when we could still look each other in the eye without flinching. But there is a reason I do not go back to the quiet blocks much anymore. The silence there leaves too much room for the old orders to echo. Out here, with neon flicker and broken pavement and the hum of illegal grav drives overhead, I can pretend that choosing my own fights makes me clean.

I know better. But tomorrow the Platoon has a meet, and this time Marcus says the client used phrases that sound uncomfortably like the ones I heard in that windowless debrief room. If they are trying to hire the ghosts they buried, they are going to find out how bad an idea that is.

I used to think the noise was the hard part. Engines, gunfire, squad comms all screaming over each other. Turns out it is the silence after that gets you. Barracks quiet. No orders. Just your own head playing back every call you followed and every one you ignored.

Grim Cohort feels like that silence weaponized. On paper we are deserters, mercs with better posture. In practice we are what is left over when you cut the chain of command and everything ugly that used to be contained inside an op order spills out into the open. We still stack gear the same way, still clear rooms on muscle memory, still snap to when Marcus Reddick gives a hand signal, but we are not answering to any flag anymore. That is supposed to feel like freedom. Some nights it just feels like falling without a target.

I keep thinking about that convoy job near the end. We were told it was logistics, high-value components, nothing civilian. Rules of engagement came down cleaner than I had heard in months, all the right words about proportional force and minimizing collateral. Then we hit the wreckage afterward and I saw those containers cracked open, not hardware, just families who paid the wrong middleman. Debrief said sensor spoof, hostile disguises, the usual excuses. Marcus stared at the floor the whole briefing, jaw clenched so hard I could hear it. Official statement went one way; every man and woman who pulled a trigger walked out knowing we had been used to send a message.

That was when the crowd I ran with started to shift. We had always been the loud ones in the mess, the ones one argument away from putting a chair through a bulkhead. After that op the arguments got quieter, sharper, all about who signed what, who knew what, whether any of us were still soldiers or just tools. A captain from upstairs vanished into "reassignment." A couple of our own disappeared into medical and never came back. The Cohort was born in those gaps, in the space where trust used to live.

I remember the night we cut loose. No speeches. Just gear bags packed a little too tight, weapons checked one extra time. Marcus came to my rack, nodded once, and that was it. Walking off base in full kit felt more wrong than any firefight I have ever been in. I kept waiting for someone to shout, for alarms, for an order to stand down. Nothing. They were happy enough to let the problem walk itself out the airlock, I guess. Easier than holding anyone higher up to account.

Out here, work comes easy. There is always some governor who wants deniable muscle, some corp exec who wants a dirty job done by people who still move like an organized unit. The Cohort keeps standards. Weapons clean. Formations tight. No chewing through civvies, no scare tactics for fun. That is the line we draw so we can still look each other in the eye. But every contract we take is another step away from the oaths we swore in cleaner uniforms, and I feel that distance stretching every time I see our insignia stenciled on a crate instead of a shoulder.

I hear rumors from the old channels sometimes, buried chatter on encrypted bands we are not supposed to still have access to. Talk of ops written off as "navigational errors," of ships that never made it to port and were quietly marked as hardware losses. People whisper about consultants and analysts rewriting routes and data so the blame never lands where it should. It sounds familiar in all the worst ways. Someone up there is still rearranging the board while grunts bleed on the tiles, and we are down here pretending we are done playing.

Thing is, I do not know if we are any better. We choose which contracts to take, but we still take them. We tell ourselves we are protecting each other now, not some abstract ideal. That is true. When the rounds start coming in, I am not thinking about flags or mottos. I am thinking about Marcus on my flank, about the others holding the line because if we do not, nobody will. That loyalty is real. It is also the same muscle they pulled on when they told us to "secure the convoy" and not look too closely at who was inside.

Most days I can live with the weight of what we walked away from. Some nights the gravity shifts. I see that line of containers again, hear the briefing officer reciting doctrine like scripture while the projector conveniently skips the worst of the footage. I remember how my old crowd vibrated with anger, how close we came to turning it inward instead of upward. Maybe that is why we left when we did. If we had stayed, the first real argument would not have stopped at a broken chair.

So here I am, writing in a cheap slate instead of filing after-action reports, trying to convince myself that this is a step toward something better, not just another variant of the same old game. Grim Cohort looks after its own. We hit hard. We get paid. We pretend the targets we take now are cleaner than the ones we used to. And when the quiet settles in after a job, when the echoes fade and nobody is issuing orders, I listen to my own breathing and wonder how many more times I can pull a trigger and still tell myself I walked away for the right reasons.

Did a lookout shift on the upper grates tonight, same as every other cold, buzzing evening in this hole.  
Breath fogging in front of the busted vent, eyes burning from recycled air and cheap smoke, counting the same three doors and the same six cameras that barely work.  
Darius Holt was late swapping with me again, said he was running a courier run down to the lower level, but I know that look he gets when he is actually off doing side work for someone other than the Lords.  
Nobody says it out loud, because as long as credits and chems land in the same crate, nobody wants to know whose logo is stamped on the underside.

The day blend is always the same grind.  
Wake up on a stained mattress with someone else's music still playing in the hallway, sweep shell casings and broken glass into the corner, then wait for Rico Vance to bang on the pipe and yell out the rota.  
Lookout shift.  
Courier run.  
Sit in the dark, guarding a door to nothing, in case a message comes from the next floor up.  
Half the time the orders never come, just rumors floating down the stairwell: a missing shipment, a rival crew moving in closer, some new boss name none of us have seen face to face.  
We run packages anyway, because standing still feels worse than getting shot.

Mara Kincaid slid me a folded scrap tonight, said it came from someone who pays attention to traffic patterns.  
Dock traffic, ship routes, strange gaps nobody wants to admit are there.  
She said a convoy went off-chart a while back, that someone has been selling bad directions on purpose, and there is word a hunter is following that trail.  
We are small-time by comparison, but the halls started buzzing the second that rumor hit, like everyone could already feel crosshairs somewhere behind the walls.  
Talon Mercer laughed it off, said the sky is always killing people, nothing new.  
But I noticed he moved his stash closer to the emergency hatch afterward.

Funny thing is, all this noise feels less stressful than regular life topside ever did.  
Back before I fell in with the Lords, I spent half my days in lines.  
Lines at the food shop, staring at flickering adverts for things I could never afford.  
Lines at clinics while some overworked medic told me to "come back next cycle" for a test that might not even matter.  
Lines at transit stations, shuffling forward in that dead, quiet crowd while waiting for a shuttle that would already be full when the doors hissed open.  
You stand there long enough, you realize nobody's watching you, nobody will remember if you step left and disappear somewhere worse.

Down here, at least, you get remembered.  
Not fondly, not gently, but your name gets said.  
Keira Morrow still owes me half a cut from that last courier job and every time she walks past, she flashes this guilty half smile that says she hasn't forgotten.  
That means something, in its own crooked way.  
We bleed together on these runs, share the same cheap med packs and the same bad liquor when the night finally slows.  
You hoist a crate next to someone while sirens echo in the distance, or sit shoulder to shoulder on the stairwell counting the seconds between footsteps above, and suddenly the person next to you feels like family in a way your blood never did.

I think that is what loyalty looks like, for people like us.  
Not speeches.  
Just sleepless nights on the same concrete, taking turns with the only half-working rifle, whispering about what we will do "once this score lands" even though it never quite does.  
You get used to the idea that if you fall, they will at least drag your body back through the door so you are not left out in the corridor for the cleaners.  
That is our version of kindness.

Still, there is a hard edge under it all.  
Darius told me in a low voice that some of the jobs we run are not just for chems and parts anymore, that messages are moving through us, codes hidden in shipping logs and transit stamps.  
He said someone upstairs is using the Lords as a relay because nobody bothers to audit criminals.  
I laughed, but it stuck with me.  
Feels like we are standing on rails someone else laid, waiting for a train we will never see, only the impact.

And then there is him.  
I almost did not write about him, but this is supposed to be honest, right.  
The one I let inside before I ever met the Lords.  
I like to pretend that the gang life broke me, that the constant tension and the blood under my nails turned me into this sharp, hollow thing.  
Truth is, the relationship broke me long before it officially ended.  
By the time he finally said the words, there was not much left to shatter.  
The Lords just picked up the pieces, filed them down, and found a use for whatever remained.

Sometimes, when I am on lookout and the corridor is quiet, I remember standing in those old lines with him.  
Arguing softly about nothing important, just to fill the empty space.  
I thought the boredom would kill me then.  
Now I know better.  
Boredom did not kill me.  
Loyalty did.  
Or whatever twisted version of it I keep chasing down here in the charred basement, waiting for the next order that might never come.

Darius is snoring again.  
Funny how that sound means "safe" to me now.

We used to joke that Outcast Platoon sleeps lighter than a minefield, but put enough klicks between you and the last artillery barrage and suddenly everyone remembers how to breathe. Marcus is on watch, pretending he is not staring holes through the horizon. Elias is stripping down that crate of rifles we lifted last week, spreading parts out on the deck like he is laying out cards to see if fate will finally give us a decent hand.

Command said we were the problem. Every argument in those last months circled back to that, no matter what started it. Civilians hit by someone else's misfire  our fault because we did not "create enough separation." Intel omissions that got us ambushed  our fault because we "should have anticipated unsanctioned hostiles." I remember sitting in that narrow debrief room, stale coffee and recycled air, listening as the brass recast their own bad calls as our "failure to adapt." Truth never stood a chance; the loop always closed on us.

Before all this, I had a tiny apartment above a freight corridor on Gagarin. Rust-stained walls, busted climate control, one flickering strip light that hummed louder than the haulers below. Dishes piled in the sink, laundry everywhere, a half-assembled rifle on the kitchen table next to an open Meal Pack. Messy, yes, but harmless. Some nights I wish I were still there, cursing the neighbors instead of trying to remember which of my friends helped bury which body.

I keep replaying that corridor on New Thessaly, the one that should have been clear. We moved as a column, armor scraping bulkheads, comms hissing with cross-talk. Then the first charge went off and everything became smoke, sound, and shrapnel. I could not see, only feel someone clamp down on my hand through two layers of glove and plate, fingers shaking but refusing to let go. Turned out it was Elias. There was nothing tender in it  just two people refusing to get separated in a kill box someone else had signed off as "secure."

Out here, we eat what we can steal, trade for, or scrape off forgotten manifests. Marcus once turned a crate of expired ration bars and a bottle of questionable whiskey into what he swore was a "proper dinner." We sat cross-legged on the cargo bay floor, passing a dented tin cup between us, picking melted wrappers off the heating element of a stolen camp stove. Our uniforms are more patch than fabric now  duct tape, field stitching, bits of Spacer and Crimson gear we have cut down to fit. Darius wears an old unit patch under his new jacket, edges frayed, colors dulled. He says it is just habit, but I see how his hand drifts there whenever someone mentions court-martials.

We never talk plainly about the operation that broke us. Officially, it does not exist. No records, no reprimands, just a series of "reassignments" and "structural realignments." Unofficially, we share fragments. Marcus remembers a briefing holo that did not match what we found on the ground. Elias remembers the smell of burned composite and something worse under it. I remember a colonel's voice over the channel telling us to hold position while the sky was already full of falling metal. Afterward they said we were insubordinate for pulling back. Afterward they said anything that did not fit the report was "fog of war."

That is how you end up crawling through abandoned bunkers and derelict stations, running jobs that would have been called treason back when we still had rank. Rumors drift our way  about hidden jump tests that went wrong, about ships whose logs do not match their wreckage, about orders given off the record and buried the same day. Sometimes the chatter lines up too neatly with what we saw, too neatly with why Outcast Platoon exists at all. I tell myself I do not care about the why anymore, only the pay and the people beside me. It is a lie I am still learning to tell convincingly.

We abandoned command, but we did not abandon each other. We still clear each other's angles, still count heads after a fight, still check seals and mags before we move. Outcast, sure. Rogue, if that makes them feel better. But the discipline is bone-deep. When Darius snaps awake mid-night, hand already on his rifle, he relaxes only when he has eyes on all of us. When Marcus sharpens his knife, it is not nerves; it is ritual. When I write like this, it is not sentiment; it is inventory. Taking stock of what we have left that is not rusted through.

I know if they ever drag us into another debrief room, the story will be the same. Whatever went wrong will be pinned to our chests like a medal we never wanted. Every question will spiral back to our supposed failures: why we left, why we fought back, why we did not just accept the version of events that kept everyone's hands clean.  

But when I remember that cramped little apartment, and that burning corridor where someone squeezed my hand so hard my fingers went numb, and this patched-up gear that keeps us alive one more day, I know who I trust. It is not the ones re-editing logs in some quiet office. It is the ones sharing the last ration bar in the dark, waiting for the next bad order we will finally refuse to follow.

I keep telling myself I am going to stop counting how many roofs we have slept under this month, but I still do the math without meaning to. Four hab-blocks, two cargo holds, one condemned barracks on a rock nobody bothered to name. Different ceilings, same feeling: bag half-packed by the door, boots pointed toward the next exit. Disavowed Guard stays alive by never letting the dust settle on our footprints, Marcus likes to say, but sometimes it just feels like we are running laps around the same drain.

The old discipline will not die, no matter how many insignia we burn. I still fold my kit the way they drilled into us back in the line, still sleep light, still hear the cadence in my head when I count ammo. Elena jokes that I am going to die with my boots aligned to regulation angles. She says it with a smile, but there is strain behind it. She was the one who signed off on those after-action reports back when we wore the uniform, the ones where the numbers did not quite match the bodies we stepped over. She never talks about that, not straight, but I see it in the way she studies orders now like they might carry a second bullet hidden between the lines.

Darius takes it different. He laughs too loud, too long, like if he stops the silence will fill up with all the things we saw and pretended not to. He is the one who reminds us why we walked away: the patrol that was never meant to come back, the evac window that mysteriously narrowed, the way command talked about "asset preservation" when we asked about missing civilians. We never got the full truth, just redacted briefings and a new deployment. Then one day the orders came down that did not make tactical or human sense, and enough of us decided we were finished dying for someone's ledger.

Still, for all the righteous talk, I do not kid myself about what the Guard is now. We hop system to system, contract to contract, making enemies on every side while pretending we are above the games. Rival crews watch us, test us, wait for us to slip. We stay ahead of them by moving faster, hitting harder, trusting less. That last one takes the biggest toll. Every new "safe spot" is just another place to study doorways and sightlines and decide who in the room you could kill first if it turned.

The worst moments are when the boss sends for us. Does not matter where we are hiding that week a rusted hangar on a forgotten moon, a converted freight bay in some overbuilt station the feeling is the same. Someone comes to the door, says my name, and my gut goes cold before my brain catches up. You walk down the corridor running two parallel sets of possibilities: it is a job, or it is judgment. He will hand you a datapad or a bullet. I have watched good operators walk in standing tall and come out in a bag, all because they thought their questions or their conscience mattered more than the unit staying "clean."

So every morning, I wake up and take stock. Rifle, armor, sidearm, knife, spare mag, backup credit chit. Then faces. Marcus, who has pulled me out of more than one burning corridor but who has also been taking extra long briefings with the boss lately. Elena, who still thinks like an officer and knows where all our skeletons are buried. Darius, who sleeps with his back to the wall and his hand on the grip, even when we are supposedly among friends. I ask myself, if one of them decided tonight was the night I disappeared, would I see it coming? Most days the honest answer is no.

When the fear gets too loud, I fix things. Stupid little things. I rewired a cracked wrist-chrono last week, spent an hour coaxing life out of bent contacts and a dying microcell. Before that it was a busted music chip Marcus salvaged from some spacer dive, and before that the cheap handheld game Elena uses to pretend she is not watching the room. It does not matter what it is as long as it is small, broken, and ignorant of orders and loyalties. Circuits do not lie. If something fails, you can find the fault with a scope and a steady hand. I wish people were that simple.

I try not to think about the classified op that never officially happened, the one where the target list changed mid-flight and somehow our own people ended up inside the blast radius. They wrote it up as equipment failure; those of us who survived signed the kind of papers that erase years from the record. Maybe that was the first time I understood that the insignia on my chest did not mean what I thought it did. Maybe that is why, when the Disavowed Guard whispered your name, it sounded less like treason and more like a lifeline.

Now the only oath that matters is the one we have to each other, thin and frayed as it is. We watch the doors, we keep our kit tight, we move before our shadows get too familiar. And every time I finish fixing some useless little gadget, I catch myself thinking about the men and women we left behind, still marching to orders written by ghosts. I tell myself we are different. That when our time comes, it will be because of the enemies we chose, not the ones our own command chose for us. Then I put the chrono back together, set the alarm, and lie down under another unfamiliar ceiling, wondering if I will wake to a job, an execution, or nothing at all.

Caleb says keeping a diary is a liability. Darius calls it evidence. They are both right, and I am writing anyway. Old habits from field debriefs, I guess. You learn to put things down clean and clinical, then scrub out anything that sounds like a feeling. Feelings got you reassigned, or evaluated, or quietly sidelined. In the Regiment, they get you killed slower. Different kind of mercy.

I remember the first time I tried to say something honest on record, back in the service. Not even a protest, just a question about a strike package that did not match the intel we had seen on the ground. The room went quiet, the recorder light blinked, and the debrief officer smiled that thin smile that never reached his eyes. The report that came back had my question neatly cut out, but my file got a new tag and my next posting was to a unit where nobody asked anything ever again. You learn: speak the party line, or do not speak. The punishment was always soft at first, like they were giving you a chance to correct yourself.

Sometimes I think that is why we walked. Not the big betrayals, not the final bad order, but the slow grind of having to pretend you did not see what you saw. Whole towns we were told were "logistical nodes" that looked a lot like civilian grids. A corridor we cleared that was supposed to be "uninhabited," except for the faces that stayed with you when you closed your eyes. The after action briefings with numbers instead of names, probabilities instead of bodies. They kept calling it collateral and necessary, like if you said those words enough times they would turn into something cleaner.

Fractured Regiment is not clean. We tell ourselves we are different from the outfits we run against, but we move the same way they do. One safe house to another, one backwater dock to the next derelict hangar, always leaving before rival crews or old flags can pin us down. We sleep in shifts, weapons within arm's reach, boots never far from the hatch. You learn to tell how long you can stay in a place by the way the locals look at you on day two. Respect turns to curiosity, curiosity turns to calculation. That is when we move.

Lena jokes that we are ghosts chasing ghosts, but I see the tension in her hands when she cleans her rifle for the third time in a night. She still calls Darius "sir" sometimes, like the rank is stuck in her throat. He pretends not to hear it. Caleb pretends he does not miss having a uniform that meant something. We all pretend a lot of things. Old discipline is hard to shake. We still stack gear like there will be an inspection, still check corners like some invisible instructor is grading us. The difference is, now when orders feel wrong, we ignore them instead of saluting.

There was a moment once, between jumps, that felt like it might be enough to make all of this worth it. We were parked in a shadowed orbit, hull lights off, engines cooling. No alarms, no rival pings on the scope. The only sound was life support and Lena's breathing where she had dozed off beside me in the crew bay, head resting against my shoulder. I remember the warmth, the weight of her there, and the way Darius had laughed, actually laughed, at some stupid story about training days. It felt...safe. That is the word I am afraid to use. Safe, like maybe we could just drift there forever and no one would come looking.

Of course, the alert chimed a few minutes later a patrol sweep coming in just wide enough to be coincidence, just close enough to be a problem. We scattered to stations, masks back on, voices clipped and professional. The softness of that moment evaporated like it had never happened, but my shoulder remembered the pressure long after the straps of the crash harness bit in. I caught Lena looking at me once during the burn, something almost like apology in her eyes, like she resented being seen as anything but mission ready. I understood. Tenderness is a liability out here. You can not count it in the plan.

The worst part is knowing that even in our stolen moments of peace, the past sits in the corner of the room. I think about that night planetside, rain hammering the shattered roofs while we huddled under a half collapsed awning, sharing a canteen and a ration bar we had not yet divided by calories. Mortars in the distance, comms full of confusion, but for a heartbeat it was just the four of us, laughing at nothing, breath fogging in the cold. I knew, with a kind of cold clarity, that it could be the last time we were together and still mostly whole. I wanted to say something real then to tell them that if one of us did not walk out, I was glad we had at least that. Instead I made a joke about the food. Everyone laughed, and the moment passed. Next morning we moved, like always.

So here we are, rogues with standards, deserters who still wake up at zero five out of habit. There are stories whispered about us now, the Fractured Regiment that takes contracts nobody else will, that walks away from payouts if the intel smells wrong. Some call us idealists, some call us cowards who flinched too late. The truth is less clean. We are just trying to find a way to live with what we have done and what we might still have to do. And I am still afraid that if I ever speak that truth out loud, someone, somewhere, will find a way to punish us for it.

Darren says today's haul was "clean," like that means anything out here.

We cracked a commuter ring over Narion this shift, just me, Darren, and two new riggers whose names I keep forgetting. Hull was buckled along the spine, atmosphere long gone, but the emergency strips were still pulsing every few meters, weak red glows chasing us through the dark. I hate when the lights still work. Makes the wreck feel like it remembers being alive.

Darren kept on the channel about fast cuts, get in, pull the drives, strip the avionics, no sightseeing. I nodded and did my thing, torch singing through bulkheads, but every time my faceplate crossed a viewport I caught my own reflection and, behind it, that endless black. I could feel those old training cams on me again, the ones they bolted into the corridors "for safety." Always watching, always logging. Back then, every misstep got replayed by some supervisor in a warm office. After a while, I stopped feeling safe anywhere I wasn't being watched, like the only thing between me and the void was somebody else's judgement.

Funny how that wires you. Even now, drifting through a dead ship with just Darren on point, I catch myself wishing there was a camera in the corner, some eye that'd see it if a brace failed or a patch let go. Then I remember there's no playback if the whole section rips loose and drifts forever.

We hit the galley and the newbies started pawing through personal lockers, looking for anything with a charge left. Scrapline rule says anything with a serial goes in the official bin, anything "personal" gets split if no family claimant shows. Unspoken rule says anything you can hide inside your suit you don't talk about. One kid tucked a pair of earrings so fast I almost laughed. Almost called him on it, too. I floated close, visor to visor, and just looked at him. Said nothing. Watched his breath fog his glass. He stammered an excuse about "tagging them for inventory" and I felt this cold weight settle in my chest when I realized he believed I could make his life miserable with three words on the crew channel. That sudden hush on comms, the way Darren turned his helmet just so, waiting to see what I'd say that was the first time I understood I could scare someone without lifting a tool. It felt ugly and good at the same time. Disturbingly easy.

Sometimes, when I think too hard about all the ways this work can kill us, my head goes back to that night on the old breaker barge, before we signed on with Scrapline proper. Docking clamps had failed and the whole habitat ring shuddered for hours, groaning like it wanted to tear itself apart. No one said it out loud, but we all thought the welds were going to go. I ended up in a storage locker with another junior tech, both of us crammed between crates of patch kits, breathing each other's recycled air. We pressed so close our harnesses dug into our ribs. I remember his gloves on my arm, just needing to feel someone solid while the metal around us flexed. We whispered whatever came to mind weather reports, old spacer jokes, how we'd rather die quick in a blowout than slow in a stuck suit. I felt more connected in that stupid cramped space than any briefing room since. And still, underneath it, there was this raw terror that if the hull opened, we'd die together and no one would ever even know we'd been afraid.

Funny the things you miss, too. Back home there was a corner kiosk under the transit line that sold these greasy seaweed snacks in crinkled foil. You could grab a pack and a lukewarm TerraBrew in one hand, feel the weight of both swinging as you walked back to a tiny room that at least had a ceiling. On bad days I can almost taste the salt and burnt oil when I crack my helmet seal after a long shift, only it is just stale air and other people's sweat.

When I started with the Breakers, they only trusted me with the "safe" jobs. Seal checks. Tagging scrap bundles. Running tether lines from the barge to hull anchors. Mundane, they called it. But every line you clip is another chance to drift, every hatch you open in a dead ship is a bet that what is on the other side is just vacuum and not a pressure pocket ready to tear it off its hinges. You learn quick or you float. First time I soloed a tether run, I remember my hands shaking so hard I could barely thumb the carabiner. Not from the cold. From imagining every screw failing at once.

And then there are the stories they only half tell. Rough talk in the mess about a freighter that jumped on a shortcut and came back wrong, or never came back at all. A survey vessel that still pings on old scanners, buried under ghost coordinates nobody will admit to owning. Darren pretends not to believe, but he cuts the power to his suit beacons whenever we hit certain long-abandoned lanes, like he is hoping not to catch the eye of whatever chewed those ships up. Some nights I tell myself it is all just bad math and worse luck. Other nights, looking at the patterns in the salvage reports, I wonder if someone out there is tracing routes on purpose, deciding which hulls get to die.

Anyway, today the wreck was "clean." We got our drives and boards. No corpses, no strange echoes, no missing hours in the logs. And still, when I closed my eyes in the airlock just now, I could feel that old camera lens searching for me, waiting to see whether I step left or right before the deck drops out.

Jordan always says this is a waste of time.  
Elena just shrugs and checks the door seals one more time while I write.  
Tara laughs and calls it "poor woman's therapy."  
Maybe they are all right.  
But tonight the hum of the reactor is too close to the pitch of old artillery, and if I do not put these ghosts somewhere, they will sit in my hands when I need them steady.

I keep thinking about that day on the carrier deck, the one we do not name out loud.  
The alarms were already howling, atmosphere bleeding off in a white scream, and I was on my back under a ruptured bulkhead when he fell into my arms.  
I had patched that man up a dozen times for stupid cuts and training burns, teased him about being too pretty for the infantry, watched him fall asleep over ration coffee more nights than I can count.  
Then the deck shook, lights went dead, and the only thing left was the weight of him and the way his fingers dug into my vest like he was trying to hold on to me and his own lungs at the same time.  
Love and loss braided together in one long exhale that ended before the medevac could even pretend to start.  
The after-action summary called it "swift casualty evacuation failure."  
They never mentioned that I kept talking to his body until the bulkhead crews pried us apart.

Feels like every argument since then loops back to that day, one way or another.  
In the unit.  
With command.  
Even with myself.  
Any time something goes sideways, you can feel it in the room, see it in the way eyes settle on me a half-second too long.  
If I step wrong, if I question an order, somebody eventually drags it in, like a knife pulled out of storage: "You froze on the deck, Ellison."  
Never mind the chaos, the impossible calculations.  
The story is simpler when I am the hinge everything broke on.  
Soon you start telling it to yourself that way, just to match the file.

Funny, I did not grow up with this constant noise.  
There were afternoons when I would sit on the stoop outside our block, boots scuffing at cracked concrete, watching people drift by with nothing sharper than grocery bags in their hands.  
No plans, no missions, just a slow river of neighbors and strangers, laughing too loudly at dumb jokes, arguing about which vendor had the better fruit.  
I would lean back against warm stone, drink something sweet and cheap from the corner stall, and imagine that the world ended at the far tram stop.  
Surface-level problems.  
Rain, rent, who owed who a drink.  
Sometimes I miss that smallness so much it hurts.

Back then, affection was a ration.  
You did the chores, you kept your voice low, you got a nod, maybe a hand in your hair if you were lucky.  
Say the wrong thing, come home with the wrong bruise, and the warmth snapped off like a switch.  
I learned pretty quickly that love arrived when I met expectations and vanished when I did not.  
By the time I put on a uniform, the pattern was already etched in.  
Stand straight, shoot straight, do not ask why.  
The pat on the shoulder after a dirty op, the extra leave chit slid across a desk, the quiet "good work, Ellison" that came right after we "re-aligned" a report about civilian traffic getting caught in the wrong corridor.  
Affection as reward.  
Silence as punishment.  
I did not notice how much it steered me until I was already too far along the vector.

Wayward Taskforce is supposed to be different.  
That is the joke.  
Jordan calls us strays who finally picked our own handler.  
Elena pretends she is only here because she has nowhere else to be, but she still polishes her rifle like we're due for inspection.  
Tara talks big about being free agents, but she flinches when someone says "debrief" too loudly.  
We left the flag, walked out of the barracks, cut the transponders, yet somehow the same patterns follow.  
We just argue louder now.  
And the crowd we run with feels permanently one breath away from violence, arguments snapping from mission planning into threats before anyone can blink.  
It is not so far from those stairwell fights outside my old block, just scaled up, with better weapons and uglier stakes.

I keep catching whispers about sanitized wrecks, about navigation data that does not match the scars on the hulls, about one engineer-turned-myth tampering with beacons in the dark.  
Classified debriefs we half-heard before we walked out spoke of "necessary adjustments" to war records, of listening posts that went quiet at very convenient times.  
Backchannel chatter says some of those messes are on our old ledger, missions we ran without knowing who was really steering the ship.  
Some nights, when we are charting our next aimless hop between systems, I wonder if Wayward Taskforce is actually walking away or just being turned like any other piece, kept where we can still be used to clean up what nobody else wants to touch.

I do not know if leaving official command was betrayal, survival, or both.  
The oaths still ring in my ears when I am half-asleep, but so do the screams and the sudden, surgical silence that always followed.  
Maybe that is why I write this instead of sleeping.  
Because for a few minutes, it feels like I am choosing my own words instead of reciting someone else's version of what happened, of who I am supposed to be, of which failures belong to me and which were baked into the orders long before I ever stepped onto the deck.

I do not know why I still do this.

Old habit from the regulars, I guess. Write it down, seal it, pretend someone in Intel is reading and cares. Out here, no one audits anything except ammo counts and fuel.

Sundered Company hit the depot this morning. Small garrison, mostly scared kids and contract techs, more worried about paperwork than perimeter checks. Naomi ghosted their sensors like she was still on their payroll, Mara walked the entry stack as if the codes were bricked into her bones, and Riley kept overwatch on the ridge, calling wind like we were back on drills instead of committing treason. It was clean, efficient, professional. Everything they trained us to be, just pointed the other way.

We took what we came for and a little extra, because we can now. That is the part that still sticks in my throat. In uniform, they told us the numbers mattered more than the names, that supply chains and objectives were all that kept the frontier from burning down. Funny how the same doctrine feels uglier without the flag patch.

There is this moment on every run, right after the breach, when my body falls into the old rhythm. Room, corner, center, breathe. Targets are shapes, not people. The sound of my own rifle is just another part of the pattern. Then it is over, the adrenaline dips, and the shapes have faces again. Today one of them looked young enough to still be arguing with instructors over field manuals. I did not let myself check his ID. I keep moving, I keep my hands busy, because that is what good soldiers do when the thinking starts to hurt.

We celebrated tonight, if you could call it that. Someone raided the liquor from the depot before we blew the logs; suddenly the barracks block we squatted turned into a makeshift cantina. Loud music bleeding from three different speakers, bad jokes shouted over worse singing. Naomi trying to arm-wrestle anyone still upright, Mara dancing with a bottle in one hand and her sidearm in the other, Riley on a crate telling a story about some patrol gone sideways until his voice cracked from laughing. For a few hours, it was chaos and light and the kind of noise that drowns out thinking. Then the bottles emptied, the music cut mid-song, and it all fell quiet like someone had flipped a breaker. Same as always. Fleeting. Leaves more echo than warmth.

I keep waiting for the moment it really feels like we left. Like there is a clean line between "before" and "after." But Sundered is just the same unit with the serial number scratched off. We still stack bunks like we are expecting an inspection. We still run drills on off-days. Jonas Mercer, soldier, except the paymaster is a shadow ledger and the mission briefings do not mention what happens if anyone ever decides to drag us back in chains.

I cannot stop thinking about Ortiz.

Lieutenant Ortiz was the first one I ever saw push back on an op. We were all crammed into that debrief room, stinking of propellant and sweat, after the dust settled on that settlement strike. The body count did not match the threat matrix, and everyone in the room knew it. Command called it a "necessary demonstration." Ortiz called it something else, right there in front of the ops chief. She did not shout. She just asked, too calmly, why our targeting package had changed mid-flight, and why the original sat-tags did not match the after-action photos.

Next cycle, she was gone.

They said reassignment at first. Then they stopped saying anything. Her bunk emptied during night rotation, footlocker stripped, name tag peeled off so clean it looked like she had never existed. No one asked where she went. We traded theories in whispers over rations, but when the section sergeant walked through, every voice cut off on the same syllable. It was the quiet that did it for me. The way even the loudmouths folded. I learned a lot from that silence.

Sometimes I look at Naomi and see the way her jaw clenches during briefings when the plan brushes up against collateral. I watch Mara counting rounds after a fight, lips moving like a prayer, tallying more than ammo in her head. Riley jokes the loudest, but his eyes always go to the exits first, like he is waiting for a squad of MPs that never comes. We all saw someone like Ortiz. We all decided, at different speeds, that we did not want to be next in line for a vanishing act.

Officially, we walked because the chain of command broke faith. Unofficially, I think we left because staying meant admitting we had already compromised too much of ourselves to ever walk straight again. Out here, in the gray, at least the lies are ours. We pick the contracts, we see the ledgers, we decide what we are willing to do and who we are willing to do it to. It sounds like freedom until I remember I used to tell myself the same thing about the old missions.

I still polish my boots before I rack out. Not because anyone will check, but because the day I stop might be the day I admit I am just another gun in the dark, no better than the ones we used to be pointed at. Maybe that is self-deception. Maybe it is the last discipline I have left.

If anyone ever asks why I left, I will probably give them a slogan about betrayal and bad orders. It is easier than telling them the truth. The truth is, I watched a good officer disappear for asking why the numbers did not line up with the bodies, and I have been pretending ever since that walking away is not the same thing as turning my back.

Malik says writing things down is a liability.  
He is not wrong.  
But if I do not put some of this somewhere, it just keeps looping in my head like bad comms echo.

Funny where loops start.  
When I was a kid I ran errands for half the building, trotting up and down four flights with lists scribbled on paper already stained with oil and tea.  
Neighbors would press a few credits into my palm, tell me to grab bread or powdered milk, sometimes that cheap instant ramen with the plastic sachets you could never get fully open.  
On the way back I always stopped at the same little corner kiosk, bought a lukewarm CAN-uck! Maple Cola and a packet of Choco Bites if I had anything left.  
I remember thinking life would always be that small and that simple: doors, stairs, lists, the familiar jangle of the kiosk's chime.  
No armor, no debriefs, no photographs you are not supposed to look at for more than three seconds.

My first real orders in uniform felt like just another errand.  
Run this crate across the tarmac.  
Escort this tech team to a "routine survey."  
Babysit a convoy through a debris corridor some analyst swore was cleared last cycle.  
Mundane, on the paper.  
But the crate hummed like a reactor about to lose its temper, the survey site still stank of burnt insulation and cooked flesh under the sterilizer, and the "cleared" corridor turned out to be very much alive, with wreckage and things no one logged officially.  
They called it cutting our teeth.  
I learned to clamp my jaw until it ached instead.

Outcast Detail started as a joke, the way all the worst ideas do.  
Malik would mutter about how we were already ghosts, how command only remembered us when they needed something done where there were no cameras.  
By the time the name stuck we had already crossed that invisible line: too dirty for clean units, too effective to discharge, wrapped in classifications so deep even our nightmares came stamped "need to know."  
They sent us to tidy up after things went sideways.  
Containment.  
Recovery.  
Denial.  
We saw wrecks that did not match the official battle reports, orbital scars that stopped exactly where certain names on the roster began.  
Sometimes our job was to stack the dead straight; other times it was to make sure no one could count them properly ever again.

I remember one op in particular, because it is when I understood what we had really become.  
We were told to secure a freighter "compromised in transit," nothing more.  
When we burned in, the thing was half-embedded in a field of old war scrap, like a coffin trying to join a mass grave that did not want more company.  
Sensor logs had been wiped, and we got a verbal order only: clear survivors, purge black boxes, transmit nothing.  
Malik did not argue.  
Outcast Detail follows orders even when it hates them.  
That is our sickness.

The cracks showed after.  
Briefings that ran too long on what we "had not seen."  
Rumors about navigational data being rewritten instead of corrected.  
A name that kept showing up on classified after-action reports, some engineer turned wild card, and instructions to tag any mention of altered beacons and feed it up the chain without discussion.  
We were not hunting him then, but the shape of his work was already in the files they would not let us keep.

When I finally walked out, I thought I was cutting the leash.  
That is the story deserters tell themselves: you step off the transport, you vanish into some underlevel bar, you become your own problem.  
But leaving Outcast Detail is not freedom.  
It is a death sentence with a longer timer.  
Command does not like loose ends that know which battles never really happened.  
The unit does not like traitors who might talk under the wrong kind of pressure.  
Malik never said it, but the last time I saw him he looked at me like a target he had not decided on yet.

The funny thing is, the discipline does not wash off.  
I still wake up before ship's dawn, still inventory my kit, still scan exits without thinking.  
Sometimes I catch myself plotting fire lanes in a crowded market, then remember I am just there to buy powdered milk and Instant Oatmeal that tastes like cardboard but lasts forever.  
I even found a kiosk in the port that sells that same Maple Cola, though it is colder and costs three times as much now.  
For a second, can in hand, I can almost pretend I am just the girl with the shopping list again.

And then I hear the unit's name on someone else's tongue.  
A bounty board whisper about a "rogue clean-up team," or some drunk spacer talking about wrecks that keep rearranging themselves into patterns nobody can quite decode.  
Bits of our old orders keep surfacing where they should not: mention of falsified crash logs, of private nav algorithms changing hands in back rooms on Neon, of officers who retired too quietly just before certain reports went missing.  
I try not to connect it all, because connecting things is what got us here.  
But every time another story leaks out, I see the familiar fingerprints, the same insistence that the past can be edited into something more convenient.

Malik would say none of this belongs on paper.  
He is probably right.  
Still, it helps to admit it somewhere: I walked away from Outcast Detail, but I am still marching along their old vectors, just a step to the side, hoping that when the timer runs out it will not be one of ours holding the gun.

I keep telling myself I only write in this thing to keep my hand steady, but that is a lie and I know it. Trigger squeeze, pen stroke, same muscle memory. The body remembers even when the brain is tired of replaying the feed.

Tonight the boys started whispering in the corner of the bay again. Caleb hunched over the crate like it was a holotable, Marcus pacing that slow circle he does when he's walking the perimeter of an idea instead of a killzone. Jonah laughed once, too loud, then caught himself. And then Elias crooked a finger at me without looking up, like he already knew I had been listening from across the room. That little gesture lit something in my chest I hate: the quiet thrill of being pulled into a conversation where every word is technically treason and none of us care anymore.

They slid the datapad my way, redacted manifests, blacked-out unit IDs, an op name someone had helpfully replaced with a skull in permanent marker. Same pattern as before: escort duty that never made the public channels, cargo no one wanted logged by an independent observer, and those casualty reports that always seemed to arrive pre-signed. We used to get briefed on runs like that with a straight face and a stamped seal, told to hold perimeter and ask no questions while the real work happened in the shadows. I never saw what was in those locked containers. Still smells like burned coolant and bleach when I think too hard about it.

Being in on the planning this time feels different. No colonel's voice on the overhead, no legal jargon to hide behind. Just Marcus, grimmer than ever, making the case that if command can run black flights and scrub the records, then so can we. Nina watching him with that measured calm of hers, the one that means she has already calculated three exit vectors and two firing solutions. Caleb nodding along because he trusts people harder than he should until they give him a reason to stop. And me, leaning over the datapad, tracing the route with my finger, pretending my heart is not racing at the thought of putting a round finally in the direction all those old orders came from.

My body still reacts before my mind, like it did back in the corridor fights. Raised voice behind me, and my shoulders tighten before I have processed the words. Dropship engines spool up outside and I am halfway to cover, looking for hard points and choke angles, before I realize it's just a freighter cycling its drives. Sometimes I catch my reflection with a hand halfway to the small of my back, reaching for a sidearm I am not supposed to carry on station. Fight, flee, freeze. The trinity drilled into our hindbrains so hard that even now, dishonorably unmoored, I twitch on the same old cues.

We built numbness around ourselves out there. Layer by layer, op after op, until it felt like a second skin. Civilians in the crossfire, targets misflagged, "collateral" we were told not to record in our own heads. You do not survive long in that line of work if you feel everything. So we stopped feeling. I remember one insertion where the shooting stopped for maybe six hours straight. No alarms, no running boots, no medevac chatter on the squad net. I lay on my bunk staring at the ceiling and what I felt was not peace, not safety, just a bone-deep relief that no one needed me to kill or triage for a few more minutes. It did not feel like being loved. It felt like the absence of burden, like putting a rucksack down and not caring if anyone else picked it up.

Now, with the Phalanx, the numbness is harder to justify. We are not following anyone's flag but our own, and every line we cross is a choice we make in the open. When we talk about hitting that convoy, about bleeding the same machine that bled us, I can feel the old armor sliding back into place around my ribs. Part of me enjoys the weight. Part of me is terrified I have forgotten how to take it off.

I think about the incident we were never debriefed on, the one where entire squads disappeared off the roster with a single keystroke, replaced by "equipment malfunction" and "orbital debris." We were rotated through cleanup on that one, told to secure a perimeter around twisted hull and vented atmosphere, no remains allowed to be visually confirmed. I heard rumors later that some of those "malfunctions" started when a junior officer refused to sign off on a safety override. Maybe that is why my ears ring when Elias speaks now, voice low, spelling out just how brittle the command chain always was. Maybe that is why I am still here, sitting with known deserters, writing this instead of burning it.

I tell myself I follow them because they are the only ones who will look me in the eye and admit what we did and what was done to us. I tell myself I stay because if someone is going to point a rifle at the people who wrote those sanitized reports, I would rather it be someone like Nina than some Spacer high on cheap chems. Truth is, I also stay because when Marcus calls everyone in and the air goes tight and electric, I feel that same small, forbidden excitement I did the first night an instructor pulled me aside and said, "You are not like the others. We have plans for you."

Maybe that is the ugliest part of all this. Not the acts, not the bodies, not the lines in the after-action logs that do not match the scars on my hands. It is how quickly I slip back into the rhythm of squad banter and target designations, how comforted I am by the click of a mag seating properly, how relieved I feel when the quiet ends and there is finally something to do.

If I keep telling myself I am only doing this to clear my head after shift, maybe I will believe it one of these days.  
Mira says writing anything down is asking for trouble, Jonas shrugs and says no one cares enough to read it, and Raul just laughs and tells me to make sure I spell his name right when I blame him for everything that goes wrong.  
Elias stays quiet, like always, eyes on the manifest, pretending he cannot hear us.

We burned out to that freighter husk today, the one just off the lane where the nav buoys keep resetting themselves.  
On approach, it was the usual noise in the comms: Mira arguing with Jonas about who tagged the hull first, Elias muttering about line tension, Raul humming that same off-key spacer ballad he uses when he is nervous.  
Once we hard-docked, the noise cut off like someone pinched a cable.  
It is always like that.  
The minute the hatch cycles, every joke dies and it is just suit seals, mag boots, and the quiet knowledge that one puncture or one bad weld is the difference between getting paid and becoming part of the scenery.

I am trying to remember when we started reaching for weapons before wrenches.  
Years back, if another crew showed up on a claim, there would be shouting across comms, maybe a bluff about filing the first mark with Trade Authority, some creative swearing, then everybody would back off or cut a deal.  
Now I watch Jonas thumb the safety on his rifle before he even runs a structural scan.  
Mira keeps a shotgun magged to her harness and calls it "pest control," meaning anyone without a Salvage Crown patch.  
Today, when a pair of independents tried to nose their tug into "our" airlock, Raul did not hail them, did not warn them off, just pulsed the maneuvering thrusters hard enough to rattle their docking collar and send them tumbling.  
We all pretended not to hear the panicked breathing over open channel.  
Violence used to be what happened when everything else failed.  
Now it is the first tool we reach for, even when the problem is just two crews trying to eat off the same carcass.

Family still thinks I work "portside support."  
That is how I phrased it the last time I sent a message to my brother, anyway.  
He asked which port, and I changed the subject, talked about food, about how the stars look the same in every system.  
Back when I started with Salvage Crown, I told myself there was no point worrying them with details.  
"Nothing dangerous," I said, "mostly cutting scrap, well within regs."  
Then the jobs got stranger: derelicts with fresh burns on the hull but no transponder history, listening posts that went dark right after some admiral's name started circulating in the news.  
The more the patterns bothered me, the more I smoothed the edges in my calls.  
Now I do not talk about work at all.  
If he ever saw what we walk into, how we step over things that should not be there and carry out the parts that should not belong to anyone, I am not sure he would recognize the person on the other end.

Inside that freighter, the air was gone but the smell still clung to the fabric: burnt plastic, cooked lubricant, that faint metallic tang that does not come from rust.  
Elias found a bundle of personal effects neatly stacked by an emergency locker, every item tagged with coordinates and dates in tidy handwriting.  
No bodies, no logs we are supposed to see, just those little altars people keep talking about in the bars.  
Mira swore under her breath and walked right past, said it looked "too arranged."  
Jonas quietly marked the location for internal records, the kind we do not share when we sell the rest.

In the mess later, someone brought up the story again, about the engineer who lost his mind in the war cleanup and started moving wrecks around like they were pieces in some private memorial.  
Last time I heard it, it was just a ghost-ship yarn, good for drinking and scaring greenhands.  
Now we keep cutting into derelicts that feel curated, not abandoned.  
Beacon logs that do not match the scars on the hull.  
Drift patterns that keep pulling ships toward old battle sites no one wants to talk about.  
Every time, someone says "just a coincidence," and every time, the room goes a little quieter.

We do not report most of what we see.  
Unspoken rule.  
If it looks like it will tank the payout or bring in too many questions from people who carry badges, it does not go into the official handoff.  
Mira keeps a private drive with all the weird finds, calls it her "puzzle box."  
Elias pretends it does not exist, but he is the one who backs it up after every job.  
Raul claims he does not believe in cursed wrecks, then triple-checks his seals whenever we board anything with fresh power readings and no crew.  
We all saw that one ship, years ago, lights still on, galley half-set for a meal no one finished.  
Salvage Crown stripped it fast and quiet, and nobody has said its registry name since.

I tell myself I am fine with this life.  
Good pay when the jobs line up, decent kit, a crew that mostly has my back.  
I like the quiet out there, the way sound dies in the suit and all that is left is my own breathing and the hiss of the recycler.  
But some nights, when I am looking at another wreck hanging against a starfield like a broken tooth, I wonder how many of these hulks were accidents and how many were nudged.  
And whether, one day, someone will climb through a torn-open hatch, step over my neatly stacked tools, and decide what parts of my story are worth writing down and what can drift nameless in the dark.

Caleb keeps saying we should all be asleep by 0200 if we want to be worth anything at 0600, but he is snoring three doors down and I am staring at a wall that will not blink first. So I might as well write.

Sometimes I think the strangest thing about Direwolf is how familiar it feels. Different insignia, cleaner guns, more zero-g time, but the same quiet calculus I grew up with: who is safe to stand next to when the room turns, who you never turn your back on, who will fold when the rounds start skipping off the bulkheads. The brass talk about honor, contracts, chain of command. The real rules live in the seconds between words.

I still remember my first job that was not supposed to lead anywhere. A part-time gig at a dockside supply kiosk, barely more than a closet with a register. Delivering sealed packages to ships, sweeping the grit off the deck, stocking crates of canned protein and discount ammo under flickering lights. I thought it was honest work. Then I noticed how the same three captains always paid in cash, how the scanner never beeped when their packages went out, how the supervisor watched them leave and pretended not to see. I learned the unspoken rules fast: knock twice, never read the label, never ask why there is no manifest.

One of the loaders handed me a bracelet once, thin links of some alloy that caught the light like ice. Said it fell off a crate, nobody would miss it. I knew it had not been bought anywhere near that kiosk. I also knew enough to smile, slip it on, and say thank you. Questions are just another kind of receipt. If you do not generate them, nobody comes looking to reconcile the books.
