Direwolf is the same shape at a higher resolution. Nadia plays the loyal professional, and she is, but she also knows who is holding back ammo, which pilots are refueling off the record, which comms tech is being paid by someone else to "accidentally" delay certain transmissions. She never says so directly. She just asks if I have enough spare mags, then glances at the requisition console and raises an eyebrow. Marcus pretends he is all muscle and drills, yet he spends extra time in the sim with the rookies he thinks might actually survive a second contract. He growls about standards, but he does not let them wash out before they learn how to keep their helmet seals clean.

Caleb is different. By-the-book, almost painfully so, but there is a reason the handlers keep putting him on the same teams as me. He believes in the job more than the paycheck, or pretends well enough that it does not matter. When he signs off on an op, he means it. When he hesitates, I listen. Tonight, he hesitated.

We got a briefing packet flagged eyes-only, something to do with "off-grid asset recovery" and a series of derelicts officially written off years ago. The language was almost bureaucratic enough to be boring, but the coordinates formed a pattern I have seen painted in rumor across mess tables and barracks chatter. Cold, distant systems. Half-erased salvage records. Names that only come up in whispers after the third drink. Someone in MAST or close to it has been quietly shuffling certain wrecks toward one shadow ledger, then hiring people like us to make the paperwork match the reality.

No one says it outright, but we all hear the rumors. A lost patrol that followed the wrong beacon. An independent hauler whose transponder data vanished from every registry overnight. An arbitrator who knew the codes too well and disappeared with a hold full of stolen cores. People say there is a place where those ghosts go, a graveyard of hulls too valuable or too embarrassing to leave in the open. Tonight's packet looked like a map with half its lines erased.

I keep wondering if this is another version of that dockside kiosk, just on a system-wide scale: deliver this, do not scan it too closely, do not ask why the manifest is redacted. The difference is that now the packages are starships and the missing receipts look like dead crews.

When I close my eyes I still see one particular hold, years ago, not on a contract but on a station that did not have emergency drills often enough. Fire, alarms warbling out of tune, artificial gravity hiccupping so that debris hung for a second before crashing down again. I was younger, holding on to the only person who had ever tried to keep me off the streets, her breath ragged against my shoulder as bulkheads shuddered and panels tore loose above us. Love and loss twisted together in that stuttering red light, the smell of melting plastic and burnt metal settling into my lungs. I remember thinking, even then, that the rules outside this compartment were already rewriting themselves. That some accountant somewhere would call the whole thing an "incident" and move on.

Maybe that is why I ended up here, in a unit named after a predator that never hunts alone. When the system collapses around you enough times, you stop believing in its protection and start learning to read the gaps. I learned to walk those gaps as a kid, to feel where the power really flows, to see which "temporary measures" quietly become permanent. In Direwolf, that sense is the difference between coming home and being a line item.

So I watch, and I listen. I note which contracts come with too much hazard pay and too little detail. I watch the way the handlers flinch when certain names cross the holo. I hear the whispers that some of our recovery work is not just cleaning up old battles, but erasing proof that they ever happened the way the records say. And I remember the bracelet on my wrist, cold and beautiful, a gift from someone who stole it because that was the only way to survive another day on the docks.

We traced a stray dataslate in the dust back to a pattern of falsified salvage, then listened to a jumpy analyst talk about orders that never made it into the log. Later, in a dead station's quiet, we saw how temporary files about missing ships had been left looping for years, unacknowledged but never erased. The trail from that forgotten kiosk feels a lot shorter now.

I can hear the reactor hum bedding down for the off-shift, the way it always does when Deepwater slips a little deeper into the dark. Feels colder tonight, even though environmental says we are well within spec. Rhea swore the air smelled like recycled fear at dinner, which made Jonas laugh until he choked on his stew. I laughed too, but it stuck halfway up my throat and never quite came out. Maybe it is just the way the grav plates kept shuddering on the mid-deck, like the ship is trying to shrug something off.

I should not have been on cargo three after lights, but Darius forgot his toolkit again and begged me to grab it before the Trade Authority inspector logs our next systems ping. So I went, like I always go, because I am the only one who remembers where everyone leaves everything. That is what I tell myself, anyway. The hold was quiet, just the clink of maglocks settling and that slow, hollow creak you only get when a ship is really alone. I almost turned around when I heard voices.

Galen and Rhea, down by the auxiliary console. They did not see me around the crate stack. I know I should have walked away, made some noise so they knew I was there, anything but stand there with my hand over my mouth like some spacer child hiding from ghosts. But I froze. I always thought Galen was just quietly ambitious, the kind of man who knows which side of a ledger to fall on and never makes waves. Hearing him talk in that low, flat voice made the hair on my arms lift.

I could not catch everything, just pieces between the cargo scanner chirps. Payment cleared. Window in the patrol net. No questions from the bosses as long as the manifests match. Rhea asked if he was sure about "the handoff" and he said it was already set, that this route "belongs to other people now" and we just keep our mouths shut and ride it out. The way he said "other people" made my stomach twist, like there was a third ship in the hold with us, listening.

I backed away, bumped into a crate, and nearly dropped Darius's damn toolkit. Galen called out, asked if someone was there, and I forced myself to step around the corner with the most casual smile I could manage. Told them I was just playing errand girl again. Rhea looked like she swallowed a whole asteroid. Galen smiled too easily, asked if I ever sleep, and my cheeks went hot for no good reason. I hate that about myself, the way my face advertises every thought I do not say.

On the walk back I kept replaying it, trying to tell myself it was nothing. Trade Authority runs side deals all the time. Priority cargo, priority clients. Maybe that is all it is. But the way he stood too close to the console when I passed, as if he did not want me to see what was on it, that is not "standard incentive." I know enough smugglers' tricks from Gagarin to recognize the shape of one, even if I pretend otherwise.

Then there was this morning in the galley, which I would erase from my memory if I could. I walked in just as Galen was rinsing his cup, and the ship had this weird half-gravity hiccup while the stabilizers recalibrated. I stumbled, grabbed the counter, and he caught my elbow at the same time. For half a second we were both braced together, his hand warm through the sleeve of my coverall, my hair floating stupidly in my face. He made some joke about me testing the inertial dampeners with my "graceful entrance," and I could not think of anything to say but "I meant to do that."

Who says that? I meant to do that. I replayed it all day, cringing at every angle. Part of me wanted to stay in that stupid almost-embrace and pretend he was just another crew mate teasing me, not someone whispering about handoffs and patrol windows in the dark. Part of me wanted to pull away, march straight to Jonas, and dump everything I heard on the table between us. Instead I mumbled something about shift reports and fled with my coffee sloshing over my hand.

I keep asking myself who I am loyal to. To Deepwater, her logs and her unremarkable corridors. To the Trade Authority, who will absolutely not hesitate to vent a whole crew for stepping out of line, then deny we ever existed. To the faces I see every day, trading bad jokes and good coffee in the galley. Or to the tiny, selfish part of me that wonders if Galen is right, if there is a way to come out of all this with more than a pension and worn-out boots.

Rhea has been quieter since that conversation. She watches Galen when she thinks no one is looking, as if trying to decide whether she is on his side or just near the blast radius. Darius buried himself in maintenance on the external relays, grumbling about how they do not pay him enough to fix old Trade Authority shortcuts. Jonas keeps talking about what he will buy after this run, like spending the credits in his head will guarantee he lives long enough to touch them.

The rumor mill has gone dry, and that is what scares me most. Normally there is always some story about pirates out past Akila or Ryujin making plays in Neon, the usual noise. Lately the stories come in whispers, like the space between systems has teeth, and someone is paying good money to sharpen them. I hear it in the way the dockers on Gagarin spoke too softly when they mentioned our route, in how a bartender on New Atlantis changed the subject as soon as he saw our ship patch.

If I bring this to anyone official, it is my word against Galen's, and he knows how to dress his lies in the right paperwork. If I stay quiet, I am complicit in something I do not understand. And in the middle of all that, there is the part of me that still feels the echo of his hand on my arm and hates myself for it. I do not know if I want him to be innocent or just honest.

For now I will do what I always do: log my shift, double-check the environmental seals, and pretend I do not notice when the course projections shift a few degrees off the standard lanes. But I have started keeping my own copy of the route data, tucked where no one looks. If this goes bad, I want someone, somewhere, to know we did not just vanish. We were steered.

I keep telling myself I will not write after missions. That sleep matters more than ink. Then I lie there staring at the ceiling of whatever tin-box bunk Bravo Ironclad has rented this week and feel the shakes coming on, and the pen starts moving by itself.

Today was simple on paper. Escort. Secure. Overwatch. No casualties on our side, minor property damage, client very impressed. "Textbook," Marcus called it in the debrief, and Jonas nodded along like he agreed, jaw clenched the way it always is when command is in the room. But there was nothing textbook about walking through that hangar and seeing the scorch patterns, the twist in the hull from a bad grav-jump, and hearing the client insist it was only "routine wear." Even Sara, who usually just takes the credstick and smiles, kept glancing at the patched bulkheads like she was reading a crime scene.

Bravo Ironclad has an unspoken rule: we do not ask what happened before the contract starts or after it ends. That is for lawyers, nav auditors, and whoever thinks they run this part of the sky. We hold the line for the hours we are paid for and then we walk away. Lately I have started to notice how often we are being hired to stand between "routine wear" and a paper trail.

There is a rumor going around that one of the big shipyards has a missing test navigator on their hands, and that some of the "anomalous incidents" we have cleaned up over the past month are all echoes from the same ghost on the lanes. Jonas says it is just spacer talk, same as always, but Marcus has been quietly running extra checks on our own jump plots. He pretends it is just caution; I see the way his eyes stay on the displays three seconds longer than they should.

Discipline keeps the unit together. Discipline and the fact that we all know what we look like without the armor. Sara is the only one who will say out loud that this is all borrowed time. Over coffee she said, "We are here until the risk profile says we are not," then laughed and changed the subject to ammo shipments. But she has been logging more range hours than usual, and she asked me, very casually, to check her will for errors. That is not nothing.

I am not afraid of dying on a job. I am afraid of dying for a lie I can see and still accept the payout for. That is the difference between us and the regulars: they can pretend they do not have a choice. We sign every contract knowing exactly how much we cost.

Maybe that is why I keep thinking about him tonight.

He was not Bravo. Not even close. Freelance security, "consultant" was the word he liked to use, as if the way he held a rifle was a theoretical exercise. We burned hard and fast, three months grabbing shore leave in the same ports, sharing bunks between contracts, promising to sit out the next op and never once actually doing it. I remember the first time he lost his temper in a bar and put a man through a table for touching my shoulder. I remember loving the way my heart pounded watching him do it, how safe and powerful and reckless it felt, like I had personally called down an orbital strike.

The same night, back in the rented room, he had hands that shook so badly lighting a cigarette he burned his fingers and did not even notice. I noticed. I did not let go.

It took me longer than it should have to understand that we were feeding each other's worst instincts. We stayed together through threats and slammed doors, through mission briefs where we pretended not to know each other, through nights where he would wake up already halfway to choking me before he recognized my face. I told myself I stayed because I could handle him. Truth is, I stayed because I liked the fire as much as I feared it. Love, lust, adrenaline, all the same chemical storm. Destructive and intoxicating, and I kept going back into the blast radius.

He took a job I turned down a year ago. High risk, poor intel, very good money. I watched his back as he walked up the ramp and I knew, in that tight little hollow behind the ribs, that the odds were bad. I still let him go. No body ever came back, just a brief mention in a casualty report that did not even spell his name right. That was the last time I believed that wanting someone enough could keep them alive.

Since then, sleep has been optional. On quiet nights like this, my brain replays every scene in slow motion. The bar fight, the way his knuckles split. The time he pinned a crew chief to the wall and hissed threats because a manifest had my name on a hazardous crate. The argument on a freight deck where we both had guns in hand and neither of us quite raised them but we thought about it. I close my eyes and it all comes back in perfect detail, like my mind is running its own debrief loop and cannot find the point where it could have turned out another way.

Now it is Bravo voices that crowd the dark. Marcus laying out insertion angles in that calm, steady way he has. Jonas arguing for a more aggressive posture while pretending he is not itching for an excuse to pull the trigger. Sara cracking some dry joke that lands just wrong enough to remind us we are all one miscalculation away from airless silence. I listen to them in the ready room, then I lie here listening to their echoes, wondering which of them is going to make a choice they cannot walk back and whether I will follow.

Somewhere out there, ships jump and do not come back on the same vector they left. Somewhere, a navigator who should be a footnote in an accident report is still nudging traffic along paths no one admits exist. Bravo Ironclad has been orbiting that shadow for a while now, cleaning around the edges for clients who do not like their names spoken. We are getting closer, whether command says it or not.

I told myself tonight that I would not get attached again. Then I signed my name to another op with the same people, in the same unmarked armor, trusting them to wake me if something goes wrong while I finally grab an hour of sleep. I am still staring at the ceiling, listening for the hum of the reactor, waiting for the old nightmares to start, and knowing that when they do, somewhere inside them will be the same pattern of threats and violence I have never really learned to walk away from.

Tomorrow we brief on the next relay. Tomorrow I will pretend my hands do not shake when I check my rifle.

Day 241, shift rotation unknown

Gamma Hardstrike says we do not keep diaries. We keep after-action reports. Evaluations. Debriefs. Nothing messy, nothing that looks like leverage. Maybe that is why I am writing this in a cheap notepad I bought for three weeks worth of loose credits at some corner stall on Jemison. Just paper and a stub of a pen. Feels harder to hack.

We got back from escort duty a few hours ago. Simple contract on paper. Hold perimeter while a corporate team pulled data from a derelict relay. No flags, no uniforms, just "authorized contractors." Riya Calder was running the entry stack, Marcus Kepler on overwatch with the long glass, Naomi Vance coordinating fire lanes from the rear ramp. I was breach two, which means close enough to die first, far enough to get blamed if someone else does.

It went smooth. Too smooth. No contacts, no surprises, client in and out like they had been here before. On the ride back, Elena Halbrook kept her helmet on, visor dark, like she was more comfortable staring at HUD flicker than at anyone's face. She has been that way since we ran that convoy job along the border and lost comms for ten full minutes. Official line is that it was just a solar flare. Unofficial line, whispered over maintenance tables, is that ships do not just blink off every scope in a sector unless someone with better toys than us wants them to.

That is the job, though. Stuff goes wrong, command rewrites the story, and we clap each other on the back and pretend we are not counting exits. Gamma's unspoken rules are simple. You do not ask about clients. You do not ask why some ops never show up on the roster. You do not ask why we still get hazard pay from contracts no one admits to signing. You keep your rifle zeroed, your gear squared, and your questions to yourself.

Most days I can do that. Then something small happens and I feel the floor tilt.

Today it was Marcus snapping at me over a clearance call. I had a bad angle on a corridor and called it cold; he swore he saw movement on his scope. We went back and forth for maybe ten seconds, but my chest locked up like I was sixteen again, waiting for the first blow to land. My palms went numb, vision tunneled, adrenaline for nothing. No threat. Just a disagreement on comms. Still, every cell in my body braced for impact, for being told I was blind, for the accusations that follow.

Old conditioning crawls up your spine like that. Does not care that you are paid now, that you have armor, that you are not trapped in some concrete room while someone bigger explains how you "misremembered" what happened.

He used to do that. My partner, before I signed on with Gamma. Whole arguments rewired in real time. I would say, "You shoved me," and he would say, "You walked into me." I would say, "You yelled for ten minutes," and he would say, "You are too sensitive; I only raised my voice once." After a while, I stopped trying to hold the lines of what was true in my head. It was easier to accept his version, let him narrate. Every correction came with that look, the one that said I was lucky he had not lost his temper "for real." Lucky the wall took the worst of it. Lucky the bruise was where a jacket could hide it.

Funny how quick you learn to call that luck.

It seeps into everything. In the old crew, beatings were just noise between jobs. Threats were punctuation. Someone steals a cut, someone mouths off, someone forgets who sits higher in the pecking order. A cracked rib here, a dislocated finger there, a knife waved inches from an eye. Nobody called it torture. It was "discipline," "banter," "just getting him back in line." The music was always loud enough to drown the shouting, but never loud enough to cover the sound of someone sniffling afterward.

Gamma is supposed to be better. Contractual. Professional. We get paid on time. We sign NDAs instead of blood oaths. But there is still that current under everything, that edge. The laughter in the ready room has the same taste as back then. Not the kind where someone tells a dumb story and everyone exhales. It is sharp, mocking, a pack sound. Someone drops a crate on their foot, everyone laughs a beat too long. Someone stumbles on a stair, and the jokes cut just a bit deeper than they need to. No one wants to be next in line for that. So we all laugh too. Part defense, part camouflage.

Riya plays that game well. She can slice a man open verbally with a raised eyebrow and a quiet remark. People are a little afraid of her, though they would never admit it. Naomi keeps things steadier. On ops, her voice is the one that cuts through my panic, pulls me back to the room. "Check your corners, Krane." Simple, factual, no judgment. Marcus is rougher, but if he says he has your back, he means it. He just does not know that when he raises his voice, my system clocks back to every slammed door I ever heard.

I hate that about myself. How fast I go from calm to white-hot inside. How one joke, one perceived slight, can flip me into wanting to break someone's teeth, then curl up and disappear. There is no warning. No build-up. One second I am checking magazine counts, the next my heart is hammering like we are mid-contact and my hands are shaking hard enough to rattle my rifle. Then I overcorrect, go quiet, lock it all down so no one sees. That is how you survive in outfits like this. You become your own prison warden.

Saving for that notebook drove the point home. Credits slide through your fingers fast out here. Armor plates, med packs, paying off some mechanic to not log your ship's serial into the wrong system. But I kept skimming small amounts off chow and cheap Erdebrau, stashing them aside. Took weeks just to buy paper and ink. Something soft. Something that did not bruise when you touched it. When the seller dropped it on the counter, he did not understand why my hands would not stop trembling around a stupid pad that cost less than we burn in ammo on a training day.

We hear things, between contracts. About convoys that vanish off the grid, about pilots who can slip whole freighter trains through patrol space like ghosts. About clients who want problems gone, not solved. Gamma takes the contracts and tells us not to think too hard. But whispers still swim through the barracks. That some routes are not just dangerous, they are wrong. That certain navigators who "got people killed" did not fail so much as they pushed too close to something the big flags do not want to talk about. That our job is to keep the noise down so nobody asks why ships are disappearing.

Maybe that is all nonsense, drunk talk and spacer superstition. Maybe it is the truest thing anyone in this line of work will ever say.

For now, I will file my report, clean my rifle, and pretend my hands do not shake when I set the safety. Gamma Hardstrike cares about performance, not ghosts. But here, in this thin-paper book, I can follow the lines nobody wants on the mission board. The ones etched into my nerves, still mapping out every threat long after the beating stops.

Didn't sleep again.

Hips still remember the crash couch, even when it is just a bunk welded to a half-rusted frame. Funny how the body clings to routine long after the orders stop. Lights out, gear stacked, weapon at arm's reach. No CO, no duty roster, but I still wake on the minute before the alarm I do not set.

Redacted Division. We picked the name as a joke, sitting in that gutted briefing room with the projectors still cycling through half-deleted slides. Now it sticks to us like gun oil. Files gone, pay records blank, commendations scrubbed. Like we were never there. Except my shoulder still aches where shrapnel went through during that corridor push and Elena Carrow still rolls her ankle before a fight because she swears it saved her life once. Ghosts do not limp. We do.

Dana Kostova said tonight that we are freer than we have ever been. Her words, clipped like she was still reporting to someone. Maybe she believes it. Maybe she needs to. I watch her eyes when she says it and all I see is someone measuring blast radii in her head. She has not stopped doing that since the operation where the map was wrong and the civilians were in the wrong tower. Wrong. That is generous. The map we got was curated. Someone made a decision. We executed it. Then we were told our helmet cam feeds were corrupted in transit.

Kira Haldane does not talk about that deployment. She just maintains the rifles like they are all that is left holding her together. You can tell which ones were hers in the old unit; she runs a finger along the barrel before she racks them. Another ritual trying to paper over the cracks. Renee Calder pretends not to remember, cracks jokes about how we were all too green to see the signs. Mira Salcedo does remember. I know because she will not stand within sightline of anyone wearing an old-issue patch from that theater. We were told the insurgent stronghold had to go. We were told the signatures were hostile. Later, in the dark corners of the debrief, I heard an officer say "acceptable trade." That phrase still tastes like copper.

We walked away after that, in different stages. Some filed resignation that never processed. Some just did not report in. I followed them when the first arrest warrant was issued for "data tampering" and we all recognized the face. He had been the only one stubborn enough to print out the raw sensor logs before the purge. Official line said he falsified them. His body never turned up. Our record did not just get sealed; it was being rewritten. If the story does not match the blood on your boots, you either change the story or burn the boots. Command chose the first. We chose the second.

Abandoning official command felt like cutting my own spine out. Years of drilled instinct do not vanish because you toss a uniform into a recycler. I still hear the cadence when I move. Formation spacing. Threat sectors. Even in this cramped hold where we squat between runs, my brain assigns fire arcs. I do not know how to be anything else. That is the worst part. It is not that they betrayed us. It is that they built us so well we still want to flinch to attention when some new voice barks an order.

Redacted Division pretends we are leaderless, just a circle of equals, but everyone still glances at Kira before we break atmosphere. Old roles die slower than reputations. We run contracts now that would have had us court-martialed once. Asset extractions. Burn jobs. Ship jacks. No insignia, no chain, just credits and a list of coordinates. We tell ourselves we pick our targets. We do not hit hospitals or schools or relief ships. We have lines, we say. But every month those lines look thinner.

Long stakeouts used to be the worst part of the job. Hours on some blasted ridge or baking rooftop, watching a doorway that never opened, pulse crawling from boredom to dread and back again. It was strange how boredom and fear braided together until you could not tell them apart. You sit there long enough, you start wanting something to happen, anything, just to prove you are not already dead and dreaming in your armor. That is where the danger lives. Right on that edge where survival and savagery start sharing a face. Every week out there shaved that edge a little sharper. Fewer questions asked when a shadow moved wrong. Fewer warnings shouted in a language you half-understood.

Those habits did not go away when we cut loose. If anything, the leash snapping only made the dog meaner. I have seen Elena put two rounds into a runner's back because he twitched toward a console. Maybe he was calling reinforcements. Maybe he was trying to surrender on a frequency she did not care about. I did not stop her. The line between staying alive and becoming the thing we used to hunt is not a line anymore; it is fog. Some days I think we are already on the wrong side and just too deep in to notice.

I catch myself justifying what we do now the same way I used to justify deployments. "We take from bastards who deserve it." "We hit facilities that have skeletons in their foundations." Dana digs up the contracts, shows us the dossiers with all the ugly little footnotes. Human trials off-grid. Smuggled weapons. Black budgets written in blood. It is easier to breach a lab when you have already decided everyone inside is guilty. But I know how files can be massaged. I saw it happen once from the other end.

What keeps me here? Part habit, part fear of what waits if I walk away. Civvy life is not made for people who can clear a room in six seconds and sleep through nothing but ordnance. There is also loyalty, though I do not say that out loud. Not to flags or mottos anymore, but to the handful of faces that were there when the building came down, who dragged me out of broken steel and did not ask if I still believed. I owe Kira my life twice over. Elena caught a round meant for me. Mira patched a hole in my side with a dressing and a lie to the medevac techs. I walk because they walk. If we are going to hell, at least I will recognize the silhouettes.

Sometimes I dream about that last official briefing we sat in. The screen flickered, the map glowed, and the major recited words someone else had written. Threat indices, collateral estimates, authorizations. I remember staring at the line that said "post-action media narrative: localized unrest." That was the first time I thought about who writes the story when the guns cool. Now, in this little metal box, I am trying to write my own, and it is not coming out clean.

Tomorrow we hit another target. Supposedly a private black site, the kind that learned all the wrong lessons from the programs we bled for. The intel says they are doing the same experiments under a different franchise banner, chopping up the same kind of lives under a new logo. Maybe if we break their machines, it makes what we did back then matter a little less. Maybe that is just another lie.

I used to sign logs with my full name, rank, unit. Now I scratch three letters on the inside of my gauntlet and tell myself it is enough: R D V.

The V stands for Velez. I am trying not to forget that part.

I used to think the worst thing that could happen in a day was the guy upstairs dropping weights at oh-five-hundred or the damned faucet in the kitchenette never fully shutting off. That drip used to drive me crazy on rest days. Funny, how that was what I thought stress was. I would sit on my bunk, patching up an old field jacket or sewing a knee on my fatigues, not because supply was short, just because my hands needed to be busy. Habit. Routine. Take something frayed and make it look inspection-ready. Back then the biggest crisis was whether the sergeant would notice a crooked stitch.

Lately I catch myself walking the parts of town command used to warn us off. The alleys where the street clinics don't ask names, where the bars don't log tabs, where nobody flinches when they hear automatic fire out past the docks. First it was just to clear my head after shift, then it became the only place my head would actually clear. I knew which corners the black-bag recruiters used, which stairwells smelled like old chem smoke and coolant. I told myself I was doing "presence patrols" out of habit, but I never filed a report.

There was this one night outside a dive near the freight yards. Some kid in a cheap jacket bumped my shoulder, hand sneaking toward my pocket. Muscle memory kicked in: step, pivot, wrist-lock. I remember how fast he folded, how his eyes went wide when I pushed him to the wall without even trying. I did not draw a weapon, did not even raise my voice. Just leaned in, let him see I was not afraid of him, or anyone he knew. He apologized, stammering, swore he did not mean anything by it. I let him go, but the part that stuck with me was not the almost-mugging. It was the way my heart slowed down after, the way the street seemed to give me a wider berth. It was disturbingly easy to enjoy that.

Caleb used to say the uniform was just cloth, that what mattered was who we were underneath it. He did not see how deep the seams ran. Even off-duty I ironed my shirts, patched my cuffs, polished boots no one inspected. Old habits from campaigns where an unbuttoned collar meant you were too tired to live through the next breach. Now, in Rogue Unit, there is no dress code, but I still find myself darning holes in the same old trousers instead of buying new ones. Everyone jokes that I am the squad quartermaster without a storehouse. The truth is, I am afraid if I stop caring about the small things, I will lose whatever line is left between soldier and something worse.

We all carry ghosts from those last official deployments. Mara never talks about the evac we were ordered to stand down on, but I have heard her grinding her teeth in her sleep. Jared will drink himself halfway under a table before he mentions the intel feed we got scrubbed before the tribunal, the one that did not match the brief we were given. Caleb still believes, or pretends to, that somebody up the chain simply "made a mistake." I remember the after-action debriefs, the careful phrasing, the statistics used like bandages over bodies we never got to see. Somewhere between those memos and the graveside detail, trust started bleeding out.

Rogue Unit is what is left when faith in the machine snaps but the training does not. We still stack on doors like we did in uniform, still clear rooms by reflex. Orders just come from a smaller table now. No flags on the wall, just a battered ops board and printed photos with faces circled. I wish I could say we are better this way, more honest, but there is a kind of freedom in not having to pretend the objectives are clean. We pick our contracts, tell ourselves we are balancing scales nobody else will touch. Some days I believe that. Some days I hear the old commands echoing in my head and I am not sure whose voice is giving them anymore.

My partner back then loved the uniform more than the person inside it, I think. There was always another family issue, another crisis, another favor that needed pulling strings. Their needs filled every off-duty hour: moving boxes, fixing visas, smoothing over arguments, visiting relatives who only called when they wanted something. I kept saying it was temporary, that once this deployment ended or that promotion posted, I would get to have a say. Instead, my world shrank down to their schedule and the next set of orders. One day I caught myself introducing myself as "his girl" before I used my own name. That was when I realized somewhere along the line I had stopped being a person and become a role, another resource to be allocated.

Walking through those bad parts of town, I started to feel more like myself than I did at home. That should have been the warning. When the first rumors surfaced about that operation we are not supposed to mention, the one with the casualty numbers that never made it onto any official ledger, I heard them in a bar that smelled like grease and cheap liquor, from people who should not have known the grid coordinates. I went back to the barracks and listened to the official brief the next morning, watched the holo-map neatly omit whole districts. That was the day Mara stopped saluting the big screens, and Jared started keeping copies of raw telemetry "just in case."

We did not all leave at once. It was more like a slow leak. Caleb tried to route complaints through channels until the channels closed around his throat. I got written up twice for "tone" in debriefs, then quietly reassigned to clerical support as if my trigger finger had gone bad. Mara vanished for a month, officially on compassionate leave, and came back with eyes that did not match her smiles. The final straw was not some grand revelation. It was sitting in our tiny apartment, listening to that damned faucet drip, sewing up a rip in my partner's jacket while he complained about a delayed shipment, and realizing I was more furious about a dry cleaning bill than the bodies we were supposed to forget. My anger had nowhere honest to go.

Rogue Unit did not recruit me with promises of justice. They just handed me a file, a burner, and a chance to stop pretending I did not see what we had done. I am not naive enough to think we are the good ones now. We are people who knew how to break things efficiently, and someone found a way to point us at different targets. But here, at least, my name is my own again. I fix my own gear, mend my own clothes, decide which lies I am willing to live with. And when I walk through those dangerous streets now, heads turn for what I chose to become, not the insignia stitched to my chest.

Still, some nights I hear that faucet. Some nights the drip sounds like a metronome counting down to the day we get caught or killed, and I wonder if we ever really left the old command behind or if we are just another off-the-books unit in a longer chain of deniability. I try not to think about the ops we took without asking who really signed the payments, about the way certain zones always seem to be redacted on our own maps. You can only ignore the patterns for so long before you have to decide whether you are going to follow them to the end or tear them apart with your bare hands.
